Week 1 · Diffusion — Why Anything Moves at All

A mosquito bite opens the week with one question: how fast can a molecule get where it needs to be, when nothing pushes it? Tab 1 prices thermal motion in \(k_BT\) and derives the gas law from bouncing molecules (1.1.1–1.1.7). Tab 2 turns the kicks into a random walk and a clock, \(t \approx L^2/2dD\) (1.2.1–1.2.8). Tab 3 shows that the same kicks that jiggle a particle also drag it, and that equilibrium then forces \(D = \mu k_BT = k_BT/6\pi\eta a\) (1.3.1–1.3.9). Tab 4 spends these on the bite, and Tab 5 previews the encounter rate that Week 2 derives (1.5.1).

Module Tab 1 · The Bouncing World
1.1.1

Equipartition — temperature is kinetic energy

Minted in Week 1 §1.2 · \(k_BT\) — the currency of the molecular world · open the module

eq. 1.1.1$$\tfrac{3}{2}k_BT \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}m\langle v^2\rangle$$

Letters

  • \(k_B\) — Boltzmann's constant, the exchange rate from kelvin to joules · J/K · 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J/K (exact)
  • \(T\) — absolute temperature · K · body: 310 K
  • \(k_BT\) — the thermal energy unit · J · 4.28 × 10⁻²¹ J = 4.28 pN·nm at 310 K
  • \(m\) — the mass of one molecule · kg
  • \(\langle v^2\rangle\) — the average of the squared speed, over many molecules or a long time · m²/s²

How it is used

§1.2 states it as one of two facts about the bath, to be derived in §1.4, where it is the last line of eq. 1.1.7. The speed-thermometer sim puts one tracer (H₂, H₂O, O₂ or a 1 kDa molecule) in a bath of 18 Da molecules. Its time-averaged ⟨KE⟩/\(k_BT\) readout sits at 1 whichever tracer you pick (the sim is 2D, so two directions at ½\(k_BT\) each), while its speed histogram slides with mass. It feeds eq. 1.1.2, and it makes \(k_BT\) the price tag for every energy in the course: lecture Q3 ranks a hydrogen bond at ~2–5 \(k_BT\) and ATP at ~20–25 \(k_BT\).

Comes back: —

Biological examplewhat one water molecule and one antibody each carry

A mast cell in the bite sits in a bath of water and proteins. How much kinetic energy does each molecule carry, and is that enough to matter to a bond?

  1. Thermal unit at 310 K: \(k_BT = (1.381\times10^{-23})(310) = 4.28\times10^{-21}\) J.
  2. Average kinetic energy: \(\tfrac32 k_BT = 6.42\times10^{-21}\) J = 6.42 pN·nm, for every molecule.
  3. Water, 18 Da: \(m = 0.018/6.022\times10^{23} = 2.99\times10^{-26}\) kg.
  4. Its mean squared speed: \(\langle v^2\rangle = 3k_BT/m = 4.30\times10^{5}\) m²/s².
  5. An antibody (IgG), 150 kDa: \(m = 2.49\times10^{-22}\) kg, so \(\langle v^2\rangle = 3k_BT/m = 51.6\) m²/s².
  6. Check: \(\tfrac12 m\langle v^2\rangle = 6.42\times10^{-21}\) J for both.
  7. Q3's price list: a hydrogen bond, 2–5 \(k_BT\) = 8.6–21 pN·nm; ATP, ~20 \(k_BT\) ≈ 86 pN·nm.

What it means. The antibody is more than 8000 times heavier than water, but it carries the same energy. It pays in speed instead: 7.2 m/s against water's 655 m/s. The average kick, 1.5 \(k_BT\), is the size of a hydrogen bond, so hydrogen bonds break and re-form all the time. ATP holds about 13 times the average, which is why it is a safe fuel packet.

Mechanical analogya heavy puck among light ones on an air-hockey table

Build the speed-thermometer sim at table scale. Fill an air-hockey table with light pucks and let motor-driven rails kick them, so they keep colliding. Then add one heavy puck. After many collisions, the heavy puck carries, on average, the same kinetic energy as each light puck. It just moves more slowly.

In the cellIn the machine
water molecules, the baththe swarm of light pucks, 20 g each
the antibody, \(m\) = 150 kDaone heavy puck, 0.5 kg
temperature \(T\)how hard the rails kick
\(\tfrac32 k_BT\) per molecule (3 directions)the same KE per puck (2 directions on a flat table)
\(\langle v^2\rangle\) falls as \(1/m\)the heavy puck is slower by \(\sqrt{25}\) = 5

If a light puck moves at a root-mean-square 1.0 m/s, it carries ½(0.020)(1.0)² = 0.01 J. The heavy puck then averages the same 0.01 J, so \(\langle v^2\rangle\) = 2(0.01)/0.5 = 0.04 m²/s², a root-mean-square 0.2 m/s. Each puck's energy is 1.56 × 10¹⁸ times a molecule's.

Where it breaks. Real pucks lose energy in every bounce and to the air film, so the table has a "temperature" only while a motor feeds it. The molecular bath needs no motor: on average its collisions lose nothing, and its energy scale is set by \(k_B\), not by a rail.

1.1.2

RMS speed — the same energy, a different speed

Minted in Week 1 §1.2 · \(k_BT\) — the currency of the molecular world · open the module

eq. 1.1.2$$v_{rms} \;=\; \sqrt{\langle v^2\rangle} \;=\; \sqrt{3k_BT/m}$$

Letters

  • \(v_{rms}\) — root-mean-square speed, the square root of the average squared speed · m/s
  • \(\langle v^2\rangle\) — mean squared speed · m²/s²
  • \(k_BT\) — thermal energy · J · 4.28 × 10⁻²¹ J at 310 K
  • \(m\) — mass of one molecule · kg (a molecule of 18 Da has \(m\) = 0.018 kg/mol ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)

How it is used

§1.2 solves eq. 1.1.1 for speed. Its worked example clocks O₂ at 310 K: \(v_{rms}\) ≈ 492 m/s, about Mach 1.4. A Deeper box separates \(v_{rms}\) from the mean speed (0.92 \(v_{rms}\) ≈ 453 m/s for O₂) and the most-probable speed (0.82 \(v_{rms}\)), which is lecture Q2's trap. In the speed thermometer, switching the tracer from H₂ to 1 kDa slides the speed histogram left by \(\sqrt{m}\) while ⟨KE⟩/\(k_BT\) stays at 1 (the 2D form is \(\sqrt{2k_BT/m}\)). Tab 4's check-yourself (b) uses it to show that a fast molecule is not a fast traveller.

Comes back: —

Biological examplehow fast histamine flies between collisions

The mast cell has just released histamine. How fast is one histamine molecule moving?

  1. Mass: 111 Da, so \(m = 0.111/6.022\times10^{23} = 1.84\times10^{-25}\) kg.
  2. Thermal budget: \(3k_BT = 3(4.28\times10^{-21}) = 1.284\times10^{-20}\) J.
  3. Mean squared speed: \(\langle v^2\rangle = 1.284\times10^{-20}/1.84\times10^{-25} = 6.97\times10^{4}\) m²/s².
  4. \(v_{rms} = \sqrt{6.97\times10^{4}}\) ≈ 264 m/s.
  5. Same law for O₂ (32 Da): 492 m/s, faster by \(\sqrt{111/32}\) = 1.86.
  6. A straight flight to the itch nerve, 120 µm away: \(1.2\times10^{-4}/264 = 4.5\times10^{-7}\) s = 0.45 µs.

What it means. Tab 4's ledger needs about 7 s for that 120 µm leg, roughly 15 million times longer than the straight flight. The speed is real, but it lasts only until the next collision. Tab 2 is about what is left of it.

Mechanical analogya pinball plunger launching two balls

The bath hands every molecule the same energy per direction, ½\(k_BT\). A pinball plunger does the same along one direction: pulled back to the same mark, it stores the same energy whatever ball sits in front of it. The ball leaves with ½(mass)(speed)² equal to that energy, so its speed is the square root of 2 × energy ÷ mass. Three plungers, one per axis, would give the 3 in \(\sqrt{3k_BT/m}\).

In the cellIn the machine
½\(k_BT\) per directionthe plunger's stored energy, 0.05 J
histamine, 111 Daa steel pinball, 80 g
O₂, 32 Daa ping-pong ball, 2.7 g
\(v_{rms} = \sqrt{3k_BT/m}\)launch speed = √(2 × 0.05 J ÷ mass)
three directionsthree plungers, one per axis

Run it: the steel ball leaves at √(2 × 0.05/0.080) = 1.12 m/s, the ping-pong ball at √(2 × 0.05/0.0027) = 6.1 m/s. Their ratio, √(80/2.7) = 5.4, is the same square-root law that makes O₂ 1.86 times faster than histamine.

Where it breaks. The plunger hands every ball exactly the same energy. The bath hands out a spread of energies (the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution) and fixes only the average. A real plunger also loses some energy to its own moving rod.

1.1.3

The ideal gas law — counting molecules from P, V and T

Minted in Week 1 §1.3 · The law the 1600s measured · open the module

eq. 1.1.3$$PV \;=\; nRT \;=\; N k_B T$$

Letters

  • \(P\) — pressure · Pa (1 atm = 101,325 Pa)
  • \(V\) — volume · m³
  • \(n\) — amount of gas · mol
  • \(R\) — gas constant, \(R = k_BN_A\) · 8.31 J/(mol·K)
  • \(N\) — number of molecules, \(N = nN_A\), with \(N_A\) = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹
  • \(k_B\), \(T\) — as in eq. 1.1.1 · \(k_BT\) = 4.28 × 10⁻²¹ J at 310 K

How it is used

§1.3 gives it as the law the 1600s–1800s measured, piece by piece: Boyle (\(P\) falls as \(1/V\)), Charles (\(V\) grows with \(T\)), Avogadro (\(n\) grows with \(V\)). Lecture Q1 uses it to count one 0.5 L breath at 310 K: 1.2 × 10²² molecules, 2.5 × 10²¹ of them O₂. Boyle's bench knows only elastic bounces, yet sweeping the piston lays the measured points on the isotherm. Raising \(T\) gives a higher hyperbola, and dropping to \(N\) = 20 scatters the points: the law is exact only for the average. §1.4 then derives it from mechanics (eq. 1.1.4–1.1.6), and eq. 1.1.7 sets the two side by side.

Comes back: —

Biological examplehow many O₂ molecules wait in one alveolus

Your lungs hold hundreds of millions of alveoli. How much oxygen sits in one of them, ready for the blood? Each gas in a mixture obeys the law with its own share of the pressure.

  1. Alveolus as a sphere 200 µm across (typical): \(V = \tfrac43\pi(1.0\times10^{-4})^3 = 4.19\times10^{-12}\) m³.
  2. Oxygen's share of the pressure, about 100 mmHg (typical alveolar value): \(P\) = 1.33 × 10⁴ Pa.
  3. Body temperature: \(k_BT = 4.28\times10^{-21}\) J.
  4. \(N = PV/k_BT = (1.33\times10^{4})(4.19\times10^{-12})/(4.28\times10^{-21}) = 1.30\times10^{13}\) O₂ molecules.
  5. In moles: \(n = N/N_A = 2.17\times10^{-11}\) mol. Check: \(nRT = (2.17\times10^{-11})(8.31)(310) = 5.6\times10^{-8}\) J \(= PV\).
  6. One red cell carries about 2.7 × 10⁸ hemoglobins (typical), each binding 4 O₂: 1.1 × 10⁹ O₂.
  7. One alveolus: \(1.30\times10^{13}/1.1\times10^{9}\) ≈ 1.2 × 10⁴ red cells' worth.

What it means. A speck of lung 0.2 mm across holds enough oxygen to load about twelve thousand red cells. The counts are so large that \(P\), \(V\) and \(T\) behave as smooth numbers. That is why a law found with pistons and mercury in the 1600s works at all.

Mechanical analogythe lung as a bicycle pump

Your diaphragm is a piston. When it drops, lung volume grows and pressure falls, so air flows in. A bicycle pump is the same machine with a valve on it.

In the cellIn the machine
alveolus, \(V\) = 4.19 × 10⁻¹² m³pump barrel, \(V\) = 3 × 10⁻⁴ m³ (0.3 L)
O₂ molecules, \(N\) = 1.3 × 10¹³air molecules, \(N\) = 7.3 × 10²¹
O₂ share of \(P\) = 13.3 kPabarrel \(P\) = 101 kPa, then 203 kPa at half stroke
\(T\) = 310 K, held by the blood\(T\) ≈ 300 K, held only if you pump slowly
diaphragmpiston

Run it: \(N = PV/k_BT = (101{,}325)(3\times10^{-4})/[(1.381\times10^{-23})(300)] = 7.3\times10^{21}\). Close the outlet and push the piston halfway. \(N\) and \(T\) stay fixed, so \(P\) doubles to 203 kPa: Boyle's law, by hand.

Where it breaks. Pump fast and the gas heats, so \(T\) is not constant; that is why a bike pump's barrel gets warm. The alveolus also trades molecules with the blood every second, so its \(N\) is never fixed.

1.1.4

One molecule's wall kick — impulse and round-trip time

Minted in Week 1 §1.4 · Why the law is true — one molecule at a time · open the module

eq. 1.1.4$$F_x = \frac{\Delta (m v_x)}{t} = \frac{2m v_x}{t}, \qquad \langle t\rangle = \frac{2L}{v_x}$$

Letters

  • \(F_x\) — the average force on the wall over one round trip · N
  • \(\Delta(mv_x)\) — momentum change in one elastic bounce, \(2mv_x\), the impulse · N·s
  • \(m\) — mass of the molecule · kg
  • \(v_x\) — its velocity component perpendicular to the wall · m/s
  • \(t\), \(\langle t\rangle\) — time between hits on the same wall, one round trip · s
  • \(L\) — the box's width along \(x\) · m

How it is used

§1.4 opens the kinetic-theory derivation with one molecule in a cube of side \(L\), bouncing off the wall perpendicular to \(x\). The one-molecule pressure gauge runs it, with sliders for \(v_x\), \(L\) and \(N\). With \(N\) = 1 the measured hit interval matches \(2L/v_x\), and the force trace is a train of spikes, each carrying \(2mv_x\). It feeds the time average in eq. 1.1.5.

Comes back: —

Biological exampleone air molecule drumming on your eardrum

Your eardrum is a membrane patch at the end of a 2.5 cm canal (typical), and air hammers it. What does one N₂ molecule deliver per hit, and how often would it come back?

  1. Mass: 28 Da, so \(m = 4.65\times10^{-26}\) kg.
  2. Speed toward the drum: each direction holds ½\(k_BT\), so \(v_x = \sqrt{k_BT/m} = \sqrt{4.28\times10^{-21}/4.65\times10^{-26}} = 303\) m/s.
  3. Impulse per bounce: \(2mv_x = 2(4.65\times10^{-26})(303) = 2.82\times10^{-23}\) N·s.
  4. Round trip down the canal and back, \(L\) = 0.025 m: \(\langle t\rangle = 2L/v_x = 0.05/303 = 1.65\times10^{-4}\) s = 165 µs.
  5. Average force over that trip: \(F_x = 2.82\times10^{-23}/1.65\times10^{-4} = 1.7\times10^{-19}\) N.

What it means. One molecule pushes with 10⁻¹⁹ N, which is nothing. A real N₂ molecule also never flies the canal straight: with the module's 70 nm free path, it hits a neighbour about 360,000 times per crossing. The derivation still holds, because collisions between molecules swap momentum without changing the total delivered to the drum, on average.

Mechanical analogya squash ball between two walls

Hit a perfectly bouncy squash ball straight down the court so that it shuttles between the front and back walls. Each hit on the front wall reverses its momentum, and it returns once per round trip.

In the cellIn the machine
N₂ molecule, \(m\) = 4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ kgsquash ball, 24 g
\(v_x\) = 303 m/s20 m/s
the eardrumthe front wall
ear canal, \(L\) = 2.5 cmcourt length, \(L\) = 9.75 m
impulse \(2mv_x\) = 2.8 × 10⁻²³ N·s2(0.024)(20) = 0.96 N·s
\(\langle t\rangle\) = 165 µs2(9.75)/20 = 0.98 s

The front wall takes 0.96 N·s about once a second, so its average push is 0.98 N.

Where it breaks. A squash ball keeps less than half its speed at each bounce, so a player must keep feeding it. The molecule's bounces are elastic on average, because the wall is at the gas's own temperature. The ball also never meets another ball; the molecule meets one every 70 nm.

1.1.5

Average force and pressure — from one molecule

Minted in Week 1 §1.4 · Why the law is true — one molecule at a time · open the module

eq. 1.1.5$$\langle F_x\rangle = \frac{2m v_x}{\langle t\rangle} = \frac{m v_x^2}{L}, \qquad \langle P_x\rangle = \frac{\langle F_x\rangle}{L^2} = \frac{m v_x^2}{V}$$

Letters

  • \(\langle F_x\rangle\) — time-averaged force of one molecule on one wall · N
  • \(\langle P_x\rangle\) — that force per wall area · Pa
  • \(m\), \(v_x\), \(L\), \(\langle t\rangle\) — as in eq. 1.1.4
  • \(L^2\) — the wall's area · m²
  • \(V\) — the box's volume, \(L^3\) · m³

How it is used

§1.4 averages eq. 1.1.4's spike train into a steady force. The impulse \(2mv_x\) arrives once per round trip \(2L/v_x\), so speed enters twice: harder hits, more often. In the one-molecule pressure gauge, the running average of the force trace converges onto the dashed line \(mv_x^2/L\). It feeds eq. 1.1.6, which adds up \(N\) molecules.

Comes back: —

Biological examplehow many drummers make one atmosphere

Stay with the ear. What pressure does one N₂ molecule exert, and how many does it take to make the 101 kPa the eardrum actually feels? The box need not be a cube: force over wall area is \(mv_x^2\) ÷ (length × area), which is \(mv_x^2/V\).

  1. The canal as a box: length \(L\) = 2.5 cm, end wall (the eardrum) ≈ 0.6 cm² (typical): \(V = (0.025)(0.6\times10^{-4}) = 1.5\times10^{-6}\) m³.
  2. One molecule: \(\langle F_x\rangle = mv_x^2/L = (4.65\times10^{-26})(303)^2/0.025 = 1.71\times10^{-19}\) N.
  3. Its pressure: \(\langle P_x\rangle = 1.71\times10^{-19}/0.6\times10^{-4} = 2.85\times10^{-15}\) Pa.
  4. Molecules needed for one atmosphere: \(101{,}325/2.85\times10^{-15} = 3.55\times10^{19}\).
  5. Check with eq. 1.1.3: \(N = PV/k_BT = (101{,}325)(1.5\times10^{-6})/(4.28\times10^{-21}) = 3.55\times10^{19}\).

What it means. The two counts agree because \(mv_x^2\) equals \(k_BT\) when \(v_x\) is the per-direction rms speed. Eq. 1.1.7 makes that formal. The eardrum feels a steady push only because 10¹⁹ separate drummers average out.

Mechanical analogya billiard ball rattling between cushions

Send one billiard ball end to end on a frictionless 9-foot table. Each cushion hit reverses it, and it comes back once per round trip, just like the molecule in the canal.

In the cellIn the machine
N₂ moleculebilliard ball, 170 g
\(v_x\) = 303 m/s1.0 m/s
canal length \(L\) = 2.5 cmtable length \(L\) = 2.54 m
a hit every \(2L/v_x\) = 165 µsa hit every 2(2.54)/1.0 = 5.08 s
\(\langle F_x\rangle = mv_x^2/L\) = 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁹ N(0.17)(1.0)²/2.54 = 0.067 N

Each hit delivers 2(0.17)(1.0) = 0.34 N·s, once every 5.08 s, so the cushion feels 0.067 N on average. Double the speed and the average force rises four times, to 0.27 N: twice the impulse, twice as often. That square is why hotter gas pushes harder.

Where it breaks. A real ball slows on the cloth, and the cushion soaks up energy at each hit. One ball also gives a spiky force, never a steady pressure. It takes ~10¹⁹ molecules to smooth the spikes away.

1.1.6

Isotropy — the pressure of N molecules

Minted in Week 1 §1.4 · Why the law is true — one molecule at a time · open the module

eq. 1.1.6$$\langle v_x^2\rangle = \langle v_y^2\rangle = \langle v_z^2\rangle = \tfrac{1}{3}\langle v^2\rangle \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; P = \frac{1}{3}\frac{m\langle v^2\rangle}{V} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; P = \frac{N}{V}\frac{m\langle v^2\rangle}{3}$$

Letters

  • \(\langle v_x^2\rangle\), \(\langle v_y^2\rangle\), \(\langle v_z^2\rangle\) — mean squared velocity along each axis · m²/s²
  • \(\langle v^2\rangle\) — mean squared speed, the sum of the three · m²/s²
  • \(P\) — pressure of the whole gas · Pa
  • \(N/V\) — molecules per volume · m⁻³
  • \(m\) — molecular mass · kg

How it is used

§1.4 notes that real molecules move in 3D with no preferred direction, so each axis carries a third of \(\langle v^2\rangle\). Summing \(N\) molecules turns one molecule's spikes into the gas's pressure. In the pressure gauge, sliding \(N\) up to 100 fuses the spikes into a steady force: pressure becoming a macroscopic quantity. A Deeper box warns that \(\langle v_x^2\rangle\) is not \(\langle v_x\rangle^2\), which is zero. Averages of squares return as the mean-squared displacement in Tab 2. It feeds eq. 1.1.7.

Comes back: —

Biological examplewhy your ears hurt when the plane lands

At cruise the cabin is held near 75 kPa (typical). If the Eustachian tube stays shut all the way down, the middle ear keeps that thin air while the canal side returns to 101 kPa. How hard is the eardrum pushed?

  1. N₂ at 310 K: \(v_{rms} = \sqrt{3k_BT/m}\) = 525 m/s, so \(\langle v^2\rangle = 2.76\times10^{5}\) m²/s².
  2. Isotropy: \(\langle v_x^2\rangle = \langle v^2\rangle/3 = 9.2\times10^{4}\) m²/s², and \(m\langle v^2\rangle/3 = 4.28\times10^{-21}\) J. O₂ carries the same (eq. 1.1.1), so the mix of gases does not matter.
  3. Canal side: \(N/V = P/(m\langle v^2\rangle/3) = 101{,}325/4.28\times10^{-21} = 2.37\times10^{25}\) m⁻³.
  4. Middle ear: \(N/V = 75{,}000/4.28\times10^{-21} = 1.75\times10^{25}\) m⁻³.
  5. Pressure difference: \((2.37-1.75)\times10^{25}\times4.28\times10^{-21} \approx 2.63\times10^{4}\) Pa.
  6. On a 0.6 cm² eardrum: \((2.63\times10^{4})(0.6\times10^{-4})\) = 1.6 N.

What it means. About 26 % fewer molecules on one side of a membrane gives 1.6 N, the weight of a 160 g apple, pressed on a membrane about 0.1 mm thick (typical). Swallowing opens the tube, molecules flow in until the two counts match, and the ear "pops".

Mechanical analogya vacuum-sealed jar lid

A sealed jar is the blocked ear at kitchen scale: fewer molecules inside than outside, and a lid pressed by the difference.

In the cellIn the machine
canal air, \(N/V\) = 2.37 × 10²⁵ m⁻³room air above the lid
trapped middle-ear air, \(N/V\) = 1.75 × 10²⁵ m⁻³thinned air inside the jar, ≈ 0.7 atm (illustrative)
eardrum, 0.6 cm²lid, 7 cm across (38.5 cm²)
\(m\langle v^2\rangle/3\), the same on both sidesthe same on both sides, once the jar has cooled to room temperature
swallowing opens the Eustachian tubeprying the lid's edge lets air in: the "pop"

Run it: (0.3 × 101,325 Pa)(π × 0.035² m²) = 117 N, which is why the lid will not turn. Pry the edge, molecules rush in until both sides have the same \(N/V\), and the lid comes off with almost no force.

Where it breaks. The lid is rigid, but the eardrum bulges inward, which shrinks the trapped volume and raises the inside pressure a little. The jar also got its thin air by cooling hot contents; the ear got its by trapping cabin air, and it stays at 310 K throughout.

1.1.7

Kinetic theory meets the gas law — what k_BT means

Minted in Week 1 §1.4 · Why the law is true — one molecule at a time · open the module

eq. 1.1.7$$PV = N\frac{m\langle v^2\rangle}{3} = Nk_BT \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; k_BT = \frac{m\langle v^2\rangle}{3} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT = \tfrac{1}{2}m\langle v^2\rangle$$

Letters

  • \(P\), \(V\), \(N\) — pressure, volume, number of molecules · Pa, m³, —
  • \(m\) — molecular mass · kg
  • \(\langle v^2\rangle\) — mean squared speed · m²/s²
  • \(k_BT\) — thermal energy · J · 4.28 × 10⁻²¹ J at 310 K

How it is used

§1.4 sets the mechanical pressure (eq. 1.1.6) against the measured law (eq. 1.1.3). Both say \(PV = N\) × an energy, so \(k_BT = m\langle v^2\rangle/3\), and multiplying by 3/2 recovers eq. 1.1.1. The fact §1.2 asserted is now derived: temperature is the average kinetic energy per molecule, read in other units. The module closes Tab 1 by noting that nothing in eq. 1.1.4–1.1.7 needed the word "gas". The same bookkeeping applies to a protein in water, which is where Tab 2 picks up.

Comes back: —

Biological examplewhat ice on the bite does to the molecules

Tab 4 asks why ice dulls the itch. Start with the molecules. Suppose the ice cools the bitten skin from 37 °C to 20 °C, 293 K (illustrative).

  1. At 310 K: \(k_BT = 4.28\times10^{-21}\) J, and for water \(\langle v^2\rangle = 3k_BT/m\) gives \(v_{rms}\) = 655 m/s.
  2. At 293 K: \(k_BT = (1.381\times10^{-23})(293) = 4.05\times10^{-21}\) J, 5.5 % less.
  3. Since \(k_BT = m\langle v^2\rangle/3\), \(\langle v^2\rangle\) falls by the same 5.5 %, to \(4.06\times10^{5}\) m²/s².
  4. \(v_{rms} = \sqrt{4.06\times10^{5}}\) = 637 m/s, 2.8 % slower.

What it means. Cooling by 17 degrees costs the molecules only a few percent of their energy, because the scale starts at absolute zero. If ice slows the itch a lot, most of the effect must come from somewhere else. Tab 4's physics answer is viscosity: water at 20 °C is about 1.0 mPa·s (typical), 1.45 times its 0.69 mPa·s at 37 °C. Its biology answer is a slower mast cell.

Mechanical analogythe tire gauge as a thermometer

A tire holds a fixed \(N\) in a nearly fixed \(V\), so its gauge reads \(PV/N = m\langle v^2\rangle/3\). It is a molecular speedometer. A cold morning plays the ice pack.

In the cellIn the machine
tissue water, warmed by the bloodair in a car tire
the ice pack, 310 → 293 Kcold morning 278 K → after a highway drive 308 K
\(k_BT = m\langle v^2\rangle/3\)\(PV/N\), read on the gauge
water's \(v_{rms}\), 655 → 637 m/sN₂'s \(v_{rms}\), 498 → 524 m/s

Run it: at fixed \(V\) and \(N\), \(P\) grows with \(T\). A tire at 3.2 bar absolute and 278 K reaches 3.2 × 308/278 = 3.55 bar at 308 K. The gauge, which reads absolute minus 1.013 bar, climbs from 2.19 to 2.53 bar. That is why tire pressure should be checked cold.

Where it breaks. The tire holds a gas, where \(PV = Nk_BT\) holds. Tissue is liquid water, where it does not. What survives in the liquid is \(k_BT = m\langle v^2\rangle/3\) itself, since equipartition holds for any classical system, not the gas law used to derive it.

Module Tab 2 · The Drunkard's Walk
1.2.1

Potential energy of a suspended particle — buoyant weight × height

Minted in Week 1 §2.2 · Why the pollen jiggles — and the sand grain doesn't · open the module

eq. 1.2.1$$U(h) = \Delta\rho\,V g\,h \qquad\text{(buoyant weight × height)}$$

Letters

  • \(U(h)\) — potential energy at height \(h\) · J
  • \(\Delta\rho\) — particle density minus fluid density · kg/m³
  • \(V\) — particle volume · m³
  • \(g\) — gravitational acceleration · 9.8 m/s²
  • \(h\) — height above the floor · m
  • \(\Delta\rho Vg\) — the buoyant weight, the net downward force · N

How it is used

§2.2 asks when a particle is small enough to be Brownian. The answer is an energy balance, and this is gravity's side of it. The jiggle-vs-sink bench (radius, \(\Delta\rho\) and \(T\) sliders on a 50-µm water column) shows the cloud collapsing into sediment somewhere near a micron, and shows gravity vanishing at any size when \(\Delta\rho\) = 0. It feeds \(\ell_g\) (eq. 1.2.2), becomes the \(U\) in the Boltzmann distribution (eq. 1.2.7), and §3.3 generalizes it to \(U = Fh\) for any constant force.

Comes back: R1 §2.2 (a 3-µm nebulizer droplet in air and a 0.6-nm drug molecule in mucus, in one gravitational field).

Biological examplewhat it costs a red cell to rise one diameter

Blood left standing separates: red cells sink and the plasma clears above them, which is what the sedimentation-rate test watches. What does gravity charge a red cell to climb?

  1. Volume: 90 fL (typical) = \(9.0\times10^{-17}\) m³.
  2. Densities: red cell ≈ 1100, plasma ≈ 1025 kg/m³ (typical), so \(\Delta\rho\) = 75 kg/m³.
  3. Buoyant weight: \(\Delta\rho Vg = (75)(9.0\times10^{-17})(9.8) = 6.6\times10^{-14}\) N = 0.066 pN.
  4. One cell diameter up, \(h\) = 8 µm (typical): \(U = (6.6\times10^{-14})(8\times10^{-6}) = 5.3\times10^{-19}\) J.
  5. In thermal units: \(5.3\times10^{-19}/4.28\times10^{-21}\) = 124 \(k_BT\).

What it means. One diameter of climb costs about 124 \(k_BT\), the energy of five or six ATP. Thermal kicks pay about one \(k_BT\) at a time, so the red cell sinks. Its force is tiny, 0.066 pN, but the bill is large because the climb is long next to the reach of one \(k_BT\).

Mechanical analogylifting a stone off the floor of a pool

Lift a stone underwater and you feel only its buoyant weight: the water it displaces pays part of the bill. That "part" is the Δ in \(\Delta\rho\).

In the cellIn the machine
red cell, \(V\) = 90 fLgranite stone, \(V\) = 1 L
plasma, 1025 kg/m³pool water, 1000 kg/m³
\(\Delta\rho\) = 75 kg/m³2650 − 1000 = 1650 kg/m³
buoyant weight 0.066 pN16.2 N (26 N in air)
\(h\) = 8 µm, \(U\) = 124 \(k_BT\)\(h\) = 1 m, \(U\) = 16.2 J

Underwater the stone feels 38 % lighter. Lifting it 1 m costs (1650)(10⁻³)(9.8)(1) = 16.2 J.

Where it breaks. Nothing in the pool lifts the stone for free. The cell's bath does: it pays about one \(k_BT\) per kick, in a random direction. For the red cell that is under 1 % of the bill.

1.2.2

Sedimentation length — gravity's toll meets the thermal budget

Minted in Week 1 §2.2 · Why the pollen jiggles — and the sand grain doesn't · open the module

eq. 1.2.2$$U(\ell_g) = k_BT \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \ell_g \;=\; \frac{k_BT}{\Delta\rho\, V g}$$

Letters

  • \(\ell_g\) — sedimentation length: the height whose climb costs one \(k_BT\), and the 1/e height of a settled cloud · m
  • \(k_BT\) — thermal energy · J · 4.28 × 10⁻²¹ J at 310 K
  • \(\Delta\rho\), \(V\), \(g\) — as in eq. 1.2.1 · \(\Delta\rho Vg\) is the buoyant weight

How it is used

§2.2 sets the climbing cost equal to the thermal budget. The verdict rule: \(\ell_g\) much larger than the particle means Brownian; \(\ell_g\) much smaller means it sediments. The worked example gives a 1-µm polystyrene bead \(\ell_g\) = 17 µm (Brownian), while a 1-mm sand grain's falls below a proton's width (it sinks). The bench's height histogram decays as \(e^{-h/\ell_g}\), the shape §2.4 names as the Boltzmann distribution (eq. 1.2.7).

Comes back: R1 §2.2 (one length decides whether a droplet or a drug molecule is "Brownian or furniture").

Biological exampledoes a neutrophil sink in a dish? does GFP?

Two members of the course's cast, at opposite ends of the size scale, in water at 37 °C.

  1. A resting neutrophil is round, about 8 µm across (typical; it spreads to 12–15 µm when it crawls): \(V = \tfrac43\pi(4\times10^{-6})^3 = 2.68\times10^{-16}\) m³.
  2. \(\Delta\rho\) ≈ 80 kg/m³ (cell ≈ 1080 against medium ≈ 1000 kg/m³, typical).
  3. Buoyant weight: \((80)(2.68\times10^{-16})(9.8) = 2.1\times10^{-13}\) N.
  4. \(\ell_g = 4.28\times10^{-21}/2.1\times10^{-13} = 2.0\times10^{-8}\) m = 20 nm, about 390 times smaller than the cell.
  5. GFP: \(a\) = 2.3 nm, so \(V = 5.1\times10^{-26}\) m³; protein ≈ 1350 kg/m³ (typical), so \(\Delta\rho\) = 350.
  6. Buoyant weight: \((350)(5.1\times10^{-26})(9.8) = 1.75\times10^{-22}\) N.
  7. \(\ell_g = 4.28\times10^{-21}/1.75\times10^{-22}\) = 24.5 m.

What it means. The neutrophil is furniture: put it in a dish and it ends up on the floor, which is where you watch it crawl. GFP's sedimentation length is 24.5 m, so no cell or test tube is tall enough for a protein to settle. The two lengths differ by a factor of 10⁹, and the bench shows the crossover near a micron.

Mechanical analogythe carnival high striker

Hit the pad with a mallet and the puck climbs the rail. The height it reaches is the energy of the blow divided by the puck's weight. That is eq. 1.2.2 with a mallet in place of the bath.

In the cellIn the machine
thermal budget \(k_BT\)the energy the blow hands the puck, 30 J (illustrative)
buoyant weight \(\Delta\rho Vg\)the puck's weight
\(\ell_g = k_BT/\Delta\rho Vg\)height reached = 30 J ÷ weight
neutrophil, \(\ell_g\) = 20 nma 10 kg puck: 30/(10 × 9.8) = 0.31 m
GFP, \(\ell_g\) = 24.5 ma 1 kg puck: 30/9.8 = 3.1 m, and the bell rings

The same blow sends a puck ten times heavier a tenth as high: height = budget ÷ weight.

Where it breaks. One blow gives one height. The bath delivers ~10¹³ small kicks a second in random directions, so \(\ell_g\) is not the peak of one launch but the 1/e height of a whole population: a cloud, not a puck. The rail's friction also takes a cut that the bath never does.

1.2.3

The random walk — ⟨x²⟩ grows with the number of steps

Minted in Week 1 §2.3 · Pearson's drunkard and the law of ⟨x²⟩ · open the module

eq. 1.2.3$$\langle x_N^2\rangle = \langle x_{N-1}^2\rangle + \delta^2 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \langle x^2\rangle = N\delta^2 = \frac{\delta^2}{\tau}\,t$$

Letters

  • \(x_N\) — position after \(N\) steps, starting from 0 · m
  • \(\langle\;\rangle\) — average over many walkers
  • \(\delta\) — step size · m
  • \(N\) — number of steps, \(N = t/\tau\)
  • \(\tau\) — time per step · s
  • \(t\) — elapsed time · s

How it is used

§2.3 answers Pearson's 1905 drunkard. Square \(x_N = x_{N-1} \pm \delta\) and average: the cross-term \(\pm 2\delta x_{N-1}\) averages to zero, leaving one \(\delta^2\) per step. The drunkard-on-a-line bench (walkers, \(\delta\), step rate \(1/\tau\), bias) shows it. With one walker the ⟨x²⟩ trace never settles; with 1000 it snaps onto a straight line while ⟨x⟩ hugs zero. Add a bias and ⟨x⟩ takes off, Week 2's advection in embryo. The microscopic details enter only through \(\delta^2/\tau\), which eq. 1.2.4 names \(D\).

Comes back: —

Biological examplehow far a swimming E. coli really gets

E. coli swims in straight runs of about 1 s at about 20 µm/s, then tumbles and sets off in a new direction (typical values). Treat each run as a step, \(\delta\) = 20 µm and \(\tau\) = 1 s, with a full re-aim at each tumble (illustrative). In 3D the same three lines give \(\langle r^2\rangle = N\delta^2\), because the cross-term still averages to zero.

  1. One minute: \(N\) = 60 runs.
  2. \(\langle r^2\rangle = N\delta^2 = 60\times(20\ \mu\mathrm{m})^2 = 24{,}000\ \mu\mathrm{m}^2\).
  3. \(r_{rms} = \sqrt{24{,}000}\) = 155 µm.
  4. Path actually swum: \(N\delta\) = 1200 µm, 7.7 times the net distance.
  5. One hour: \(N\) = 3600, so \(r_{rms} = \sqrt{3600}\times20\) = 1200 µm = 1.2 mm.
  6. Path swum in that hour: 72 mm.

What it means. A bacterium that swims 72 mm in an hour ends up about a millimetre from where it started. Distance grows only as \(\sqrt{N}\), so swimming longer buys little. To reach food the cell must bias its runs: the small "nudge toward home" that collapses the search time in §2.6.

Mechanical analogya Galton board

Drop a ball into a board of pegs. Each row knocks it left or right at random, and the next row knows nothing of the last. That is the drunkard's walk with rows for steps.

In the cellIn the machine
E. colithe ball
one run, \(\delta\) = 20 µmone peg row: a shift of ±1 cm
a tumble, a fresh directionthe next peg, a fresh coin flip
\(N\) runs\(N\) rows (12 here)
\(\langle x^2\rangle = N\delta^2\)the spread of the heap at the bottom

Run it: after 12 rows, \(x_{rms} = \sqrt{12}\times1\) cm = 3.5 cm, though a ball knocked the same way every time would land 12 cm out. Pour in a thousand balls and the heap is the bell curve the drunkard bench draws.

Where it breaks. The board's clock is rows, not seconds, and its steps go only left or right. E. coli steps in 3D with run lengths that vary, and one tumble does not fully erase its old heading.

1.2.4

The diffusion coefficient — the one number that survives

Minted in Week 1 §2.3 · Pearson's drunkard and the law of ⟨x²⟩ · open the module

eq. 1.2.4$$D \;\equiv\; \frac{\delta^2}{2\tau} \qquad \left[\frac{\mathrm{m^2}}{\mathrm{s}}\right]$$

Letters

  • \(D\) — diffusion coefficient · m²/s (GFP in water at 25 °C: ≈ 87 µm²/s, the measured value the module quotes from Milo & Phillips)
  • \(\delta\) — step size · m
  • \(\tau\) — time per step · s

How it is used

§2.3 defines \(D\) because \(\delta^2/\tau\) is all of the walk that survives. A million tiny, fast steps and a few large, slow ones spread identically if their \(\delta^2/\tau\) match. The units are area per time, not a speed. The factor 2 is bookkeeping, chosen so that this \(D\) is the same number as Fick's \(D\) in eq. 1.3.5. The drunkard bench's \(\delta\) and \(1/\tau\) sliders set it; the constants box gives the \(D\) ladder from dissolved O₂ (~2 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s) to vesicles (~10⁻¹² m²/s). It feeds eq. 1.2.5.

Comes back: —

Biological exampletracking GFP on a camera

You film single GFP molecules in water (\(D\) ≈ 87 µm²/s, measured). What "step" does the camera see between frames?

  1. Video at 30 frames/s: \(\tau = 1/30\) s = 33 ms.
  2. Solve the definition for the per-axis step: \(\delta = \sqrt{2D\tau} = \sqrt{2\times87\times0.0333}\) = 2.41 µm.
  3. A fast camera at 1000 frames/s: \(\tau\) = 1 ms, so \(\delta = \sqrt{2\times87\times0.001}\) = 0.417 µm.
  4. Read \(D\) back from each: \(2.41^2/(2\times0.0333)\) = 87 µm²/s, and \(0.417^2/(2\times0.001)\) = 87 µm²/s.

What it means. The step you see is set by your camera, not by the molecule. \(D\) comes out the same either way. The molecule's own steps are far too small and fast to film: its velocity memory, \(m/\zeta\), lasts about 1.16 × 10⁻¹² s (Tab 3). At video rate a GFP moves about a quarter of a cell's width per frame, which is why single-molecule tracking needs fast cameras.

Mechanical analogytwo coin-flip stepper carts

Put two carts on a long track. Each is driven by a stepper motor that flips a coin before every step to choose its direction. Give them very different steps and clocks, but the same \(\delta^2/\tau\).

In the cellIn the machine
GFPa cart
thermal kickscoin-flip motor pulses
camera frame \(\tau\)the motor's step time
per-frame step \(\delta\)the step length
\(D = \delta^2/2\tau\) = 87 µm²/s5 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s for both carts

Cart A steps 1 mm every 0.01 s: \(D = (10^{-3})^2/(2\times0.01) = 5\times10^{-5}\) m²/s. Cart B steps 1 cm every second: \(D = (10^{-2})^2/(2\times1) = 5\times10^{-5}\) m²/s. Watch either for 100 s and \(\langle x^2\rangle = (\delta^2/\tau)t\) = 0.01 m², an rms of 0.1 m. Up close they differ; from a distance they spread identically.

Where it breaks. Look closer than one step and the carts are easy to tell apart, each with a definite speed. The molecule has no fixed step to find: its velocity memory dies in picoseconds, and below that its motion is not a walk.

1.2.5

⟨x²⟩ = 2Dt — the law of the walk, in one dimension

Minted in Week 1 §2.3 · Pearson's drunkard and the law of ⟨x²⟩ · open the module

eq. 1.2.5$$\langle x^2\rangle = 2Dt \qquad\text{(one dimension)}$$

Letters

  • \(\langle x^2\rangle\) — mean squared displacement along a line · m²
  • \(D\) — diffusion coefficient · m²/s
  • \(t\) — elapsed time · s

How it is used

§2.3 writes the walk's law with \(D\) named. The average position never moves, while the average squared position grows linearly in time, with \(D\) the only material parameter. Rearranged, \(D = \langle x^2\rangle/2t\) is how HW1 measures it. The drunkard bench draws the \(2Dt\) line, and its histogram carries ±\(\sqrt{2Dt}\) whiskers. A Deeper box warns that one track's \(x^2/2t\) never converges; only the average does. §2.4 then reads \(\sqrt{2Dt}\) as the width of a probability cloud (about 68 % inside, in 1D), not as a position.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea protein loose in an axon

An axon is a thin tube, so a protein inside it effectively walks in 1D along its length. Take a GFP-sized protein: \(D\) ≈ 87 µm²/s in water, divided by 4 for crowded cytoplasm (the module's ÷3–5 rule for small proteins), so \(D\) ≈ 22 µm²/s.

  1. One second: \(\langle x^2\rangle = 2(22)(1) = 44\ \mu\mathrm{m}^2\), so \(x_{rms}\) = 6.6 µm.
  2. One minute: \(2(22)(60) = 2640\ \mu\mathrm{m}^2\), so 51 µm.
  3. One hour: \(2(22)(3600) = 1.58\times10^{5}\ \mu\mathrm{m}^2\), so 398 µm.
  4. One day: \(2(22)(86{,}400) = 3.8\times10^{6}\ \mu\mathrm{m}^2\), so 1950 µm ≈ 2 mm.
  5. The longest axons run about 1 m (typical, spinal cord to foot): 2 mm is 0.2 % of the way.

What it means. Sixty times more time buys only about 8 times more distance. To cover the metre would take \(t = L^2/2D = 1/(2\times22\times10^{-12}) = 2.3\times10^{10}\) s, about 720 years. A neuron cannot supply its axon's far end by diffusion, which is why it ships cargo on motors (Week 4).

Mechanical analogya ball bearing in a pipe on a shaking table

Lay a long straight pipe on a table that shakes, and drop a ball bearing in. Each shake knocks it a little left or right. The pipe keeps it to one dimension, like the axon.

In the cellIn the machine
the proteina ball bearing
the axona long straight pipe
thermal kicksthe table's shakes: ±1 cm, 20 times a second
\(D\) = 22 µm²/s\(D = (0.01)^2/(2\times0.05) = 10^{-3}\) m²/s
\(x_{rms} = \sqrt{2Dt}\)0.14 m after 10 s; 1.41 m after 1000 s

A hundred times the shaking buys ten times the distance: the same square root as in the axon.

Where it breaks. The bearing rolls on between shakes, because it has inertia, and friction drains it. So its short-time motion is not a clean walk. The protein's velocity memory dies in picoseconds, so on any timescale we can watch, its walk is clean.
