1.2.6

⟨r²⟩ = 2dDt — the walk in any dimension

Minted in Week 1 §2.3 · Pearson's drunkard and the law of ⟨x²⟩ · open the module

eq. 1.2.6$$\langle r^2\rangle = 2d\,Dt, \qquad d = \text{number of dimensions the walker explores}$$

Letters

  • \(\langle r^2\rangle\) — mean squared distance from the start · m²
  • \(d\) — number of dimensions the walker explores: 1, 2 or 3
  • \(D\) — diffusion coefficient · m²/s
  • \(t\) — elapsed time · s

How it is used

§2.3 notes that each axis is its own independent 1D walk contributing \(2Dt\), so the contributions add. Its table: \(d\) = 1 along a line (the drunkard bench), \(d\) = 2 for a particle track on a microscope image, a projection (\(4Dt\)), and \(d\) = 3 for a molecule loose in a cell (\(6Dt\)). "Which \(d\) you use is not a style choice", and HW1 grades it. §2.4's probability ring uses \(r = \sqrt{4Dt}\), which holds 63 % of a 2D cloud, and Tab 5 names this equation as the one HW1 uses to read \(D\) off particle tracks. It feeds eq. 1.2.8.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea receptor, its ligand, and the microscope's view

At the itch nerve ending, the H1 receptor drifts in the membrane, a true 2D walk. Histamine walks in 3D through the tissue. What does each cover in one minute?

  1. Receptor in a membrane: \(D\) ≈ 0.1 µm²/s (typical for a membrane protein), \(d\) = 2: \(\langle r^2\rangle = 4(0.1)(60) = 24\ \mu\mathrm{m}^2\), so \(r_{rms}\) = 4.9 µm.
  2. Histamine in tissue: \(D\) ≈ 330 µm²/s (Tab 4), \(d\) = 3: \(\langle r^2\rangle = 6(330)(60) = 118{,}800\ \mu\mathrm{m}^2\), so 345 µm.
  3. A microscope image of that histamine sees a 2D projection: \(\langle r^2\rangle = 4(330)(60) = 79{,}200\ \mu\mathrm{m}^2\), so 281 µm.
  4. The classic error: fit the image's 79,200 µm² with \(6Dt\). That gives \(D = 79{,}200/(6\times60)\) = 220 µm²/s, a third too low.

What it means. In a minute the receptor barely leaves its own few-micron patch, while histamine spreads over a third of a millimetre. Choosing \(d\) wrong does not change the physics, but it changes your measured \(D\) by a factor of 1.5.

Mechanical analogya robot vacuum, a toy drone, and the drone's shadow

A robot vacuum wandering at random is stuck on the floor. A toy drone wandering at random has the whole room. The drone's shadow on the floor is what a microscope sees of a 3D walker.

In the cellIn the machine
H1 receptor in the membrane (\(d\) = 2)robot vacuum on the floor
histamine in tissue (\(d\) = 3)a toy drone flying at random
the microscope image (a 2D projection)the drone's shadow on the floor
each axis adds \(2Dt\)left–right, front–back and up–down are separate walks

Give each the same per-axis \(D\) = 0.1 m²/s (illustrative) and watch for 10 s. The drone's \(\langle r^2\rangle = 6Dt\) = 6 m², an rms of 2.45 m. Its shadow's is \(4Dt\) = 4 m², or 2.0 m, the same as the robot vacuum, which really is 2D. The shadow is honest about two axes and blind to the third.

Where it breaks. Robots and drones move in straight legs between turns, and walls stop them. A molecule's path turns ~10¹³ times a second, and on this scale the tissue has no walls.

1.2.7

The Boltzmann distribution — each k_BT of cost makes a state e times rarer

Minted in Week 1 §2.4 · Where is the particle? What √(2Dt) actually tells you (Tilt the cloud: the Boltzmann distribution) · open the module

eq. 1.2.7$$C(h) = C_0\, e^{-U(h)/k_BT}$$

Letters

  • \(C(h)\) — concentration (number per volume) at height \(h\); read as the relative odds of finding a particle there · m⁻³
  • \(C_0\) — the concentration where \(U\) = 0 · m⁻³
  • \(U(h)\) — the energy cost of being at \(h\) · J
  • \(k_BT\) — thermal energy, the exchange rate · J · 4.28 × 10⁻²¹ J at 310 K

How it is used

§2.4 names the shape that §2.2's settling histogram showed. With \(U = \Delta\rho Vgh\), linear in height, \(e^{-U/k_BT}\) is a plain exponential whose 1/e height is \(\ell_g\). It is a probability statement: one \(k_BT\) of cost makes a state 2.7 times rarer, two make it 7.4 times rarer, and ten make it 22,000 times rarer. That is why a cell builds an enzyme rather than wait for an event costing tens of \(k_BT\). §3.3 re-boxes it ("same law, general \(U\)") as Step 1 of Einstein's derivation; the flux-standoff sim's histogram lands on its curve, and Perrin tested it with resin beads (Nobel 1926).

Comes back: Week 3 §1.3 (the exponential tail of kick energies that frees a bound ligand) and §1.5 (the odds of sitting ΔU above a bond's floor); R1 §2.2 (where the aerosol dose lands).

Biological examplewhy a climber gasps on Everest

Air molecules feel gravity too, so each one pays \(U(h) = mgh\). How much air is left at the summit, 8849 m up?

  1. Air's average molecule, 29 Da: \(m = 4.82\times10^{-26}\) kg.
  2. Assume one temperature for the whole column, 288 K (typical sea-level air): \(k_BT = 3.98\times10^{-21}\) J.
  3. Cost at the summit: \(U = mgh = (4.82\times10^{-26})(9.8)(8849) = 4.18\times10^{-21}\) J = 1.05 \(k_BT\).
  4. \(C/C_0 = e^{-1.05}\) = 0.35.
  5. The 1/e height, \(k_BT/mg\) = 8.4 km, is the atmosphere's \(\ell_g\).
  6. Oxygen's share: 21 % of 101.3 kPa is 21.3 kPa at sea level, and 0.35 × 21.3 = 7.4 kPa at the summit.

What it means. One \(k_BT\) of climb leaves about a third of the air, so each summit breath carries about a third of the oxygen it would at sea level. The real summit pressure is also about a third of sea level (typical). The estimate is rough, because real air gets colder as it rises, so it is not a single-temperature column.

Mechanical analogya shaken box of ball bearings

Shake a tall, clear box of steel ball bearings hard from below. They form a small atmosphere: crowded at the floor, thinning upward. The shaking floor plays the bath.

In the cellIn the machine
air molecules1 g steel ball bearings
\(k_BT\), the bath's energythe floor's energy per bead, ~1 mJ (illustrative)
\(U = mgh\)\(U = mgh\)
1/e height, 8.4 km10⁻³/(10⁻³ × 9.8) = 10.2 cm
the summit, 1.05 \(k_BT\) up: 35 %30 cm up: 5.3 %

At 30 cm the bead density is \(e^{-0.30/0.102}\) = 5.3 % of the floor's.

Where it breaks. The beads lose energy in every collision, so the box is "colder" near the top and the profile is only roughly exponential. That is the same flaw that keeps the real atmosphere from being a single-temperature Boltzmann column.

Featured in HW1 · Problem 3(b), Challenge
1.2.8

Diffusion time — distance costs quadratically

Minted in Week 1 §2.5 · √t runs biology · open the module

eq. 1.2.8$$t \;\approx\; \frac{L^2}{2dD} \qquad \text{(d = dimensionality; } L^2/6D \text{ in 3D)}$$

Letters

  • \(t\) — typical time to diffuse a distance \(L\) · s
  • \(L\) — distance · m
  • \(d\) — dimensions explored: 1, 2 or 3
  • \(D\) — diffusion coefficient · m²/s

How it is used

§2.5 inverts eq. 1.2.6 into the travel-time formula the course uses more than any other. Its ladder for histamine (\(D\) ≈ 10⁻⁹ m²/s, 3D) runs from a 20 nm synaptic cleft (70 ns) to a 10 µm cell (17 ms), the bite's 1 mm wheal (170 s) and 1 m (5 years). The spreading-bite sim draws the front at \(\sqrt{6Dt}\) for four diffusers, with a tissue-crowding divider; its "equivalent speed" readout collapses with time. Tab 4's ledger runs on it: detection in ~3 s, histamine to the nerve in ~7 s, the bump in ~33 min. §3.4 chains it after Stokes–Einstein.

Comes back: Week 7 §1.2 (a vesicle's diffusion clock against a motor, down a metre-long axon); C1 §1.3 (O₂ crosses the alveolar wall in a fraction of a millisecond) and §2.1 (how far TGF-β1 carries from an injured alveolus); R1 §2.1 (a drug crossing a 50-µm mucus film) and §2.5 (the 15-minute dose); R2 §1.2 (TGF-β1 leaving the clot) and §1.4 (a fibroblast's walk to the middle of the wound).

Biological exampleoxygen from a capillary to a cell

Dissolved O₂ diffuses at \(D\) ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s (constants box). Tissue is 3D, so \(t \approx L^2/6D\).

  1. A cell midway between capillaries about 100 µm apart (typical), \(L\) = 50 µm: \(t = (5\times10^{-5})^2/(6\times2\times10^{-9})\) = 0.21 s.
  2. A cell 1 mm away: \(t = (10^{-3})^2/(1.2\times10^{-8})\) = 83 s.
  3. A cell 1 cm away: \(t = (10^{-2})^2/(1.2\times10^{-8})\) = 8300 s ≈ 2.3 h.

What it means. Within 50 µm, oxygen arrives in a fifth of a second. At a millimetre it takes over a minute, and at a centimetre hours, which is far too slow for a working tissue. So capillaries run within about 100 µm of most cells (typical), and anything thicker needs plumbing (Weeks 9 and 11).

Mechanical analogyheat creeping up a pan handle

Heat in a solid spreads by the same random-walk arithmetic, with the metal's thermal diffusivity in place of \(D\). The pan is the capillary; the handle is the tissue.

In the cellIn the machine
the capillary, the sourcethe hot pan on the burner
tissue between capillary and cellthe handle, 15 cm long
O₂heat
\(D\) = 2 × 10⁻⁹ m²/sthermal diffusivity: cast iron ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻⁵, stainless ≈ 4 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s (typical)
\(t \approx L^2/2dD\), \(d\) = 3\(t \approx L^2/2D\), \(d\) = 1 along the handle

Run it: cast iron, (0.15)²/(2 × 1.5 × 10⁻⁵) = 750 s ≈ 12.5 min; stainless, (0.15)²/(2 × 4 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 47 min. That is why a stainless handle stays cool through a short fry.

Where it breaks. The handle loses heat to the air along its length, so its far end may never get hot at all. Tissue does the same to O₂ by consuming it on the way, and then the clock is no longer the whole story.

Module Tab 3 · Einstein's Bargain
1.3.1

Mobility — speed per unit force

Minted in Week 1 §3.1 · The bargain, watched — one bath, two jobs · open the module

eq. 1.3.1$$v_{drift} = \mu F \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mu \equiv \frac{v_{drift}}{F} \qquad \left(\ \zeta \equiv \frac{1}{\mu}\ \text{is the same fact stated as a price}\right)$$

Letters

  • \(v_{drift}\) — the steady speed under a steady push · m/s
  • \(F\) — the applied force · N (cell scale: pN)
  • \(\mu\) — mobility, speed per unit force · m/(N·s)
  • \(\zeta = 1/\mu\) — the drag coefficient, force per unit speed · N·s/m

How it is used

§3.1 introduces the tab's central character. At the cell scale a push gives an instant steady speed, not an acceleration (§3.2 shows why), so speed per force is the right variable. It is measured the way it is defined: pull with a known \(F\), read \(v\), divide. An optical tweezer does this, and HW1 hands you one. The bargain bench pulls its orange team with a steady force, half each way, and reads \(\mu = v_{drift}/F\). It feeds the claim (eq. 1.3.2) and Stokes' law (eq. 1.3.3).

Comes back: —

Biological examplethe mobility of a sinking red cell

Gravity is a free, known force. Eq. 1.2.1 gave a red cell's buoyant weight in plasma: \(F\) = 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ N. Film one isolated cell in a thin chamber, and suppose it falls 60 µm in a minute, \(v\) = 1 µm/s (illustrative, the right size for a single cell).

  1. \(\mu = v/F = 10^{-6}/6.6\times10^{-14} = 1.5\times10^{7}\) m/(N·s).
  2. As a price: \(\zeta = 1/\mu = 6.6\times10^{-8}\) N·s/m.
  3. Predict a spin at 1000 g: \(F\) = 1000 × 0.066 pN = 66 pN.
  4. \(v = \mu F = (1.5\times10^{7})(6.6\times10^{-11}) = 1.0\times10^{-3}\) m/s = 1 mm/s.
  5. A 3 cm tube clears in \(0.03/10^{-3}\) = 30 s.

What it means. One measurement at 1 g predicts the centrifuge, because speed is proportional to force with no coasting. A real tube of whole blood takes longer, since packed cells hinder each other. Eq. 1.3.3 will confirm the 1 µm/s: a sphere of the cell's volume (\(a\) = 2.8 µm) in plasma of about 1.2 mPa·s (typical) sinks at about 1 µm/s.

Mechanical analogya car's shock absorber

A shock absorber is a dashpot. Push harder and it moves faster in proportion; stop pushing and it stops. That is mobility in a part you can hold.

In the cellIn the machine
the red cellthe damper's piston
buoyant weight \(F\) = 0.066 pNa 500 N push on the damper
plasma resisting the motionoil forced through holes in the piston
\(\zeta\) = 6.6 × 10⁻⁸ N·s/m\(\zeta\) ≈ 2000 N·s/m (a typical car damper)
\(\mu\) = 1.5 × 10⁷ m/(N·s)\(\mu\) = 1/2000 = 5 × 10⁻⁴ m/(N·s)
\(v\) = 1 µm/s\(v\) = 500/2000 = 0.25 m/s

Where it breaks. The piston and the car have mass, and the car rides on springs, so a real car bounces before it settles. A damper's valves also open at high speed, so it is linear only over a range. The red cell has no bounce: its momentum dies in about 1.5 µs.

1.3.2

Einstein's claim — D = μk_BT

Minted in Week 1 §3.1 · The bargain, watched — one bath, two jobs · open the module

eq. 1.3.2$$D \;\overset{?}{=}\; \mu\,k_BT$$

Letters

  • \(D\) — diffusion coefficient, from the free jiggle (the slope of ⟨r²⟩) · m²/s
  • \(\mu\) — mobility, from a steady pull · m/(N·s)
  • \(k_BT\) — thermal energy · J · 4.28 × 10⁻²¹ J at 310 K
  • \(\overset{?}{=}\) — a claim to be tested, proved in §3.3

How it is used

§3.1 states Einstein's bargain: the kicks and the resistance are the same collisions, so thermal energy must convert one into the other. The bargain bench runs two teams in one bath. The purple team is left alone (\(D\) from ⟨r²⟩); the orange team is pulled (\(\mu = v/F\)). The starred readout \(D/(\mu k_BT)\) wanders toward 1 with honest ±20 % noise. Heating moves both measurements but not the ratio, and pulling too hard makes it sag (probe gently). §3.3 proves it as eq. 1.3.8 and finishes it as eq. 1.3.9.

Comes back: —

Biological examplepredicting the red cell's jiggle from its sinking

Eq. 1.3.1 measured the red cell's mobility by letting it sink. The bargain says that number also fixes how much it jiggles.

  1. From eq. 1.3.1: \(\mu = 1.5\times10^{7}\) m/(N·s).
  2. \(D = \mu k_BT = (1.5\times10^{7})(4.28\times10^{-21}) = 6.5\times10^{-14}\) m²/s = 0.065 µm²/s.
  3. On a microscope image (\(d\) = 2), in one second: \(r_{rms} = \sqrt{4Dt}\) = 0.51 µm.
  4. Cross-check: \(D/v = 6.5\times10^{-14}/10^{-6}\) = 65 nm \(= k_BT/F\), the red cell's sedimentation length (eq. 1.2.2).
  5. After 100 s it has sunk 100 µm, but wandered only \(\sqrt{4\times6.5\times10^{-14}\times100}\) = 5.1 µm.

What it means. A pulling measurement predicts a jiggle: half a micron per second, easy to see. Sinking grows as \(t\) and wander as \(\sqrt{t}\), so drift wins for anything that waits long enough. The length where they trade places is \(\ell_g\).

Mechanical analogythe heavy puck on the air-hockey table, again

Return to the table from eq. 1.1.1. The swarm of light pucks does two jobs on the heavy puck. Parked, it gets kicked around (jiggle). Towed, it meets more pucks on its front face than its back (drag). Einstein's claim says one measures the other.

In the cellIn the machine
the red cellthe heavy puck
plasma moleculesthe swarm of light pucks
\(\mu\) from sinking\(\mu\) from towing: 0.05 N gives 0.1 m/s, so \(\mu\) = 2 m/(N·s) (illustrative)
\(k_BT\)the swarm's energy per puck, 0.01 J
\(D = \mu k_BT\)predicted \(D\) = 2 × 0.01 = 0.02 m²/s

Where it breaks. The table's swarm is kept going by a motor and loses energy in every bounce, so it is not in equilibrium, and the bargain is an equilibrium result. On a driven table nothing forces the ratio to be exactly 1. In a thermal bath, §3.3 shows that it must be.

1.3.3

Stokes' law — drag grows with radius, not area

Minted in Week 1 §3.2 · Mobility has a law: μ = 1/6πηa · open the module

eq. 1.3.3$$v = \mu F, \quad \mu = \frac{1}{6\pi\eta a} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad F_{drag} = \zeta v, \quad \zeta = 6\pi\eta a$$

Letters

  • \(v\) — the steady (drift) speed · m/s
  • \(F\) — the applied force, balanced by \(F_{drag}\) · N (cell scale: pN)
  • \(\mu\) — mobility, speed per unit force · m/(N·s)
  • \(\zeta = 1/\mu\) — the drag coefficient, force per unit speed · N·s/m
  • \(\eta\) — the fluid's viscosity · Pa·s (water: 0.69 mPa·s at 37 °C, 0.89 mPa·s at 25 °C)
  • \(a\) — the sphere's radius · m

How it is used

§3.2 mints it to give §3.1's measured mobility a law. At low Reynolds number (\(Re = \rho va/\eta\) ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁹ for a 2-nm protein) velocity exists only while a force acts. The drag-race bench pulls four spheres (10–300 nm) with the same force: ten times the radius gives a tenth of the speed, not a hundredth, and mass appears nowhere. Raising the viscosity toward cytoplasm (×30) or honey (×1000) never leaves the low-\(Re\) world. §3.2 and §3.4 price a vesicle's haul with it (lecture Q5: 0.002 pN in water, 0.2–2 pN in cytoplasm, against kinesin's 5–6 pN stall). It is the bottom half of Stokes–Einstein (eq. 1.3.9): once \(\mu\) is known from geometry, \(D = \mu k_BT\) follows.

Comes back: R1 §2.2 (two cargoes in one gravitational field).

Biological examplewhat a swimming E. coli pays to move

A gut bacterium swims at about 20 µm/s, roughly ten body lengths a second. How hard must its flagella push?

  1. Treat the cell as a sphere: \(a\) ≈ 1 µm = 10⁻⁶ m.
  2. Body fluid ≈ water at 37 °C: \(\eta\) = 6.9 × 10⁻⁴ Pa·s.
  3. Drag coefficient: \(\zeta = 6\pi\eta a = 6\pi(6.9\times10^{-4})(10^{-6}) = 1.3\times10^{-8}\) N·s/m.
  4. Speed: \(v\) = 20 µm/s = 2 × 10⁻⁵ m/s.
  5. Thrust: \(F = \zeta v = (1.3\times10^{-8})(2\times10^{-5}) = 2.6\times10^{-13}\) N ≈ 0.26 pN.

What it means. A quarter of a piconewton moves a whole bacterium, about a twentieth of the 5–6 pN at which a kinesin motor stalls (§3.2). Drag at this scale is cheap in force but has no memory. Its Reynolds number, \(\rho va/\eta\), is 2.9 × 10⁻⁵, so the instant the flagella stop, so does the cell; Purcell's coasting distance is a tenth of an ångström.

Mechanical analogya steel ball sinking through glycerol

The falling-ball viscometer is this equation, built at bench scale. In place of the flagella's thrust, a constant force pulls: the ball's buoyant weight. In place of water, a fluid two thousand times thicker than body-temperature water keeps the motion slow and free of inertia. The ball reaches terminal speed almost at once, and that speed is \(F/\zeta\).

In the cellIn the machine
flagellar thrust \(F\)buoyant weight of the ball, \(\Delta\rho\tfrac{4}{3}\pi a^3 g\)
water, \(\eta\) = 0.69 mPa·sglycerol, \(\eta\) ≈ 1.41 Pa·s (typical, 20 °C)
bacterium, \(a\) ≈ 1 µmsteel ball, \(a\) = 1 mm
swimming speed 20 µm/sterminal speed \(v = F/6\pi\eta a\) ≈ 1.0 cm/s

A 1 mm steel ball (7800 kg/m³) weighs 2.7 × 10⁻⁴ N in glycerol (1260 kg/m³, both typical). With \(\zeta = 6\pi\eta a\) = 0.027 N·s/m, it sinks at about 1.0 cm/s. That is slow enough that the flow is still Stokes flow: \(Re = \rho va/\eta\) ≈ 0.009. Time the fall and you have measured \(\eta\).

Where it breaks. Make the ball much faster or larger and its own inertia starts to matter (\(Re\) approaching 1), so the law fails. The bacterium never gets there. The ball is also far too heavy to show the thermal jiggle that Stokes–Einstein builds on.

1.3.4

The drift flux — concentration times drift speed

Minted in Week 1 §3.3 · Why the bargain is forced: \(D = \mu k_BT\) · open the module

eq. 1.3.4$$J_{drift} = -\,C\,\mu\,\frac{\partial U}{\partial h}$$

Letters

  • \(J_{drift}\) — particles crossing unit area per second because of the force · m⁻²s⁻¹
  • \(C\) — number concentration · m⁻³
  • \(\mu\) — mobility · m/(N·s)
  • \(\partial U/\partial h\) — the slope of the energy landscape; for \(U = Fh\) it is the force \(F\) · N
  • the minus sign — the flux runs downhill in \(U\)

How it is used

§3.3 Step 2 names the first of two currents. The force settles particles downward at the mobility speed \(\mu\,\partial U/\partial h\), and the flux is concentration times that speed. The flux-standoff sim (tilting force \(F\), radius \(a\), \(T\), and a Break Einstein toggle) is §2.2's settling column revisited; this current is what piles particles at the floor. It meets its opposite in eq. 1.3.8.

Comes back: —

Biological exampleyeast settling in a flask on the bench

Leave a culture of baker's yeast on the bench and it settles. How fast do cells arrive on the floor?

  1. Yeast cell as a sphere, \(a\) ≈ 2.5 µm (typical, 5 µm across): \(V = 6.5\times10^{-17}\) m³.
  2. \(\Delta\rho\) ≈ 100 kg/m³ (cell ≈ 1100 against medium ≈ 1000, typical): \(\partial U/\partial h = \Delta\rho Vg = 6.4\times10^{-14}\) N.
  3. Mobility, water at 25 °C: \(\zeta = 6\pi(8.9\times10^{-4})(2.5\times10^{-6}) = 4.2\times10^{-8}\) N·s/m, so \(\mu = 2.4\times10^{7}\) m/(N·s).
  4. Drift speed: \(\mu\,\partial U/\partial h = (2.4\times10^{7})(6.4\times10^{-14}) = 1.5\times10^{-6}\) m/s, about 5.5 mm per hour.
  5. A dense culture: \(C\) ≈ 10⁸ cells/mL = 10¹⁴ m⁻³ (typical).
  6. \(J_{drift} = -(10^{14})(1.5\times10^{-6}) = -1.5\times10^{8}\) cells/(m²·s): 150 cells per mm² per second, downward.
  7. Onto 1 cm² of floor in one hour: \((1.5\times10^{8})(10^{-4})(3600) = 5.5\times10^{7}\) cells.

What it means. A cream-coloured layer builds on the bottom of the flask within hours, and this is that flux. The upward leak of eq. 1.3.5 cannot stop it: yeast's sedimentation length is only 64 nm.

Mechanical analogya baggage conveyor

A conveyor delivers bags at a rate equal to bags per metre times belt speed. The drift flux has the same shape: concentration times drift speed.

In the cellIn the machine
yeast cells per volume, \(C\)bags per metre of belt, 2 /m
drift speed \(\mu\,\partial U/\partial h\)belt speed, 0.5 m/s
gravitythe belt's motor
\(J_{drift}\)bags arriving per second: 2 × 0.5 = 1 bag/s
the flask's floorthe end of the belt

Where it breaks. Every bag rides at exactly the belt's speed. Each yeast cell also jiggles, and in a pile the jiggle leaks some back up: the second current, eq. 1.3.5. For yeast the leak is negligible; for a protein it wins.

Featured in HW1 · Problem 1(c)
1.3.5

Fick's first law — the diffusive flux

Minted in Week 1 §3.3 · Why the bargain is forced: \(D = \mu k_BT\) · open the module

eq. 1.3.5$$J_{diff} = -\,D\,\frac{\partial C}{\partial h}$$

Letters

  • \(J_{diff}\) — particles crossing unit area per second by diffusion · m⁻²s⁻¹
  • \(D\) — diffusion coefficient · m²/s
  • \(\partial C/\partial h\) — the concentration gradient · m⁻⁴
  • the minus sign — the flux runs from crowded to sparse

How it is used

§3.3 Step 2 borrows it "on credit" as the leak that carries the pile at the floor back up; next week derives it. In the flux-standoff sim it is the upward current that meets the drift. Its convention fixes the factor 2 in eq. 1.2.4: with that 2, the walker's \(D\) and Fick's \(D\) are the same number. Tab 5 points out that it was hiding inside Einstein's derivation, and HW1's FRAP measurement leans on it.

Comes back: Week 2 §1.2 (derived and measured as its own bench: counting makes a current); Week 3 §3.6 (Fick I across the unstirred film in front of the receptors); R1 §2.4 (oxygen supply into a CF mucus layer full of bacteria).

Biological exampleoxygen crossing the alveolar wall

Blood arrives at a lung capillary low in oxygen. How many O₂ molecules cross each patch of the wall per second?

  1. Oxygen pressure: alveolus ≈ 100 mmHg, blood arriving ≈ 40 mmHg (typical).
  2. Dissolved O₂ ≈ 1.3 µM per mmHg (typical, plasma at 37 °C): 130 µM on the air side, 52 µM on the blood side.
  3. \(\Delta C\) = 78 µM = 0.078 mol/m³; times \(N_A\), 4.7 × 10²² molecules/m³.
  4. Barrier ≈ 1 µm thick (typical; the thinnest parts are about half that): \(\partial C/\partial h \approx -4.7\times10^{22}/10^{-6} = -4.7\times10^{28}\) m⁻⁴, with \(h\) measured from the air into the blood.
  5. \(D\) ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s (constants box).
  6. \(J = -D\,\partial C/\partial h = (2\times10^{-9})(4.7\times10^{28}) = 9.4\times10^{19}\) molecules/(m²·s), into the blood.
  7. Per square micron: 9.4 × 10⁷ molecules each second.

What it means. About 10⁸ O₂ molecules cross each square micron each second at the start of the capillary. The flux falls as the blood loads and \(\Delta C\) shrinks. Breathing harder raises the alveolar side and steepens the gradient: that, not \(D\), is the lever the body pulls.

Mechanical analogywater through an espresso puck

Flow through a packed bed obeys Darcy's law: flow per area is a coefficient times the pressure gradient. That is Fick's law with pressure in place of concentration, and an espresso machine runs it every morning.

In the cellIn the machine
O₂ moleculeswater
concentration gradient \(\partial C/\partial h\)pressure gradient: 8 bar across 1 cm = 8 × 10⁷ Pa/m
\(D\)the puck's permeability over water's viscosity, set by the grind
alveolar wall, 1 µmcoffee puck, 1 cm
\(J\) = 9.4 × 10¹⁹ m⁻²s⁻¹30 mL in 25 s through a 58 mm basket: 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ m/s

Flow per area ÷ gradient = 4.5 × 10⁻⁴/8 × 10⁷ = 5.7 × 10⁻¹² m²/(Pa·s). That is the grind's number, as \(D\) is the barrier's. Grind finer and it falls, and the shot runs slow.

Where it breaks. The pump pushes all the water one way, but nothing pushes the O₂. Fick's flux is the net of random walks in both directions: more molecules start on the crowded side, so more cross from it.

1.3.6

The slope of a Boltzmann profile — proportional to C itself

Minted in Week 1 §3.3 · Why the bargain is forced: \(D = \mu k_BT\) · open the module

eq. 1.3.6$$\frac{\partial C}{\partial h} = C_0\,e^{-U/k_BT}\cdot\left(-\frac{1}{k_BT}\frac{\partial U}{\partial h}\right) = -\,\frac{C}{k_BT}\,\frac{\partial U}{\partial h}$$

Letters

  • \(\partial C/\partial h\) — the slope of the settled profile · m⁻⁴
  • \(C = C_0e^{-U/k_BT}\) — the Boltzmann profile, eq. 1.2.7 · m⁻³
  • \(\partial U/\partial h\) — the force each particle feels, as an energy slope · N
  • \(k_BT\) — thermal energy · J

How it is used

§3.3 Step 3 differentiates eq. 1.2.7 by the chain rule, holding \(C_0\) and \(k_BT\) constant. The result says the Boltzmann profile's slope is proportional to \(C\) itself, which is what makes it exponential. It is substituted into Fick's law next (eq. 1.3.7).

Comes back: —

Biological examplehow fast the air thins as you climb

Take eq. 1.2.7's single-temperature atmosphere at 288 K, where \(U = mgh\), so \(\partial U/\partial h = mg\).

  1. Weight per molecule: \(mg = (4.82\times10^{-26})(9.8) = 4.72\times10^{-25}\) N.
  2. Fractional slope: \((1/C)\,\partial C/\partial h = -mg/k_BT = -4.72\times10^{-25}/3.98\times10^{-21} = -1.19\times10^{-4}\) per metre.
  3. Per 100 m of climb: 1.19 % of the air, wherever you start.
  4. At sea level, \(C = P/k_BT = 101{,}325/3.98\times10^{-21} = 2.55\times10^{25}\) m⁻³, so \(\partial C/\partial h = -3.0\times10^{21}\) m⁻⁴.
  5. At the summit (\(C\) = 0.35 \(C_0\)): \(-1.06\times10^{21}\) m⁻⁴, about a third as steep.

What it means. The percentage lost per metre stays fixed while the absolute loss shrinks with \(C\). A slope proportional to what is left is the signature of an exponential: the air never ends at a sharp edge, it thins.

Mechanical analogyan aircraft's barometric altimeter

An altimeter turns this slope into height. Multiply eq. 1.3.6 by \(k_BT\). Since pressure is \(Ck_BT\) (eq. 1.1.3 per volume), pressure falls by \(C\,mg\) per metre: the weight of the air in a 1 m² column one metre tall.

In the cellIn the machine
air molecules at concentration \(C\)air outside the aircraft
\(\partial U/\partial h = mg\)the weight of one molecule
\(\partial C/\partial h\)the pressure slope the sensor reads, \(k_BT\,\partial C/\partial h\)
−1.19 × 10⁻⁴ per metre12.0 Pa per metre at sea level
\(k_BT\)the temperature the instrument assumes

Run it: \(Cm = (2.55\times10^{25})(4.82\times10^{-26})\) = 1.23 kg/m³ of air, so pressure drops (1.23)(9.8) = 12.0 Pa per metre. A sensor that resolves 12 Pa resolves one metre of height.

Where it breaks. Real air cools with height, and the weather moves \(C_0\) up and down. That is why altimeters assume a standard atmosphere that cools as it rises, and why pilots reset them before landing.

1.3.7

The diffusive flux, rewritten with U — the leak runs uphill

Minted in Week 1 §3.3 · Why the bargain is forced: \(D = \mu k_BT\) · open the module

eq. 1.3.7$$J_{diff} = -\,D\,\frac{\partial C}{\partial h} = +\,\frac{D}{k_BT}\,C\,\frac{\partial U}{\partial h}$$

Letters

  • \(J_{diff}\) — diffusive flux · m⁻²s⁻¹
  • \(D\) — diffusion coefficient · m²/s
  • \(C\), \(\partial C/\partial h\) — concentration and its slope · m⁻³, m⁻⁴
  • \(\partial U/\partial h\) — the energy slope, the force per particle · N
  • \(D/k_BT\) — has the units of a mobility · m/(N·s)

How it is used

§3.3 puts eq. 1.3.6 into Fick's law (eq. 1.3.5). In a Boltzmann profile the leak runs uphill (the + sign), and it now has the same shape as the drift, \(C\times\)(a mobility)\(\times\partial U/\partial h\), with \(D/k_BT\) in the place of \(\mu\). Comparing the two currents is then one line (eq. 1.3.8).

Comes back: —

Biological examplehemoglobin in an ultracentrifuge

A sedimentation-equilibrium run spins a protein until its profile stops changing. Take hemoglobin at 10⁴ g (illustrative) and 25 °C.

  1. Mass 64.5 kDa (typical): \(m = 1.07\times10^{-22}\) kg. Protein density 1350 kg/m³, so \(\Delta\rho V = 350\times m/1350 = 2.78\times10^{-23}\) kg.
  2. \(\partial U/\partial h = \Delta\rho V\times10^{4}g = (2.78\times10^{-23})(9.8\times10^{4}) = 2.72\times10^{-18}\) N.
  3. \(D\) ≈ 7 × 10⁻¹¹ m²/s (typical, water at 25 °C) and \(k_BT = 4.11\times10^{-21}\) J, so \(D/k_BT = 1.70\times10^{10}\) m/(N·s).
  4. The leak's uphill speed: \((D/k_BT)\,\partial U/\partial h = (1.70\times10^{10})(2.72\times10^{-18}) = 4.6\times10^{-8}\) m/s = 46 nm/s.
  5. At 1 mg/mL (9.3 × 10²¹ molecules/m³): \(J_{diff} = (9.3\times10^{21})(4.6\times10^{-8}) = 4.3\times10^{14}\) m⁻²s⁻¹, upward.
  6. The profile's 1/e height: \(k_BT/(\partial U/\partial h)\) = 1.5 mm.

What it means. The leak behaves as if a force as large as the centrifuge's pushed each molecule uphill through a mobility \(D/k_BT\). The 1.5 mm profile fits inside a centrifuge cell, which is how sedimentation equilibrium weighs a protein without touching it.

Mechanical analogyshoppers wandering on a staircase

Picture a long staircase crowded at the bottom and thinning upward. Each shopper steps up or down at random. No one aims upward, yet more of them start each step from below than from above, so the crowd leaks up.

In the cellIn the machine
hemoglobin moleculesshoppers on a long staircase
thermal kickseach shopper steps 0.3 m up or down, once a second
\(D\) = 7 × 10⁻¹¹ m²/s\(D\) = (0.3)²/(2 × 1) = 0.045 m²/s
profile thinning e-fold every 1.5 mmcrowd thinning e-fold every 3 m of stairs
uphill speed \((D/k_BT)\,\partial U/\partial h\) = 46 nm/snet upward flow, as if each rode up at 0.045/3 = 0.015 m/s

Where it breaks. Shoppers choose where to go and get tired; molecules do neither. And a crowd that thins upward will not stay that way unless something pulls it down: the down escalator of eq. 1.3.8.

1.3.8

Flux balance — equilibrium forces the bracket to zero

Minted in Week 1 §3.3 · Why the bargain is forced: \(D = \mu k_BT\) · open the module

eq. 1.3.8$$J_{drift}+J_{diff} = \left(\frac{D}{k_BT} - \mu\right) C\,\frac{\partial U}{\partial h} \;=\; 0$$

Letters

  • \(J_{drift}\), \(J_{diff}\) — the two currents, eq. 1.3.4 and eq. 1.3.7 · m⁻²s⁻¹
  • \(D/k_BT\) — diffusion's effective mobility · m/(N·s)
  • \(\mu\) — the mechanical mobility · m/(N·s)
  • \(C\), \(\partial U/\partial h\) — concentration and energy slope · m⁻³, N

How it is used

§3.3 adds the two currents and demands zero net current everywhere. Since \(C\) is not zero and the tilt is not zero, the bracket must vanish: \(D = \mu k_BT\), the bargain of eq. 1.3.2. The flux-standoff sim shows the settled column on the Boltzmann curve. Its Break Einstein toggle sets \(D\) freely; the column then settles into the wrong exponential, with 1/e height \(\zeta D/F\) and an effective temperature \(\zeta D/k_B\) that disagrees with the bath. That would be an engine running on nothing, which the second law forbids.

Comes back: —

Biological examplewhat a settled tube of red cells looks like

Let a dilute suspension of red cells stand until nothing changes. What profile does the balance demand?

  1. Drift: from eq. 1.3.1, \(\mu = 1.5\times10^{7}\) m/(N·s).
  2. Diffusion: from eq. 1.3.2, \(D = 6.5\times10^{-14}\) m²/s, so \(D/k_BT = 6.5\times10^{-14}/4.28\times10^{-21} = 1.5\times10^{7}\) m/(N·s). The bracket is zero.
  3. The balanced profile is eq. 1.2.7, with 1/e height \(\ell_g = k_BT/F\) = 65 nm.
  4. One cell diameter up, 8 µm = 124 \(\ell_g\): \(C/C_0 = e^{-124} \approx 10^{-54}\).
  5. A plasma protein in the same tube, albumin (66.5 kDa, typical): \(\ell_g\) at 1 g ≈ 15 m.

What it means. The red cells' equilibrium is a pellet. Their dilute profile is thinner than one cell, so in practice they stack until packed, where the dilute picture fails (§5.2). The albumin above them stays mixed from top to bottom. Both currents still run at full strength in the settled profile, since the cells still sink and jiggle, but they cancel at every height.

Mechanical analogythe down escalator

Put eq. 1.3.7's wandering shoppers on a down escalator. The escalator is the drift; their random stepping is the leak. The crowd stops changing when the two cancel.

In the cellIn the machine
red cellsshoppers stepping at random, \(D\) = 0.045 m²/s
drift down at \(\mu\,\partial U/\partial h\)the escalator's speed
leak up at \((D/k_BT)\,\partial U/\partial h\)the crowd's net upward wander
bracket = 0the crowd's profile stops changing
\(\ell_g = D/v\) = 65 nmcrowd height = \(D\) ÷ escalator speed

Run the escalator at 0.015 m/s and the crowd settles with a 1/e height of 0.045/0.015 = 3 m: a cloud. Run it at 1.5 m/s and the height is 3 cm. Everyone piles up at the bottom, like the red cells' pellet.

Where it breaks. The shoppers' wander and the escalator's speed are set separately, so any pair is possible. In a thermal bath both are set by the same collisions, and only \(D = \mu k_BT\) survives. That is the point of the bracket.

Featured in HW1 · Problem 1(a), ChallengeFeatured in HW2 · Problem 4(e), Problem 5(a)
1.3.9

Stokes–Einstein — D from size, viscosity and temperature

Minted in Week 1 §3.3 · Why the bargain is forced: \(D = \mu k_BT\) · open the module

eq. 1.3.9$$D = \mu\,k_BT \;=\; \frac{k_BT}{6\pi\eta a}$$

Letters

  • \(D\) — diffusion coefficient · m²/s
  • \(\mu\) — mobility, \(1/6\pi\eta a\) (eq. 1.3.3) · m/(N·s)
  • \(k_BT\) — thermal energy · J · 4.28 × 10⁻²¹ J at 310 K, 4.11 × 10⁻²¹ J at 298 K
  • \(\eta\) — viscosity · Pa·s · water: 0.69 mPa·s at 37 °C, 0.89 mPa·s at 25 °C
  • \(a\) — hydrodynamic radius · m

How it is used

§3.3 finishes the derivation with Stokes's mobility: "the whole of Week 1 in one line". The worked example predicts GFP (\(a\) ≈ 2.3 nm, 25 °C) at 107 µm²/s against a measured ≈ 87 µm²/s; the ~20 % gap is GFP's barrel shape and its shell of water. §3.4 runs it as an assembly line, \(a \rightarrow \mu \rightarrow D \rightarrow t = L^2/6D\). In the biomolecule speedometer six cargos race: a ribosome ~78,000 times O₂'s mass arrives only ~100 times later, and every line has slope ½ on log–log axes. Lecture Q4 sends a 2-nm protein across a 10-µm cell in ~0.1 s (water) or 0.3–0.5 s (cytoplasm). Tab 4 builds the bite's cast with it: histamine 1300 → 330 µm²/s in tissue, the saliva protein ≈ 140 → 34 µm²/s. HW1's tweezer pairs it with eq. 1.3.3.

Comes back: C1 §2.1 (run backwards on GFP for TGF-β1's size, then forwards at 37 °C); R1 §2.3 (the viscosity trap: CF sputum's bulk \(\eta\) is the wrong \(\eta\) for a small drug); R2 §1.2 (TGF-β1 leaving the clot).

Biological examplean antibody coming to the bite

Once antibodies have leaked out of a capillary near the bite, how fast do they diffuse to the saliva pocket?

  1. IgG hydrodynamic radius: \(a\) ≈ 5.5 nm (typical).
  2. At 37 °C: \(\eta = 6.9\times10^{-4}\) Pa·s and \(k_BT = 4.28\times10^{-21}\) J.
  3. Drag price: \(6\pi\eta a = 6\pi(6.9\times10^{-4})(5.5\times10^{-9}) = 7.15\times10^{-11}\) N·s/m.
  4. \(D = 4.28\times10^{-21}/7.15\times10^{-11} = 6.0\times10^{-11}\) m²/s = 60 µm²/s in water.
  5. In tissue, with the module's ÷4 crowding: ≈ 15 µm²/s.
  6. Capillary to pocket, \(L\) ≈ 60 µm (Tab 4's cast): \(t = L^2/6D = 60^2/(6\times15)\) = 40 s.
  7. Histamine over the same 60 µm, at 330 µm²/s: \(60^2/(6\times330)\) = 1.8 s.

What it means. The antibody is 22 times wider than histamine and diffuses 22 times more slowly, though it is 1350 times heavier: \(D\) prices radius, not mass. Forty seconds is still quick next to the bite's minutes-long timeline, so the last 60 µm is not the slow step.

Mechanical analogythe falling-ball viscometer, asked to jiggle

Take eq. 1.3.3's machine and ask Stokes–Einstein about the ball itself. Same law, same parts, machine-scale numbers.

In the cellIn the machine
antibody, \(a\) = 5.5 nmsteel ball, \(a\) = 1 mm
tissue fluid, \(\eta\) = 0.69 mPa·sglycerol, \(\eta\) = 1.41 Pa·s
\(k_BT\) at 310 K\(k_BT\) at 293 K, 4.05 × 10⁻²¹ J
\(6\pi\eta a\) = 7.15 × 10⁻¹¹ N·s/m\(6\pi\eta a\) = 0.027 N·s/m
\(D\) = 60 µm²/s\(D\) = 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ m²/s

Run it: \(D = 4.05\times10^{-21}/0.027 = 1.5\times10^{-19}\) m²/s, so in a full day the ball wanders \(\sqrt{2Dt}\) = 0.16 µm. The law holds; the ball is simply far too big and the fluid far too thick.

Where it breaks. Nothing in the law breaks, but you could never see it. The ball sinks at 1 cm/s anyway, and the faintest convection current in the glycerol would move it farther than 0.16 µm a day.

Module Tab 5 · Next Week
Featured in HW1 · Problem 4, ChallengeFeatured in HW2 · Problem 1(b), Problem 4(e)
1.5.1

Smoluchowski's encounter rate — the diffusion speed limit

Minted in Week 1 §5.1 · Next week's headline, measured today — the hungry receptor · open the module

eq. 1.5.1$$k_s = 4\pi (D_1 + D_2)(a_1 + a_2)$$

Letters

  • \(k_s\) — encounter rate constant: arrivals per second per unit concentration · m³/s (× \(N_A\) × 1000 L/m³ gives M⁻¹s⁻¹)
  • \(D_1\), \(D_2\) — the two partners' diffusion coefficients · m²/s
  • \(a_1\), \(a_2\) — the two partners' radii · m

How it is used

§5.1 previews Week 2's headline: the diffusion-limited rate that caps how fast any reaction in a cell can run. The hungry-receptor sim puts a perfectly absorbing sphere of radius \(a\) in a 3D bath that is resupplied at the rim. It hollows out a \((1 - a/r)\) depletion halo and captures at \(4\pi DaC_\infty\), eq. 1.5.1 with the target held still (\(D_2\) = 0, \(a_2\) = 0). Doubling \(a\) doubles the captures (radius, not area), and doubling \(D\) doubles them too; at the defaults, \(4\pi Da = 4\pi(20)(0.7)\) = 176 µm³/s. Lecture Q6(ii) and HW1's absorber use it.

Comes back: Week 2 §3.3 (derived line by line from eq. 2.3.1); Week 3 §1.2 (delivery to a pocket whose surface concentration is \(C_s\)); R1 §3.1 (drug molecules finding an immobile P. aeruginosa); Report 1 §A.1 (the transport step in series with the cell's binding sites).

Biological examplehow often histamine finds an H1 receptor

The bite's histamine has reached the nerve ending. How often does it arrive at one receptor's binding pocket?

  1. Histamine: \(D_1 = 1.3\times10^{-9}\) m²/s (water, 37 °C, Tab 4) and \(a_1\) = 0.25 nm.
  2. H1 receptor, anchored in the membrane: \(D_2\) ≈ 10⁻¹³ m²/s (typical for a membrane protein), under 0.01 % of \(D_1\), so drop it.
  3. The target is the binding pocket, \(a_2\) ≈ 0.5 nm (illustrative): \(a_1 + a_2\) = 0.75 nm.
  4. \(k_s = 4\pi(1.3\times10^{-9})(0.75\times10^{-9}) = 1.23\times10^{-17}\) m³/s.
  5. In chemist's units: \(\times N_A\times1000\) gives \(7.4\times10^{9}\) M⁻¹s⁻¹.
  6. At 1 µM histamine (illustrative), \(C = 6.0\times10^{20}\) m⁻³, so \(k_sC = 7.4\times10^{3}\) arrivals per second.

What it means. At micromolar histamine, each receptor pocket is visited thousands of times a second. About 10⁹–10¹⁰ M⁻¹s⁻¹ is the ceiling for a reaction between small partners in water (typical). Real binding is slower, because not every touch sticks, and the membrane blocks half the directions of approach, which roughly halves this. Weeks 2 and 3 refine both.

Mechanical analogybumper cars in an arena

Fill an arena with bumper cars driven at random. A bump is an encounter. The formula's two sums are §5.1's two riddles, and the arena answers both.

In the cellIn the machine
histaminea bumper car wandering at random
the H1 receptora second car, barely moving
\(D_1 + D_2\)only the gap between two cars matters, and it wanders with both cars' wandering added
\(a_1 + a_2\)two cars touch when their centres are \(a_1 + a_2\) apart
\(k_sC\)bumps per minute for one car, given how crowded the arena is

Two wandering cars bump more often than one car passing a parked one, and two big cars bump more often than two small ones.

Where it breaks. Bumper cars drive straight between turns, so over a car's length they move ballistically, and their bump rate is set by their width and speed, as in a gas, not by a \(D\). Smoluchowski's \((D_1 + D_2)(a_1 + a_2)\) needs paths that turn many times within the contact distance. That is true for molecules, whose velocity memory lasts picoseconds. And an arena is flat: in 2D, diffusion gives no steady encounter rate at all (§5.1's honesty note), so the formula needs the third dimension the cars lack.

Week 2 · Gradients & Encounters — How Molecules Find Their Targets

Week 1 followed one molecule; Week 2 counts a crowd of them and asks which way the crowd flows and how often two molecules meet. Tabs 1–2 build Fick's laws from a head-count of random walkers (2.1.1–2.2.3), and Tab 3 solves the hungry sphere line by line to earn Smoluchowski's \(k_s = 4\pi D a\), with \(\lambda\) and Pe deciding how local a signal stays (2.3.1–2.3.8). Tab 4 turns those concentrations into probabilities (2.4.1–2.4.7). The answer line: a molecule released 30 µm from a mast cell has a one-in-six chance of ever reaching it, yet the cell fires about 1.3 s after the bite, because the mosquito sent ten billion.
