Module Tab 1 · The Crowd Becomes a Current
2.1.1

Flux from a lattice random walk — the net current is a small imbalance between two torrents

Minted in Week 2 §1.2 · Counting makes a current — Fick's first law, measured · open the module

eq. 2.1.1$$J \;=\; \frac{\delta}{2\tau}\left(C_L - C_R\right) \;=\; \frac{\delta^2}{2\tau}\,\frac{C_L - C_R}{\delta} \;\;\xrightarrow{\ \delta\to 0\ }\;\; -\frac{\delta^2}{2\tau}\frac{\partial C}{\partial x}$$

Letters

  • \(J\) — net flux, crossings per area per second · #/(m²·s) (the 1D cartoon counts crossings of a point, #/s)
  • \(\delta\) — the walker's step length · m
  • \(\tau\) — the time per step · s
  • \(C_L, C_R\) — the concentrations in the bins just left and just right of the booth · #/m³
  • \(\partial C/\partial x\) — the concentration gradient; \((C_L - C_R)/\delta\) is minus its one-step version · #/m⁴
  • \(\delta^2/2\tau\) — Week 1's definition of \(D\) (eq. 1.2.4) · m²/s (bench default 10 µm²/s)

How it is used

§1.2 mints it by counting at a tollbooth: walkers within one step of the booth cross in one step-time, half of them each way, so the net is \(\tfrac{\delta}{2\tau}(C_L - C_R)\). The tollbooth bench measures it first. On a flat census the gross traffic runs to hundreds per second each way and the net hugs zero; with a gradient held, the net settles onto \(-D\,\partial C/\partial x\) (the measured-to-predicted ratio rides near 1), and doubling \(D\) doubles the net. The coefficient \(\delta^2/2\tau\) is exactly Week 1's \(D\), so the limit is Fick's first law, re-boxed right after as eq. 1.3.5. That law then drives eqs. 2.1.2, 2.2.1 and 2.3.4.

Comes back: —

Biological examplethe nucleus's supply line, counted at mid-cell

Take the module's Q4 cell. Ribosomes hold a protein at 100 /µm³ on one side; the nucleus, 10 µm away, consumes it and holds \(C \approx 0\); \(D\) = 100 µm²/s. Stand a booth at mid-cell and count with a lattice step \(\delta\) = 0.1 µm, a bookkeeping choice, not a property of the protein. How big are the two torrents, and the net?

  1. Step time: \(\tau = \delta^2/2D = (0.1)^2/(2\times100) = 5\times10^{-5}\) s = 50 µs.
  2. The census falls 100 /µm³ over 10 µm, 10 /µm³ per µm. Bins either side of the booth: \(C_L\) = 50.5, \(C_R\) = 49.5 /µm³.
  3. Rightward: \(\tfrac{\delta}{2\tau}C_L = (1000\ \mu\mathrm{m/s})(50.5) = 50{,}500\) /(µm²·s).
  4. Leftward: \((1000\ \mu\mathrm{m/s})(49.5) = 49{,}500\) /(µm²·s).
  5. Net: \(J\) = 1000 /(µm²·s).
  6. Check with the limit: \(\tfrac{\delta^2}{2\tau}\cdot\tfrac{C_L - C_R}{\delta} = 100 \times 1/0.1 = 1000\) /(µm²·s) ✓.

What it means. The supply that feeds the nucleus is 2% of the traffic running each way. The torrents are not even physical: halve \(\delta\) to 0.05 µm and each one doubles (to 100,500 and 99,500), while the net stays at 1000. Only the imbalance is real, which is why Fick's law holds \(D\) and the gradient and nothing about steps.

Mechanical analogyball bearings on a shaker tray

Put ball bearings in a long, narrow channel on a vibrating table. Each shake knocks every ball one hop left or right at random, like a blind walker. Cut a counting gate across the middle and load more balls on the left. No ball is pushed toward the sparse side, yet balls stream through the gate both ways, and slightly more go right.

In the cellIn the machine
a protein moleculea ball bearing
thermal kicks, step \(\delta\) every \(\tau\)the shaker: a 1-cm hop every 0.1 s
\(D = \delta^2/2\tau\) = 100 µm²/s\(D = (0.01)^2/(2\times0.1) = 5\times10^{-4}\) m²/s
\(C_L, C_R\) = 50.5 and 49.5 /µm³300 and 200 balls per metre either side of the gate
net \(J\) = 1000 /(µm²·s)net 5 balls/s through the gate

At tray scale eq. 2.1.1 gives \((0.01/0.2)\times300 = 15\) balls/s rightward and \(0.05\times200 = 10\) leftward, a net of 5 balls/s, as \(D\,(C_L - C_R)/\delta = 5\times10^{-4}\times100/0.01\) also gives. In 1D, \(J\) is a count per second, as in the module's cartoon.

Where it breaks. The shaker must supply the jiggle that heat supplies for free, and crowded balls collide and lose energy, so their hops stop being independent. The proteins almost never meet each other; they only bump solvent.

Featured in HW1 · Problem 1(c)
2.1.2

Steady flux between two reservoirs — a straight line, and the same flux at every station

Minted in Week 2 §1.3 · Steady state: nature's straight line · open the module

eq. 2.1.2$$C(x) = C_L + \left(C_R - C_L\right)\frac{x}{L}, \qquad J = D\,\frac{C_L - C_R}{L} \quad\text{(steady state)}$$

Letters

  • \(C(x)\) — the steady concentration at position \(x\) in the gap · #/m³
  • \(C_L, C_R\) — the concentrations pinned at the two ends · #/m³
  • \(x\) — distance from the left end · m
  • \(L\) — the gap's length · m
  • \(J\) — the steady flux, the same at every station · #/(m²·s)
  • \(D\) — diffusion coefficient · m²/s (dissolved O₂: 2000 µm²/s, constants box)

How it is used

§1.3 mints it from eq. 1.3.5: in steady state nothing piles up, so the flux is the same at every station, and a constant flux needs a constant slope. The "Two reservoirs, one channel" bench shows it: start empty or start full and the census locks onto the same line; the three station fluxes disagree while filling and agree at steady state; doubling \(D\) changes the flux but not the profile. The module prices oxygen across a 5-µm gap and the Q4 supply line to the nucleus (1000 /(µm²·s)) with it. Zero curvature is why it is the only profile that stands still under eq. 2.2.1; eqs. 2.3.1–2.3.3 are its spherical cousin.

Comes back: C1 §1.3 (Fick's steady flux, times the area); C1 §1.4 (summed over patches in parallel); R1 §2.4 (how deep oxygen gets in mucus).

Biological exampleoxygen from a capillary to a cell 20 µm away

Capillaries sit within about 20 µm of nearly every cell (§1.3). Treat the gap as a slab: the capillary side holds dissolved O₂ at \(C_L\), and the cell's mitochondria hold the far side near \(C_R \approx 0\). What steady flux can the gap carry?

  1. \(D\) = 2000 µm²/s (dissolved O₂, constants box).
  2. \(C_L\): dissolved O₂ in tissue fluid is about 50 µM (typical) = \(5\times10^{4}\) nM × 0.6022 = \(3.0\times10^{4}\) /µm³.
  3. \(C_R \approx 0\); \(L\) = 20 µm.
  4. \(J = D\,(C_L - C_R)/L = 2000 \times 3.0\times10^{4}/20 = 3.0\times10^{6}\) /(µm²·s).
  5. Mid-gap: \(C(10\ \mu\mathrm{m}) = C_L + (0 - C_L)(10/20) = 1.5\times10^{4}\) /µm³, half, as a straight line must be.
  6. Halve the gap to 10 µm: \(J = 6.0\times10^{6}\) /(µm²·s).

What it means. Three million O₂ molecules cross each µm² every second, with no pump. A 100-µm² patch of cell facing the capillary could receive at most \(3\times10^{8}\) per second. Biology cannot raise \(D\), so it shortens \(L\): halve the gap and the ceiling doubles.

Mechanical analogyheat through a brick wall

A house wall in winter is the same slab. The room pins one face at 20 °C, the outside air pins the other at 0 °C, and after a day or so the temperature inside the brick is a straight line. Heat flow per square metre is the brick's conductivity times the temperature drop, divided by the thickness. Temperature plays \(C\); conductivity plays \(D\).

In the cellIn the machine
capillary side, \(C_L = 3.0\times10^{4}\) /µm³room face, 20 °C
cell side, \(C_R \approx 0\)outside face, 0 °C
gap \(L\) = 20 µmwall thickness \(L\) = 0.2 m
\(D\) = 2000 µm²/sbrick conductivity ≈ 0.7 W/(m·K) (typical)
\(J = 3.0\times10^{6}\) /(µm²·s)heat loss 0.7 × 20/0.2 = 70 W/m²
mid-gap: half of \(C_L\)mid-wall: 10 °C

Double the wall to 0.4 m and the loss halves to 35 W/m². Evolution shrinks \(L\) to deliver more; a builder thickens \(L\) to deliver less. It is the same lever, pulled the other way.

Where it breaks. Sun and wind change the outer face through the day, so a real wall seldom sits on its steady line for long. And heat is not counted in molecules, so the wall has none of the census noise of §1.1.

Module Tab 2 · Clouds Have Laws
2.2.1

Fick's second law — concentration changes where the profile curves

Minted in Week 2 §2.1 · Watch a cloud obey · open the module

eq. 2.2.1$$\frac{\partial C}{\partial t} \;=\; -\frac{\partial J}{\partial x} \;=\; D\,\frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial x^2} \qquad\text{(in 3D: } \partial C/\partial t = D\nabla^2 C\text{)}$$

Letters

  • \(C(x,t)\) — concentration · #/m³
  • \(t\) — time · s
  • \(J\) — flux, given by eq. 1.3.5 · #/(m²·s)
  • \(x\) — position · m
  • \(D\) — diffusion coefficient · m²/s (bench default 10 µm²/s)
  • \(\partial^2 C/\partial x^2\) — the curvature of the profile · #/m⁵
  • \(\nabla^2 C\) — the 3D curvature (the Laplacian) · #/m⁵

How it is used

§2.1 mints it from two Tab 1 ideas: molecules are conserved, so a bin gains only what its neighbours lose (\(\partial C/\partial t = -\partial J/\partial x\)), and \(J\) is Fick's first law. The pulse bench catches it first: a dropped spike softens into a plain, the cloud's variance climbs in a straight line of slope \(2D\) (the "D recovered" stat), and two pulses pass through each other and simply add, because the law is linear. Eq. 2.2.2 is its point-source solution, FRAP (eq. 2.2.3) runs on it, and its steady spherical form is eq. 2.3.1. §2.4 marks its limit: in crowded cytoplasm, where \(\langle r^2\rangle \propto t^{\alpha}\) with \(\alpha < 1\), it no longer holds.

Comes back: R1 §2.5 (fifteen minutes on, twelve hours off).

Biological examplethe middle of a fresh histamine cloud

Moments after a mast cell releases histamine, read three census bins 2 µm apart along a line through the cloud: 300, 600 and 300 /µm³ (0.5, 1.0 and 0.5 µM; illustrative). Take the cloud as varying along this line only, the pulse bench's 1D picture; a round cloud curves the same way along all three axes, so its middle falls three times faster. Is the middle bin rising or falling, and how fast?

  1. \(D\) = 330 µm²/s (histamine in tissue, Week 1); bin spacing \(\Delta x\) = 2 µm.
  2. Curvature: \((300 - 2\times600 + 300)/(2)^2 = -150\) /µm⁵.
  3. \(\partial C/\partial t = D \times\) curvature \(= 330 \times (-150) = -4.95\times10^{4}\) /(µm³·s).
  4. In molar units: \(4.95\times10^{4}/602\) ≈ 82 µM lost per second.
  5. Same answer by flux: out each wall, \(J = 330 \times (600 - 300)/2 = 4.95\times10^{4}\) /(µm²·s); two walls drain a 2-µm bin by \(2 \times 4.95\times10^{4}/2 = 4.95\times10^{4}\) /(µm³·s) ✓.
  6. A flank bin on a straight stretch, 600, 400, 200 /µm³: curvature 0, so \(\partial C/\partial t = 0\), even though \(J = 330 \times 200/2 = 3.3\times10^{4}\) /(µm²·s) flows through it.

What it means. At this pace the middle bin would empty in about 12 ms. It will not, because the curvature softens as the cloud widens, and the fall slows. The flank bin shows the law's real content: flux can pour through a bin without changing it. Only curvature changes concentration, and diffusion shaves it until nothing curves.

Mechanical analogya torch-heated steel bar

Heat a long, thin steel bar at one spot with a torch and walk away. Three thermocouples 1 cm apart read 80, 200 and 80 K above room temperature. Heat obeys eq. 2.2.1 with temperature in place of \(C\) and steel's thermal diffusivity in place of \(D\).

In the cellIn the machine
census bins 2 µm apartthermocouples 1 cm apart
\(C\) = 300, 600, 300 /µm³excess temperature 80, 200, 80 K
\(D\) = 330 µm²/ssteel, \(D\) ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s (typical)
curvature −150 /µm⁵curvature \((80 - 400 + 80)/(0.01)^2 = -2.4\times10^{6}\) K/m²
\(\partial C/\partial t = -4.95\times10^{4}\) /(µm³·s)middle cools at \(1.2\times10^{-5}\times2.4\times10^{6}\) ≈ 29 K/s
straight flank: no changethermocouples reading 200, 150, 100: no change

Where it breaks. The bar also sheds heat from its surface to the air, a loss eq. 2.2.1 leaves out (the cell's version is clearance, eq. 2.3.7). And temperature is smooth at every scale; the bar has no ±√N flicker.

2.2.2

The point-source Gaussian — a released cloud widens as √(2Dt) while its peak falls

Minted in Week 2 §2.2 · The Gaussian is the atom of diffusion · open the module

eq. 2.2.2$$C(x,t) = \frac{N}{\sqrt{4\pi D t}}\,e^{-x^2/4Dt} \qquad\text{(3D: } C(r,t) = \frac{N}{(4\pi D t)^{3/2}}\,e^{-r^2/4Dt}\text{)}$$

Letters

  • \(C(x,t)\), \(C(r,t)\) — concentration at distance \(x\) (1D) or \(r\) (3D) from the release point · #/m (1D), #/m³ (3D)
  • \(N\) — the number of molecules released at \(t = 0\) · #
  • \(D\) — diffusion coefficient · m²/s
  • \(t\) — time since release · s
  • \(x\), \(r\) — distance from the release point · m
  • width \(\sigma = \sqrt{2Dt}\) per axis — Week 1's probability radius · m

How it is used

§2.2 mints it as the diffusion equation's response to a point release (its Green's function). In the pulse bench's "field + theory" view, a red curve drawn from it with no fitting rides the histogram all the way down. Its width is Week 1's \(\sqrt{2Dt}\); its prefactor says the peak falls as \(t^{-1/2}\) in 1D and \(t^{-3/2}\) in 3D, because the same \(N\) spreads over more room. Linearity makes it the "atom" that every other solution is summed from. Tab 4's 566 box uses the 3D form for the quick estimate \(\dot n \approx 4\pi D a\,C(r,t)\).

Comes back: —

Biological exampleone mast cell's histamine, read at the itch nerve

A mast cell holds about 3 pg of histamine (§4.5). The module releases it over about 300 s; here, take the upper bound and let it all out at once. Does the puff reach the H1 threshold of about 10 nM at the nerve 120 µm away? At 1 mm?

  1. \(N = 3\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{g}/(111 \times 1.66\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g}) = 1.6\times10^{10}\) molecules.
  2. \(D\) = 330 µm²/s (tissue, Week 1); \(r\) = 120 µm.
  3. At a fixed \(r\) the 3D curve peaks where its time-derivative is zero: \(t = r^2/6D = 14{,}400/1{,}980 = 7.3\) s.
  4. Then \(4\pi D t = 3.0\times10^{4}\) µm², so \((4\pi D t)^{3/2} = 5.2\times10^{6}\) µm³.
  5. At that moment the exponent is always \(r^2/4Dt = 3/2\), and \(e^{-1.5} = 0.22\).
  6. \(C = (1.6\times10^{10}/5.2\times10^{6}) \times 0.22 = 6.9\times10^{2}\) /µm³ ≈ 1.15 µM.
  7. At \(r\) = 1 mm the peak comes at 505 s and reaches only 1.2 /µm³ ≈ 2.0 nM.

What it means. At the nerve the puff overshoots the threshold about 115-fold, within seconds. At 1 mm it never reaches threshold, even with no clearance at all, because the 3D peak falls as \(1/r^3\): 8.3 times the distance, about 580 times less. Spreading is dilution, and dilution alone already goes a long way toward keeping the itch local.

Mechanical analogya heat pulse along a steel wire

Touch a soldering iron to the middle of a long steel wire for an instant. The pulse of heat spreads both ways as the 1D Gaussian, with temperature in place of \(C\). It is the histamine puff with one dimension instead of three.

In the cellIn the machine
\(N\) molecules released at onceone pulse of heat
tissue, \(D\) = 330 µm²/ssteel, \(D\) ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s (typical)
width \(\sqrt{2Dt}\) ≈ 69 µm at 7.3 swidth \(\sqrt{2Dt}\) = 1.5 cm at 10 s
3D: peak falls as \(t^{-3/2}\)1D wire: peak falls as \(t^{-1/2}\)
molecules conservedheat conserved, if the wire is insulated

At 40 s the warm stretch is 3.1 cm wide and its peak has halved. In tissue the same fourfold wait cuts the peak eightfold: a wire dilutes slowly because it has only one direction to spread in.

Where it breaks. A bare wire loses heat to the air along its length, so the area under its curve shrinks; the molecules of eq. 2.2.2 are conserved until something clears them.

Featured in HW1 · Bench 2
2.2.3

The FRAP half-time — recovery scales as the spot's radius squared

Minted in Week 2 §2.3 · Filling the hole — Fick's second law with a stopwatch · open the module

eq. 2.2.3$$\tau_{1/2} \;=\; 0.224\,\frac{w^2}{D}$$

Letters

  • \(\tau_{1/2}\) — time for the bleached spot to win back half its lost brightness · s
  • \(w\) — radius of the bleached disk · m (bench default 3.0 µm)
  • \(D\) — diffusion coefficient of the fluorescent molecule · m²/s (bench default 10 µm²/s)
  • 0.224 — the exact prefactor for a sharp circular spot (Soumpasis 1983) · dimensionless

How it is used

§2.3 mints it for FRAP: the laser carves a hole in the visible census, and eq. 2.2.1 fills it. Dimensional analysis says the only time built from \(w\) and \(D\) is \(w^2/D\); Soumpasis's exact solution supplies the 0.224. The bleach bench measures it first: bleach at 1.5, 3 and 6 µm and the points fall on a slope-2 line on log–log axes; change \(D\) and the points slide while the slope stays 2. The worked example rehearses the HW1 move, exponent first: doubling \(w\) must give 4×, and only then \(w\) = 3 µm, \(\tau_{1/2}\) = 0.20 s gives \(D \approx 10.1\) µm²/s. §2.4 bounds it: if crowding makes \(\alpha \neq 1\), there is no single \(D\) to report.

Comes back: —

Biological examplesizing a FRAP spot for a GFP-sized protein

A lab bleaches a spot in a cell expressing a GFP-sized protein, about the size of Week 1's saliva protein (radius ≈ 2.4 nm). How fast will the hole fill, and what does the \(w^2\) test look like?

  1. Week 1's assembly line: \(k_BT/6\pi\eta a = 1.37\times10^{-10}\) m²/s = 137 µm²/s in water; ÷4 for a crowded interior gives \(D\) ≈ 34 µm²/s.
  2. Spot \(w\) = 2 µm: \(\tau_{1/2} = 0.224 \times 4/34 = 0.026\) s = 26 ms.
  3. Spot \(w\) = 4 µm: \(\tau_{1/2} = 0.224 \times 16/34 = 0.105\) s.
  4. Ratio 0.105/0.026 = 4: the \(w^2\) fingerprint of diffusion.
  5. Suppose the 4-µm spot actually reads 0.11 s. Then \(D = 0.224 \times 16/0.11 = 33\) µm²/s.

What it means. The hole fills in tens of milliseconds, faster than one frame of video at 30 frames per second, so the camera sets the smallest usable spot. Had the 4-µm spot recovered only twice as slowly as the 2-µm one, binding or flow would be running the recovery, and the number in step 5 would mean nothing.

Mechanical analogyrefilling a cold spot on a steel plate

Press a chilled metal puck onto a large, warm steel plate, lift it, and time how long the cold disk takes to win back half its lost heat. The cold spot is the bleach: the missing heat, like the missing brightness, is filled in by diffusion from the surroundings. With its faces insulated the plate is 2D, as the FRAP formula assumes.

In the cellIn the machine
bleached disk, \(w\) = 2 µmchilled disk, \(w\) = 1 cm
missing brightnessmissing heat
\(D\) ≈ 34 µm²/ssteel, \(D\) ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s (typical)
\(\tau_{1/2}\) = 26 ms\(\tau_{1/2} = 0.224 \times (0.01)^2/1.2\times10^{-5}\) = 1.9 s
doubled spot: 4× longerdoubled puck, \(w\) = 2 cm: 7.5 s, 4× longer

Where it breaks. Bare faces lose heat to the air, which adds a second clock that does not scale as \(w^2\). In a cell that role is played by binding, and the \(w^2\) test is how you catch it. And the plate has one kind of heat, while FRAP tracks two kinds of molecule, dark and bright, that are otherwise identical.

Module Tab 3 · The Meeting Problem
2.3.1

Steady spherical diffusion — the same current crosses every shell

Minted in Week 2 §3.3 · The derivation, line by line: eq. 2.3.1 → eq. 1.5.1 · open the module

eq. 2.3.1$$\nabla^2 C(r) = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{d}{dr}\!\left(r^2\,\frac{dC}{dr}\right) = 0$$

Letters

  • \(\nabla^2\) — the Laplacian, the 3D curvature of eq. 2.2.1 · 1/m²
  • \(C(r)\) — concentration at distance \(r\) from the sphere's centre · #/m³
  • \(r\) — radial distance · m
  • \(dC/dr\) — the radial gradient · #/m⁴
  • \(r^2\,dC/dr\) — the quantity the equation holds constant; times \(4\pi D\) it is the current through a shell · #/m²

How it is used

Step 1 of §3.3: with the halo steady and spherically symmetric, eq. 2.2.1 collapses to this. §3.1's absorber bench measured its consequences first (rate ∝ \(D\), rate ∝ \(a\), halo \(1 - a/r\)), and the Derive box there reads it as a molecule count: the current \(I = 4\pi r^2 J\) is the same through every shell. In 2D the same count gives a logarithm and no steady halo (§5.2). §4.3 re-boxes it as "eq. 2.3.1 again", with the capture probability \(u(r)\) as the unknown; that version yields eq. 2.4.1.

Comes back: —

Biological exampleoxygen into a respiring bacterium

A bacterium (\(a\) ≈ 0.5 µm) burns about 10⁶ O₂ molecules per second (typical; R1 uses the same value). In steady state that whole current crosses every shell around it. What flux and gradient does that demand at its surface, and 5 µm out?

  1. \(I = 10^{6}\) /s through every shell.
  2. At \(r\) = 0.5 µm: \(J = I/4\pi r^2 = 10^{6}/(4\pi \times 0.25) = 3.2\times10^{5}\) /(µm²·s).
  3. At \(r\) = 5 µm: \(J = 10^{6}/(4\pi \times 25) = 3.2\times10^{3}\) /(µm²·s), 100 times less.
  4. Gradient by Fick I with \(D\) = 2000 µm²/s: \(dC/dr = J/D\) = 159 /µm⁴ at the surface, 1.6 /µm⁴ at 5 µm.
  5. The bracket: \(r^2\,dC/dr = 0.25 \times 159 = 25 \times 1.59 = 40\) /µm² at both radii ✓. It equals \(I/4\pi D\).

What it means. All the steepness sits within a few radii of the cell; ten radii out, the gradient is a hundred times gentler. The shell count says so before \(C\) is even solved for.

Mechanical analogya buried drain in wet sand

Bury a spherical well screen, 5 cm in radius, deep in saturated sand and pump it at a steady 1 L/min. Water seeps toward it from every side. In steady state no shell of sand fills or drains, so the same 1 L/min crosses every shell. Darcy's law plays Fick's: the seepage speed is the sand's hydraulic conductivity times the slope of the water head.

In the cellIn the machine
bacterium, \(a\) = 0.5 µmscreen, \(a\) = 5 cm
O₂ current \(I = 10^{6}\) /spump rate 1 L/min = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s
\(C(r)\)water head (height of the water column)
\(D\) = 2000 µm²/ssand conductivity ≈ 10⁻⁴ m/s (typical clean sand)
\(J\) at \(a\) and \(10a\): 3.2 × 10⁵ and 3.2 × 10³ /(µm²·s)seepage at 5 and 50 cm: 0.53 mm/s and 5.3 µm/s

The head slope is 5.3 m per metre at the screen and 0.053 at 50 cm; times \(r^2\), both give the same number.

Where it breaks. Water on a steep slope can drag sand into the screen and erode the bed, so the medium changes; oxygen's gradient never rearranges the fluid around the bacterium.

2.3.2

The general solution — a constant plus a 1/r

Minted in Week 2 §3.3 · The derivation, line by line: eq. 2.3.1 → eq. 1.5.1 · open the module

eq. 2.3.2$$C(r) = c_1 + \frac{c_2}{r}$$

Letters

  • \(C(r)\) — concentration at radius \(r\) · #/m³
  • \(c_1\) — the constant term, the level the profile approaches far away · #/m³
  • \(c_2\) — the strength of the \(1/r\) term · #/m² (concentration × length)
  • \(r\) — distance from the centre · m

How it is used

Step 2 of §3.3: integrate eq. 2.3.1 twice and two constants appear; the \(1/r\) is gravity's and Coulomb's shape, for the same reason. Eq. 2.3.3 spends the constants on the boundaries. §3.1's honesty line uses it with a finite rim: the absorber bench resupplies walkers at \(R\) = 5 µm, so its prediction carries a factor \(1/(1 - a/R)\) ≈ 1.16. §4.3 reuses this general solution for the capture probability.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea receptor patch fed from a nearby rim

The absorber bench's geometry is a fair cartoon of a hungry receptor patch (\(a\) = 0.7 µm) that the rest of the cell tops up from a rim at \(R\) = 5 µm. Let the rim hold ligand at 6.0 /µm³ (10 nM, illustrative) and let the patch eat on contact. Spend the two constants on the two surfaces.

  1. Patch surface: \(C(0.7) = 0\), so \(c_1 + c_2/0.7 = 0\).
  2. Rim: \(C(5) = 6.0\), so \(c_1 + c_2/5 = 6.0\).
  3. Subtract: \(c_2\,(1/5 - 1/0.7) = 6.0\), so \(c_2 = 6.0/(-1.229) = -4.9\) /µm².
  4. Then \(c_1 = -c_2/0.7 = 7.0\) /µm³, which is \(6.0/(1 - 0.7/5) = 1.16 \times 6.0\).
  5. At \(r\) = 1.4 µm (two radii): \(C = 7.0 - 4.9/1.4 = 3.5\) /µm³.
  6. An infinite sea at 6.0 /µm³ would give \(6.0\,(1 - 0.5) = 3.0\) /µm³ there.

What it means. A rim only seven radii out already behaves almost like an infinite sea; the whole profile, and the catch, is 16% higher. Two surfaces fix two numbers, and that is all the problem needs.

Mechanical analogythe insulation around a liquid-nitrogen tank

A spherical tank of liquid nitrogen, 0.5 m in radius and held at −196 °C, sits inside a foam shell whose outer skin, at 1.0 m, is at room temperature, 20 °C. In steady state the temperature in the foam obeys eq. 2.3.1, so it is \(c_1 + c_2/r\). The cold tank plays the hungry patch; the warm skin plays the rim.

In the cellIn the machine
patch, \(a\) = 0.7 µm, \(C\) = 0tank wall, 0.5 m, −196 °C
rim, \(R\) = 5 µm, 6.0 /µm³outer skin, 1.0 m, 20 °C
\(C(r)\)temperature in the foam
\(c_1\) = 7.0 /µm³\(c_1\) = 236 °C
\(c_2\) = −4.9 /µm²\(c_2\) = −216 °C·m

From the two surfaces: \(c_2 = 216/(1/1.0 - 1/0.5) = -216\) °C·m and \(c_1 = -196 + 432 = 236\) °C. At 0.75 m the foam is at \(236 - 288 = -52\) °C, not the straight-line −88 °C: the \(1/r\) profile packs its steep part against the cold surface, as the halo does against the patch.

Where it breaks. Foam conducts differently at −196 °C than at 20 °C, while the cell's \(D\) is the same everywhere in the halo. And this thick shell makes \(c_1\) a fictitious "temperature at infinity" that no point in the foam reaches.

2.3.3

The depletion halo — an absorber hollows out its neighbourhood

Minted in Week 2 §3.3 · The derivation, line by line: eq. 2.3.1 → eq. 1.5.1 · open the module

eq. 2.3.3$$C(r) = C_\infty\left(1 - \frac{a_{rel}}{r}\right)$$

Letters

  • \(C(r)\) — steady concentration at distance \(r\) · #/m³
  • \(C_\infty\) — the concentration far away, the undisturbed sea · #/m³
  • \(a_{rel}\) — the contact distance, \(a_1 + a_2\) (§3.2) · m
  • \(r\) — centre-to-centre distance · m

How it is used

Step 3 of §3.3: the far sea sets \(c_1 = C_\infty\), and "reacts on contact" sets \(C(a_{rel}) = 0\), so \(c_2 = -C_\infty a_{rel}\). This is the halo the absorber bench of §3.1 measured: the census hugs \(1 - a/r\), half-depleted at \(2a\) and 90% recovered only at \(10a\). The module flags "reacts on contact" as an idealization with an expiration date; Tab 5 breaks it as the receptor fills. Eq. 2.3.4 differentiates it, and in Tab 4 its \(1/r\) shape, wearing eq. 2.3.7's exponential screen, gives the histamine field at the nerve.

Comes back: —

Biological exampleone mast cell shadows its neighbour

A mast cell (\(a\) = 5 µm) eats allergen on contact from a steady background \(C_\infty\). A second mast cell sits 30 µm away, centre to centre. How much does the first cell's halo take from the second's neighbourhood?

  1. Contact distance: \(a_{rel}\) = 5 µm + 2.4 nm (the allergen's radius, Week 1) ≈ 5.0 µm.
  2. At \(r\) = 10 µm: \(C/C_\infty = 1 - 5/10 = 0.50\).
  3. At \(r\) = 30 µm: \(C/C_\infty = 1 - 5/30 = 0.83\).
  4. At \(r\) = 50 µm: \(C/C_\infty = 1 - 5/50 = 0.90\).
  5. With \(C_\infty\) = 10 nM (illustrative), the neighbour sits in 8.3 nM.

What it means. The neighbour loses a sixth of its supply to the first cell's halo. The halo has no edge, only a \(1/r\) tail, so cells within a few radii of each other compete for the same molecules, while cells ten radii apart barely notice each other.

Mechanical analogytwo drains in one aquifer

Return to the buried drain of 2.3.1, now 0.1 m in radius and pumped hard enough to hold the screen at zero head. Far away the water stands 2 m high. The steady head around the drain is then 2 m × \((1 - a/r)\): a drawdown halo. Well engineers call the effect on a neighbour "well interference".

In the cellIn the machine
mast cell, \(a\) = 5 µmdrain screen, \(a\) = 0.1 m
\(C(a) = 0\): eats on contacthead held at zero at the screen
far sea, \(C_\infty\)far water head, 2 m
at \(2a\): half of \(C_\infty\)at 0.2 m: 1.0 m of head
neighbour at \(6a\): 0.83 \(C_\infty\)second drain at 0.6 m: 1.67 m of head

Where it breaks. A real aquifer has a floor and a roof, so flow toward a well is closer to two-dimensional. Then the drawdown is a logarithm that keeps spreading, with no steady halo, which is the module's own warning about receptors on 2D membranes (§5.2).

2.3.4

Flux around the absorber — inward traffic thins as 1/r²

Minted in Week 2 §3.3 · The derivation, line by line: eq. 2.3.1 → eq. 1.5.1 · open the module

eq. 2.3.4$$J(r) = -D_{rel}\,\frac{dC}{dr} = -D_{rel}\,C_\infty\,\frac{a_{rel}}{r^2}$$

Letters

  • \(J(r)\) — radial flux at distance \(r\); negative means inward · #/(m²·s)
  • \(D_{rel}\) — relative diffusion coefficient, \(D_1 + D_2\) (§3.2) · m²/s
  • \(dC/dr\) — the halo's gradient · #/m⁴
  • \(C_\infty\) — far concentration · #/m³
  • \(a_{rel}\) — contact distance · m
  • \(r\) — distance from the centre · m

How it is used

Step 4 of §3.3: Fick's first law, the law that ran the tollbooth, applied to the gradient of eq. 2.3.3. The flux falls as \(1/r^2\), so the current \(4\pi r^2 J\) has the same size, \(4\pi D_{rel} a_{rel} C_\infty\), through every shell: the number the absorber bench's stats panel calls "prediction". Eq. 2.3.5 evaluates it at contact.

Comes back: —

Biological exampleallergen traffic toward a mast cell

The same mast cell (\(a\) = 5 µm, effectively still) sits in steady allergen at \(C_\infty\) = 6.0 /µm³ (10 nM, illustrative), with \(D\) = 10 µm²/s (Tab 4). How heavy is the inward traffic near the cell and far from it?

  1. \(D_{rel} = 10 + 0 = 10\) µm²/s.
  2. \(D_{rel}C_\infty a_{rel} = 10 \times 6.0 \times 5 = 300\) /s.
  3. At \(r\) = 5 µm (contact): \(J = -300/25 = -12\) /(µm²·s).
  4. At 10 µm: −3.0 /(µm²·s). At 30 µm: −0.33 /(µm²·s).
  5. Current through any shell: \(4\pi \times 300 = 3.8\times10^{3}\) /s, inward.

What it means. Each µm² of the cell's surface is hit 12 times a second; at the neighbour's distance the traffic is 36 times thinner. But the total crossing every shell is the same 3800 per second, and that total is what the cell collects.

Mechanical analogya vacuum nozzle in open air

A vacuum nozzle held away from any surface draws air from every direction. The same volume per second must cross every sphere around it, so the inward air speed falls as \(1/r^2\). That is why a vacuum has to nearly touch the crumb. Treat the nozzle as a sphere 5 cm in radius.

In the cellIn the machine
mast cell surfacenozzle mouth
current through a shell, 3800 /sair drawn, ≈ 0.03 m³/s (typical household vacuum)
\(J(r) \propto 1/r^2\)inward air speed ∝ \(1/r^2\)
−12 /(µm²·s) at contact0.03/(4π × 0.05²) ≈ 0.95 m/s at 5 cm
36 times thinner at six radii2.7 cm/s at 30 cm

Where it breaks. Air is pushed by pressure and carries momentum; its flow is advection, not diffusion. Only the bookkeeping half of eq. 2.3.4 carries over (the same current through every shell), and nothing in the nozzle plays \(D\). Close to a real nozzle the flow is not spherical either.

2.3.5

Flux at contact — small targets are fed hardest per area

Minted in Week 2 §3.3 · The derivation, line by line: eq. 2.3.1 → eq. 1.5.1 · open the module

eq. 2.3.5$$J(a_{rel}) = -\,\frac{D_{rel}\,C_\infty}{a_{rel}}$$

Letters

  • \(J(a_{rel})\) — flux at the contact surface · #/(m²·s)
  • \(D_{rel}\) — relative diffusion coefficient · m²/s
  • \(C_\infty\) — far concentration · #/m³
  • \(a_{rel}\) — contact distance · m

How it is used

Step 5 of §3.3: set \(r = a_{rel}\) in eq. 2.3.4. The flux per area at contact goes as \(1/a_{rel}\); when eq. 2.3.6 multiplies by the area \(4\pi a_{rel}^2\), one power of \(a\) survives. That is the module's answer to §3.1's measured "rate ∝ \(a\), not \(a^2\)": supply, not surface.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea receptor pocket against the whole cell

The same allergen sea (\(D\) = 10 µm²/s, \(C_\infty\) = 6.0 /µm³). Compare the flux at contact for the whole mast cell (\(a\) = 5 µm) with that for one binding pocket taken on its own (\(a\) ≈ 1 nm = 10⁻³ µm, §4.3).

  1. Cell: \(J = -D C_\infty/a = -10 \times 6.0/5 = -12\) /(µm²·s).
  2. Pocket: \(J = -10 \times 6.0/10^{-3} = -6.0\times10^{4}\) /(µm²·s).
  3. Ratio: 5000, which is 5 µm/1 nm.
  4. Totals, × \(4\pi a^2\): cell \(3.8\times10^{3}\) /s; pocket 0.75 /s. Ratio 5000 the other way.

What it means. Per µm², the pocket is fed 5000 times harder than the cell, yet it catches 5000 times less in total. The area brings \(a^2\), the flux brings \(1/a\), and the catch keeps one power of \(a\). §4.3 finds the same factor of 5000 in capture odds.

Mechanical analogywhy sprays use small drops

A water drop evaporating in still, dry air is the hungry sphere run backwards. Its surface holds saturated vapour, the far air holds none, and vapour diffuses outward. The flux at the surface is \(D\) times the vapour difference, divided by the radius. That is why spray nozzles break liquid into tiny drops.

In the cellIn the machine
far allergen, \(C_\infty\) = 6.0 /µm³vapour difference ≈ 0.017 kg/m³ (saturated at 20 °C, typical)
\(D\) = 10 µm²/swater vapour in air, \(D\) ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s (typical)
whole cell, \(a\) = 5 µm: 12 /(µm²·s)raindrop, \(a\) = 1 mm: 4.3 × 10⁻⁴ kg/(m²·s)
pocket, \(a\) = 1 nm: 6.0 × 10⁴ /(µm²·s)spray drop, \(a\) = 10 µm: 0.043 kg/(m²·s)
ratio 5000ratio 100

The raindrop line is \(2.5\times10^{-5} \times 0.017/10^{-3}\). Break a big drop into small ones and every square millimetre of liquid surface evaporates a hundred times faster.

Where it breaks. Evaporation cools the drop, which lowers its surface vapour, and the drop shrinks as it goes, so the steady formula holds only for a moment. A moving spray also has its vapour stripped away by flow, a Péclet effect (eq. 2.3.8).

2.3.6

Rate constant from the flux — the total catch per unit concentration is 4πDa

Minted in Week 2 §3.3 · The derivation, line by line: eq. 2.3.1 → eq. 1.5.1 · open the module

eq. 2.3.6$$k_s = \frac{J\,A}{C_\infty} = \frac{J}{C_\infty}\,4\pi a_{rel}^2 = -\,4\pi D_{rel}\,a_{rel}$$

Letters

  • \(k_s\) — encounter rate constant: arrivals per second per unit far concentration · m³/s
  • \(J\) — flux at contact (eq. 2.3.5) · #/(m²·s)
  • \(A = 4\pi a_{rel}^2\) — area of the contact sphere · m²
  • \(C_\infty\) — far concentration · #/m³
  • \(D_{rel}\), \(a_{rel}\) — relative diffusion coefficient and contact distance · m²/s, m

How it is used

Step 6 of §3.3 defines the rate as the total flow over the target per unit ambient concentration, \(k_s = JA/C_\infty\); the minus sign only records that the flux points inward. §3.1 measured it first: the absorber bench's captures double when \(D\) doubles and when \(a\) doubles. With §3.2's camera trick (the pair bench reads the separation's MSD slope as \(D_1 + D_2\); contact is at \(a_1 + a_2\)), it becomes eq. 1.5.1.

Comes back: —

Biological examplehow often a mast cell meets allergen

The mast cell again (\(a\) = 5 µm, still) in allergen with \(D\) = 10 µm²/s. What is its rate constant, and what does it mean at 1 nM?

  1. \(D_{rel} = 10 + 0 = 10\) µm²/s; \(a_{rel}\) = 5 µm + 2.4 nm ≈ 5.0 µm.
  2. Sign check with 2.3.5's numbers: \(JA/C_\infty = (-12)(4\pi \times 25)/6.0 = -628\) µm³/s.
  3. Magnitude: \(k_s = 4\pi D_{rel} a_{rel} = 4\pi \times 10 \times 5 = 628\) µm³/s.
  4. In chemistry's units: \(628 \times 6.022\times10^{8} = 3.8\times10^{11}\) M⁻¹s⁻¹.
  5. At 1 nM (0.6022 /µm³): \(628 \times 0.6022 = 378\) arrivals per second.

What it means. A whole cell sits about a hundredfold above the 3.4 × 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹ ceiling the module computes for an enzyme. No law is broken: \(k_s\) grows with \(a\), and a mast cell is more than a thousand times wider than an enzyme–substrate pair. Even at 1 nM, nearly 400 allergen molecules reach it every second.

Mechanical analogya drain's specific capacity

Well engineers rate a drain by its specific capacity: the flow it yields per metre of drawdown. That is a rate constant, flow per unit driving head, just as \(k_s\) is arrivals per second per unit concentration. For the spherical screen of 2.3.3 in uniform sand, it is \(4\pi\) × conductivity × radius.

In the cellIn the machine
\(k_s\) = 628 µm³/sspecific capacity, m³/s per metre of head
\(D_{rel}\) = 10 µm²/ssand conductivity ≈ 10⁻⁴ m/s (typical)
\(a_{rel}\) = 5 µmscreen radius 0.1 m
rate = \(k_s C_\infty\)yield = specific capacity × drawdown
∝ \(a\), not \(a^2\)double the screen, double the yield, not four times

Run it: \(4\pi \times 10^{-4} \times 0.1 = 1.26\times10^{-4}\) m³/s per metre, about 7.5 L/min per metre of drawdown. At the 2-m drawdown of 2.3.3 the drain yields 0.25 L/s.

Where it breaks. The drain has no partner to wander. In the cell, \(D_{rel}\) adds two walkers' \(D\)s; the sand's conductivity has nothing to add to. A mast cell barely moves either, which is why \(D_{rel} \approx D\) here.

2.3.7

Reaction–diffusion length — clearance sets the radius of "here"

Minted in Week 2 §3.4 · Expiration dates: what reactions and flow do to a cloud · open the module

eq. 2.3.7$$\lambda = \sqrt{D\,\tau} \qquad\Big(\text{steady point source with clearance: } C(r) \propto \tfrac{1}{r}\,e^{-r/\lambda}\Big)$$

Letters

  • \(\lambda\) — reaction–diffusion length · m
  • \(D\) — diffusion coefficient · m²/s (bench default 300 µm²/s)
  • \(\tau\) — mean lifetime before clearance · s (bench default 60 s)
  • \(C(r)\) — steady concentration around a continuous point source · #/m³
  • \(r\) — distance from the source · m

How it is used

§3.4 mints it as the first of two expiration dates: a molecule cleared with lifetime \(\tau\) diffuses only while it lasts, so a steady source's \(1/r\) tail picks up an exponential guillotine. The "Source, clearance, flow" bench shows it: with clearance the profile freezes with an edge at \(\lambda\), and halving \(\tau\) pulls the edge in as \(\sqrt\tau\) (the measured-λ stat). Tab 4 spends it twice: \(\lambda\) = 42 µm shrinks the alarm horizon from 50 m to 0.5 mm (through eq. 2.4.4), and \(\lambda\) ≈ 200 µm keeps histamine's itch local. The Q6 check-yourself uses it for glutamate reuptake: a \(\lambda\) far below 2 µm keeps a synapse private.

Comes back: C1 §2.1 (the halo of a cleared signal; again on each clock); R2 §1.2 (the clearance length); P1 §3.3 (the calcium ion's reach).

Biological examplehow far the itch reaches

A degranulating mast cell releases histamine at about \(S = 5\times10^{7}\) per second for a few minutes (§4.5). Histamine is cleared with \(\tau\) = 120 s and diffuses at \(D\) = 330 µm²/s. Where does the steady field fall below the H1 threshold of about 10 nM, that is, 6.0 /µm³?

  1. \(\lambda = \sqrt{D\tau} = \sqrt{330 \times 120} = 199\) µm ≈ 0.2 mm.
  2. The field (the module's §4.5 form): \(C(r) = \frac{S}{4\pi D r}\,e^{-r/\lambda}\).
  3. At \(r\) = 500 µm without clearance: \(5\times10^{7}/(4\pi \times 330 \times 500) = 24\) /µm³ ≈ 40 nM.
  4. With clearance: \(\times\,e^{-500/199} = \times\,0.081\), giving 1.95 /µm³ ≈ 3.2 nM.
  5. Threshold radius with clearance (solved numerically): about 350 µm.
  6. Without clearance the steady \(1/r\) tail would stay above 10 nM out to \(S/(4\pi D \times 6.0)\) ≈ 2 mm.

What it means. Clearance shrinks the itchy zone from millimetres to about 0.35 mm, under two \(\lambda\). The \(1/r\) geometry loses signal slowly; the exponential does the work within a few multiples of \(\lambda\). (A no-clearance field 2 mm out would take longer to build than the release lasts, so step 6 is an upper bound.)

Mechanical analogya soldering iron on a fan-cooled steel sheet

Hold a soldering iron on a thin steel sheet while a fan blows across both faces. Heat spreads through the steel, as histamine spreads through tissue, and the moving air carries it off, as enzymes and lymph clear histamine. After a minute or so the hot zone stops growing. Its size is set by \(\lambda = \sqrt{D\tau}\).

In the cellIn the machine
mast cell releasing \(S\) per secondsoldering iron feeding heat steadily
tissue, \(D\) = 330 µm²/ssteel, \(D\) ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s (typical)
clearance lifetime \(\tau\) = 120 scooling lifetime of a patch of 2-mm sheet in a fan's breeze, \(\tau\) ≈ 60 s (typical)
\(\lambda\) ≈ 0.2 mm\(\lambda\) ≈ 2.7 cm
itchy zone ≈ 0.35 mmhot zone a few cm across

Run it: \(\sqrt{1.2\times10^{-5} \times 60} = 0.027\) m. A stronger fan that halves \(\tau\) to 30 s pulls the edge in to 1.9 cm, as \(\sqrt\tau\).

Where it breaks. The sheet is 2D, so the profile around the iron is a flatter cousin of \((1/r)\,e^{-r/\lambda}\), though \(\lambda\) is the same. And air cooling is only roughly a fixed lifetime; a very hot spot sheds heat faster than first-order.

2.3.8

The Péclet number — flow beats diffusion when Lv/D ≫ 1

Minted in Week 2 §3.4 · Expiration dates: what reactions and flow do to a cloud · open the module

eq. 2.3.8$$\mathrm{Pe} = \frac{L\,v}{D} \qquad \mathrm{Pe}\ll1:\ \text{diffusion wins} \quad\big|\quad \mathrm{Pe}\gg1:\ \text{flow wins}$$

Letters

  • \(\mathrm{Pe}\) — Péclet number, advective over diffusive transport · dimensionless
  • \(L\) — the distance that matters · m
  • \(v\) — flow speed of the medium · m/s (bench default 0 µm/s)
  • \(D\) — diffusion coefficient · m²/s

How it is used

§3.4 mints it as the second expiration date: advection carries a molecule \(vt\) while diffusion covers \(\sqrt{2Dt}\), and over a distance \(L\) the ratio of the two rates is Pe. The same bench's "clearance + flow" view smears the halo downstream and shows the Pe readout crossing 1. The module's punchline is that Pe grows with \(L\): at cell scale (10 µm, µm/s) Pe ≪ 1, while in a capillary (\(L\) ~ 500 µm, \(v\) ~ 500 µm/s, \(D\) ~ 500 µm²/s) Pe ≈ 500. §4.5 uses it for histamine that reaches a capillary (Pe ≈ 760), and HW1's map problem grades it.

Comes back: R1 §3.2 (the mucus escalator, and what happens when it stops).

Biological examplea neutrophil's chemokine, in tissue and in blood

A neutrophil follows a chemokine gradient through tissue at about 0.3 µm/s (18 µm/min, typical). Does its own crawling, or the seep of interstitial fluid, smear the cloud it reads? And what happens to the same chemokine in a venule's blood?

  1. Chemokine \(D\): a small protein; use \(D\) ≈ 34 µm²/s, Week 1's saliva-sized protein in tissue, as a cautious stand-in.
  2. Crawling, over one cell length: \(L\) = 10 µm, \(v\) = 0.3 µm/s, so \(\mathrm{Pe} = 10 \times 0.3/34 = 0.088\).
  3. Interstitial seep, \(v\) ≈ 1 µm/s (typical upper value): \(\mathrm{Pe} = 10 \times 1/34 = 0.29\).
  4. Venule blood, \(v\) ≈ 1 mm/s (typical), over \(L\) = 100 µm of vessel: \(\mathrm{Pe} = 100 \times 1000/34 = 2.9\times10^{3}\).

What it means. In tissue Pe is below 1: diffusion keeps the gradient smooth faster than the cell or the fluid can smear it, so the cell reads a clean signal. In blood Pe is in the thousands: chemokine released into the stream is carried off long before it can diffuse across. A soluble gradient only makes sense once the cell is out in the tissue.

Mechanical analogythe hot-water pipe

Open a hot tap at the end of 10 m of pipe from the heater. Heat can reach you by flow, or by conduction along still water. Pe decides which, with water's thermal diffusivity in place of \(D\).

In the cellIn the machine
chemokineheat
blood in a venule, \(v\) ≈ 1 mm/shot water, \(v\) ≈ 1 m/s
\(L\) = 100 µm of vessel\(L\) = 10 m of pipe
\(D\) = 34 µm²/swater's thermal diffusivity ≈ 1.4 × 10⁻⁷ m²/s (typical)
Pe ≈ 2.9 × 10³Pe = 10 × 1/(1.4 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 7 × 10⁷
tissue around the cell, Pe below 1still water in a cup: conduction only

By flow the hot water arrives in \(L/v\) = 10 s. By conduction alone the 10 m would take \(L^2/2D\) ≈ 3.6 × 10⁸ s, about 11 years (Week 1's eq. 1.2.8). That is why a house has plumbing, and why you have a heart.

Where it breaks. Blood in a venule is laminar, so its sideways mixing really is molecular. Pipe flow at 1 m/s is turbulent, and its eddies mix heat far faster than conduction does, which only widens the flow's win.

Module Tab 4 · The First Alarm
2.4.1

Capture probability — a molecule's odds of ever arriving are a/r

Minted in Week 2 §4.3 · Why it is \(a/r\) — and why \(D\) is nowhere in it · open the module

eq. 2.4.1$$\boxed{\;P_\infty = \frac{a}{r}\;}\qquad\text{(probability of ever being captured; exact, unbounded 3D)}$$

Letters

  • \(P_\infty\) — probability that a molecule released at \(r\) is ever captured · dimensionless
  • \(a\) — radius of the absorbing cell · m (bench default 5.0 µm)
  • \(r\) — release distance from the cell's centre · m (bench default 30 µm)

How it is used

§4.3 mints it to explain the "One bolus, one cell" bench. A cohort of 300 molecules is released, and the captured fraction climbs, then flattens onto a ceiling near 0.167 at \(a\) = 5 µm, \(r\) = 30 µm; moving the cell to 60 µm halves it, and dragging \(D\) slides the curve sideways without moving the ceiling. The derivation re-boxes eq. 2.3.1 for the capture probability \(u(r)\), with fates as the boundary conditions: \(u(a) = 1\), \(u(\infty) = 0\). Pólya's theorem is why the answer is below 1: a 3D random walk can escape forever. The worked example compares the whole cell with one of its receptor pockets (a factor of 5000), and eqs. 2.4.2, 2.4.4 and 2.4.5 carry it as their prefactor.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea neutrophil and a bacterium's peptide

A bacterium sheds a formyl peptide, a chemoattractant, 40 µm from the centre of a neutrophil (\(a\) ≈ 4 µm, typical, for a cell about 8 µm across). Suppose the neutrophil catches every molecule that touches it. What are the odds that a given molecule ever reaches it?

  1. \(a\) = 4 µm, \(r\) = 40 µm.
  2. \(P_\infty = a/r = 4/40 = 0.10\).
  3. A source ten times farther, \(r\) = 400 µm: \(P_\infty = 0.010\).
  4. One receptor pocket on its own (\(a\) ≈ 1 nm = 10⁻³ µm) at 40 µm: \(P_\infty = 2.5\times10^{-5}\).
  5. \(D\) is absent: a fast peptide and a slow protein released from the same spot have the same odds.

What it means. Nine molecules in ten wander off forever, from only ten radii out. But the odds fall as \(1/r\), not \(1/r^2\): a source ten times farther is ten times fainter, not a hundred times.

Mechanical analogya charged metal dome

The capture odds \(u(r)\) solve Laplace's equation with \(u = 1\) on the sphere and \(u = 0\) far away. A charged metal sphere in open air, like a Van de Graaff generator's dome, poses the same problem for voltage: full voltage on the dome, zero at a distant ground. So the voltage at distance \(r\) is the dome's voltage times \(a/r\).

In the cellIn the machine
capture odds \(u(r)\)voltage as a fraction of the dome's
\(u(a) = 1\): touching means caughtdome surface at full voltage
\(u(\infty) = 0\)distant ground
neutrophil, \(a\) = 4 µm, source at 40 µmdome, \(a\) = 0.2 m, probe at 2 m
\(P_\infty\) = 0.10100 kV × 0.2/2 = 10 kV, a fraction of 0.10
no \(D\) in the answerno property of the air in the answer

At 20 m the probe reads 1 kV, 0.01 of the dome, just as the source at 400 µm gives the neutrophil 0.01.

Where it breaks. The voltage is one steady number at each point; a molecule either arrives or does not, and only the average over many releases equals \(a/r\). Walls and floors near the dome distort its field, much as a second cell nearby would change the odds.

2.4.2

Capture by time t — the same odds, with a diffusion clock in front

Minted in Week 2 §4.3 · Why it is \(a/r\) — and why \(D\) is nowhere in it · open the module

eq. 2.4.2$$P(t) = \frac{a}{r}\,\mathrm{erfc}\!\left(\frac{r-a}{\sqrt{4Dt}}\right)$$

Letters

  • \(P(t)\) — probability of having been captured by time \(t\) · dimensionless
  • \(a\), \(r\) — cell radius and release distance · m
  • \(r - a\) — the gap to cross, from the release point to the cell's surface · m
  • \(D\) — diffusion coefficient · m²/s (bench default 10 µm²/s)
  • \(t\) — time since release · s
  • \(\mathrm{erfc}\) — the complementary error function: 1 at zero argument, falling toward 0 · dimensionless

How it is used

§4.3 Step 3 solves the same problem with the time-dependent equation. The prefactor is eq. 2.4.1, the fraction that ever arrives; the erfc is the fraction of those that have arrived yet, with the gap measured in diffusion lengths \(\sqrt{4Dt}\). It is the captured-fraction curve of the "One bolus, one cell" bench. The worked "\(D\) stress test" inverts it for the half-arrival time, \(t_{1/2} \approx 1.10\,(r-a)^2/D\): 69 s at \(D\) = 10 µm²/s and 17 s at 40, with \(P_\infty\) unchanged. \(D\) sets when; geometry sets whether. Eq. 2.4.3 differentiates it, and eq. 2.4.5 scales it by the bolus.

Comes back: —

Biological examplewhen the neutrophil's peptide arrives

The same neutrophil and source as in 2.4.1 (\(a\) = 4 µm, \(r\) = 40 µm, \(P_\infty\) = 0.10). A small peptide (radius ≈ 0.5 nm, typical) gets its \(D\) from Week 1's assembly line. How much of the eventual catch is in by 1 s, and by 10 s?

  1. In water, with the peptide's radius: \(4.28\times10^{-21}/(6\pi \times 6.9\times10^{-4} \times 5\times10^{-10}) = 6.6\times10^{-10}\) m²/s; ÷4 in tissue gives \(D\) ≈ 165 µm²/s.
  2. Gap: \(r - a\) = 36 µm.
  3. At 1 s: \(\sqrt{4Dt}\) = 25.7 µm, so \(P = 0.10 \times \mathrm{erfc}(1.40) = 0.10 \times 0.048 = 0.0048\).
  4. At 10 s: \(\sqrt{4Dt}\) = 81.2 µm, so \(P = 0.10 \times \mathrm{erfc}(0.44) = 0.10 \times 0.53 = 0.053\).
  5. Half the eventual catch: \(t_{1/2} = 1.10 \times 36^2/165 = 8.6\) s.
  6. A saliva-sized protein (\(D\) ≈ 34 µm²/s, Week 1): \(t_{1/2}\) = 42 s, with the same final 0.10.

What it means. Within ten seconds the neutrophil has half of all it will ever get from one release. A slower molecule makes it wait five times longer for the same final share. Speed buys latency, not sensitivity.

Mechanical analogya heater bead cast in aluminium

Cast a small spherical heater, 1 cm in radius, into a large aluminium block. Switch it on at a fixed surface temperature and watch a thermometer 6 cm from its centre. The thermometer's rise, as a share of the heater's, is exactly \((a/r)\,\mathrm{erfc}\big((r-a)/\sqrt{4Dt}\big)\): the same boundary problem as the capture odds, with "hot" in place of "caught".

In the cellIn the machine
neutrophil, \(a\) = 4 µmheater bead, \(a\) = 1 cm
release point, \(r\) = 40 µmthermometer, \(r\) = 6 cm
\(P(t)\), the share caught by \(t\)the thermometer's rise as a share of the heater's
\(P_\infty = a/r\) = 0.10final share \(a/r\) = 1/6
\(D\) = 165 µm²/saluminium, \(D\) ≈ 8 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s (typical)
\(t_{1/2}\) = 8.6 s\(t_{1/2} = 1.10 \times (0.05)^2/8\times10^{-5}\) ≈ 34 s

After 10 s the thermometer shows \((1/6)\,\mathrm{erfc}(0.88)\) ≈ 0.035 of the heater's rise. A steel block (\(D\) ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s) would take 6.7 times longer to get halfway, and would end at the same 1/6.

Where it breaks. The block is finite, so once heat reaches its edges the reading drifts away from \(a/r\). And a real heater cannot hold its surface at the set temperature from the very first instant.

2.4.3

The encounter rate — arrivals per second rise, peak, and trail off

Minted in Week 2 §4.3 · Why it is \(a/r\) — and why \(D\) is nowhere in it · open the module

eq. 2.4.3$$\dot n(t) = N_0\,\frac{dP}{dt} = N_0\,\frac{a}{r}\cdot\frac{r-a}{\sqrt{4\pi D t^{3}}}\; e^{-(r-a)^{2}/4Dt}$$

Letters

  • \(\dot n(t)\) — arrivals per second at the cell · #/s
  • \(N_0\) — number of molecules in the bolus · # (module: 10¹⁰)
  • \(dP/dt\) — the rate of change of eq. 2.4.2 · 1/s
  • \(a\), \(r\), \(D\), \(t\) — as in eq. 2.4.2

How it is used

§4.3 Step 4 differentiates eq. 2.4.2 and multiplies by the bolus; it is the capstone's answer to "what encounter rate do we expect for a given time". The bench's bolus view plots it: zero at first, a peak at \(t = (r-a)^2/6D\) (10.4 s at the defaults), then a \(t^{-3/2}\) decay; the "with clearance" view erases the tail. The check-yourself moves the cell to 60 µm and the peak to 50.4 s, a factor of 4.84, not 4. The 566 box compares it with the quick estimate \(4\pi D a\,C(r,t)\) from eq. 2.2.2, which peaks later (15 s) but has the same time integral, \(N_0 a/r\).

Comes back: —

Biological examplerush hour at the mast cell

The bite at the module's defaults: \(N_0 = 10^{10}\) allergen molecules, \(a\) = 5 µm, \(r\) = 30 µm, \(D\) = 10 µm²/s. When is the traffic heaviest, how heavy is it, and how much of the total has arrived by then?

  1. Peak time: \(t = (r-a)^2/6D = 625/60 = 10.4\) s.
  2. There, \(\sqrt{4\pi D t^3} = \sqrt{4\pi \times 10 \times 10.4^3} = 377\) µm·s.
  3. At the peak the exponent is always \((r-a)^2/4Dt = 3/2\), and \(e^{-1.5} = 0.223\).
  4. \(\dot n = 10^{10} \times (5/30) \times (25/377) \times 0.223 = 2.5\times10^{7}\) /s.
  5. At \(t\) = 100 s: \(\dot n = 3.2\times10^{6}\) /s, still 13% of the peak.
  6. Share of the eventual total in by the peak: \(\mathrm{erfc}(\sqrt{1.5}) = 0.083\). By 100 s: 0.58.

What it means. About 25 million arrivals per second at rush hour, ten seconds after the bite. Yet only 8% of the eventual total is in by then; the \(t^{-3/2}\) tail carries most of it. That is why clearance, which cuts the tail, lowers the total so much.

Mechanical analogythe thermometer's warming rate

Return to the heater bead in aluminium (2.4.2) and hold the heater 60 K above the block. The rate at which the thermometer at 6 cm warms plays \(\dot n\): zero at first, fastest at \((r-a)^2/6D\), then tapering as \(t^{-3/2}\).

In the cellIn the machine
\(N_0 = 10^{10}\) moleculesheater held 60 K above the block
\(\dot n(t)\), arrivals per secondthe thermometer's warming rate, K/s
peak at 10.4 speak at \((0.05)^2/(6 \times 8\times10^{-5})\) = 5.2 s
2.5 × 10⁷ /s at the peak0.30 K/s at the peak
8% of the total in at the peak8% of the final 10-K rise in at the peak

The 8% is no coincidence: at the peak the erfc's argument is always \(\sqrt{1.5}\), for any cell and any block.

Where it breaks. The analogy runs the problem backwards: the heater's temperature plays the certainty of capture on contact, not the molecules, so it reproduces the arrival curve but not where the molecules are. And heat has no counting noise, so the thermometer never flickers the way the 300-molecule cohort does.

2.4.4

Capture probability with clearance — an exponential screen brings D back

Minted in Week 2 §4.3 · Why it is \(a/r\) — and why \(D\) is nowhere in it · open the module

eq. 2.4.4$$P_\infty = \frac{a}{r}\,e^{-(r-a)/\lambda}, \qquad \lambda = \sqrt{D\tau} \quad \text{(eq. 2.3.7)}$$

Letters

  • \(P_\infty\) — probability of ever being captured, now with clearance · dimensionless
  • \(a\), \(r\) — cell radius and release distance · m
  • \(\lambda = \sqrt{D\tau}\) — the reaction–diffusion length (eq. 2.3.7) · m
  • \(D\) — diffusion coefficient · m²/s
  • \(\tau\) — the molecule's mean lifetime before clearance · s (Tab 4: ~180 s)

How it is used

§4.3 Step 5 gives each molecule a lifetime \(\tau\), so the steady equation gains a sink, \(\nabla^2 u = u/\lambda^2\), and its solution multiplies eq. 2.4.1 by \(e^{-(r-a)/\lambda}\). The bench's "with clearance" view shows it: early arrivals barely change, the long tail is erased, and the ceiling drops. Because \(\lambda\) contains \(D\), the odds now depend on speed; the verdict bench's "per-molecule chance" moves with \(D\) only when clearance is on. The worked "fifty-metre bite" uses it with \(\lambda\) = 42 µm to shrink the alarm horizon from 50 m to about 0.5 mm.

Comes back: C1 §2.1 (the odds of ever arriving, with clearance); R2 §1.2 (the odds a released molecule is ever caught).

Biological examplethe second mast cell, with clearance

Tab 4's allergen is cleared with \(\tau\) = 180 s and diffuses at \(D\) = 10 µm²/s. Compare mast cells (\(a\) = 5 µm) at 30 µm and at 60 µm, with and without clearance. Then ask what a faster allergen buys.

  1. \(\lambda = \sqrt{10 \times 180} = 42.4\) µm.
  2. At 30 µm: no clearance, 5/30 = 0.167; with clearance, \(0.167 \times e^{-25/42.4} = 0.167 \times 0.555 = 0.092\).
  3. At 60 µm: no clearance, 0.083; with clearance, \(0.083 \times e^{-55/42.4} = 0.083 \times 0.274 = 0.023\).
  4. Near-to-far ratio: 2.0 without clearance, 4.1 with.
  5. Double \(D\) to 20 µm²/s: \(\lambda\) = 60 µm, and at 30 µm \(P_\infty = 0.167 \times e^{-25/60} = 0.110\).

What it means. Clearance almost halves the near cell's odds and cuts the far cell's by nearly three-quarters; distance now costs exponentially. And \(D\) is back in the answer: a molecule twice as fast has 19% better odds at 30 µm, because it covers more ground before it is destroyed.

Mechanical analogyaluminium and steel cooling fins

A long rod sticks out of a hot engine block into still air. Heat runs along the rod by conduction, as allergen spreads by diffusion, and the air takes heat off the surface, as clearance removes allergen. Far along a long rod the temperature excess is the base excess times \(e^{-x/\lambda}\), with \(\lambda = \sqrt{D\tau}\) and \(x\) the distance along the rod. The rod is 1D, so there is no \(a/r\) factor.

In the cellIn the machine
allergenheat
mast cell at 30 µmthermometer 10 cm along the rod
clearance, \(\tau\) = 180 sair cooling of a 5-mm rod in still air: \(\tau\) ≈ 300 s for aluminium, ≈ 450 s for steel (typical)
no clearance: \(a/r\), whatever \(D\)insulated rod: the far end reaches the base temperature, whatever the metal
\(\lambda\) = 42 µm; doubling \(D\) gives 19% better oddsaluminium (\(D\) ≈ 8 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s): \(\lambda\) = 15.5 cm; steel (\(D\) ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s): \(\lambda\) = 7.3 cm

At 10 cm the aluminium rod keeps \(e^{-0.10/0.155}\) = 0.52 of the base excess and the steel rod \(e^{-0.10/0.073}\) = 0.26. Insulated, both would end at the base temperature, steel only later; cooled, the better conductor delivers twice as much. That is \(D\) coming back through \(\lambda\).

Where it breaks. A fin is one-dimensional, so it has no \(a/r\) geometry to combine with the exponential. And air cooling depends on how hot the rod is, so its lifetime is only roughly fixed.

2.4.5

Expected arrivals — the bolus times the odds

Minted in Week 2 §4.4 · Does it fire, and when? · open the module

eq. 2.4.5$$\mu(t) = N_0\,P(t) = N_0\,\frac{a}{r}\,\mathrm{erfc}\!\left(\frac{r-a}{\sqrt{4Dt}}\right)$$

Letters

  • \(\mu(t)\) — expected number of molecules captured by time \(t\), a mean, not a count (not Week 1's mobility) · #
  • \(N_0\) — bolus size · # (module: 10¹⁰)
  • \(P(t)\) — eq. 2.4.2 · dimensionless
  • \(a\), \(r\), \(D\), \(t\) — as in eq. 2.4.2

How it is used

§4.4 mints it because one molecule's 1-in-6 says nothing about a bite: multiply by the bolus. The verdict bench's alarm-clock chart plots it against the threshold line. The worked example sets it equal to \(N_{th}\) = 10³ and inverts the erfc to get \(t_{\rm alarm}\) ≈ 1.3 s, paying off Week 1's asserted "~3 s" with a mechanism. At that instant \(P = N_{th}/N_0 = 10^{-7}\): individually hopeless, collectively certain. Halving the bolus delays the alarm by only about 70 ms. Eq. 2.4.6 turns the mean into a probability of firing.

Comes back: —

Biological examplethe second mast cell's count

The same bite (\(N_0 = 10^{10}\), \(D\) = 10 µm²/s, no clearance), read at the mast cell 60 µm away (\(a\) = 5 µm). How many allergen molecules does it expect by 5 s, 10 s and 60 s, and when does the mean pass 1000?

  1. Ceiling: \(N_0\,a/r = 10^{10} \times 5/60 = 8.3\times10^{8}\).
  2. Gap: \(r - a\) = 55 µm.
  3. At 5 s: \(55/\sqrt{4 \times 10 \times 5} = 3.89\), erfc = 3.8 × 10⁻⁸, so \(\mu\) ≈ 32.
  4. At 10 s: the argument is 2.75, erfc = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴, so \(\mu = 8.4\times10^{4}\).
  5. At 60 s: the argument is 1.12, erfc = 0.112, so \(\mu = 9.4\times10^{7}\).
  6. \(\mu\) = 1000 needs erfc = \(1000/8.3\times10^{8} = 1.2\times10^{-6}\), an argument of 3.43, so \(t = 55^2/(40 \times 3.43^2) = 6.4\) s.

What it means. Between 5 and 10 s the expected count jumps from about thirty to nearly a hundred thousand: the front of arrivals is steep. The far cell's mean passes 1000 at 6.4 s, about five times later than the near cell's 1.3 s. Each number is a mean; the actual count scatters by about \(\pm\sqrt\mu\).

Mechanical analogythe heater's push, scaled up

Use the heater bead of 2.4.2 again. There, the thermometer's share of the heater's rise played \(P(t)\). Now hold the heater 60 K above the block: the thermometer reads 60 K × that share, the size of the push times the odds, just as \(\mu = N_0 P\).

In the cellIn the machine
bolus, \(N_0 = 10^{10}\)heater excess, 60 K
\(P(t)\), the odds by \(t\)the thermometer's share, \((1/6)\,\mathrm{erfc}(\ldots)\)
\(\mu(t)\), expected arrivalsthe thermometer's rise, K
ceiling \(N_0 a/r = 8.3\times10^{8}\)final rise 60/6 = 10 K
\(\mu\) passes 1000 at 6.4 sthe rise passes 1 K at 5.8 s

The readings at 5, 10 and 60 s are 0.77, 2.1 and 6.1 K. To reach 1 K the erfc must equal 0.1, so its argument is 1.16 and \(t = (0.05)^2/(4 \times 8\times10^{-5} \times 1.16^2)\) = 5.8 s.

Where it breaks. The thermometer reads the mean and nothing else; the cell's count is a mean plus Poisson scatter of \(\pm\sqrt\mu\), which matters when \(\mu\) is near threshold (eq. 2.4.6). And a count comes in whole molecules, while a temperature is continuous.

2.4.6

The activation probability — the chance the count clears a threshold

Minted in Week 2 §4.4 · Does it fire, and when? · open the module

eq. 2.4.6$$P(\text{fire by } t) = 1 - \sum_{k=0}^{N_{th}-1} \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{k}}{k!}$$

Letters

  • \(P(\text{fire by } t)\) — probability that the cell has fired by \(t\) · dimensionless
  • \(N_{th}\) — activation threshold, the arrivals needed · # (module: ~10³, "the softest number")
  • \(k\) — a possible count, summed from 0 to \(N_{th} - 1\) · #
  • \(\mu\) — expected arrivals by \(t\) (eq. 2.4.5) · #
  • \(e^{-\mu}\mu^k/k!\) — the Poisson probability of exactly \(k\) arrivals · dimensionless

How it is used

§4.4 mints it from eq. 2.4.5: each molecule wanders independently, so the count is binomial over \(N_0\) trials, which for large \(N_0\) and small \(P\) is Poisson with mean \(\mu\); the cell fires when the count reaches \(N_{th}\). The verdict bench reads the result as "deafening", "coin flip" or "silence"; dragging the distance outward passes through all three, and the crossing is the alarm horizon \(r^\ast\) on the second chart. "Roll 200 bites" checks the formula against actual dice. At the defaults the bite is about 10⁶ times over threshold, so the sum is effectively 1.

Comes back: —

Biological examplehow sharp is the alarm horizon?

With clearance (\(\tau\) = 180 s, \(\lambda\) = 42.4 µm), Tab 4's horizon sits at \(r^\ast\) ≈ 494 µm, where \(\mu = N_0\,(a/r)\,e^{-(r-a)/\lambda}\) (eq. 2.4.4 × the bolus) equals \(N_{th}\) = 1000. How fast does the verdict change across it?

  1. At \(r^\ast\): \(\mu\) = 1000, and the Poisson spread is \(\sqrt{1000}\) ≈ 32.
  2. Summing eq. 2.4.6 at \(\mu\) = 1000: \(P(\text{fire})\) = 0.50.
  3. At \(\mu\) = 900: \(P(\text{fire}) = 5.5\times10^{-4}\).
  4. At \(\mu\) = 1100: \(P(\text{fire})\) = 0.999.
  5. Where those cells sit: \(\mu\) = 900 at \(r\) ≈ 498 µm, and \(\mu\) = 1100 at \(r\) ≈ 490 µm.
  6. Compare a factor of two in \(N_{th}\) (500 or 2000): the horizon moves about 27 µm.

What it means. The verdict flips from "almost never" to "almost always" across about 8 µm, less than one mast-cell diameter. Counting noise is real but thin at \(N_{th}\) = 1000. The uncertainty in \(N_{th}\) itself, which the module calls the softest number in the tab, moves the horizon several times farther.

Mechanical analogythe tipping-bucket rain gauge

A tipping-bucket rain gauge sends one click when its small bucket has caught a fixed amount of water. Count that amount in drops and it is a threshold. In steady rain, the number of drops entering the funnel in a window is Poisson, with mean \(\mu\) = drops per second × window. Whether the bucket has tipped by the end of the window is eq. 2.4.6.

In the cellIn the machine
allergen arrivalsraindrops into the funnel
\(N_{th}\) = 1000bucket full at ≈ 1500 drops
\(\mu\), expected arrivalsexpected drops in the window
spread \(\sqrt\mu\) ≈ 32spread \(\sqrt{1500}\) ≈ 39
fires or nottips or not

The 1500: a 20-cm funnel and a bucket that tips at 0.2 mm of rain (typical) collect \(0.2\times10^{-3} \times \pi (0.1)^2\) m³ = 6.3 mL, and a 2-mm raindrop holds 4.2 µL. With \(\mu\) = 1350, 1500 and 1650 drops in the window, the bucket has tipped with probability 3 × 10⁻⁵, 0.50 and 0.9999.

Where it breaks. Raindrops come in many sizes, so the bucket really counts volume, not drops, and its threshold in drops is fuzzy. And the bucket empties and resets after each tip, while a mast cell that has degranulated is spent.

Featured in HW2 · Problem 1(c)–(d)
2.4.7

The Berg–Purcell patchy sphere — a few findable receptors catch almost everything

Minted in Week 2 §4.4 · Does it fire, and when? · open the module

eq. 2.4.7$$k_s = 4\pi D a\,\cdot\,\frac{N_{\rm rec}\,a_s}{N_{\rm rec}\,a_s + \pi a}$$

Letters

  • \(k_s\) — encounter rate constant of the patchy cell · m³/s
  • \(D\) — the ligand's diffusion coefficient · m²/s
  • \(a\) — cell radius · m
  • \(N_{\rm rec}\) — number of receptor pockets · #
  • \(a_s\) — radius of one pocket · m (module: ~1 nm)
  • \(4\pi D a\) — the perfect absorber's rate, eq. 1.5.1 for a still cell · m³/s

How it is used

§4.4 mints it to tie a loose end: §4.2's bench let the whole cell swallow anything that touched it, but real cells are mostly inert membrane. The correction is a ratio of lengths, not the area fraction, for §3.1's reason: a molecule that hits bare membrane rattles in the depleted layer and tries again. No bench measures it directly; it rests on §3.1's measured \(a\)-not-\(a^2\) law. The worked example finds that \(N_{\rm rec} = \pi a/a_s\) ≈ 1.6 × 10⁴ pockets (0.016% of the surface) give half the perfect rate, and 3 × 10⁵ give 95% at 0.3% coverage, which licenses the perfect-absorber cartoon (Berg & Purcell 1977).

Comes back: —

Biological examplehow many transporters an E. coli needs

An E. coli cell (\(a\) ≈ 1 µm, Week 1's value) takes up a sugar through pockets with \(a_s\) ≈ 1 nm. How many pockets make it half as good as a perfect absorber, what share of its surface is that, and what does it catch at 1 µM?

  1. Half the perfect rate when \(N_{\rm rec}a_s = \pi a\): \(N_{\rm rec} = \pi \times 1/10^{-3} = 3.1\times10^{3}\).
  2. Surface share: \(N_{\rm rec}a_s^2/4a^2 = 3142 \times 10^{-6}/4 = 7.9\times10^{-4}\), about 0.08%.
  3. With 10⁴ pockets: \(10/(10 + 3.14) = 0.76\) of the perfect rate.
  4. The sugar (radius ≈ 0.4 nm, typical) in water at 37 °C: \(4.28\times10^{-21}/(6\pi \times 6.9\times10^{-4} \times 4\times10^{-10}) = 8.2\times10^{-10}\) m²/s = 820 µm²/s.
  5. Perfect rate: \(4\pi \times 820 \times 1 = 1.03\times10^{4}\) µm³/s; with 10⁴ pockets, \(7.9\times10^{3}\) µm³/s.
  6. At 1 µM (602 /µm³): \(7.9\times10^{3} \times 602 = 4.7\times10^{6}\) sugar molecules per second.

What it means. A few thousand findable doors, under a tenth of a percent of its skin, give a bacterium half of what a fully sticky cell would catch. Because the half-way count is \(\pi a/a_s\), a small cell needs fewer pockets than a big one: the mast cell needs 1.6 × 10⁴.

Mechanical analogya drain ball with a few holes

Take the buried drain of 2.3.3, but make it a sealed steel ball, 0.1 m in radius, drilled with holes 1 mm in radius. How many holes give half the yield of a fully open screen? The water around the ball obeys the same Laplace problem, so the same formula answers.

In the cellIn the machine
E. coli, \(a\) = 1 µmdrain ball, \(a\) = 0.1 m
pocket, \(a_s\) = 1 nmhole, \(a_s\) = 1 mm
\(N_{\rm rec}\) = 3.1 × 10³ for half\(\pi \times 0.1/0.001\) = 314 holes for half
0.08% of the surface0.8% of the surface
a molecule that misses tries againwater that meets bare steel flows on to the next hole

With 3000 holes, 7.5% of the surface, the ball yields 0.91 of a fully open screen.

Where it breaks. The holes must be spread out; bunched on one side they act like one big hole and lose the advantage. And water converging on a 1-mm hole moves fast enough to drag sand in and clog it, a failure no receptor pocket has.

1.3.5

Fick's first law — now derived from the tollbooth count

Re-boxed in Week 2 §1.2 · Counting makes a current — Fick's first law, measured

eq. 1.3.5 again$$J \;=\; -D\,\frac{\partial C}{\partial x}$$

Week 1 met it inside Einstein's argument, as the diffusive half of the flux standoff. Week 2 derives it as the \(\delta \to 0\) limit of the tollbooth count (eq. 2.1.1), with Week 1's \(D \equiv \delta^2/2\tau\) (eq. 1.2.4) dropping in with no stray factor. Here \(J\) is the net crossing rate down the gradient (#/(m²·s); #/s in the 1D cartoon), \(C\) the census of walkers and \(x\) position along the box; the tollbooth bench checks the measured net against it, and eqs. 2.1.2, 2.2.1 and 2.3.4 all run on it.

Full entry: eq. 1.3.5, Week 1

1.5.1

Smoluchowski's encounter rate — previewed in Week 1, earned here

Re-boxed in Week 2 §3.3 · The derivation, line by line: eq. 2.3.1 → eq. 1.5.1

eq. 1.5.1 again$$\boxed{\;k_s = 4\pi\,(D_1+D_2)\,(a_1+a_2)\;}\qquad \left[\mathrm{m^3/s}\right]$$

Week 1 measured it on the hungry receptor; Week 2 derives it as the magnitude of eq. 2.3.6 with §3.2's camera trick, \(D_{rel} = D_1 + D_2\) and \(a_{rel} = a_1 + a_2\). \(D_1, D_2\) are the partners' diffusion coefficients, \(a_1, a_2\) their radii, and \(k_s\) times a concentration is encounters per second. The module spends it three ways: a transcription factor's ~265-s search for one 10-bp site, the ~3.4 × 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹ ceiling for an enzyme, and ~10⁷ glutamate encounters per second on one receptor.

Full entry: eq. 1.5.1, Week 1

Week 3 · Binding — How a Cell Reads a Concentration

A cell never sees a concentration, only how many of its receptors are occupied, and Tab 1 builds that occupancy from three rates: arrival by diffusion (\(J = DC/\delta\)), sticking (\(k_{on} = Pk_s\)), and release, a rare thermal escape from a well (\(k_{off} = k_0e^{-\Delta U/k_BT}\)). Tab 2 turns many sites into curves: one-way filling, Langmuir's isotherm with its window around \(K_D\), BET's pile, Hill's switch and Michaelis–Menten's saturating rate. Tab 3 follows the occupancy into decisions (a threshold, a direction, a position in a gradient), checks with the Damköhler number when the bulk concentration may be used, and ends at the Berg–Purcell counting limit, the floor under any reading. Tab 4 sets a neutrophil and a bacterium in one infected bite: the big cell reads its gradient across its body in one glance, while the small one must read in time.

Module Tab 1 · The Door and the Delivery
3.1.1

Arrival flux — delivery is Fick's law across the emptied layer

Minted in Week 3 §1.1 · Arrival: how often does a diffusing protein reach a surface? · open the module

eq. 3.1.1$$J_{\text{arr}} = \frac{D\,C}{\delta} \qquad\text{(the sim: } \delta = L,\ C = 2N/L^2 \text{ at the supply, so arrivals/s} = 2ND/L^2\text{)}$$

Letters

  • \(J_{\text{arr}}\) — arrival flux: fresh molecules reaching the surface per area per second · #/(m²·s), here µm⁻²s⁻¹
  • \(D\) — the ligand's diffusion coefficient · m²/s · the module's peptide: ≈ 500 µm²/s
  • \(C\) — the bulk concentration, far from the surface · #/m³ · 1 nM = 0.6022 µm⁻³
  • \(\delta\) — the thickness of the layer the surface has emptied: a film, the distance to the supply, or a whole cell's radius · m
  • \(N, L\) — the sim's protein count and box width; arrivals per second should read \(2ND/L^2\)

How it is used

§1.1 mints it to ask how often a fresh molecule reaches a surface in water. The sticky-wall bench counts arrivals against \(2ND/L^2\): double the proteins and arrivals double, double \(D\) and they double too, and the profile settles into a straight line falling to zero at the wall. It is Fick's first law (eq. 1.3.5) across the layer the surface digs; with \(\delta = a\) for a whole sphere it is Week 2's \(4\pi DaC\). The worked example puts a 1 nM peptide's delivery at ≈ 300 µm⁻²s⁻¹ across a micron and 3.8 s⁻¹ into one 1 nm pocket. §1.2 reuses it as the delivery side of the flux balance (eq. 3.1.3).

Comes back: —

Biological examplehistamine reaching an itch-nerve terminal

Week 2 left histamine at about 55 molecules/µm³ (≈ 90 nM) at a nerve ending 120 µm from the mast cell. How many fresh histamine molecules reach each square micron of the terminal's membrane every second?

  1. Histamine's diffusion coefficient in tissue (Week 2): \(D\) ≈ 330 µm²/s.
  2. Concentration at the nerve (Week 2 §4.5): \(C\) ≈ 55 µm⁻³.
  3. Treat the terminal as a sphere about 1 µm in radius (illustrative). Its own radius sets the layer: \(\delta\) ≈ 1 µm.
  4. Flux: \(J_{\text{arr}} = DC/\delta = (330)(55)/1 ≈ 1.8\times10^{4}\) µm⁻²s⁻¹.
  5. Whole terminal: \(4\pi a^2 J_{\text{arr}} = 4\pi(1)^2(1.8\times10^{4}) ≈ 2.3\times10^{5}\) s⁻¹.
  6. Time to cross the layer (Week 1's walk): \(\delta^2/2D = 1/660\) s ≈ 1.5 ms.

What it means. Eighteen thousand fresh molecules reach each square micron every second, and the last micron costs each one only a millisecond or two. Delivery is not why an itch takes a minute. It is the ceiling: no receptor on that membrane can bind faster than this.

Mechanical analogya drain pipe under a sand bed

A field drain is a perforated pipe buried in sand. It takes every drop that reaches it, so the water table slopes down to it, as the concentration slopes to zero at the sticky wall. The water seeps rather than falls, at a rate set by the sand, the head at the far side and the distance. Darcy's law, \(q = Kh/L\), has the shape of eq. 3.1.1.

In the cellIn the machine
bulk concentration \(C\)water head \(h\) at the far side of the bed
diffusion coefficient \(D\)hydraulic conductivity of the sand, \(K\)
emptied layer \(\delta\)distance \(L\) through the sand to the pipe
arrival flux \(J_{\text{arr}}\)seepage flux \(q\) into the pipe face
sticky wall, \(C = 0\) at contactopen drain, zero head at the pipe

Take clean sand (\(K\) ≈ 10⁻⁴ m/s, typical), a 0.5 m head and 1 m of sand: \(q = (10^{-4})(0.5)/1 = 5\times10^{-5}\) m/s, or 180 litres an hour through each square metre of pipe face. Double the head and the flow doubles; double the distance and it halves.

Where it breaks. Water in sand is pushed by a pressure gradient. Histamine is not pushed at all: its "flow" is the net of random walks, and with no gradient each molecule would still jiggle, which still water in sand does not.

3.1.2

Binding flux — the surface drinks at a speed κ

Minted in Week 3 §1.2 · Which arrivals count: the site, and the stick · open the module

eq. 3.1.2$$J_{\text{bind}} = k_r\,\Gamma_{max}(1-\theta)\,C_s \;\equiv\; \kappa\,C_s, \qquad \kappa \equiv k_r\,\Gamma_{max}(1-\theta)$$

Letters

  • \(J_{\text{bind}}\) — bindings per area per second · #/(m²·s)
  • \(k_r\) — intrinsic rate of one open site: the volume of liquid it clears of ligand per second · m³/s (µm³/s)
  • \(\Gamma_{max}\) — sites per area · #/m² · neutrophil: ≈ 75 µm⁻²
  • \(\theta\) — fraction of sites occupied, so \(1-\theta\) are open
  • \(C_s\) — concentration in the liquid touching the surface · #/m³
  • \(\kappa\) — the surface's uptake speed · m/s

How it is used

§1.2 mints it when the wall gets sites. On its bench a walker that touches an open site sticks with odds \(p_c\), and the stats print \(\kappa\): more sites, stickier sites or more of them open all raise it. The module insists \(k_r\) is chemistry, not a count of touches: a Brownian path touches a wall infinitely often, so touches are not a physical count. Setting this flux equal to the delivery of eq. 3.1.1 gives the flux balance, eq. 3.1.3.

Comes back: —

Biological examplehow fast a neutrophil's surface drinks fMLP

Tab 4's neutrophil sits where the bacterial peptide is at its \(K_D\). How fast does its surface clear peptide from the liquid touching it, and how does that compare with delivery?

  1. Site density: \(\Gamma_{max} = N/4\pi a^2 = 53{,}000/4\pi(7.5)^2 ≈ 75\) µm⁻².
  2. Intrinsic site rate: \(k_r ≈ k_{on} ≈ 0.028\) µm³/s (§1.2 found this pocket reaction-limited).
  3. At \(C = K_D\) half the receptors are open: \(1-\theta = 0.5\).
  4. Uptake speed: \(\kappa = (0.028)(75)(0.5) ≈ 1.05\) µm/s.
  5. Binding flux, with \(C_s ≈ C = 0.36\) µm⁻³: \(J_{\text{bind}} = (1.05)(0.36) ≈ 0.38\) µm⁻²s⁻¹.
  6. Whole cell: \(0.38 \times 4\pi(7.5)^2 ≈ 270\) bindings per second.
  7. Delivery speed for comparison, \(D/\delta\) with \(\delta = a\): 500/7.5 ≈ 67 µm/s.

What it means. The surface drinks at about 1 µm/s while diffusion refills at 67 µm/s, so it binds only ~1.6 % of what diffusion could deliver (the ceiling \(DC/\delta\)) and \(C_s\) stays essentially at \(C\). That is why Tab 4 may read this cell with the bulk concentration.

Mechanical analogya vacuum hold-down table with some holes plugged

A router shop holds sheets flat on a vacuum table: a plate drilled with holes, each drawing a fixed volume of air per second, some plugged by chips. The draw per hole, times the holes per square metre, times the fraction still open, is a speed: the face velocity. Multiply it by what the air carries and you have the uptake flux.

In the cellIn the machine
one open site's clearing rate \(k_r\)one hole's air draw (m³/s)
site density \(\Gamma_{max}\)holes per square metre
occupied fraction \(\theta\)fraction of holes plugged by chips
uptake speed \(\kappa\)face velocity of the table
\(C_s\), ligand beside the membranedust concentration at the plate

Holes on a 5 cm grid (400 per m²), each drawing 0.1 L/s = 10⁻⁴ m³/s, half of them plugged: \(\kappa = (10^{-4})(400)(0.5) = 0.02\) m/s, a face velocity of 2 cm/s. Plug more holes and the table drinks more slowly, exactly as filling sites lowers \(\kappa\).

Where it breaks. The table moves the air itself toward the plate. A receptor moves nothing; it only removes ligand that diffusion has already brought to its door. And a chip stays in its hole until someone clears it, while a bound ligand can leave on its own (§1.3).

3.1.3

The flux balance — delivery and chemistry in series

Minted in Week 3 §1.2 · Which arrivals count: the site, and the stick · open the module

eq. 3.1.3$$\frac{D\,(C - C_s)}{\delta} = \kappa\,C_s \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; C_s = \frac{C}{1 + \kappa\delta/D}, \qquad J_{\text{bind}} = \frac{C}{\delta/D + 1/\kappa}$$

Letters

  • \(D\), \(\delta\) — diffusion coefficient and layer thickness; \(\delta/D\) is the resistance of the delivery · s/m
  • \(\kappa\) — the surface's uptake speed (eq. 3.1.2); \(1/\kappa\) is the resistance of the chemistry · s/m
  • \(C\) — bulk concentration · #/m³
  • \(C_s\) — concentration in the liquid touching the surface · #/m³
  • \(J_{\text{bind}}\) — the one steady flux: what is delivered is what is bound · #/(m²·s)

How it is used

§1.2 sets delivery (eq. 3.1.1, with the surface no longer empty) equal to binding (eq. 3.1.2) and solves for \(C_s\). The sim's dotted prediction line is this equation with the box's \(\delta\) and the sim's \(\kappa\): the \(p_c = 1\) chip rides near the ceiling \(DC/\delta\) (fast surface, \(C_s \to 0\)) and the \(p_c = 0.01\) chip near \(\kappa C\) (slow surface, \(C_s \to C\)). The ratio \(J_{\text{bind}}/(DC/\delta) = 1/(1 + D/\kappa\delta)\) is the sticking probability per arrival \(P\), the stats' "fraction of the ceiling". One pocket at a time, the same series law becomes eq. 3.1.4; Tab 3 turns the ratio of the two resistances into the Damköhler number.

Comes back: —

Biological exampleE. coli, if its receptors bound on contact

Tab 3's "receptors at the ceiling" chip asks what would happen if each of E. coli's ~1,200 aspartate receptors bound every molecule that reached its pocket. Would the cell still read the true concentration?

  1. Cell radius (Tab 4's cast): \(a\) = 0.5 µm, so \(\delta = a\) = 0.5 µm.
  2. Site density: \(\Gamma_{max} = 1200/4\pi(0.5)^2 ≈ 382\) µm⁻².
  3. Each pocket at the diffusion ceiling, with aspartate's \(D\) = 900 µm²/s (the chip's value): \(k_r = 4\pi Da_s = 4\pi(900)(10^{-3}) ≈ 11.3\) µm³/s.
  4. Fresh surface (\(\theta ≈ 0\)): \(\kappa = (11.3)(382) ≈ 4{,}320\) µm/s.
  5. Delivery speed: \(D/\delta = 900/0.5 = 1{,}800\) µm/s, so \(\kappa\delta/D = 2.4\).
  6. Surface concentration: \(C_s = C/(1 + 2.4) ≈ 0.29\,C\).
  7. Flux: \(J = C/(5.6\times10^{-4} + 2.3\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{s/\mu m}) ≈ 0.71\,DC/\delta\).

What it means.
