With receptors covering only about 0.12 % of its surface, this cell would catch 71 % of what a perfect absorber catches, yet its receptors would sit in liquid at 29 % of the true concentration and read the world 3.4 times too low. \(D\) cancels in \(\kappa\delta/D = Na_s/a\): the verdict is geometry. Real Tar binds far below the ceiling, which is what keeps E. coli's reading honest.

Mechanical analogya garden hose with a nozzle

Water from a tank runs through a long hose to a nozzle. The flow is the tank's head over the sum of the two resistances, and the pressure just upstream of the nozzle sits between full and zero, depending on which resistance is larger. At slow, smooth flow both resistances are constants, and the arithmetic is eq. 3.1.3.

In the cellIn the machine
bulk concentration \(C\)tank head
delivery resistance \(\delta/D\)hose resistance
chemistry resistance \(1/\kappa\)nozzle resistance
surface concentration \(C_s\)pressure at the nozzle inlet
binding flux \(J_{\text{bind}}\)water flow

Give the hose a conductance of 0.5 L/s per metre of head and the nozzle 1.2 L/s per metre (2.4 times the hose, as in E. coli), with a 2.0 m head. The flow is \(2.0/(1/0.5 + 1/1.2) ≈ 0.71\) L/s, 71 % of the flow with the nozzle off. The nozzle inlet sits at \(0.71/1.2 ≈ 0.59\) m, 29 % of the head. Same numbers as the bacterium.

Where it breaks. A hose at full tap is turbulent, so its pressure drop grows faster than the flow and its resistance is not a constant. Diffusion has no such regime: \(\delta/D\) is fixed by geometry and temperature.

Featured in HW2 · Problem 4(e)
3.1.4

Collins–Kimball — association is arrive, then stick

Minted in Week 3 §1.2 · Which arrivals count: the site, and the stick · open the module

eq. 3.1.4$$s + p \;\xrightarrow{\;k_{on}\;}\; sp, \qquad \frac{d\Gamma_{sp}}{dt} = k_{on}\,C\,\Gamma_s, \qquad k_{on} = \frac{k_r\,k_s}{k_r + k_s} = P\,k_s, \quad k_s = 4\pi D a_s,\ \ P = \frac{k_r}{k_r + k_s}$$

Letters

  • \(s\), \(p\), \(sp\) — a free site, a free protein (the ligand), a bound pair
  • \(\Gamma_s\), \(\Gamma_{sp}\) — free and occupied sites per area · #/m²
  • \(t\) — time · s
  • \(k_{on}\) — association rate constant: one open site's binding rate per unit of bulk concentration · m³/s · \(10^{9}\ \mathrm{M^{-1}min^{-1}}\) = 0.028 µm³/s
  • \(C\) — bulk concentration · #/m³
  • \(k_r\) — the site's intrinsic chemistry (eq. 3.1.2) · m³/s
  • \(k_s = 4\pi Da_s\) — encounter rate constant of one pocket, eq. 1.5.1 · m³/s
  • \(D\) — ligand diffusion coefficient · m²/s; \(a_s\) — pocket radius · m · 1 nm
  • \(P\) — sticking probability per arrival, 0 to 1

How it is used

§1.2's derivation balances Smoluchowski's delivery to one pocket, \(4\pi Da_s(C - C_s)\), against its chemistry, \(k_rC_s\), and reads \(k_{on}\) off as arrivals times the odds of sticking. Inverted, \(1/k_{on} = 1/k_r + 1/k_s\): the same two resistances as eq. 3.1.3. On the bench, the \(p_c = 1\) chip rides the diffusive ceiling (\(P \to 1\), diffusion-limited) and \(p_c = 0.01\) the reaction-limited floor (\(k_{on} \to k_r\)). The worked example finds Tab 4's neutrophil receptor binds one arrival in ~220 (\(P\) = 0.0044). \(k_{on}\) is one of the three rates every later model is built from (§1.6).

Comes back: —

Biological examplebarnase and barstar, with and without steering

§1.4 quotes Schreiber and Fersht: without electrostatic attraction, the bacterial enzyme barnase binds its inhibitor barstar at a basal 10⁵ M⁻¹s⁻¹; with it, at over 5 × 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹, the diffusive ceiling. What is the sticking probability each way?

  1. Units: 1 M = 6.022 × 10⁸ µm⁻³, so 1 M⁻¹s⁻¹ = 1.66 × 10⁻⁹ µm³/s.
  2. Ceiling: \(k_s ≈ 5\times10^{9} \times 1.66\times10^{-9} ≈ 8.3\) µm³/s.
  3. Basal: \(k_{on} = 10^{5} \times 1.66\times10^{-9} = 1.66\times10^{-4}\) µm³/s.
  4. Basal odds: \(P = k_{on}/k_s = 1.66\times10^{-4}/8.3 = 2.0\times10^{-5}\), one arrival in 50,000.
  5. Its chemistry: \(k_r = k_{on}k_s/(k_s - k_{on}) ≈ 1.66\times10^{-4}\) µm³/s. Reaction-limited: \(k_{on} ≈ k_r\).
  6. Steered: \(k_{on} ≈ k_s\), so \(P ≈ 1\). Diffusion-limited.
  7. At 1 nM barstar (0.602 µm⁻³): basal \(k_{on}C ≈ 1.0\times10^{-4}\) s⁻¹, one binding every ~2.8 h; steered \(k_{on}C ≈ 5\) s⁻¹.

What it means. Same two proteins, same diffusion, same delivery. Charge moves the pair from one end of eq. 3.1.4 to the other, a 50,000-fold change in \(P\), and turns a three-hour wait into a fifth of a second.

Mechanical analogya vibratory bowl feeder with an orientation gate

Assembly lines feed caps or screws from a vibrating bowl. The shaking walks parts up a spiral track to a gate that passes only parts lying the right way round; a part in the wrong pose is knocked back to try again. Two limits act in series: how fast the bowl delivers parts to the gate, and how fast the gate passes them.

In the cellIn the machine
encounter rate \(k_sC\)parts delivered to the gate per second
site chemistry \(k_rC\)gate's pass rate with parts crowded at it
sticking probability \(P\)fraction of delivered parts that pass
bound pair \(sp\)part through the gate, gone for good
electrostatic steeringa guide rail that pre-orients the parts

Delivery 10 parts/s and a gate that passes 2 parts/s: throughput \(1/(1/10 + 1/2) ≈ 1.67\) parts/s, \(P ≈ 0.167\), gate-limited. Add a guide rail so the gate could pass 200 parts/s: \(1/(1/10 + 1/200) ≈ 9.5\) parts/s, \(P ≈ 0.95\), delivery-limited. The rail did what barnase's charges do.

Where it breaks. The bowl is driven and its parts have inertia; a refused part is thrown back on purpose. A refused protein is not thrown anywhere. It stays near the pocket by diffusion, which is why it gets many touches per arrival.

3.1.5

The revolving door — both arrows run at once

Minted in Week 3 §1.3 · Bombarded: what a bound molecule feels · open the module

eq. 3.1.5$$s + p \;\underset{k_{off}}{\overset{k_{on}}{\rightleftharpoons}}\; sp$$

Letters

  • \(s\), \(p\), \(sp\) — a free site, a free ligand, a bound pair
  • \(k_{on}\) — association rate constant (eq. 3.1.4) · m³/s; the forward rate per open site is \(k_{on}C\) · s⁻¹
  • \(k_{off}\) — dissociation rate per bound pair · s⁻¹ · typical receptor 10⁻³–10⁻² s⁻¹; the neutrophil's 0.010 s⁻¹

How it is used

§1.3 gives §1.2's one-way door its reverse arrow. §1.2's bench had already shown what it does: with the unbinding dial up, the sites stop filling to the top, and bindings per second hold steady instead of dying. The rest of Tab 1 is about what sets \(k_{off}\): the kick law (eq. 3.1.6), the depth ledger (eq. 3.1.7) and the survival law (eq. 3.1.8). In §1.6's switchboard this is case 3, which Tab 2 solves as Langmuir (eq. 3.2.4).

Comes back: —

Biological examplethe churn under a neutrophil's steady reading

A neutrophil sits where fMLP is at its \(K_D\), and its receptor reading is steady. Is anything happening?

  1. Forward rate per open receptor: \(k_{on}C = (0.028)(0.36) ≈ 0.010\) s⁻¹.
  2. Reverse rate per bound receptor: \(k_{off}\) = 0.010 s⁻¹.
  3. At \(C = K_D\) half of the 53,000 receptors are bound (Tab 2's isotherm): 26,500 open, 26,500 bound.
  4. Bindings: 26,500 × 0.0101 ≈ 267 s⁻¹.
  5. Releases: 26,500 × 0.010 = 265 s⁻¹.
  6. Each receptor waits ~100 s for a peptide, then holds it ~100 s.

What it means. A steady reading is not a still one. About 270 peptides arrive and 270 leave every second, and the count holds only because the two arrows balance. Double \(C\) and only the forward arrow doubles; the bath, not the concentration, runs the reverse one.

Mechanical analogya Velcro board on a shaking wall

Throw fuzzy balls at a Velcro board hung on a vibrating wall. A ball that hits a bare patch sticks; one that hits an occupied patch bounces off. Each stuck ball drops off now and then as the wall shakes. Throwing harder does nothing to the dropping, and shaking harder does nothing to the sticking.

In the cellIn the machine
open site \(s\)bare Velcro patch
ligand \(p\) at concentration \(C\)balls in the air, set by the throw rate
forward rate \(k_{on}C\) per open sitehits per bare patch per minute
bound pair \(sp\)stuck ball
reverse rate \(k_{off}\)drop-off rate per stuck ball

A board of 100 patches, 0.4 hits per bare patch per minute, and a drop-off rate of 0.1 per minute settles at 80 stuck balls: 20 bare × 0.4 = 8 sticking and 80 × 0.1 = 8 dropping each minute. Double the throw rate and it settles near 89, with 8.9 each way.

Where it breaks. The balls drop because a motor shakes the wall and gravity pulls. A bound peptide leaves because the bath, at body temperature, eventually hands it enough energy. Stop the motor and the board freezes; nobody can stop a bath.

3.1.6

The kick law — leaving is a rare kick, exponentially sensitive to depth

Minted in Week 3 §1.3 · Bombarded: what a bound molecule feels · open the module

eq. 3.1.6$$k_{off} = k_0\,e^{-\Delta U/k_BT} \qquad (k_0 = \text{the attempt rate — here, kicks per second on the bound ligand})$$

Letters

  • \(k_{off}\) — dissociation rate · s⁻¹
  • \(k_0\) — the attempt rate · s⁻¹ · §1.3: the raw kick count, ≈ 6 × 10¹³ s⁻¹; §1.5: the rattle rate to the rim, ≈ 10⁷ s⁻¹
  • \(\Delta U\) — the depth of the well, a binding free energy · J, quoted in \(k_BT\)
  • \(k_BT\) — thermal energy, Boltzmann's constant times absolute temperature · 4.28 × 10⁻²¹ J = 4.28 pN·nm at 310 K

How it is used

§1.3 mints it from two measurements on the bombardment bench: kick energies are Boltzmann-distributed (eq. 1.2.7), and the ligand leaves when a kick clears \(\Delta U\). Raising \(\Delta U\) from 3 to 6 \(k_BT\) leaves the hit rate alone and cuts the shaded tail, and the unbinding rate, twenty-fold. The worked example shows that counting kicks gets the exponential right but \(k_0\) a million times too high. §1.5 re-boxes the same law ("eq. 3.1.6 again") from the well bench, where the mean stay climbs as \(e^{\Delta U/k_BT}\) and \(k_0\) becomes the rattle rate set by the well and the bath's friction (Kramers). Eq. 3.1.7 then supplies \(\Delta U\).

Comes back: —

Biological examplethe fMLP receptor in a fever

§1.5 found that the neutrophil's receptor holds fMLP in a well 21.2 \(k_BT\) deep, with a one-minute half-life (\(k_{off}\) ≈ 0.0116 s⁻¹, mean stay ≈ 87 s) at 37 °C. A fever takes the body to 40 °C. How much shorter is the stay? And what would one extra hydrogen bond do?

  1. Depth in joules, taken as fixed: \(\Delta U = 21.2 \times 4.28\times10^{-21} ≈ 9.07\times10^{-20}\) J.
  2. Thermal energy at 313 K: \(k_BT' = 4.28\times10^{-21} \times 313/310 ≈ 4.32\times10^{-21}\) J.
  3. New exponent: \(\Delta U/k_BT' ≈ 21.0\), down by 0.20.
  4. Ratio, with \(k_0\) unchanged: \(k_{off}'/k_{off} = e^{0.20} ≈ 1.23\).
  5. Mean stay: 87 s → 87/1.23 ≈ 71 s.
  6. One more hydrogen bond (≈ 3 \(k_BT\) deeper): \(k_{off}\) falls by \(e^{3} ≈ 20\), and the mean stay grows from 87 s to ≈ 29 min.

What it means. A 3 °C fever shortens the grip by about a fifth; one hydrogen bond changes it twenty-fold. Temperature acts through the exponent's denominator, but depth is the big dial. (A real \(\Delta U\) is a free energy with an entropy part, so it also shifts a little with temperature; see §1.4's 566 box.)

Mechanical analogya ball in a dimpled tray on a shaker

Set a steel ball in a dimple on a tray bolted to a shaker that delivers random jolts. Most jolts rattle it around the bottom; once in a while one throws it over the lip. The escape rate is the jolt rate times the fraction of jolts big enough, and if jolt energies are spread exponentially about a mean \(E_0\), that fraction is \(e^{-\Delta U/E_0}\).

In the cellIn the machine
bound ligandball in the dimple
well depth \(\Delta U\)energy to lift the ball over the lip
\(k_BT\)mean jolt energy \(E_0\), the shaker's "temperature"
attempt rate \(k_0\)jolts per second
\(k_{off}\)escapes per second

At 50 jolts a second and a lip of 5 \(E_0\): \(k_{off} = 50\,e^{-5} ≈ 0.34\) s⁻¹, a mean stay of 3 s. Deepen the dimple to 7 \(E_0\): 0.046 s⁻¹ and 22 s, a factor \(e^{2} ≈ 7.4\). Shake 10 % harder instead: the lip is now 4.5 \(E_0\), \(k_{off} ≈ 0.53\) s⁻¹, a stay of 1.9 s.

Where it breaks. The steel ball keeps a jolt's energy long enough to use it, so one big jolt can throw it out. That is §1.3's kick-count picture. A ligand in water loses each kick's energy in the next collision and escapes only when a run of kicks carries it to the rim, which is why §1.3's naive \(k_0\) was a million times too high.

3.1.7

The depth ledger — shape contacts plus charge pairs

Minted in Week 3 §1.4 · What sets the depth: shape and charge · open the module

eq. 3.1.7$$\Delta U \;\approx\; N_c\,\varepsilon_c \;+\; \big(N_{+-} - N_{++}\big)\,\varepsilon_q$$

Letters

  • \(\Delta U\) — well depth, the net binding free energy · \(k_BT\)
  • \(N_c\) — patches of the two surfaces in van der Waals contact (a bump in a dip)
  • \(\varepsilon_c\) — net worth of one patch · ≈ 0.5 \(k_BT\) per ~30 Å²; the sim uses 0.5
  • \(N_{+-}\) — charged or polar pairs facing an opposite partner
  • \(N_{++}\) — pairs facing a like charge, a clash
  • \(\varepsilon_q\) — worth of one pair · ≈ 1–3 \(k_BT\); the sim uses 1.2

How it is used

§1.4 turns \(\Delta U\) from a slider into a sum. The epitope–paratope bench sets how many bumps fit their dips and how many charges face an opposite, then builds the well and measures the stay: the perfect fit is 8(0.5) + 3(1.2) = 7.6 \(k_BT\), flipped charges drive the ligand to a worse pose, and spoiling the shape costs roughly a factor \(e\) of stay per \(k_BT\). Fed into eq. 3.1.6, each entry becomes a factor in the residence. The module's antibody ledger gives ≈ 19 \(k_BT\), a 6 nM \(K_D\) and an 18 s grip.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea viral escape mutation that flips one charge

Take §1.4's antibody: about 800 Å² buried on each side, three charged pairs facing opposites, an 18 s grip. A virus mutates one epitope residue so that its charge is reversed, and the paratope's partner now faces a like charge. What does that cost, against a mutation that merely removes the charge?

  1. Shape term: \(N_c ≈ 800/30 ≈ 26.7\) patches, so \(N_c\varepsilon_c ≈ 13.3\) \(k_BT\).
  2. Charge term before: \((3 - 0) \times 2 = 6\) \(k_BT\). Total \(\Delta U ≈ 19\) \(k_BT\), as §1.4 rounds it.
  3. Stay before (eq. 3.1.6, \(k_0 = 10^{7}\) s⁻¹): \(e^{19}/10^{7} ≈ 18\) s.
  4. Charge flip: \(N_{+-}\) goes 3 → 2 and \(N_{++}\) 0 → 1, so the charge term is \((2 - 1) \times 2 = 2\) \(k_BT\). The well is 4 \(k_BT\) shallower.
  5. Stay after: shorter by \(e^{4} ≈ 55\), so 18 s → ≈ 0.33 s.
  6. Neutral swap instead (pair lost, no clash): 2 \(k_BT\) shallower, shorter by \(e^{2} ≈ 7.4\), so 18 s → ≈ 2.4 s.

What it means. In the ledger a wrong charge is a penalty, not a blank. A flip costs twice the exponent of a loss: a 55-fold shorter grip against 7-fold. One residue turns an antibody that holds a virion for 18 s into one that lets go in a third of a second. The bare ledger is the gentle estimate, though: §1.4's worked example adds what a charge left without a partner costs once it has given up its water (Fersht's ≈ 4 kcal/mol ≈ 6.5 \(k_BT\)), so even the neutral swap shortens this grip about 700-fold.

Mechanical analogya Lego plate with magnets

Press a Lego plate onto a baseplate that also carries a few small magnets. Its grip is a ledger: every stud seated in a tube adds a fixed amount, every magnet pair facing north-to-south adds more, and every pair facing north-to-north subtracts the same. Shift the plate one stud and studs land on studs, so almost nothing seats.

In the cellIn the machine
patches in contact \(N_c\)studs seated in tubes
\(\varepsilon_c\)work to unseat one stud
opposite pairs \(N_{+-}\)magnet pairs facing north-to-south
like pairs \(N_{++}\)magnet pairs facing north-to-north
\(\varepsilon_q\)work to part one magnet pair
\(\Delta U\)total work to pull the plate off

In stud units, with a magnet pair worth 2: eight studs and three attracting pairs make 8 + 3 × 2 = 14. Flip one magnet: 8 + (2 − 1) × 2 = 10. Remove it instead: 8 + 2 × 2 = 12. The same sign rule as the antibody.

Where it breaks. On a shelf, a 10-unit plate and a 14-unit plate both stay put forever, because nothing in a room kicks that hard. Those 4 units matter in the cell only because the bath kicks on the same scale, so each \(k_BT\) of the ledger is a factor \(e\) in the stay.

3.1.8

Survival — a bond's stay has no memory

Minted in Week 3 §1.5 · A bond is a well the bath kicks you out of · open the module

eq. 3.1.8$$P(\text{still bound at } t) = e^{-k_{off}t}, \qquad \langle t_{\text{bound}}\rangle = \frac{1}{k_{off}}$$

Letters

  • \(P(\text{still bound at } t)\) — the fraction of a cohort bound at \(t = 0\) that is still bound at \(t\)
  • \(k_{off}\) — dissociation rate · s⁻¹
  • \(t\) — time since binding · s
  • \(\langle t_{\text{bound}}\rangle\) — mean residence, the average stay · s; the half-life is \(\ln 2/k_{off}\)

How it is used

§1.5's well bench measures it: with a thousand wells, the survival curve is a straight line on a log axis and the spread of stays equals their mean, the signature of a memoryless process. In every short interval \(dt\) a bound molecule leaves with the same probability \(k_{off}\,dt\), however long it has stayed. The worked example turns a one-minute half-life into \(k_{off}\) ≈ 0.012 s⁻¹ and a mean stay of ≈ 87 s. §1.6 files it beside eq. 3.1.6 as how \(k_{off}\) is read, and Tab 2's Langmuir equation empties occupied sites at exactly this rate.

Comes back: —

Biological examplewhat E. coli's receptors remember from the start of a run

A swimming E. coli runs for about a second before it tumbles (Berg & Brown, Tab 4). Its aspartate receptor is fast, \(k_{off}\) ≈ 1 s⁻¹ (§3.7). Of the aspartate molecules bound when a run begins, how many are still bound when it ends, and three seconds on?

  1. Mean stay: \(1/k_{off}\) = 1 s.
  2. Half-life: \(\ln 2/k_{off}\) ≈ 0.69 s.
  3. Still bound after a 1 s run: \(e^{-1} ≈ 0.37\).
  4. Still bound after 3 s (the memory time of §4.3's sim): \(e^{-3} ≈ 0.05\).

What it means. Within one run most of the bound aspartate has been swapped for fresh molecules, and three seconds later 95 % has. The receptors forget in about a second, so they cannot be what remembers. The bacterium's few-second memory lives downstream, in the slow methylation of its receptors (§4.3's note).

Mechanical analogymarbles in an egg crate on a shaker

Seat 100 marbles in an egg crate on a shaker table driven with random jolts, and count how many are still seated every minute. Each marble's chance of escaping in the next minute is the same whether it has sat for ten seconds or ten minutes. So the count falls by the same fraction each minute: a straight line on a log plot.

In the cellIn the machine
bound ligandseated marble
a cohort of bound receptorsthe 100 marbles
\(k_{off}\)escape rate per marble
\(P(\text{still bound at } t)\)fraction still seated
\(\langle t_{\text{bound}}\rangle = 1/k_{off}\)mean seat time

At 0.2 escapes per marble per minute, 37 marbles remain at 5 min (\(100e^{-1}\)) and about 5 at 15 min (\(100e^{-3}\)). The half-life is \(\ln 2/0.2 ≈ 3.5\) min and the mean seat time 5 min.

Where it breaks. A marble that has just landed is still moving and may bounce straight out, so very short stays are not memoryless, and a shaker with a steady rhythm would add memory of its own. The bath has neither problem: its kicks are random and the ligand forgets each one at once.

3.1.9

The master equation — one scheme, every model a switch setting

Minted in Week 3 §1.6 · One setup for every model · open the module

eq. 3.1.9$$s + p \;\underset{k_{off}}{\overset{P\,k_s}{\rightleftharpoons}}\; sp \;\xrightarrow{\;k_{cat}\;}\; s + q, \qquad \frac{d\Gamma_{sp}}{dt} = P\,k_s\,C\,\Gamma_s \;-\; k_{off}\,\Gamma_{sp} \;-\; k_{cat}\,\Gamma_{sp}, \qquad \frac{d\theta}{dt} = k_{on}\,C\,(1-\theta) \;-\; (k_{off} + k_{cat})\,\theta$$

Letters

  • \(s\), \(p\), \(sp\), \(q\) — a free site, a free ligand, a bound pair, a product
  • \(P\,k_s = k_{on}\) — arrive times stick (eq. 3.1.4) · m³/s
  • \(k_{off}\) — release (eq. 3.1.6, 3.1.8) · s⁻¹
  • \(k_{cat}\) — conversion of the bound ligand to product, which frees the site · s⁻¹
  • \(\Gamma_s\), \(\Gamma_{sp}\) — free and occupied sites per area, \(\Gamma_{max} = \Gamma_s + \Gamma_{sp}\) · #/m²
  • \(\theta = \Gamma_{sp}/\Gamma_{max}\) — fraction occupied
  • \(C\) — the concentration the sites see: the bulk \(C_\infty\) for isolated pockets, \(C_s\) when a surface empties its neighbourhood · #/m³
  • \(t\) — time · s

How it is used

§1.6 writes every arrow at once and turns the scheme into a rate equation by mass action: sites fill as protein meets an open site and sticks, and empty by letting go or by finishing a conversion. It has no bench of its own; it is the bookkeeping every later bench is a special case of. The switchboard names the cases: \(k_{off} = 0\) gives one-way doors (eq. 3.2.2–3.2.3), \(k_{off} > 0\) Langmuir (eq. 3.2.4–3.2.9), \(k_{cat} > 0\) Michaelis–Menten (eq. 3.2.13–3.2.15), \(k_{off}(\theta)\) Hill, a second layer BET, \(C \to C_s\) Tab 3's Damköhler fine print, and two readings across one cell Tab 4. When a model looks new, ask first which switches it has thrown.

Comes back: —

Biological examplethree cast members, three switch settings

Set \(d\theta/dt = 0\) in the master equation to get the steady occupancy, \(\theta = k_{on}C/(k_{on}C + k_{off} + k_{cat})\), and read three surfaces off it.

  1. E. coli's aspartate receptor at \(C = K_D\) (case 3): \(k_{on}C = k_{off}\) = 1 s⁻¹ and \(k_{cat}\) = 0, so \(\theta = 1/(1 + 1) = 0.5\).
  2. A tight capture antibody on a short assay (case 2): \(k_{off} ≈ 0\), \(k_{cat} = 0\). Now \(d\theta/dt = k_{on}C(1-\theta)\) stops only at \(\theta = 1\).
  3. §2.7's enzyme at \(C\) = 100 nM (case 4a): \(k_{on}C = (0.02\ \mathrm{nM^{-1}s^{-1}})(100\ \mathrm{nM}) = 2\) s⁻¹, and \(k_{off} + k_{cat} = 0.5 + 10 = 10.5\) s⁻¹.
  4. Its occupancy: \(\theta = 2/(2 + 10.5) = 0.16\).
  5. The same enzyme with catalysis switched off (back to case 3): \(\theta = 2/(2 + 0.5) = 0.80\).

What it means. One equation gives a receptor at half occupancy, a capture surface that fills to the top, and an enzyme that sits at 16 % although its bond alone would hold it at 80 %. Nothing new was derived; three switches were thrown.

Mechanical analogya tank with an inlet valve and two drains

A tank stands beside a header tank whose water is level with the tank's brim. A pipe from the header feeds the tank from below, so the inflow is proportional to the head still unfilled, \(H - h\). Two narrow drain pipes leave from the bottom, each passing a flow proportional to the level \(h\). At slow flow the level obeys \(dh/dt \propto g_{in}(H - h) - (g_1 + g_2)h\): the master equation, with \(\theta = h/H\).

In the cellIn the machine
occupancy \(\theta\)fill fraction \(h/H\)
open sites \(1 - \theta\)unfilled head \(H - h\)
\(k_{on}C\)inlet conductance \(g_{in}\)
\(k_{off}\)drain-1 conductance \(g_1\)
\(k_{cat}\)drain-2 conductance \(g_2\)
setting a switchopening or shutting a valve

The level settles at \(h/H = g_{in}/(g_{in} + g_1 + g_2)\). With conductances in the enzyme's ratio, 2 : 0.5 : 10, the tank stands 16 % full. Shut drain 2 and it rises to 80 %; shut both and it fills to the brim, the one-way surface.

Where it breaks. The water level is smooth. A receptor population is a count of discrete sites, each flipping at random, so a real \(\theta\) flickers about the tank's level by roughly \(\sqrt{N}\) sites (Tab 3).

Module Tab 2 · Three Ways to Cover a Surface
3.2.1

Fractional occupancy — the only number a surface reports

Minted in Week 3 §2.1 · Same surface, three rules · open the module

eq. 3.2.1$$\theta = \frac{\Gamma_{sp}}{\Gamma_s + \Gamma_{sp}} = \frac{\Gamma_{sp}}{\Gamma_{max}} \qquad (0 \le \theta \le 1 \text{ for a monolayer})$$

Letters

  • \(\theta\) — fractional occupancy, 0 to 1 for a monolayer
  • \(\Gamma_{sp}\) — occupied sites per area (or a count)
  • \(\Gamma_s\) — free sites per area (or a count)
  • \(\Gamma_{max} = \Gamma_s + \Gamma_{sp}\) — all sites per area (or the total count)

How it is used

§2.1 mints it as the quantity the three rules share, after the "one surface, switched on" bench runs one-way doors, revolving doors and stacking side by side and deposits each rule's steady \(\theta\) against \(C\). With one site, \(\theta\) is the fraction of time that site is occupied; with two hundred, it is a fraction of sites at one instant, and the 24-site chip shows the flicker of Week 2's √N census noise. Every model in Tab 2 is an equation for \(\theta\); Tab 3 treats \(N_s\theta\) as the count a cell decides on, and §3.7 prices its flicker.

Comes back: —

Biological exampleE. coli's 1,200 receptors at half occupancy

E. coli swims in aspartate at its receptor's \(K_D\) (5 µM), so \(\theta = 0.5\). What does that number look like for one receptor over time, and for the whole cell at one instant?

  1. One receptor: bound for a mean \(1/k_{off}\) = 1 s, then free for a mean \(1/k_{on}C\) = 1 s (at \(K_D\), \(k_{on}C = k_{off}\)).
  2. So its \(\theta\) is a time fraction: 1 s/(1 s + 1 s) = 0.5.
  3. Whole cell at one instant: \(N_s\theta = 1200 \times 0.5 = 600\) receptors bound.
  4. Census flicker: \(\sqrt{N_s\theta(1-\theta)} = \sqrt{300} ≈ 17\) receptors.
  5. As a fraction: \(\theta = 0.500 \pm 0.014\).
  6. The neutrophil's 53,000 at the same \(\theta\): 26,500 ± 115 bound, or \(\theta = 0.500 \pm 0.002\).

What it means. Same \(\theta\), two very different instruments. One snapshot of E. coli wobbles by 1.4 %, the neutrophil's by 0.2 %, and that difference drives most of Tab 4's story.

Mechanical analogya bike-share dock

A bike-share station is a row of docks with latches. Its app shows one number, and that number is exactly \(\theta\): bikes docked over docks in total.

In the cellIn the machine
sitedock
occupied site, counted in \(\Gamma_{sp}\)docked bike
free site, counted in \(\Gamma_s\)empty dock
\(\Gamma_{max}\)docks in the station
\(\theta\) over time, one sitefraction of the day one dock is full
\(\theta\) at an instant, many sitesthe app's fill fraction

A 20-dock station with 15 bikes reads \(\theta = 0.75\). Watch one dock all day and it is full about 18 of 24 hours, the same 0.75. If docks filled independently, the station's count would wobble by \(\sqrt{20 \times 0.75 \times 0.25} ≈ 1.9\) bikes, ±0.10 in \(\theta\): the sim's 24-site chip.

Where it breaks. Docks are not independent: the morning rush fills or empties them all together, so the real wobble is larger than √N. Receptors flip independently, driven by the bath, not by a commute.

3.2.2

One-way doors — the filling rate

Minted in Week 3 §2.2 · One-way doors: a surface that fills and forgets · open the module

eq. 3.2.2$$\frac{d\theta}{dt} = k_{on}\,C\,(1-\theta)$$

Letters

  • \(\theta\) — fraction of sites occupied
  • \(t\) — time · s
  • \(k_{on}\) — association rate constant per site · m³/s
  • \(C\) — concentration, held constant and the same at the surface as in bulk · #/m³
  • \(1-\theta\) — the fraction of sites still open

How it is used

§2.2 gets it from the master equation (eq. 3.1.9) with \(k_{off} = 0\), \(k_{cat} = 0\) and \(C_s = C\). On §2.1's bench the one-way chip at 1 nM and at 30 nM both climb to \(\theta = 1\); the higher concentration only gets there sooner, so the deposits lie on a flat line at 1. The module's test for when to use it is \(k_{off}t_{\text{obs}} \ll 1\): covalent bonds, very tight capture on a short assay, proteins fouling bare plastic. Integrated from an empty surface it gives eq. 3.2.3.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea neutrophil's receptors over a 10-second glance

fMLP appears at 1 nM around a neutrophil whose receptors are empty. Over the first ten seconds, may we ignore release, and how fast do the receptors fill?

  1. Fill rate per open receptor: \(k_{on}C = (0.028)(0.602) ≈ 0.0169\) s⁻¹.
  2. One-way test: \(k_{off}t_{\text{obs}} = (0.010)(10) = 0.1 \ll 1\). Release is negligible on this clock.
  3. Empty surface: \(d\theta/dt = 0.0169 \times (1 - 0)\), about 1.7 % of receptors per second.
  4. As a count: 0.0169 × 53,000 ≈ 890 receptors per second.
  5. By 10 s (\(\theta ≈ 0.155\), from eq. 3.2.3) the rate has slowed to \(0.0169 \times 0.845 ≈ 0.0143\) s⁻¹.
  6. Over a 10-minute watch, \(k_{off}t_{\text{obs}} = 6\). Not one-way: Langmuir is needed.

What it means. Whether a door is one-way depends on your clock, not on the bond. For its first glance, the neutrophil's receptor is a one-way door filling ~900 receptors a second; on the clock of a crawl it is a revolving door.

Mechanical analogya muffin tin under a ball hopper

Hold a 24-cup muffin tin under a hopper that rains balls evenly. A ball landing in an empty cup stays. A ball landing on a full cup bounces away. The tin fills at the rain per cup times the number of empty cups, so it slows as it fills.

In the cellIn the machine
sites24 cups
\(k_{on}C\)balls landing per cup per second
\(1 - \theta\)fraction of cups still empty
\(d\theta/dt\)cups filled per second, ÷ 24
\(k_{off} = 0\)nothing ever lifts a ball out

At 0.05 balls per cup per second, the empty tin fills at 24 × 0.05 = 1.2 cups/s; with 18 cups full, at 6 × 0.05 = 0.3 cups/s. A heavier rain fills it sooner, never fuller.

Where it breaks. A ball that bounces off a full cup is gone. A ligand refused by an occupied receptor stays nearby and touches again, so in water the refused molecules are delayed, not lost.

3.2.3

One-way filling — the concentration lives in the clock

Minted in Week 3 §2.2 · One-way doors: a surface that fills and forgets · open the module

eq. 3.2.3$$\theta(t) = 1 - e^{-k_{on}C\,t}$$

Letters

  • \(\theta(t)\) — occupancy at time \(t\), starting from an empty surface
  • \(k_{on}\) — association rate constant · m³/s
  • \(C\) — concentration, held constant · #/m³
  • \(t\) — time since the ligand appeared · s; \(1/k_{on}C\) is the filling time constant

How it is used

§2.2 integrates eq. 3.2.2 from \(\theta(0) = 0\). It says what the one-way chip showed: every one-way surface ends at \(\theta = 1\), and \(C\) appears only in the exponent. The worked example times a capture chip to 90 % (64 min at 1 nM, 6.4 min at 10 nM). §2.5's ruler table files it as the model whose steady state reports nothing; only a timed reading, caught mid-fill, carries \(C\).

Comes back: —

Biological examplean antibody coating a bacterium

An antibody that does not let go on a ten-minute clock (the module's "nM antibodies on a 10-minute assay") coats the antigens on a bacterium. Take the module's typical per-site \(k_{on} = 10^{-3}\) µm³/s and an antibody concentration of 10 nM (illustrative), in excess, so it is not used up. When are the antigens 30 %, 84 % and 95 % covered?

  1. \(C\) = 10 nM = 6.02 µm⁻³, so \(k_{on}C = 6.02\times10^{-3}\) s⁻¹.
  2. Time constant: \(1/k_{on}C ≈ 166\) s.
  3. After 1 min: \(\theta = 1 - e^{-0.36} ≈ 0.30\).
  4. After 5 min: \(\theta = 1 - e^{-1.81} ≈ 0.84\).
  5. To 95 %: \(t_{95} = \ln 20/k_{on}C ≈ 3.0/(6.02\times10^{-3}) ≈ 500\) s, about 8.3 min.
  6. At 1 nM: ten times longer, \(t_{95}\) ≈ 83 min, long enough that the one-way test \(k_{off}t_{\text{obs}} \ll 1\) needs checking again.

What it means. Both concentrations end with the bacterium fully coated; only the time to get there differs. A phagocyte that arrives two hours later sees the same coat either way. The coat says "present", not "how much".

Mechanical analogyshot-peening coverage

Shot peening blasts a steel part with small balls until its surface is dented all over. Each spot is dented or not, and a spot hit twice is no more dented than a spot hit once: a one-way door. With impacts landing at random, the covered fraction grows as \(1 - e^{-kt}\). Peening shops call 98 % "full coverage".

In the cellIn the machine
sitepatch of surface
bound sitedented patch
\(C\)shot flow rate
\(k_{on}C\)impacts per patch per second
\(\theta(t)\)coverage

At \(k\) = 0.2 s⁻¹, full coverage takes \(t_{98} = \ln 50/0.2 ≈ 19.6\) s; at half the shot flow it takes ≈ 39 s. Either way the part ends fully covered, and the operator learns the flow rate only from the clock.

Where it breaks. A dent is a circle that overlaps its neighbours, so coverage is about area, not discrete sites. And a dent never heals, while even a tight antibody does let go eventually: "one-way" is a statement about the clock.

3.2.4

Langmuir's rate equation — fill the open, empty the full

Minted in Week 3 §2.3 · Revolving doors: Langmuir · open the module

eq. 3.2.4$$\frac{d\theta}{dt} = k_{on}\,C\,(1-\theta) \;-\; k_{off}\,\theta$$

Letters

  • \(\theta\) — fraction of sites occupied
  • \(t\) — time · s
  • \(k_{on}C\) — fill rate per open site · s⁻¹ (\(k_{on}\) in m³/s, \(C\) in #/m³)
  • \(C\) — concentration at the surface, here taken equal to the bulk
  • \(k_{off}\) — release rate per occupied site · s⁻¹

How it is used

§2.3 flips one switch of eq. 3.1.9 (\(k_{off} > 0\)) and names Langmuir's rate law, the sentence the revolving-door chip was speaking. It is linear in \(\theta\), so it relaxes exponentially (eq. 3.2.5, with its constant eq. 3.2.6) toward the balance point that becomes the isotherm (eq. 3.2.7–3.2.8), at the half-time of eq. 3.2.9. §2.5's worked example "a step up and a washout" shows the reading rises at \(k_{on}C + k_{off}\) but falls at \(k_{off}\) alone. It assumes delivery keeps up (\(C_s = C\)); Tab 3's eq. 3.3.7 multiplies it by \(\Gamma_{max}\) and evaluates it honestly at \(C_s\).

Comes back: Week 5 §3.3, as Langmuir counting clutches in the motor–clutch loop (\(n\) is the bound fraction).

Biological examplea neutrophil's receptors filling at 1 nM

fMLP steps to 1 nM around a neutrophil whose receptors are empty, and this time the release term stays. Read the two columns of the ledger at three moments.

  1. Rates: \(k_{on}C = (0.028)(0.602) ≈ 0.0169\) s⁻¹ per open receptor; \(k_{off}\) = 0.010 s⁻¹ per bound one.
  2. At \(\theta = 0\): \(d\theta/dt = 0.0169 - 0 ≈ 0.0169\) s⁻¹.
  3. At \(\theta = 0.30\): filling 0.0169 × 0.70 ≈ 0.0118, release 0.010 × 0.30 = 0.0030, net ≈ 0.0088 s⁻¹ (about 470 receptors a second).
  4. Balance, where filling equals release: \(\theta = 0.0169/(0.0169 + 0.010) ≈ 0.63\).
  5. Check at \(\theta = 0.63\): filling 0.0169 × 0.37 ≈ 0.0063, release 0.010 × 0.63 ≈ 0.0063. Net zero.

What it means. The rate equation is a two-column ledger. At first it is all filling; as the receptors fill, the filling column shrinks and the release column grows, and the reading stops at 63 % where they cross. Release is why the surface does not go deaf: the balance point moves when \(C\) moves.

Mechanical analogya parking garage

A garage with 400 spaces sits on a busy street. Each free space is claimed at a rate set by the passing traffic, and each parked car leaves at its own pace whatever the traffic does. Cars in per minute are the claim rate per free space times the free spaces; cars out are the leaving rate times the parked cars.

In the cellIn the machine
sites400 spaces
\(\theta\)fraction of spaces taken
\(C\)traffic past the entrance
\(k_{on}C\)rate one free space is claimed
\(k_{off}\)rate one parked car leaves

Say each free space is claimed at 0.05 per minute and a car stays 2 h on average (\(k_{off}\) = 1/120 per minute). At opening, 20 cars a minute come in and none leave. At 200 parked: 10 in, 1.67 out. It settles at \(0.05/(0.05 + 0.0083) ≈ 0.86\) full, 343 cars, with ≈ 2.9 cars a minute each way.

Where it breaks. Drivers who find the garage nearly full may circle and try again, and departures follow the clock (offices close at five). A receptor's release rate is the same at every hour, and a refused peptide simply diffuses on.

Featured in HW2 · Microscope
3.2.5

Langmuir's solution — exponential relaxation to the balance point

Minted in Week 3 §2.3 · Revolving doors: Langmuir · open the module

eq. 3.2.5$$\theta(t) = c_1\,e^{-(k_{on}C + k_{off})\,t} + \frac{k_{on}C}{k_{on}C + k_{off}}$$

Letters

  • \(\theta(t)\) — occupancy at time \(t\) (s)
  • \(c_1\) — the starting gap, fixed by eq. 3.2.6
  • \(k_{on}C + k_{off}\) — the relaxation rate, how fast a site changes its mind · s⁻¹
  • \(k_{on}C/(k_{on}C + k_{off})\) — the balance point \(\theta^\ast\), the steady occupancy

How it is used

§2.3's derivation collects the \(\theta\) terms of eq. 3.2.4, finds the fixed point, and substitutes \(\phi = \theta - \theta^\ast\) to leave \(d\phi/dt = -k\phi\). The rate is the one the revolving-door chip measured, faster at higher \(C\). §2.5's worked example times a rise to 30 % with it (22 s). Its constant is eq. 3.2.6, its \(t \to \infty\) limit the isotherm (eq. 3.2.8), its half-time eq. 3.2.9.

Comes back: —

Biological exampleE. coli swims up a 20 % rise

Tab 4 says a 20 µm run up the gradient raises the aspartate concentration by about 20 %. Treat it as a step from \(C = K_D\) to \(1.2\,K_D\). How much of the change have E. coli's receptors registered half a second later?

  1. Rates: \(k_{off}\) ≈ 1 s⁻¹, and at \(K_D\) \(k_{on}C = k_{off}\), so after the step \(k_{on}C\) = 1.2 s⁻¹.
  2. Start \(\theta_0 = 0.5\); new balance \(\theta^\ast = 1.2/2.2 ≈ 0.545\).
  3. Gap (eq. 3.2.6): \(c_1 = 0.5 - 0.545 ≈ -0.045\).
  4. Relaxation rate: 1.2 + 1 = 2.2 s⁻¹.
  5. At \(t\) = 0.5 s: \(\theta = 0.545 - 0.045\,e^{-1.1} ≈ 0.530\), two-thirds of the change.
  6. By the end of a 1 s run: \(1 - e^{-2.2} ≈ 89\) % of the change.

What it means. The receptors register a change within the run that caused it, so occupancy always says where the cell is now. The 4.5-point rise is the whole signal; comparing it with the recent past is the job of the circuit downstream (§4.3).

Mechanical analogya leaky tyre on a compressor hose

Connect a slowly leaking tyre to a compressor through a narrow hose. Air flows in at a rate proportional to the pressure still missing, \(P_s - P\), and leaks out at a rate proportional to \(P\). At gentle flows both are close to linear, so the pressure climbs exponentially to a balance below the supply.

In the cellIn the machine
\(\theta\)tyre pressure over supply pressure, \(P/P_s\)
\(k_{on}C\)hose fill rate (per minute)
\(k_{off}\)leak rate (per minute)
\(\theta^\ast\)balance pressure
\(c_1\)starting gap, e.g. a flat tyre

With a 3.0 bar supply, a hose rate of 0.5 per minute and a leak of 0.1 per minute, the tyre heads for 3.0 × 0.5/0.6 = 2.5 bar at 0.6 per minute; from flat it reaches ≈ 1.75 bar in 2 min. Open the hose valve to 1.0 per minute and it heads higher (≈ 2.7 bar) and faster (1.1 per minute). Opening the valve is raising \(C\).

Where it breaks. Air through a valve is only roughly linear in the pressure difference, and the tyre's volume changes a little as it fills. The receptor's two terms are exactly linear in \(\theta\), so its relaxation is exactly exponential.

3.2.6

The starting gap — c₁ from θ₀

Minted in Week 3 §2.3 · Revolving doors: Langmuir · open the module

eq. 3.2.6$$c_1 = \theta_0 - \frac{k_{on}C}{k_{on}C + k_{off}} \qquad\text{(from } \theta(0) = \theta_0\text{, with } C \text{ held constant)}$$

Letters

  • \(c_1\) — the starting gap: initial occupancy minus the balance point; its sign says which way the reading will move
  • \(\theta_0\) — occupancy at \(t = 0\)
  • \(k_{on}C/(k_{on}C + k_{off})\) — the new balance point \(\theta^\ast\)
  • \(C\) — concentration after the change, held constant · #/m³
  • \(k_{on}\), \(k_{off}\) — association rate constant (m³/s) and release rate (s⁻¹)

How it is used

§2.3 fixes the constant of eq. 3.2.5 by setting \(t = 0\). An empty surface has \(c_1 = -\theta^\ast\), the rise in §2.5's worked example; a surface already above its new balance has \(c_1 > 0\) and falls, as in that example's washout. The constant carries how far, and which way, the change surprised the surface; the exponential carries how fast it recovers.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea neutrophil's bath switched up, then down

In a chamber, a neutrophil's fMLP bath is switched between 0.6 nM (\(C = K_D\) = 0.36 µm⁻³, \(\theta = 0.5\)) and 0.15 nM (\(0.25\,K_D\) = 0.09 µm⁻³, \(\theta = 0.2\)). Compare the two switches.

  1. Up, 0.25 → 1 \(K_D\): \(c_1 = 0.20 - 0.50 = -0.30\).
  2. Its rate: \(k_{on}C + k_{off} = (0.028)(0.36) + 0.010 ≈ 0.020\) s⁻¹.
  3. After 60 s: \(\theta = 0.50 - 0.30\,e^{-1.2} ≈ 0.41\); 30 % of the gap is left.
  4. Down, 1 → 0.25 \(K_D\): \(c_1 = 0.50 - 0.20 = +0.30\).
  5. Its rate: \((0.028)(0.09) + 0.010 ≈ 0.0125\) s⁻¹.
  6. After 60 s: \(\theta = 0.20 + 0.30\,e^{-0.75} ≈ 0.34\); 47 % of the gap is left.

What it means. The two surprises are the same size with opposite signs, but the cell hears good news faster than bad. The clock contains \(C\), and at the lower concentration it runs on little more than \(k_{off}\).

Mechanical analogya stirred tank being flushed

A well-stirred tank of dyed water is fed with water of a new dye strength and overflows at the same rate. Its strength moves exponentially from where it started toward the feed's, and the starting gap, tank minus feed, is the whole size of the change.

In the cellIn the machine
\(\theta_0\)starting dye strength
\(\theta^\ast\)feed strength
\(c_1 = \theta_0 - \theta^\ast\)starting gap
\(k_{on}C + k_{off}\)flush rate, flow ÷ volume

A 100 L tank fed 10 L/min flushes at 0.1 per minute. Start at 0.5 with a feed of 0.2: \(c_1 = +0.3\), and after 10 min the tank reads \(0.2 + 0.3e^{-1} ≈ 0.31\). Start at 0.2 with a feed of 0.5: \(c_1 = -0.3\), and it reads ≈ 0.39.

Where it breaks. The tank flushes at the same rate in both directions, because its clock is flow over volume and does not care where it is heading. The receptor's clock contains \(C\), so its two directions run at different speeds.

Featured in HW2 · Problem 1(a)
3.2.7

The equilibrium constant — K_eq, and K_D upside down

Minted in Week 3 §2.3 · Revolving doors: Langmuir · open the module

eq. 3.2.7$$K_{eq} = \frac{k_{on}}{k_{off}} \qquad\text{(units of volume; } 1/K_{eq} \text{ is a concentration — biochemists call it } K_D\text{)}$$

Letters

  • \(K_{eq}\) — equilibrium constant · m³ (µm³)
  • \(k_{on}\) — association rate constant · m³/s
  • \(k_{off}\) — dissociation rate · s⁻¹
  • \(K_D = 1/K_{eq}\) — the concentration at half occupancy · #/m³ or M · 1 nM = 0.6022 µm⁻³

How it is used

§2.3 folds the two rate constants into one as \(t \to \infty\), so the isotherm (eq. 3.2.8) reads cleanly. The revolving-door chip asks you to find the \(C\) where \(\theta = ½\) and compare it with \(k_{off}/k_{on}\). Tab 4's cast table runs it backward, \(k_{off} = k_{on}/K_{eq}\), to get the neutrophil's 0.010 s⁻¹ from Sklar's \(K_D\) and \(k_{on}\). §2.7 sets \(K_M\) beside it, and §3.6 prices it: a fast \(k_{off}\) buys a quick reading at the cost of a weaker bond.

Comes back: —

Biological exampletwo receptors, two volumes

What does \(K_{eq}\) mean as a volume, for the neutrophil's peptide receptor and for E. coli's aspartate receptor?

  1. Neutrophil: \(K_{eq} = 0.028/0.010 = 2.8\) µm³.
  2. Its \(K_D = 1/2.8 ≈ 0.357\) µm⁻³ = 0.357/0.6022 ≈ 0.59 nM, matching Sklar's measured 0.6 nM.
  3. Read it: half occupancy when there is one peptide per 2.8 µm³, a cube about 1.4 µm on a side.
  4. E. coli: \(K_D\) = 5 µM = 5000 × 0.6022 ≈ 3,000 µm⁻³, so \(K_{eq} ≈ 3.3\times10^{-4}\) µm³.
  5. As a cube: 3.3 × 10⁵ nm³, about 69 nm on a side.
  6. Ratio: \(2.8/(3.3\times10^{-4}) ≈ 8{,}400\).

What it means. The neutrophil's receptor is half full when peptides are a micron and a half apart. The bacterium's needs an aspartate every 70 nm. Each \(K_{eq}\) is tuned to the concentrations its owner must navigate: trace peptides from a distant colony, or a nutrient at micromolar levels.

Mechanical analogya baited longline

A longline is a fishing line strung with many baited hooks. A free hook is taken at a rate proportional to how many fish are about; a hooked fish shakes loose at its own rate. The ratio of the two constants is a volume: the water per fish at which half the hooks hold a fish.

In the cellIn the machine
sitebaited hook
\(k_{on}\)volume of water a free hook "fishes" per hour
\(k_{off}\)rate a hooked fish shakes loose
\(K_{eq} = k_{on}/k_{off}\)water per fish at which half the hooks are taken
\(K_D\)fish density at which half the hooks are taken

If a free hook fishes 50 m³ of water an hour and a hooked fish shakes loose at 0.25 per hour, \(K_{eq}\) = 50/0.25 = 200 m³. Half the hooks hold a fish when there is one fish per 200 m³. A barbed hook lowers \(k_{off}\), raises \(K_{eq}\), and fills the line at thinner fish.

Where it breaks. Fish swim with purpose and may be drawn to the bait from afar; a peptide only diffuses. And a hooked fish can be eaten or the bait stripped, killing the hook, which never happens to a receptor's pocket.

Featured in HW2 · Problem 1(a), Problem 2
3.2.8

The Langmuir isotherm — the reading, and its window

Minted in Week 3 §2.3 · Revolving doors: Langmuir · open the module

eq. 3.2.8$$\theta_{eq} = \frac{K_{eq}\,C}{1 + K_{eq}\,C}$$

Letters

  • \(\theta_{eq}\) — steady occupancy
  • \(K_{eq}\) — equilibrium constant (eq. 3.2.7) · m³
  • \(C\) — concentration at the surface; the bulk value when delivery keeps up · #/m³
  • \(K_{eq}C\) — concentration in units of \(K_D\); it equals 1 at half occupancy

How it is used

§2.3 lets \(t \to \infty\) in eq. 3.2.5. This is the curve the revolving-door deposits traced: linear at \(K_{eq}C \ll 1\), half at \(C = K_D\), saturating at \(K_{eq}C \gg 1\). §2.5's ruler bench shows its slope \(d\theta/d\ln C\) peaks at ¼ per e-fold at \(K_D\), and that outside a range of roughly two decades centred on \(K_D\) the reading is pinned near 0 or 1. Every later model is read against it: BET contains it when dilute, Hill adds a steepness, Michaelis–Menten moves its midpoint. Tab 3 opens with it as \(\theta = C/(K_D + C)\) (eq. 3.3.1), §3.7 inverts it to infer \(C\), and Tab 4 applies it at the front and back of a cell (eq. 3.4.2).

Comes back: —

Biological examplehistamine on the itch nerve's H1 receptors

Week 2 left histamine at ≈ 55 µm⁻³ (≈ 90 nM) at the nerve ending. Take the H1 receptor's \(K_D\) as the ~10 nM Week 2 used as its threshold (illustrative). How full are the receptors, and how does the reading move?

  1. \(K_D\) = 10 nM = 6.02 µm⁻³, so \(K_{eq} = 1/6.02 ≈ 0.166\) µm³.
  2. At the nerve: \(K_{eq}C = (0.166)(55) ≈ 9.1\).
  3. Occupancy: \(\theta_{eq} = 9.1/10.1 ≈ 0.90\).
  4. Twice the histamine (≈ 180 nM): \(K_{eq}C ≈ 18\), so \(\theta_{eq} ≈ 0.95\).
  5. Where it has thinned to 1 nM: \(K_{eq}C ≈ 0.10\), so \(\theta_{eq} ≈ 0.09\).
  6. At exactly \(K_D\): \(\theta_{eq} = 0.5\).

What it means. At the nerve the H1 receptors are 90 % full, well past half, so the itch fires. But the reading is pinned near the top: doubling the histamine moves it by only five points. A receptor reports "how much" only within about a decade of its \(K_D\); far above it, it reports "plenty".

Mechanical analogythe parking garage at different traffic

Run 3.2.4's garage to steady state at several traffic levels. Its occupancy is \(Kx/(1 + Kx)\), where \(x\) is the traffic and \(K\) is the claim constant divided by the leaving rate.

In the cellIn the machine
\(C\)traffic past the entrance
\(K_{eq}\)claim constant ÷ leaving rate
\(K_{eq}C\)0.05 ÷ (1/120) = 6 at normal traffic
\(\theta_{eq}\)steady fraction of spaces taken
\(K_D\)the traffic that half-fills the garage

At normal traffic \(Kx\) = 6 and the garage is 86 % full; at half traffic, 75 %; at double, 92 %; at a tenth, 38 %. It is half full at one-sixth of normal traffic. From the occupancy sign, busy days and very busy days look nearly alike.

Where it breaks. A full garage turns cars away and they may queue in the street, changing the traffic it sees. Receptors never queue ligand: a refused peptide diffuses on, and the bulk is untouched as long as delivery keeps up.

3.2.9

The half-time — how fast the reading follows the world

Minted in Week 3 §2.3 · Revolving doors: Langmuir · open the module

eq. 3.2.9$$\tau_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{k_{on}C + k_{off}}$$

Letters

  • \(\tau_{1/2}\) — time to close half the gap to \(\theta_{eq}\) · s
  • \(k_{on}C + k_{off}\) — the relaxation rate of eq. 3.2.5 · s⁻¹
  • \(\ln 2\) ≈ 0.693

How it is used

§2.3 takes it from eq. 3.2.5: two half-times close 75 % of the gap and three close 88 %. §2.5's worked example gets 25 s for a receptor stepped to 1 nM. §3.2 uses it as the length of one independent glance; §3.6 makes it the second piece of fine print (a receptor whose ligand stays a minute cannot report a change faster than about a minute); §3.7's correlation time (eq. 3.3.13) is the reciprocal of the same rate. Tab 4's ledger prices the neutrophil's reading at τ½ ≈ 35 s.

Comes back: —

Biological exampletwo readers, two clocks

How fast does each of the module's two readers register a change? E. coli: \(k_{off}\) ≈ 1 s⁻¹, with \(k_{on}C = k_{off}\) at \(K_D\). Neutrophil: \(k_{on}\) = 0.028 µm³/s, \(k_{off}\) = 0.010 s⁻¹, \(K_D\) = 0.36 µm⁻³.

  1. E. coli at \(0.1\,K_D\): \(\tau_{1/2} = 0.693/(0.1 + 1) ≈ 0.63\) s.
  2. E. coli at \(K_D\): \(0.693/2 ≈ 0.35\) s.
  3. E. coli at \(10\,K_D\): \(0.693/11 ≈ 0.063\) s.
  4. Neutrophil at \(K_D\): \(0.693/(0.028 \times 0.36 + 0.010) ≈ 0.693/0.020 ≈ 35\) s.

What it means. The bacterium's receptors settle in about a third of a second, well inside its one-second run, so its reading is always current. The neutrophil's take half a minute, which is still quick for a cell that crawls ~10 µm a minute. The hundred-fold gap is the hundred-fold gap in \(k_{off}\), paid for in affinity (eq. 3.2.7).

Mechanical analogya cistern fed from a header tank

Take 3.1.9's tank with a single drain. Its level closes half the gap to balance in \(\ln 2\) over the sum of the inlet and drain rates, so opening the inlet both raises the balance level and shortens the wait.

In the cellIn the machine
\(k_{on}C\)inlet rate (per minute)
\(k_{off}\)drain rate (per minute)
\(\theta_{eq}\)balance fill fraction
\(\tau_{1/2}\)half-time to balance

With an inlet of 0.2 per minute and a drain of 0.05 per minute, the tank balances 80 % full with \(\tau_{1/2} = 0.693/0.25 ≈ 2.8\) min. Open the inlet to 1.0 per minute: it balances 95 % full, with \(\tau_{1/2} ≈ 0.66\) min.

Where it breaks. The cistern follows its own level smoothly. A receptor population's reading carries counting noise on top of the relaxation, so "half-way" is only an average over many receptors.

3.2.10

The BET isotherm — Langmuir plus a pile

Minted in Week 3 §2.4 · Stacking: BET, or what happens when the doors are not the limit · open the module

eq. 3.2.10$$\theta_{tot} = \frac{c_B\,x}{(1-x)\,\bigl(1 + (c_B - 1)\,x\bigr)}, \qquad x = \frac{C}{C_{sat}}, \quad C_{sat} = \frac{k_{off,L}}{k_{on}}$$

Letters

  • \(\theta_{tot}\) — total coverage in monolayer equivalents, free to exceed 1
  • \(x = C/C_{sat}\) — concentration relative to saturation; for a vapour, the relative humidity
  • \(C\) — concentration of the adsorbate · #/m³
  • \(C_{sat}\) — the concentration at which landing on the pile balances leaving it, \(k_{on}C_{sat} = k_{off,L}\)
  • \(c_B = k_{off,L}/k_{off,1} = e^{(E_1 - E_L)/k_BT}\) — how much more the surface is liked than the liquid · the sim's default: 50
  • \(k_{off,1}\), \(k_{off,L}\) — release rates from the first layer and from the layers above · s⁻¹
  • \(k_{on}\) — landing rate constant, assumed the same on bare surface and on the pile · m³/s

How it is used

§2.4 keeps Langmuir's kinetics and adds one balance per layer, which sum as a geometric series. On §2.1's bench the stacking chip passes \(\theta = 1\) and refuses to stop near \(C_{sat}\): the \((1-x)\) in the denominator. The worked example finds two monolayers at \(x = 0.5\), and agreement with Langmuir to 2 % at \(x = 0.01\). §2.5's table files it as the model for non-specific layering (vapours on powders, coronas, coatings) and the one to refuse for a receptor, whose pocket holds one ligand.

Comes back: —

Biological examplewater vapour on a freeze-dried collagen sponge

A freeze-dried collagen sponge, used as a wound dressing, takes up water vapour from the air, and water can stack on water: the case BET was built for. Use the module's sim value \(c_B = 50\) (illustrative), with \(x\) the relative humidity. How many monolayers does the sponge hold?

  1. Dry room, \(x = 0.2\): \(\theta_{tot} = (50)(0.2)/[(0.8)(1 + 49 \times 0.2)] = 10/8.64 ≈ 1.16\).
  2. Langmuir for the first layer alone, \(K_{eq}C = c_Bx = 10\): \(10/11 ≈ 0.91\).
  3. Humid room, \(x = 0.8\): \(40/[(0.2)(40.2)] ≈ 5.0\) monolayers. Langmuir says 0.98.
  4. Near saturation, \(x = 0.95\): \(47.5/[(0.05)(47.55)] ≈ 20\) monolayers.

What it means. In dry air the sponge holds about one layer of water and Langmuir is nearly right. In humid air the pile is five layers deep and runs toward condensation as \(x \to 1\): the sponge is getting wet, not filling sites. A receptor can never do this.

Mechanical analogysteel washers on a magnet

Rain steel washers onto a magnet plate on a gently shaken table. The first layer is held by the magnet itself and is rarely shaken off. Washers on washers are held only by the weaker magnetism induced through the layer below, so they shake off much faster. Rain them faster than the upper layers can shed and the pile grows without limit.

In the cellIn the machine
first-layer release \(k_{off,1}\)rate a washer shakes off the magnet
upper-layer release \(k_{off,L}\)rate a washer shakes off other washers
\(c_B\)how much better the magnet holds than washers do
\(x = C/C_{sat}\)rain rate ÷ upper-layer shedding rate
\(\theta_{tot}\)washers per spot on the plate

With the magnet holding 50 times better (\(c_B = 50\)) and the rain at 80 % of the upper-layer shedding (\(x = 0.8\)), the plate carries about five washers per spot. Push \(x\) toward 1 and the pile runs away.

Where it breaks. A magnet reaches through several washers, so the first layer is not the only special one, and washers heap in cones, not flat layers. BET's ideal layers are the same cartoon.

3.2.11

The Hill isotherm — cooperative sites make a switch

Minted in Week 3 §2.6 · When sites talk to each other — Hill · open the module

eq. 3.2.11$$\theta = \frac{(K_{eq}C)^{\,n}}{1 + (K_{eq}C)^{\,n}}$$

Letters

  • \(\theta\) — fraction of sites occupied
  • \(K_{eq}\) — equilibrium constant; \(C = 1/K_{eq}\) is still the half point · m³
  • \(C\) — concentration; for oxygen, proportional to its partial pressure · #/m³
  • \(n\) — Hill coefficient, an empirical steepness: 1 is Langmuir, above 1 positive cooperativity, below 1 negative

How it is used

§2.6's ring of sixty sites lets each occupied neighbour deepen a bound molecule's well by \(J\); sweeping \(C\) at \(J\) = 0, 1.5 and 2.5 \(k_BT\) steepens the isotherm until, at 2.5 \(k_BT\), it is a switch: 10 % to 90 % in a factor of ~3. In the master equation this is switch 4b, \(k_{off} = k_{off}(\theta)\); Hill's empirical form fits the result, and the Hill plot (eq. 3.2.12) measures \(n\). The module's warning: \(n\) is a steepness, not a count, since haemoglobin has four sites and \(n ≈ 2.8\). Tab 3's switch range, \(C_{90}/C_{10} = 81^{1/n}\), is this curve's width.

Comes back: R2 §1.7 ("Month 6 — why doesn't it stop?").

Biological examplehaemoglobin unloading oxygen

Hill fitted this curve to oxygen on haemoglobin. Take \(n\) = 2.8 (module), half saturation at \(P_{50}\) ≈ 26.6 mmHg, and oxygen pressures of 100 mmHg in the lung, 40 in resting tissue and 20 in hard-working muscle (typical textbook values). Dissolved oxygen is proportional to its pressure, so \(K_{eq}C = p_{O_2}/P_{50}\). How much does each pass unload, against a Langmuir carrier with the same midpoint?

  1. Lung: \((100/26.6)^{2.8} ≈ 40.8\), so \(\theta ≈ 0.976\).
  2. Resting tissue: \((40/26.6)^{2.8} ≈ 3.13\), so \(\theta ≈ 0.758\).
  3. Working muscle: \((20/26.6)^{2.8} ≈ 0.45\), so \(\theta ≈ 0.310\).
  4. Unloaded per pass: at rest 0.976 − 0.758 ≈ 0.22 of the sites; in exercise 0.976 − 0.310 ≈ 0.67.
  5. Langmuir (\(n\) = 1, same \(P_{50}\)) gives 0.790, 0.601 and 0.429, so it unloads 0.19 at rest and 0.36 in exercise.
  6. Gain from cooperativity in exercise: 0.666/0.361 ≈ 1.85.

What it means. The steep curve loads almost fully in the lung and drops two-thirds of its cargo where muscle is starved, nearly twice what a Langmuir carrier with the same midpoint could deliver. That carrier would also leave the lung only 79 % full. Steepness turns a sensor into a delivery switch.

Mechanical analogya ring of dimples where neighbours brace each other

Space dimples around a ring so that seated marbles touch. A marble with seated neighbours is wedged in and rarely shaken out; a lone marble escapes easily. Feed marbles onto the shaken ring. At a low feed the few seated marbles are lonely and soon leave. Past a point they brace each other and the ring fills in patches: the module's ring sim, in steel.

In the cellIn the machine
haem sitedimple
oxygen at concentration \(C\)marbles, at a feed rate
neighbour coupling \(J\)bracing by a seated neighbour
\(k_{off}(\theta)\)escape rate falling as neighbours fill
Hill coefficient \(n\)steepness of fill against feed

How steep? From eq. 3.2.11, 10 % full needs \((K_{eq}C)^n = 1/9\) and 90 % needs 9, so the feed must rise \(81^{1/n}\)-fold. A ring of independent dimples (\(n\) = 1) needs 81-fold; with \(n\) = 2.8 it takes only \(81^{1/2.8} ≈ 4.8\)-fold.

Where it breaks. The marbles brace each other by contact. Haemoglobin's sites talk through a change of shape of the whole protein. Hill's \(n\) describes the steepness of both and says nothing about how.

3.2.12

The Hill plot — n is a slope you measure

Minted in Week 3 §2.6 · When sites talk to each other — Hill · open the module

eq. 3.2.12$$\log\frac{\theta}{1-\theta} = n\,\log C + n\,\log K_{eq}$$

Letters

  • \(\log\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}\) — the log of the odds that a site is occupied
  • \(\theta\) — fraction occupied
  • \(n\) — Hill coefficient, the slope of the plot
  • \(C\) — concentration (or partial pressure), plotted as \(\log C\)
  • \(K_{eq}\) — equilibrium constant; \(n\log K_{eq}\) is the intercept, and the line crosses zero log-odds at \(C = 1/K_{eq}\)

How it is used

§2.6 rearranges eq. 3.2.11 so that the exponent becomes a slope you can measure from deposited points. The ring bench's right-hand chart is this plot: a line of slope 1 for independent sites (Langmuir re-plotted), climbing above 1 as the coupling \(J\) grows. The worked example reads \(n ≈ 2.5\) from two occupancies (20 % at 2 nM, 80 % at 6 nM). The module's advice: take five points and check they are straight, because a curved Hill plot signals sites that are not equivalent, not cooperativity.

Comes back: —

Biological examplereading haemoglobin's n from two blood gases

Mixed venous blood at 40 mmHg is about 75 % saturated, and arterial blood at 100 mmHg about 97.5 % (typical textbook values). What \(n\) and what \(P_{50}\) do these two points give?

  1. Odds at 40 mmHg: 0.75/0.25 = 3, and \(\log 3 ≈ 0.477\).
  2. Odds at 100 mmHg: 0.975/0.025 = 39, and \(\log 39 ≈ 1.591\).
  3. Pressure step: \(\log(100/40) ≈ 0.398\).
  4. Slope: \(n = (1.591 - 0.477)/0.398 ≈ 2.8\).
  5. Intercept from the first point: \(\log K_{eq} = 0.477/2.8 - \log 40 ≈ -1.43\), so \(K_{eq} ≈ 0.037\) mmHg⁻¹.
  6. Half point: \(P_{50} = 1/K_{eq} ≈ 27\) mmHg.

What it means. Two routine blood-gas numbers recover the textbook \(n ≈ 2.8\) and \(P_{50} ≈ 27\) mmHg. Four sites but a slope of 2.8: \(n\) measures how steep, not how many.

Mechanical analogymeasuring the braced ring

To learn how strongly 3.2.11's marbles brace each other, you do not need a model of the bracing. Measure the fill at two feed rates, then plot the log of the odds of a filled dimple against the log of the feed. The slope is the steepness.

In the cellIn the machine
\(\theta\)fraction of dimples filled
\(C\)feed rate
\(\log\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}\)log odds that a dimple is filled
\(n\)slope of the log-odds line
a curved plotdimples that are not all alike

Say the ring is 30 % full at a feed of 1 unit and 63 % full at 2 units. The odds are 0.43 and 1.71, so \(n = \log(1.71/0.43)/\log 2 ≈ 2.0\). Add a third point: if it falls off the line, some dimples are deeper than others.

Where it breaks. The steel ring braces the same way at every feed, so its plot is straight. Haemoglobin's plot is steep only in the middle and flattens toward slope 1 at both ends, where nearly every molecule is in one shape. Read \(n\) where the data are.

3.2.13

The enzyme's scheme — a revolving door with a third exit

Minted in Week 3 §2.7 · The door that eats — Michaelis–Menten · open the module

eq. 3.2.13$$s + p \;\underset{k_{off}}{\overset{k_{on}}{\rightleftharpoons}}\; sp \;\xrightarrow{\;k_{cat}\;}\; s + q$$

Letters

  • \(s\) — a free enzyme site; \(p\) — a substrate molecule; \(sp\) — the enzyme–substrate complex; \(q\) — the product
  • \(k_{on}\) — binding rate constant · m³/s (or nM⁻¹s⁻¹)
  • \(k_{off}\) — release of the substrate unchanged · s⁻¹
  • \(k_{cat}\) — turnover: conversion to product, which frees the site · s⁻¹

How it is used

§2.7 switches on the third arrow of the master equation (case 4a). Its bench runs two hundred enzymes with \(k_{on}\), \(k_{off}\) and \(k_{cat}\) dials. The "sticky, slow" chip (\(k_{cat} \ll k_{off}\)) behaves like a Langmuir surface that now and then eats what it holds, with its midpoint at \(K_D\); the "fast turnover" chip sits below Langmuir's occupancy at every \(C\), its midpoint slid right to \(K_M\). The scheme becomes a rate equation in eq. 3.2.14 and is solved in eq. 3.2.15.

Comes back: —

Biological examplewhat happens to a bound substrate

Once bound, the complex has two exits, and the odds it leaves as product are \(k_{cat}/(k_{off} + k_{cat})\). Compare §2.7's worked enzyme (\(k_{off}\) = 0.5 s⁻¹, \(k_{cat}\) = 10 s⁻¹) with the bench's "sticky, slow" defaults (\(k_{off}\) = 2.0 s⁻¹, \(k_{cat}\) = 0.2 s⁻¹).

  1. Worked enzyme, odds of product: 10/10.5 ≈ 0.95.
  2. Its complex lasts \(1/(k_{off} + k_{cat}) = 1/10.5 ≈ 0.095\) s.
  3. Bindings per product: 1/0.95 ≈ 1.05.
  4. Sticky-slow enzyme, odds of product: 0.2/2.2 ≈ 0.09.
  5. Its complex lasts 1/2.2 ≈ 0.45 s.
  6. Bindings per product: 2.2/0.2 = 11.

What it means. The worked enzyme converts nearly everything it catches, so its bond hardly matters. The sticky-slow enzyme lets ten substrates go for every one it converts, so its occupancy is set by the bond, like a receptor's. The ratio \(k_{cat}/k_{off}\) decides whether a midpoint means affinity.

Mechanical analogyan automatic car-wash bay

A car pulls into an empty bay. Either the driver changes their mind and backs out, and the car leaves unchanged, or the wash runs and the car leaves clean. Either way the bay is free for the next car.

In the cellIn the machine
free site \(s\)empty bay
substrate \(p\)dirty car
complex \(sp\)car in the bay
\(k_{off}\)rate drivers back out
\(k_{cat}\)rate washes finish
product \(q\)clean car

A one-minute wash (\(k_{cat}\) = 1 per minute) with drivers backing out at 0.05 per minute cleans 1/1.05 ≈ 95 % of the cars that enter. A twenty-minute wash (0.05 per minute) with impatient drivers (0.5 per minute) cleans only 0.05/0.55 ≈ 9 %.

Where it breaks. A driver decides to back out, and the wash runs on a motor. The enzyme's two exits are both thermal: the bath carries the complex apart, or over the barrier to product.

3.2.14

The enzyme's occupancy balance — Langmuir with a second drain

Minted in Week 3 §2.7 · The door that eats — Michaelis–Menten · open the module

eq. 3.2.14$$\frac{d\theta}{dt} = k_{on}\,C\,(1-\theta) \;-\; (k_{off} + k_{cat})\,\theta$$

Letters

  • \(\theta\) — fraction of enzyme sites busy
  • \(t\) — time · s
  • \(k_{on}C\) — fill rate per free site · s⁻¹
  • \(C\) — substrate concentration, held constant (the initial-rate condition) · #/m³
  • \(k_{off} + k_{cat}\) — total emptying rate per busy site, by release or by conversion · s⁻¹

How it is used

§2.7 writes it as eq. 3.1.9 with \(k_{cat} > 0\): Langmuir's rate law (eq. 3.2.4) with one more way to empty a site. Setting \(d\theta/dt = 0\) gives \(\theta_{ss} = C/(C + K_M)\), and multiplying by \(k_{cat}N_s\) gives eq. 3.2.15. It explains the fast-turnover chip: the enzyme empties its own sites by working, so its occupancy sits below Langmuir's for the very same bond. §3.7 meets it from the noise side, where a third exit shortens the correlation time just as a larger \(k_{off}\) would.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea working enzyme is emptier, and quicker

§2.7's enzyme at \(C\) = 100 nM has \(k_{on}C\) = 2 s⁻¹, \(k_{off}\) = 0.5 s⁻¹ and \(k_{cat}\) = 10 s⁻¹. Compare it with the same enzyme with catalysis switched off.

  1. Working: relaxation rate 2 + 0.5 + 10 = 12.5 s⁻¹, steady \(\theta_{ss} = 2/12.5 = 0.16\).
  2. Its half-time: 0.693/12.5 ≈ 0.055 s.
  3. Catalysis off: rate 2 + 0.5 = 2.5 s⁻¹, steady \(\theta = 2/2.5 = 0.80\).
  4. Its half-time: 0.693/2.5 ≈ 0.28 s.
  5. A working enzyme that were somehow half busy: \(d\theta/dt = 2(0.5) - 10.5(0.5) = -4.25\) s⁻¹. It drains fast.

What it means. Turnover does two things. It holds the sites mostly empty (16 % against 80 %), and it makes the enzyme five times quicker to follow a change in substrate. Busy enzymes are not full enzymes.

Mechanical analogya car wash with many bays

Run 3.2.13's car wash as a business with several bays. Cars pull into free bays; busy bays empty either when a driver backs out or when a wash finishes. The fraction of bays busy settles where the two flows balance.

In the cellIn the machine
\(\theta\)fraction of bays busy
\(k_{on}C\)rate a free bay is taken
\(k_{off}\)back-out rate
\(k_{cat}\)wash completion rate
catalysis switched offthe washer breaks down

With free bays taken at 0.2 per minute, back-outs at 0.05 per minute and one-minute washes (1.0 per minute), the bays are 0.2/1.25 = 16 % busy and settle with a half-time of 0.55 min. Break the washer and only back-outs empty the bays: 0.2/0.25 = 80 % busy, with a half-time of 2.8 min.

Where it breaks. A broken car wash soon loses its customers, so the traffic changes. Here the substrate concentration is held fixed, a reservoir. In a real assay the enzyme eats its substrate and \(C\) falls (§2.7's honesty note).

Featured in HW2 · Microscope, Problem 3(a),(c)
3.2.15

Michaelis–Menten — a saturating rate, with K_M above K_D

Minted in Week 3 §2.7 · The door that eats — Michaelis–Menten · open the module

eq. 3.2.15$$v = k_{cat}N_s\,\theta_{ss} = \frac{V_{max}\,C}{K_M + C}, \qquad K_M \equiv \frac{k_{off}+k_{cat}}{k_{on}}, \quad V_{max} \equiv k_{cat}N_s$$

Letters

  • \(v\) — rate of product formation · products per second
  • \(k_{cat}\) — turnover per busy site · s⁻¹
  • \(N_s\) — number of enzyme sites · the sim: 200
  • \(\theta_{ss}\) — the steady fraction busy, \(C/(C + K_M)\)
  • \(V_{max}\) — the plateau rate, every site busy
  • \(C\) — substrate concentration · M or #/m³
  • \(K_M\) — Michaelis constant, the substrate concentration at half the maximum rate; \(K_M = K_D(1 + k_{cat}/k_{off})\)
  • \(k_{off}\), \(k_{on}\) — release rate (s⁻¹) and binding rate constant (m³/s)

How it is used

§2.7 multiplies the busy fraction from eq. 3.2.14 by each busy site's rate. The curve has Langmuir's shape, with two differences the bench shows: the midpoint slides from \(K_D\) to \(K_M\) as \(k_{cat}\) grows, and the plateau \(V_{max} = k_{cat}N_s\) holds nothing about the bond. The worked enzyme has \(K_D\) = 25 nM but \(K_M\) = 525 nM, so it is 16 % busy where a binding assay would show 80 %. The module's rule: report \(K_M\) and \(V_{max}\) separately, and do not call a \(K_M\) a \(K_D\) until \(k_{cat}/k_{off}\) is checked. Tab 3's signalling cascades are chains of such factories.

Comes back: Week 4 §2.3, as a motor's cycle rate against ATP, with ATP as the substrate.

Biological examplewhy the liver clears alcohol at a constant rate

Liver alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) turns ethanol into acetaldehyde. Its \(K_M\) for ethanol is about 1 mM (typical; the isoforms span roughly 0.05–4 mM). After a few drinks the blood alcohol is 0.08 g/dL, and the body clears about 0.015 g/dL per hour (typical). Treat the liver's ADH as one pool of \(N_s\) sites bathed at the blood concentration. Is it saturated, and when does clearance slow?

  1. Concentration: 0.08 g/dL = 0.8 g/L, ÷ 46.07 g/mol ≈ 17.4 mM.
  2. Fraction of \(V_{max}\): \(17.4/(1 + 17.4) ≈ 0.95\).
  3. So \(V_{max} ≈ 0.015/0.95 ≈ 0.016\) g/dL per hour, set by how much ADH the liver holds (\(N_s\)) and its \(k_{cat}\), not by the bond.
  4. At 0.01 g/dL (≈ 2.2 mM): \(v ≈ 0.016 \times 2.2/3.2 ≈ 0.011\) g/dL per hour, still about 69 % of \(V_{max}\).
  5. Half speed only at \(C = K_M\) ≈ 1 mM, about 0.0046 g/dL.

What it means. Over almost the whole range people drink in, \(C \gg K_M\), so ADH runs on its plateau and alcohol leaves at a nearly fixed amount per hour ("zero-order" clearance). Drinking more does not make the liver work faster. It only makes the clearing take longer.

Mechanical analogya toll plaza that saturates

A toll plaza has 10 booths, each taking 12 s per car, so it can never pass more than 50 cars a minute. In light traffic throughput rises with traffic; in heavy traffic every booth is busy and throughput sits at the limit while the queue grows.

In the cellIn the machine
\(N_s\)10 booths
\(k_{cat}\)5 cars per minute per booth
\(V_{max} = k_{cat}N_s\)50 cars per minute
\(C\)traffic density on the approach
\(K_M\)the traffic that gives 25 cars per minute
\(v\)cars through per minute

Say \(K_M\) is 10 cars per km of approach. At 5 cars/km the plaza passes 50 × 5/15 ≈ 16.7 cars a minute; at 10, 25; at 100, 45; at 200, 48. Doubling heavy traffic barely moves the throughput, like ADH at 0.08 g/dL.

Where it breaks. Traffic piles up behind a saturated plaza, so the approach density is not held constant; the enzyme's substrate here is a reservoir. And a driver who finds every booth busy waits in line, while a substrate that finds every enzyme busy just diffuses on.

Module Tab 3 · From Reading to Fate
3.3.1

The reading — a cell's response is a function of its occupancy

Minted in Week 3 §3.1 · What the cell reads · open the module

eq. 3.3.1$$R = g(\theta), \qquad \theta = \frac{C}{K_D + C}$$

Letters

  • \(R\) — the cell's response: secretion, transcription, crawling · whatever unit the response is measured in
  • \(g\) — the map from occupancy to response. The simplest is proportional, a dimmer · —
  • \(\theta\) — the fraction of the cell's \(N_s\) receptors occupied right now · dimensionless, 0 to 1. The cell's only input is the count \(N_s\theta\)
  • \(C\) — the ligand concentration around the cell · nM or molecules/µm³ (1 nM = 0.6022 µm⁻³) · sim default 10 nM
  • \(K_D\) — the receptor's dissociation constant, \(k_{off}/k_{on} = 1/K_{eq}\): the concentration at half occupancy · nM · sim default 10 nM

How it is used

§3.1 opens Tab 3 with it: a cell never sees a concentration, only how many of its receptors are full. The "One cell, one reading" sim gives one cell 1,000 receptors and lets them flicker. Its deposits trace Tab 2's Langmuir isotherm (eq. 3.2.8, written here with \(K_D\)): gentle, 81-fold in \(C\) from 10 % to 90 % full, with a flicker that shrinks as \(1/\sqrt{N_s}\). The rest of the tab asks what \(g\) can be: a step (eq. 3.3.2–3.3.3), a front–back comparison (eq. 3.3.4), a steep cascade (eq. 3.3.5), and a step laid along a gradient (eq. 3.3.6).

Comes back: C1 §2.2 and R2 §1.3 (the occupancy, in the "the signal is everywhere" paradox of the lung and wound cases).

Biological examplethe itch nerve reads the histamine cloud

Week 2 put the bite's histamine at about 90 nM at the nerve ending, 120 µm from the mast cell. What does the nerve actually read? Give its H1 receptors \(K_D\) = 10 nM (the §3.1 sim's default; illustrative), give it 1,000 of them, and let \(g\) be a plain dimmer.

  1. At the nerve: \(C\) = 90 nM, \(K_D\) = 10 nM.
  2. Occupancy: \(\theta = 90/(10 + 90) = 0.90\).
  3. The count: \(N_s\theta = 1000 \times 0.90 = 900\) receptors full.
  4. Its flicker (a binomial count, Week 2's √N): \(\sqrt{N_s\theta(1-\theta)} = \sqrt{90} \approx 9.5\).
  5. Dimmer response: \(R = 0.90\) of the maximum.
  6. Where the window starts: \(\theta = 0.10\) at \(C = K_D/9 = 1.1\) nM. From 1.1 to 90 nM is 81-fold.
  7. Double the histamine to 180 nM: \(\theta = 180/190 = 0.95\).

What it means. The nerve sits at the top of its useful window: 90 nM is exactly where a 10 nM receptor reaches 90 % full. Doubling the histamine moves the reading only from 0.90 to 0.95. The receptor reports "a lot" clearly but can barely tell "a lot" from "far too much".

Mechanical analogyan egg crate on a shaker table, on a scale

A crate with 1,000 dimples sits on a shaker table, with a weighing scale under it. Ping-pong balls rain down on it. A ball that lands in an empty dimple settles; one that lands on a full dimple bounces away. The shaking knocks each seated ball out now and then, at random. The scale's needle shows how many balls are seated. That needle is \(R\), and the way the dial is marked is \(g\).

In the cellIn the machine
\(N_s\) = 1,000 receptors1,000 dimples
arrivals per free receptor, \(k_{on}C\)balls landing per empty dimple per second (the pour)
unbinding, \(k_{off}\)the shake knocking a seated ball out, once per 10 s on average
\(K_D\)the pour that half-fills the crate: 0.1 ball per dimple per second
occupancy \(\theta\)the fraction of dimples holding a ball
response \(R = g(\theta)\)the needle on the scale

Run it. With a seated ball knocked out once per 10 s, a pour of 0.1 ball per dimple per second half-fills the crate. Turn the pour up to 0.9 and \(\theta = 0.9/(0.1 + 0.9) = 0.90\): the needle reads 900 balls, wobbling by about ±9.5. To bring it down to 10 % the pour must fall to 0.011, an 81-fold change.

Where it breaks. The balls have weight and bounce, and a shaker's kicks are regular, not a thermal bath. And the crate has a scale that weighs every ball at once; a cell has no scale, only the chemistry each bound receptor sets off downstream.

3.3.2

The decision concentration — where a threshold sits on the concentration axis

Minted in Week 3 §3.2 · Deciding yes or no: a threshold · open the module

eq. 3.3.2$$C^* = K_D\,\frac{\theta^*}{1-\theta^*}$$

Letters

  • \(C^*\) — the concentration at which the cell commits · nM
  • \(K_D\) — the receptor's dissociation constant · nM · the neutrophil's formyl-peptide receptor ≈ 0.6 nM (Sklar 1984); E. coli's aspartate receptor ≈ 5 µM (Clarke & Koshland 1979)
  • \(\theta^*\) — the threshold occupancy: the cell commits when \(\theta > \theta^*\) · dimensionless · sim: ½

How it is used

§3.2 mints it by inverting the isotherm at \(\theta = \theta^*\). In the "A threshold at θ* = ½" sim, the fate lamp flips at the dashed line \(C^*\); with \(\theta^* = ½\) it sits exactly at \(K_D\), and changing \(K_D\) drags it along. The module's point: a cell picks the concentration it answers to by picking which receptor to express. The worked example puts the neutrophil's \(C^*\) at 0.6 nM. Eq. 3.3.3 then says how reliably the cell decides near \(C^*\), and §3.5 lays several thresholds along a gradient (eq. 3.3.6).

Comes back: C1 §2.2 and R2 §1.3 (the decision threshold, in the lung and wound cases).

Biological exampleone rule, two receptors

Two cells use the same rule: commit when 70 % of the receptors are full (\(\theta^*\) = 0.7, one of §3.5's flag thresholds). One is a neutrophil reading formyl peptide. The other is E. coli reading aspartate. Where does each commit?

  1. The threshold's factor: \(\theta^*/(1-\theta^*) = 0.7/0.3 = 2.33\).
  2. Neutrophil, \(K_D\) = 0.6 nM: \(C^* = 0.6 \times 2.33 = 1.4\) nM.
  3. E. coli, \(K_D\) = 5 µM = 5,000 nM: \(C^* = 5000 \times 2.33 = 11{,}700\) nM ≈ 11.7 µM.
  4. The two triggers differ by 11,700/1.4 ≈ 8,300-fold, the ratio of the \(K_D\)s.
  5. Move the threshold instead, on the neutrophil: \(\theta^*\) = 0.9 gives \(C^* = 0.6 \times 9 = 5.4\) nM.
  6. And \(\theta^*\) = 0.1 gives \(C^* = 0.6/9 = 0.067\) nM. From 0.067 to 5.4 nM is only 81-fold.

What it means. Same rule, triggers four decades apart, set entirely by the receptor. Sliding the threshold from 10 % to 90 % on one receptor covers less than two decades. To answer a concentration far from its current range, a cell changes its receptor, not its threshold.

Mechanical analogythe egg crate gets a bell

Fit the egg-crate scale of eq. 3.3.1 with an electrical contact at the 70 % mark. When the needle passes it, a bell rings. Which pour rings the bell? The half-fill pour, set by how hard the table shakes, times the contact's factor.

In the cellIn the machine
threshold \(\theta^*\) = 0.7the contact, at the 70 % mark
\(K_D\)the pour that half-fills the crate
\(C^*\)the pour that rings the bell
expressing a different receptorfitting a gentler or harder shaker

Run it. With a seated ball knocked out once per 10 s, the crate half-fills at 0.1 ball per dimple per second, and the bell rings at \(0.1 \times 2.33 = 0.23\). Fit a shaker that knocks a ball out only once per 100 s: the crate half-fills at 0.01, and the same contact rings at 0.023, ten times less pour.

Where it breaks. A receptor's \(K_D\) is set by chemistry at both ends, \(k_{off}/k_{on}\); the crate's half-fill pour is set mostly by the shake. And a contact on a wobbling needle chatters near its mark, which is exactly the band eq. 3.3.3 prices.

3.3.3

The decision band — how close to the threshold a cell can still decide

Minted in Week 3 §3.2 · Deciding yes or no: a threshold · open the module

eq. 3.3.3$$\frac{\delta C}{C} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N_s\,\theta(1-\theta)}} \qquad\text{(the band around } C^* \text{ where the fate is undecided)}$$

Letters

  • \(\delta C/C\) — the fractional half-width of the band around \(C^*\) where one glance cannot tell which side the cell is on · dimensionless
  • \(C\) — the concentration, near \(C^*\) · nM
  • \(N_s\) — receptors on the cell · count · neutrophil ≈ 53,000; E. coli ≈ 1,200; sim default 1,000
  • \(\theta\) — the occupancy there, \(\theta \approx \theta^*\) · dimensionless

How it is used

§3.2 derives it in three lines. One glance at \(N_s\) independent receptors is a binomial count with spread \(\delta\theta = \sqrt{\theta(1-\theta)/N_s}\). The isotherm's slope, \(d\theta/d\ln C = \theta(1-\theta)\), turns that into a spread in concentration. The threshold sim shows the band: at \(\theta = ½\) it is ±20 % for 100 receptors and ±2 % for 10,000. The worked example gives the neutrophil 0.9 % and E. coli 6 % in one glance. The band becomes a position error in §3.5 (eq. 3.3.6), and §3.7 narrows it by averaging past the receptors' turnover time (eq. 3.3.13–3.3.14).

Comes back: —

Biological examplehow many receptors does a T cell need?

HW2's T cell (§3.7's worked example) must notice a 15 % step in chemoattractant. Suppose it had to do it in one glance, with its threshold receptors. How many receptors would it need?

  1. Target: \(\delta C/C\) = 0.15, so \((\delta C/C)^2\) = 0.0225.
  2. Invert eq. 3.3.3: \(N_s = 1/\bigl((\delta C/C)^2\,\theta(1-\theta)\bigr)\).
  3. Threshold at half occupancy, \(\theta(1-\theta)\) = 0.25: \(N_s = 1/(0.0225 \times 0.25) \approx 180\).
  4. Threshold up at \(\theta\) = 0.9, \(\theta(1-\theta)\) = 0.09: \(N_s = 1/(0.0225 \times 0.09) \approx 490\).
  5. §3.7's fine print: a step is a difference of two readings and carries √2 more error. Double both counts: ≈ 360 and ≈ 990.

What it means. A few hundred receptors at \(K_D\) suffice for one glance at a 15 % step. Put the threshold up in the saturated shoulder and the same task costs nearly three times the receptors. A threshold near \(K_D\) is cheap precision.
