Mechanical analogya thermostat that chatters at its set point

A digital thermostat reads a temperature sensor and switches the furnace at a set point. Each reading wobbles a little. Near the set point the wobble flips the switch back and forth, and the furnace chatters. The band of room temperatures where it chatters is the sensor's wobble divided by how steeply its reading changes with temperature. That is eq. 3.3.3's structure: noise over slope.

In the cellIn the machine
one glance at the occupancy \(\theta\)one sensor reading
binomial wobble, \(\sqrt{\theta(1-\theta)/N_s}\)sensor noise, ±2 mV (illustrative)
the ruler's slope, \(\theta(1-\theta)\) per e-fold of \(C\)the sensor's slope, 10 mV per °C
the decision band \(\delta C/C\)the chatter band, ±0.2 °C
more receptors, \(N_s\)more readings averaged

Run it. Noise of ±2 mV over a slope of 10 mV/°C gives a ±0.2 °C band. Average 16 readings and the noise falls by √16 = 4, to ±0.05 °C. The cell's \(N_s\) receptors are its averaged readings, all taken at once.

Where it breaks. An engineer stops the chatter with hysteresis: one set point to switch on, a lower one to switch off, so the furnace commits and stays committed. The bare receptor reading has no such memory. It can narrow its band only with more receptors or a longer look (§3.7).

3.3.4

The direction signal — front against back, and what saturates it

Minted in Week 3 §3.3 · Deciding a direction — and what saturates it · open the module

eq. 3.3.4$$\Delta\theta = \theta(1-\theta)\,\frac{\Delta C}{C}, \qquad \frac{\text{signal}}{\text{noise}} = \frac{\Delta\theta}{2\sqrt{\theta(1-\theta)/N_s}} = \tfrac12\,\frac{\Delta C}{C}\,\sqrt{N_s\,\theta(1-\theta)}$$

Letters

  • \(\Delta\theta\) — the occupancy difference between the cell's front half and back half · dimensionless
  • \(\theta\) — the occupancy at the cell's centre · dimensionless
  • \(\Delta C/C\) — the fractional concentration difference across the cell · dimensionless · sim default 10 %
  • \(\theta(1-\theta)\) — the ruler's slope, \(d\theta/d\ln C\): ¼ at \(K_D\), about 0.01 at \(100\,K_D\) and at \(K_D/100\)
  • \(N_s\) — receptors on the whole cell, \(N_s/2\) on each half · count · neutrophil 53,000
  • signal/noise — \(\Delta\theta\) over the flicker of the difference, \(2\sqrt{\theta(1-\theta)/N_s}\), in one glance · dimensionless

How it is used

§3.3 mints it for the neutrophil's real decision: which way to crawl. In the "Front against back" sim at \(C = K_D\), with the default 10 % gradient, the front half reads about 0.025 fuller than the back and the arrow points steadily. At \(100\,K_D\) both read 0.99 and the arrow wanders; at \(K_D/100\) neither half reads anything. The worked example, with a 10 % difference and 53,000 receptors, gives a one-glance signal/noise of 5.8 at \(K_D\) and 1.1 at \(100\,K_D\). It explains Tab 0's "flooded" crowd, and Tab 4 runs it in the bite's real field as eq. 3.4.2.

Comes back: —

Biological exampleZigmond's one-percent gradient

Zigmond (1977) found that neutrophils orient to a 1 % concentration difference across the cell. How well does one glance at 53,000 receptors see it?

  1. At \(C = K_D\): \(\Delta C/C\) = 0.01, \(\theta(1-\theta)\) = 0.25.
  2. Signal: \(\Delta\theta = 0.25 \times 0.01 = 0.0025\).
  3. Noise of the difference: \(2\sqrt{0.25/53{,}000} = 0.0043\).
  4. One glance: signal/noise = 0.0025/0.0043 ≈ 0.58.
  5. Independent glances add as the square root of their number. Reaching 1 takes \((1/0.58)^2 \approx 3\) glances.
  6. Flooded ten-fold, \(C = 10\,K_D\): \(\theta\) = 0.91, \(\theta(1-\theta)\) = 0.083.
  7. Signal/noise = \(\tfrac12(0.01)\sqrt{53{,}000 \times 0.083} \approx 0.33\), so about 9 glances.

What it means. A 1 % gradient sits below one glance's noise even at the best concentration, so the cell must look about three times (§3.7 prices how long a glance lasts). Flood it ten-fold and the same gradient costs three times as many looks. At \(K_D/10\) it costs exactly the same, because \(\theta(1-\theta)\) is symmetric about \(K_D\) on a log axis.

Mechanical analogydetail in a photograph

Film records a scene in grains. Each grain either develops or not, with a probability that climbs with exposure along an S-shaped curve. An edge in the scene is a difference in exposure between two neighbouring patches. It shows up as a difference in the fraction of developed grains. In mid-grey the curve is steep and the edge is crisp. In a blown-out sky both patches are nearly all developed; in deep shadow nearly none are. Either way the edge vanishes, though it is just as sharp in the scene. The grain is the noise.

In the cellIn the machine
front and back halvestwo neighbouring patches of film
\(N_s/2\) receptors per halfgrains per patch
\(\Delta C/C\) across the cellthe edge's contrast in exposure
\(\theta(1-\theta)\), largest at \(K_D\)the film's contrast, largest at mid-grey
flooded, \(C \gg K_D\)blown highlights
tuning \(K_D\) to the fieldsetting the exposure

Run it, taking Langmuir's curve for the film's: 20,000 grains (10,000 per patch) and a 10 % edge. At mid-grey, signal/noise = \(\tfrac12(0.10)\sqrt{20{,}000 \times 0.25} = 3.5\). In the highlights, at \(\theta\) = 0.99, \(\theta(1-\theta)\) = 0.0099 and signal/noise = \(0.05\sqrt{198} = 0.70\): the edge is lost in the grain.

Where it breaks. Film's real curve has its own toe and shoulder, not Langmuir's. And an exposed grain is fixed for good, while a receptor lets go and reads again, so a cell can take another look and a photograph cannot.

3.3.5

The switch's range — steepness narrows the 10–90 % window

Minted in Week 3 §3.4 · From decision to behaviour: signalling sharpens the reading · open the module

eq. 3.3.5$$\frac{C_{90}}{C_{10}} = 81^{1/n} \qquad (81 \text{ for } n = 1;\ 3 \text{ for } n = 4;\ 1.13 \text{ for } n = 35)$$

Letters

  • \(C_{90}\), \(C_{10}\) — the concentrations giving 90 % and 10 % of the maximal response · any concentration unit; only the ratio matters
  • \(n\) — the Hill coefficient of the response, an empirical steepness (eq. 3.2.11) · dimensionless · Langmuir \(n\) = 1; haemoglobin ≈ 2.8; the frog-oocyte cascade ≥ 35

How it is used

§3.4 mints it to say how much a signalling cascade can sharpen the receptors' gentle reading. It follows from Hill's form (eq. 3.2.11): the response is 10 % and 90 % at \(C/K_D = 9^{-1/n}\) and \(9^{1/n}\). Langmuir needs 81-fold; \(n\) = 4 needs 3-fold; Ferrell and Machleder's \(n \ge 35\) for the oocyte needs 1.13, so a 13 % change in hormone flips the cell. The worked example inverts it: committing within ±10 % of the threshold needs \(n \approx 22\), beyond any binding cooperativity, so fate switches are built from cascades. The price is information: a switch can no longer tell \(0.5\,C^*\) from \(0.1\,C^*\).

Comes back: R2 §1.7 (a switch's steepness).

Biological examplehaemoglobin, a dimmer turned partway to a switch

Haemoglobin's four oxygen sites bind with \(n \approx 2.8\) (§2.6). Here \(C\) is oxygen's partial pressure, in mmHg. Take the half-saturation point at 26 mmHg (typical textbook value).

  1. Range: \(C_{90}/C_{10} = 81^{1/2.8} = 4.8\).
  2. Lower edge: \(C_{10} = 26 \times 9^{-1/2.8} = 26/2.19 \approx 12\) mmHg.
  3. Upper edge: \(C_{90} = 26 \times 2.19 \approx 57\) mmHg.
  4. The blood's own range: about 100 mmHg in the lung, about 20 mmHg in working muscle (typical).
  5. Unloaded in working muscle (eq. 3.2.11): 0.977 − 0.324 ≈ 0.65 of capacity.
  6. A Langmuir carrier (\(n\) = 1) with the same midpoint: 0.79 − 0.43 = 0.36.

What it means. \(n\) = 2.8 squeezes the 81-fold window to 4.8-fold and parks it across the range the blood actually swings through. That nearly doubles the oxygen dropped where it is needed. It is still far from Ferrell's all-or-none switch: blood must deliver in proportion, not decide.

Mechanical analogyan engine's centrifugal governor

A governor holds an engine's speed by closing the throttle as the speed rises. Spinning weights swing outward and pull the throttle linkage. How far the speed must change to swing the throttle across its travel is the governor's \(C_{90}/C_{10}\).

In the cellIn the machine
concentration \(C\)engine speed
response, 10 % → 90 %throttle closing, 10 % → 90 % of its travel
\(n\) = 1, an 81-fold rangea sloppy linkage that needs a huge speed change
a cascade, \(n \ge 35\)a tight governor
\(C_{90}/C_{10} = 81^{1/n}\)the speed ratio across the throttle's travel

Run it. Suppose the throttle swings across its travel over a 5 % change in speed (illustrative of a tight governor). Read as a Hill switch, \(n = \ln 81/\ln 1.05 \approx 90\), far steeper than Ferrell's cascade. Loosen it to 10 % and \(n \approx 46\).

Where it breaks. A governor's response is roughly a straight line across its band, not a Hill curve, so its "\(n\)" is only a way of comparing. It is also a feedback loop that holds a speed, while the oocyte's cascade commits once and stays committed.

3.3.6

Positional information — a threshold laid along a gradient

Minted in Week 3 §3.5 · Position from concentration: the French flag · open the module

eq. 3.3.6$$x_i = \lambda\,\ln\frac{C_0}{C_i^*}, \qquad \delta x = \lambda\,\frac{\delta C}{C} = \frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{N_s\,\theta^*(1-\theta^*)}}$$

Letters

  • \(x_i\) — the position of fate boundary \(i\), measured from the source · µm (cell widths in the sim)
  • \(\lambda\) — the morphogen's decay length, \(\sqrt{D\tau}\) (eq. 2.3.7) · µm · sim default 6 cell widths; Bicoid ≈ 100 µm
  • \(C_0\) — the morphogen concentration at the source · nM · sim default \(100\,K_D\)
  • \(C_i^*\) — the threshold concentration for boundary \(i\), from eq. 3.3.2 · nM
  • \(\delta x\) — the jitter in a boundary's position · µm
  • \(\delta C/C\) — one glance's decision band (eq. 3.3.3) · dimensionless
  • \(N_s\) — receptors (or binding sites) per cell · count · sim default 300
  • \(\theta^*\) — the threshold occupancy · sim's flag: 0.7 and 0.3

How it is used

§3.5 puts Wolpert's French flag in the week's symbols. A cell at \(x\) reads \(C_0e^{-x/\lambda}\) and switches fate where that equals \(C_i^*\). In the "Forty cells read one gradient" sim, boundaries fall on the dashed \(\lambda\ln(C_0/C_i^*)\). Doubling the source slides every boundary by \(\lambda\ln 2\), raising \(\lambda\) stretches the flag, and \(N_s\) = 30 makes the edges ragged by \(\lambda\,\delta C/C\). The worked example places a Bicoid boundary to about one nucleus (\(\delta x \approx 10\) µm) with about 400 independent binding events.

Comes back: —

Biological exampletwo stripes from one Bicoid gradient

Take the module's fly embryo: \(\lambda\) ≈ 100 µm, nuclei about 8 µm apart. Suppose two target genes read Bicoid with thresholds at \(\theta^*\) = 0.7 and 0.3 (the sim's flag), and the anterior tip sits at \(C_0 = 20\,K_D\) (illustrative). Where do the boundaries fall?

  1. Thresholds (eq. 3.3.2): \(C_1^* = K_D(0.7/0.3) = 2.33\,K_D\); \(C_2^* = K_D(0.3/0.7) = 0.43\,K_D\).
  2. First boundary: \(x_1 = 100\ln(20/2.33) = 100 \times 2.15 \approx 215\) µm.
  3. Second boundary: \(x_2 = 100\ln(20/0.43) = 100 \times 3.84 \approx 384\) µm.
  4. The stripe between them: 384 − 215 ≈ 169 µm \(= \lambda\ln(49/9)\), whatever \(C_0\) is.
  5. Jitter, with 400 independent sites per nucleus: \(\delta x = 100/\sqrt{400 \times 0.21} \approx 11\) µm, one to two nuclei.
  6. Double the dose: both boundaries move \(100\ln 2 \approx 69\) µm posteriorly. The stripe keeps its 169 µm.

What it means. In a 500 µm embryo, two thresholds on one gradient cut a stripe a third of the embryo wide, with edges sharp to about a nucleus. Dose moves the stripe; only \(\lambda\) and the two thresholds set its width.

Mechanical analogya wax-coated rod with one end in boiling water

Hold one end of a long copper rod (radius 3 mm) in boiling water, in still room air at 20 °C. Heat spreads along the rod by the same law as Fick's, with temperature in place of concentration. It also leaks out of the rod's sides into the air, and that leak plays clearance. At steady state the rod's temperature above the room falls as \(e^{-x/\lambda}\). Coat it in two waxes, one melting at 70 °C and one at 50 °C, and you get three bands: a French flag on a rod.

In the cellIn the machine
the source, \(C_0\)the hot end, 80 K above the room
clearance, lifetime \(\tau\)heat leaking out through the rod's sides
\(\lambda = \sqrt{D\tau}\)√(conductivity × radius / (2 × surface-loss coefficient))
thresholds \(C_i^*\)the waxes' melting points, 50 K and 30 K above the room
boundaries \(x_i\)the melt lines
doubling the sourceraising the hot end to 160 K above the room

Run it. Copper conducts about 400 W/(m·K), and still air takes about 10 W/(m²·K) from a surface (both typical). So \(\lambda = \sqrt{400 \times 0.003/(2 \times 10)} \approx 0.245\) m. The 70 °C wax melts out to \(0.245\ln(80/50) \approx 0.115\) m; the 50 °C wax to \(0.245\ln(80/30) \approx 0.24\) m. Heat the end in oil at 180 °C and both lines move out by \(0.245\ln 2 \approx 0.17\) m, keeping their 0.125 m gap.

Where it breaks. The melt line is razor-sharp because the rod's temperature is an average over some 10²³ atoms: there is no counting noise, so \(\delta x \approx 0\). The embryo's boundary is only as sharp as a few hundred binding events allow. And the rod must be several \(\lambda\) long for the simple exponential to hold.

3.3.7

The relay's flux balance — delivery equals uptake

Minted in Week 3 §3.6 · Fine print: is the reading honest, and how fast is it? · open the module

eq. 3.3.7$$J = k_m\,(C - C_s) \;=\; k_{on}\,C_s\,(\Gamma_{max} - \Gamma_{sp}) \;-\; k_{off}\,\Gamma_{sp}$$

Letters

  • \(J\) — molecules crossing the film per area per second, which equals the net uptake by the surface · µm⁻² s⁻¹
  • \(k_m\) — the mass-transfer coefficient, the delivery speed (eq. 3.3.8) · µm/s
  • \(C\) — the bulk concentration · µm⁻³
  • \(C_s\) — the concentration in the liquid touching the surface · µm⁻³
  • \(k_{on}\) — the per-site association rate constant · µm³/s
  • \(\Gamma_{max}\) — total sites per area · µm⁻²
  • \(\Gamma_{sp}\) — occupied sites per area, so \(\theta = \Gamma_{sp}/\Gamma_{max}\) · µm⁻²
  • \(k_{off}\) — the dissociation rate · s⁻¹

How it is used

§3.6 opens Tab 3's fine print with it. The rules of §3.1–3.5 assumed the receptors feel the bulk \(C\); a surface that eats faster than diffusion feeds it does not. In steady operation the molecules crossing the film must be the molecules taken up, because there is nowhere else for them to go. The right side is Langmuir's rate equation (eq. 3.2.4) times \(\Gamma_{max}\), evaluated honestly at \(C_s\); the left side is Fick's first law across the film (eq. 1.3.5 again). Setting \(\Gamma_{sp} = 0\) gives the referee and the fresh surface's \(C_s\) and \(J\) (eq. 3.3.9–3.3.11); as the surface fills, the working Damköhler number falls to \(\mathrm{Da}(1-\theta)\).

Comes back: —

Biological example§3.6's bacterium, part-way through filling

§3.6's worked example puts 10⁵ receptors for a peptide on a 1 µm bacterium, with \(D\) = 500 µm²/s, \(k_{on}\) = 0.03 µm³/s, \(k_{off}\) = 0.01 s⁻¹. Fresh, it reads \(C_s\) = 0.68 \(C\). What does it read later, at \(\theta\) = 0.3, with the peptide at 1 nM (0.602 µm⁻³)?

  1. Sites: \(\Gamma_{max} = 10^5/(4\pi \times 1^2) = 7{,}960\) µm⁻²; \(\Gamma_{sp} = 0.3 \times 7{,}960 = 2{,}390\) µm⁻².
  2. Delivery speed: \(k_m = D/a = 500\) µm/s.
  3. Uptake speed of the open sites: \(k_{on}\Gamma_{max}(1-\theta) = 0.03 \times 7{,}960 \times 0.7 = 167\) µm/s.
  4. Release: \(k_{off}\Gamma_{sp} = 0.01 \times 2{,}390 = 23.9\) µm⁻² s⁻¹.
  5. Balance: \(500(0.602 - C_s) = 167\,C_s - 23.9\), so \(C_s = (301 + 23.9)/667 = 0.487\) µm⁻³.
  6. Reading: \(C_s/C\) = 0.81.
  7. Flux: \(J = 500 \times (0.602 - 0.487) = 57.5\) µm⁻² s⁻¹, about 720 molecules/s for the cell.

What it means. Part-way to full, the cell's receptors feel 81 % of the bulk instead of 68 %: filled sites stop eating and bound ones hand some ligand back. At equilibrium (\(\theta\) = 0.64 here) the net flux is zero and \(C_s = C\) exactly. The relay matters while the surface is filling, which is when a cell most needs its reading.

Mechanical analogya row of cisterns on one supply pipe

A street main feeds a building through one service pipe into a manifold. The manifold feeds a row of toilet cisterns, each through its float valve. An empty cistern's valve is wide open; a full one's is shut. Suppose each full cistern also bleeds a little water back into the manifold. The water through the service pipe equals the water into the cisterns, net of the bleed: one flow, written two ways.

In the cellIn the machine
bulk \(C\)the main's pressure
\(C_s\)the pressure in the manifold
delivery, \(k_m(C - C_s)\)flow through the service pipe, driven by the pressure drop along it
open sites, \(\Gamma_{max} - \Gamma_{sp}\)cisterns still filling, valves open
uptake, \(k_{on}C_s(\Gamma_{max} - \Gamma_{sp})\)flow into the cisterns: manifold pressure × open valves
release, \(k_{off}\Gamma_{sp}\)the bleed from full cisterns back into the manifold

When every cistern is empty at once, the manifold pressure sags; as they fill, it recovers. That is \(C_s\) rising from 0.68 \(C\) to 0.81 \(C\) and on toward \(C\).

Where it breaks. Real pipes and valves lose pressure roughly as the square of the flow, so the plumbing's balance is not linear. The cell's version is linear on both sides, which is why \(C_s\) comes out in closed form.

3.3.8

The mass-transfer coefficient — delivery as a speed

Minted in Week 3 §3.6 · Fine print: is the reading honest, and how fast is it? · open the module

eq. 3.3.8$$k_m = \frac{D}{\delta} \qquad\text{(a film)}; \qquad k_m = \frac{D}{a} \qquad\text{(a sphere of radius } a\text{, from eq. 2.3.5)}$$

Letters

  • \(k_m\) — the mass-transfer coefficient: how fast the bath replaces what the surface removes · µm/s
  • \(D\) — the ligand's diffusion coefficient · µm²/s · small peptide ≈ 500
  • \(\delta\) — the thickness of the unstirred film the ligand must cross · µm
  • \(a\) — the radius of a spherical cell · µm · neutrophil 7.5; E. coli 0.5

How it is used

§3.6 sweeps the whole geometry of delivery into one speed. For a film, Fick's first law (eq. 1.3.5 again) gives \(D/\delta\). For a sphere, Week 2's flux at contact (eq. 2.3.5) gives \(D/a\), and \(k_m \times 4\pi a^2 \times C = 4\pi D a\,C\) recovers Smoluchowski's rate (eq. 1.5.1) from the delivery side alone. In §3.6's worked example the neutrophil's \(D/a\) = 67 µm/s licenses Langmuir at the bulk \(C\), while the crowded bacterium's 500 µm/s is not enough. It is the denominator of the referee Da (eq. 3.3.9), and the module adds a warning: also check the delivery clock, \(\delta^2/D\) or \(a^2/D\).

Comes back: —

Biological examplethree cells, three delivery speeds

A small peptide, \(D\) = 500 µm²/s, reaches three different surfaces.

  1. Neutrophil, \(a\) = 7.5 µm: \(k_m = 500/7.5 = 67\) µm/s; clock \(a^2/D\) = 0.113 s.
  2. E. coli, \(a\) = 0.5 µm: \(k_m = 500/0.5 = 1{,}000\) µm/s; clock 0.5 ms.
  3. A confluent cell layer on the floor of a culture well, under 3 mm of still medium (typical): \(k_m = 500/3{,}000 = 0.167\) µm/s.
  4. Its clock: \(\delta^2/D = 3{,}000^2/500 = 18{,}000\) s, five hours.
  5. Check the sphere against Smoluchowski at 1 nM: \(67 \times 4\pi(7.5)^2 \times 0.602 = 28{,}400\) /s \(= 4\pi(500)(7.5)(0.602)\).

What it means. Smaller is faster: the bacterium's surface is refilled 15 times faster per area than the neutrophil's. The dish floor is refilled 400 times slower than the suspended neutrophil. Spread the neutrophil's receptor density (75 µm⁻², \(k_{on}\) = 0.028 µm³/s) over that layer and Da = 2.1/0.167 ≈ 12.6. The same chemistry that is reaction-limited in suspension is transport-limited in a still dish.

Mechanical analogyheat leaking through still air

Heat crossing still air obeys the same law as Fick's, with temperature for concentration. So it has its own \(k_m\): the conductance per area of a still-air slab is the air's conductivity over the slab's thickness, and around a small ball it is the conductivity over the ball's radius.

In the cellIn the machine
\(D\) = 500 µm²/sair's thermal conductivity, about 0.025 W/(m·K) (typical)
film thickness \(\delta\)the air gap in a double-glazed window, 12 mm
\(k_m = D/\delta\)the gap's conductance, 0.025/0.012 ≈ 2.1 W/(m²·K)
sphere, \(k_m = D/a\)a ball in still air: 0.025/radius
small cell, fast refilla bead of 1 mm radius: 25 W/(m²·K); a ball of 10 cm radius: 0.25

Halve the window's gap and it leaks twice as fast. The bead loses heat per area 100 times faster than the ball, for the same reason a bacterium is refilled faster than a neutrophil.

Where it breaks. Real air convects. Widen the gap past a couple of centimetres, or warm a ball bigger than a few millimetres, and rising air carries heat faster than conduction alone. The water around a cell never stirs itself at the micron scale (Week 2's Pe ≪ 1).

3.3.9

The surface Damköhler number — the referee

Minted in Week 3 §3.6 · Fine print: is the reading honest, and how fast is it? · open the module

eq. 3.3.9$$\mathrm{Da} = \frac{k_{on}\,\Gamma_{max}}{k_m} \quad\begin{cases} \ll 1 & \text{reaction-limited: doors are slow, } C_s \approx C\text{, Langmuir kinetics (eq. 3.2.4) apply as written} \\[4pt] \gg 1 & \text{transport-limited: the surface is hungry, } C_s \ll C\text{, flux saturates at } J \approx k_m C \end{cases}$$

Letters

  • \(\mathrm{Da}\) — the surface Damköhler number: the uptake speed the surface would have at the bulk concentration, over the delivery speed · dimensionless
  • \(k_{on}\) — per-site association rate constant · µm³/s
  • \(\Gamma_{max}\) — site density · µm⁻². For a sphere carrying \(N\) receptors, \(\Gamma_{max} = N/4\pi a^2\) and \(\mathrm{Da} = k_{on}N/(4\pi D\,a)\)
  • \(k_m\) — the delivery speed (eq. 3.3.8) · µm/s
  • \(C_s\), \(C\) — surface and bulk concentrations · µm⁻³
  • \(J \approx k_mC\) — the flux ceiling of a transport-limited surface · µm⁻² s⁻¹

How it is used

§3.6 names it out of the fresh-surface derivation of eq. 3.3.7. Da ≪ 1 licenses Langmuir at the bulk \(C\); Da ≫ 1 makes the surface Week 2's absorber, its flux pinned at \(k_mC\). The "Damköhler, for a sphere" sim has four chips: the neutrophil (Da ≈ 0.03), E. coli with receptors at the diffusion ceiling, a dense GPCR patch, and tobramycin on Pseudomonas (Da ≈ 10⁻⁷, which closes the review module's factor of 10⁷). The module's warning: "a dimensionless number ranks; it does not rate", so always check the clocks \(1/(k_{on}C)\) and \(a^2/D\). It licenses Tab 4's reading (§4.2: Da = 0.031) and reconciles Week 2's patchy sphere (eq. 2.4.7).

Comes back: — in a box. Week 4 §1.5 borrows its form for eq. 4.1.10, the leading edge's Damköhler number.

Biological exampleE. coli, if its receptors bound on contact

The referee's E. coli chip: \(a\) = 0.5 µm, 1,200 aspartate receptors, \(D\) = 900 µm²/s, and every receptor at the diffusion ceiling of a 1 nm pocket.

  1. Ceiling: \(k_{on} = 4\pi D a_s = 4\pi(900)(0.001) = 11.3\) µm³/s.
  2. Site density: \(\Gamma_{max} = 1{,}200/(4\pi \times 0.5^2) = 382\) µm⁻².
  3. Uptake speed: \(k_{on}\Gamma_{max} = 11.3 \times 382 = 4{,}320\) µm/s.
  4. Delivery: \(k_m = D/a = 900/0.5 = 1{,}800\) µm/s.
  5. Referee: Da = 4,320/1,800 = 2.4. Transport-limited; fresh, \(C_s = C/3.4\).
  6. Drag \(k_{on}\) two decades lower, as the sim suggests (0.113 µm³/s; the module says only that real values are "far lower" than the ceiling): Da = 0.024, \(C_s\) = 0.98 \(C\).
  7. Clocks at 1 nM: delivery \(a^2/D\) = 0.28 ms; filling \(1/(k_{on}C)\) = 0.147 s at the ceiling, 14.7 s two decades below it.

What it means. The same cell flips from hungry absorber to honest Langmuir reader on one chemistry number. Either way the clocks show delivery is near instant; what the cell waits for is sticking. The ratio said which runner is slower; only the clocks say by how much.

Mechanical analogya bottling line

A filling machine that could fill 600 bottles a minute sits at the end of a conveyor that brings 60 a minute. The ratio, 10, is the line's Damköhler number: the filler is starved.

In the cellIn the machine
\(k_{on}\Gamma_{max}\), uptake if fedthe filler's capacity, 600 bottles/min
\(k_m\), deliverythe conveyor's delivery, 60 bottles/min
\(\mathrm{Da}\)600/60 = 10
\(C_s \ll C\), a hungry surfacean empty stretch of belt in front of the filler
\(J \approx k_mC\)output ≈ what the conveyor brings

A faster filler changes nothing here; only a faster conveyor helps. Swap the machines (a 60/min filler, a 600/min conveyor, Da = 0.1) and bottles pile up waiting; now only the filler matters. And if the shop needs just 30 bottles a minute, Da = 10 is irrelevant. It ranks the two machines; it does not say either is too slow.

Where it breaks. Bottles arrive one by one and queue, and a line's output is set by the slower machine alone. Molecules diffuse, the "queue" is a depleted layer of liquid, and the cell's flux blends the two speeds smoothly, \(J = k_mC\,\mathrm{Da}/(1+\mathrm{Da})\).

3.3.10

Surface concentration of a fresh surface — what the receptors actually feel

Minted in Week 3 §3.6 · Fine print: is the reading honest, and how fast is it? · open the module

eq. 3.3.10$$C_s = \frac{k_m}{k_m + k_{on}\Gamma_{max}}\,C = \frac{C}{1 + \mathrm{Da}}$$

Letters

  • \(C_s\) — the concentration in the liquid touching a fresh surface (\(\Gamma_{sp} \approx 0\)) · µm⁻³
  • \(C\) — the bulk concentration · µm⁻³
  • \(k_m\) — the delivery speed (eq. 3.3.8) · µm/s
  • \(k_{on}\Gamma_{max}\) — the uptake speed the sites would have at the bulk concentration · µm/s
  • \(\mathrm{Da}\) — the surface Damköhler number (eq. 3.3.9) · dimensionless

How it is used

§3.6's derive box sets \(\Gamma_{sp} = 0\) in eq. 3.3.7 and solves for \(C_s\): "the sim's readout, predicted from the two speeds alone". A tie, \(C_s/C = ½\), is Da = 1 exactly. The worked example: the neutrophil reads \(C_s \approx 0.94\,C\) and may use eq. 3.2.4 with the bulk; the crowded bacterium reads 0.67 \(C\), a third low. "Fresh" matters: as the surface fills, the working Da is \(\mathrm{Da}(1-\theta)\) and \(C_s\) recovers. The equation also reconciles Week 2's patchy sphere (eq. 2.4.7): "the two ends of eq. 3.3.10". Tab 4 uses it for the neutrophil's licence, \(C_s = C/1.031\).

Comes back: — in a box. Week 4 §1.5's relay, \(G_f = G_b/(1+\mathrm{Da})\) in eq. 4.1.10, is its form.

Biological examplea dense receptor patch against the neutrophil

The referee's "dense GPCR patch" chip is a small cell, \(a\) = 1.8 µm, carrying 600 receptors per µm². Each binds at the ceiling for a 5 nm pocket, reading a protein ligand with \(D\) = 100 µm²/s.

  1. \(k_{on} = 4\pi(100)(0.005) = 6.28\) µm³/s.
  2. Uptake speed: \(6.28 \times 600 = 3{,}770\) µm/s.
  3. Delivery: \(k_m = 100/1.8 = 55.6\) µm/s.
  4. Referee: Da = 3,770/55.6 = 68.
  5. Fresh: \(C_s = C/(1 + 68) = 0.0145\,C\). The receptors feel 1.45 % of the bulk.
  6. The neutrophil chip: Da = (0.028 × 75)/(500/7.5) = 0.0315, so \(C_s = C/1.0315 = 0.97\,C\).

What it means. Fresh, the patch's 24,000 receptors bathe in about one-seventieth of the room's concentration. They fill at the rate diffusion delivers, about 70 times slower than their chemistry allows. Langmuir with the bulk \(C\) is licensed for the neutrophil to 3 %, and for the patch only once binding and release have come to balance.

Mechanical analogythe far end of an extension cord

A heater on a long, thin extension cord. The cord and the heater are two resistances in series. The voltage at the outlet is the wall voltage divided by (1 + cord resistance/heater resistance).

In the cellIn the machine
bulk \(C\)the wall voltage, 120 V
\(C_s\)the voltage at the cord's far end
delivery speed \(k_m\)the cord's conductance (one over its resistance)
uptake speed \(k_{on}\Gamma_{max}\)the heater's conductance
\(\mathrm{Da}\)cord resistance / heater resistance
\(C_s = C/(1+\mathrm{Da})\)far-end voltage = 120/(1 + Da)

Run it. A 15 m cord of 16-gauge wire has about 0.4 Ω out and back (typical), and a 1,500 W heater is 9.6 Ω. Da = 0.4/9.6 = 0.042, and the far end sits at 120/1.042 = 115 V, 4 % low; a lamp on the same cord dims a little. A thin cord feeding a big load, Da = 68, would leave 1.74 V.

Where it breaks. The heater's load is fixed, but a surface's "load" shrinks as it fills, because Da(1 − θ) falls as sites close. The circuit also has no counterpart of release, the bound ligand handed back to the film.

3.3.11

Flux of a fresh surface — stickier doors help only when the doors are slow

Minted in Week 3 §3.6 · Fine print: is the reading honest, and how fast is it? · open the module

eq. 3.3.11$$J = \frac{k_m\,C}{1 + \mathrm{Da}}\cdot\mathrm{Da} \;=\; \frac{k_{on}\Gamma_{max}\,C}{1 + \mathrm{Da}}$$

Letters

  • \(J\) — molecules taken up per area per second by a fresh surface · µm⁻² s⁻¹
  • \(k_mC\) — the transport ceiling: every molecule delivered is taken · µm⁻² s⁻¹
  • \(k_{on}\Gamma_{max}C\) — the reaction rate the sites would manage at the bulk concentration · µm⁻² s⁻¹
  • \(\mathrm{Da}\) — the surface Damköhler number (eq. 3.3.9) · dimensionless
  • \(k_m\), \(k_{on}\), \(\Gamma_{max}\), \(C\) — as in eq. 3.3.7

How it is used

§3.6 substitutes \(C_s\) back into the delivery term. Read it, the module says, as "the reaction rate you would have had, \(k_{on}\Gamma_{max}C\), knocked down by \((1+\mathrm{Da})\)". For Da ≫ 1 it is \(k_mC\), pure delivery; for Da ≪ 1 it is \(k_{on}\Gamma_{max}C\), pure reaction at the bulk. "A surface with Da = 9 binds at one-tenth of its chemistry's pace; making its receptors stickier would change nothing." That is the referee's decision, which knob is worth turning, and the referee sim's verdicts say it for each chip.

Comes back: —

Biological exampleshould a cell make stickier receptors?

§3.6's example gives two cells the same 10⁵ receptors (\(k_{on}\) = 0.03 µm³/s) and the same peptide (\(D\) = 500 µm²/s) at 1 nM (0.602 µm⁻³). Whole-cell uptake is \(J \times 4\pi a^2 = k_{on}NC/(1+\mathrm{Da})\), and \(k_{on}NC = 1{,}806\) /s.

  1. Bacterium, \(a\) = 1 µm: Da = 0.48; uptake = 1,806/1.48 = 1,220 /s.
  2. Its ceiling, as a perfect absorber: \(4\pi D a\,C = 4\pi(500)(1)(0.602) = 3{,}780\) /s.
  3. Ten-fold stickier receptors: Da = 4.8; uptake = 18,060/5.8 = 3,130 /s, only 2.6 times more.
  4. Neutrophil, \(a\) = 7.5 µm: Da = 0.064; uptake = 1,806/1.064 = 1,700 /s, 6 % of its 28,400 /s ceiling.
  5. Ten-fold stickier: Da = 0.64; uptake = 18,060/1.64 = 11,000 /s, 6.5 times more.

What it means. The bacterium already takes a third of what reaches it, so better chemistry buys little. The large neutrophil takes 6 %, so most of a ten-fold improvement goes straight through. Which knob pays depends on Da, not on how good the receptor is.

Mechanical analogysprinkler heads on one garden hose

A long hose feeds a manifold of sprinkler heads. With few heads, adding one adds nearly its full share of water. With many, the hose cannot keep up, and each new head mostly steals pressure from the others.

In the cellIn the machine
uptake, \(k_{on}\Gamma_{max}\)the heads' combined conductance
delivery, \(k_m\)the hose's conductance
\(\mathrm{Da}\)heads' conductance / hose's conductance
ceiling \(k_mC\)the flow from the hose with its end wide open
\(J = k_mC\,\mathrm{Da}/(1+\mathrm{Da})\)the total flow from the heads

Run it. If one head has half the hose's conductance (Da = 0.5), the heads deliver 0.5/1.5 = 33 % of the open-hose flow. Two heads (Da = 1): 50 %. Four (Da = 2): 67 %. Eight (Da = 4): 80 %. Doubling from four heads to eight buys a fifth more water.

Where it breaks. Water in a hose is turbulent, so pressure losses grow as the square of the flow and the clean \(1+\mathrm{Da}\) form is only approximate; diffusion's resistances are exactly linear. And a sprinkler head never fills up, while receptors do, so a cell's working Da fades as \(\theta\) rises.

3.3.12

The Berg–Purcell limit — the counting floor under every reading

Minted in Week 3 §3.7 · The counting limit — how good can any reading be? · open the module

eq. 3.3.12$$\frac{\delta C}{C} \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt N} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi D a\,C\,t_{avg}}}$$

Letters

  • \(\delta C/C\) — the fractional error in the inferred concentration · dimensionless
  • \(N\) — molecules counted in the averaging time, \(N = k_sCt_{avg}\) · count
  • \(D\) — the ligand's diffusion coefficient · µm²/s
  • \(a\) — the radius of the counting sphere · µm
  • \(C\) — the concentration · µm⁻³
  • \(t_{avg}\) — the averaging time · s
  • \(4\pi D a = k_s\) — the encounter rate constant (eq. 1.5.1) · µm³/s

How it is used

§3.7 asks whether there is a floor no cell can read below. Berg and Purcell's answer is the simplest instrument: a sphere that swallows every molecule touching it and counts. Arrivals are independent, so the count wobbles by \(\sqrt N\) (Week 2's census noise). Only size, \(D\), \(C\) and time appear; nothing about wiring. (The constant in front is model-dependent: \(3/(5\pi)\) for a sphere that watches its interior.) In the "Reading a concentration for a while" sim, "count every arrival" lands on the orange floor and falls as \(1/\sqrt{t_{avg}}\) with no plateau. The worked example is HW2's T cell: 88 molecules in a 0.25 s pause give 10.7 %. Eq. 3.3.14 prices a receptor reading against it, and eq. 3.3.15 the gap.

Comes back: Report 1 §A.1 (two resistances in series). Week 4 §4.4 also spends it in prose, for the bacterium's reading time.

Biological exampleE. coli's best possible reading in one run

E. coli (\(a\) = 0.5 µm) reads aspartate (\(D\) = 900 µm²/s, the §3.6 referee chip's value) during a run of about 1 s. Put the aspartate at 1 nM (illustrative). Even counting every molecule, how well can it know \(C\)?

  1. Encounter rate: \(4\pi D a\,C = 4\pi(900)(0.5)(0.602) \approx 3{,}400\) /s.
  2. One run, \(t_{avg}\) = 1 s: \(N \approx 3{,}400\) molecules.
  3. Floor: \(\delta C/C = 1/\sqrt{3{,}400} \approx 1.7\,\%\).
  4. The across-body task (Tab 4.3) is a 1.4 % difference. Time it needs: \(t_{avg} = 1/(3{,}400 \times 0.014^2) \approx 1.5\) s.
  5. The along-the-run task: a 20 µm run changes \(C\) by about 20 % (Tab 4.3). A difference of two readings carries \(\sqrt2 \times 1.7\,\% \approx 2.4\,\%\).

What it means. At 1 nM, physics alone forbids reading the 1.4 % front-to-back difference within one run, even with a perfect counter; no receptor design can fix that. The 20 % change along a run is more than eight times the noise. Comparing now with a second ago is not a workaround; it is the reading the floor allows.

Mechanical analogya Geiger counter

A Geiger counter measures a radioactive source by counting clicks. Decays are random and independent, so \(N\) clicks carry a ±\(\sqrt N\) wobble. That is the whole of eq. 3.3.12.

In the cellIn the machine
a perfect absorber of radius \(a\)a tube that clicks for every particle that enters
arrivals, \(4\pi D a\,C\) per secondthe click rate
\(t_{avg}\)the counting time
\(N = 4\pi D a\,C\,t_{avg}\)clicks counted
\(\delta C/C = 1/\sqrt N\)the count's relative error

Run it. A check source gives 50 clicks a second. Counted for a minute, that is 3,000 clicks, ±1.8 %. Reaching ±1 % needs 10,000 clicks: 200 s. Halving the error always costs four times the wait, which is §3.7's first design rule.

Where it breaks. Radiation flies in straight lines, so a counter catches particles in proportion to its window's area. Diffusing molecules arrive in proportion to the collector's radius (Week 2), which is why a cell gains only linearly by growing. And the Geiger tube really does count every click; a cell's receptors do not (eq. 3.3.14).

Featured in HW2 · Problem 2
3.3.13

The correlation time — how long one glance lasts

Minted in Week 3 §3.7 · The counting limit — how good can any reading be? · open the module

eq. 3.3.13$$\tau_c = \frac{1}{k_{on}C + k_{off}} = \frac{1-\theta}{k_{off}}$$

Letters

  • \(\tau_c\) — the correlation time of the receptor population: how long the occupancy takes to forget its past · s
  • \(k_{on}C\) — the rate at which an empty receptor fills · s⁻¹
  • \(k_{off}\) — the rate at which a full receptor empties · s⁻¹ · neutrophil 0.010
  • \(\theta\) — the occupancy. The second form uses equilibrium, \(k_{on}C = k_{off}\,\theta/(1-\theta)\) · dimensionless

How it is used

§3.7 mints it because a real cell does not swallow. Its receptors are §1.5's telegraph, and a receptor bound now is probably still bound a second from now, so consecutive glances are the same glance until the population turns over. \(\tau_c\) is that turnover clock: about 50 s for the neutrophil at \(C = K_D\). It is the same rate at which Langmuir relaxes (eq. 3.2.9's \(k_{on}C + k_{off}\)). In the sim the receptor reading's error is flat for \(t_{avg} < \tau_c\) and only then falls; raising \(k_{off}\) ten-fold ends the plateau sooner. Eq. 3.3.14 counts independent looks as \(t_{avg}/2\tau_c\).

Comes back: — in a box. Week 4 Tab 0 lists it among the tools it brings.

Biological examplethe neutrophil's glance, at three concentrations

The formyl-peptide receptor: \(k_{on}\) = 0.028 µm³/s and \(k_{off}\) = 0.010 s⁻¹, so \(K_D\) = 0.36 µm⁻³. Tab 0's cells compare their receptors every 10 s. Are those looks independent?

  1. At \(C = K_D/10\): \(\theta\) = 0.091, \(\tau_c = (1 - 0.091)/0.010 = 91\) s.
  2. At \(C = K_D\): \(\theta\) = 0.5, \(\tau_c\) = 50 s.
  3. At \(C = 10\,K_D\): \(\theta\) = 0.91, \(\tau_c\) = 9.1 s.
  4. Correlation between two looks 10 s apart, \(e^{-10/\tau_c}\): 0.90, 0.82 and 0.33.
  5. At \(K_D\), a truly independent look comes every \(2\tau_c\) = 100 s.

What it means. A neutrophil at its \(K_D\) that looks every 10 s sees nearly the same receptors each time; ten looks are one. Flooded, the receptors turn over faster, but there the reading itself has saturated (eq. 3.3.4). A quick glance is bought with \(k_{off}\), and \(k_{off}\) is paid for in affinity (eq. 3.2.7).

Mechanical analogysnapshots of a laundromat

A laundromat owner photographs the row of washers to judge how busy the place is. Each free washer is claimed now and then; each busy one frees up when its wash ends. Two photos five minutes apart show mostly the same busy machines. They are not two independent looks.

In the cellIn the machine
a receptora washer
filling, \(k_{on}C\)customers claiming a free washer, 2 per hour
emptying, \(k_{off}\)washes ending, 2 per hour (30 min on average)
\(\theta\)the fraction busy, 2/(2 + 2) = 0.5
\(\tau_c = 1/(k_{on}C + k_{off})\)1/(4 per hour) = 15 min

Run it. Photos 15 min apart are still correlated by \(e^{-1}\) = 0.37; photos 45 min apart by 0.05, nearly independent. A busier evening, with more customers, shortens \(\tau_c\), just as more ligand does.

Where it breaks. A wash cycle has a fixed length, not a memoryless one, so the photos' correlation does not fall as a clean exponential. A bound ligand's stay is memoryless (eq. 3.1.8), which is why the formula is exact for receptors.

Featured in HW2 · Problem 2
3.3.14

The receptor reading — Berg–Purcell, for a cell's receptors

Minted in Week 3 §3.7 · The counting limit — how good can any reading be? · open the module

eq. 3.3.14$$\Bigl(\frac{\delta C}{C}\Bigr)^2 \approx \frac{2\tau_c}{t_{avg}}\cdot\frac{1}{N_s\,\theta(1-\theta)} = \frac{2}{N_s\,k_{off}\,\theta\,t_{avg}} \qquad (t_{avg} \gg \tau_c)$$

Letters

  • \((\delta C/C)^2\) — the variance of the concentration inferred from the averaged occupancy · dimensionless
  • \(\tau_c\) — the correlation time (eq. 3.3.13) · s
  • \(t_{avg}\) — the averaging window, much longer than \(\tau_c\) · s
  • \(N_s\) — receptors · count
  • \(\theta\) — the occupancy · dimensionless
  • \(k_{off}\) — the dissociation rate · s⁻¹

How it is used

§3.7: averaging for \(t_{avg} \gg \tau_c\) buys \(t_{avg}/2\tau_c\) independent looks, so the one-glance band (eq. 3.3.3) shrinks by the square root of that number. The derive box gives the exact window variance, \(g(u)\) with \(u = t_{avg}/\tau_c\), and shows that the right-hand form is \(2/(\text{new molecules captured in } t_{avg})\): the reading is a count of captures, not arrivals. For \(N_s\) = 1 it is Berg and Purcell's eq. 51. In the sim, "read with receptors" is flat below \(\tau_c\), then falls with slope −½. The worked example has the bacterium (1,200 receptors, a 1.4 % task) needing about 17 s at \(k_{off}\) = 1 s⁻¹, against runs of 1 s, so it reads in time (Tab 4.3).

Comes back: — in a box. Week 4 §4.4 reuses its scaling in prose, for the bacterium's reading time.

Biological examplethe neutrophil reads its concentration for five minutes

At \(C = K_D\): \(N_s\) = 53,000, \(\theta\) = ½, \(k_{off}\) = 0.010 s⁻¹, so \(\tau_c\) = 50 s. One glance reads \(C\) to 0.87 % (eq. 3.3.3). What do five minutes of averaging buy?

  1. \(t_{avg}\) = 300 s = 6 \(\tau_c\): \(t_{avg}/2\tau_c\) = 3 independent looks.
  2. New molecules captured: \(N_sk_{off}\theta t_{avg} = 53{,}000 \times 0.010 \times 0.5 \times 300 = 79{,}500\).
  3. \((\delta C/C)^2 = 2/79{,}500\), so \(\delta C/C\) = 0.50 %.
  4. The first form agrees: \(0.87\,\%/\sqrt3 = 0.50\,\%\).
  5. The derive box's exact window, at \(u\) = 6: 0.46 %. The box's long-window form is a slight overestimate this close to \(\tau_c\).
  6. To halve the error to 0.25 %: four times the wait, 20 min.

What it means. About five million peptides reach the cell in those five minutes (eq. 3.3.12 would give 0.044 %), but only 79,500 are captured: most arrivals leave without binding (Da ≈ 0.03), and half the receptors are already holding a peptide they keep for ~100 s. Captures per arrival, \(\mathrm{Da}(1-\theta)\) ≈ 1/64, sets the gap of eq. 3.3.15. Twenty minutes for 0.25 % is most of the crawl's whole clock (Tab 4.4: ~30 min). Precision beyond a glance is expensive.

Mechanical analogyjudging demand from a car park's occupancy

A town wants to know how many drivers want to park, but its only instrument is a camera on a 200-space car park; it cannot see the road. Cars stay 2 hours on average, and the lot is half full.

In the cellIn the machine
\(N_s\) receptors200 spaces
\(k_{off}\)0.5 per hour (2 h average stay)
\(\theta\)half the spaces full
\(\tau_c = (1-\theta)/k_{off}\)1 hour
new captures, \(N_sk_{off}\theta t_{avg}\)cars newly parked

Run it. One photo reads demand to \(1/\sqrt{200 \times 0.25}\) = 14 %. Over an 8-hour day (four independent looks), \((\delta C/C)^2 = 2/(200 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 \times 8) = 2/400\), so 7.1 %. The 400 are the cars that parked that day. A photo every minute adds nothing beyond them.

Where it breaks. A driver who finds the lot full drives away for good, but a released ligand often wanders back to a neighbouring receptor (the rebinding in §3.7's fine print). And real parking stays are not memoryless.

3.3.15

The gap to the floor — an honest reading is not a perfect one

Minted in Week 3 §3.7 · The counting limit — how good can any reading be? · open the module

eq. 3.3.15$$\frac{(\delta C/C)^2_{\text{receptors}}}{(\delta C/C)^2_{\text{absorber}}} = \frac{2\,k_s}{N_s\,k_{on}\,(1-\theta)} = \frac{2}{(1-\theta)\,\mathrm{Da}}, \qquad \mathrm{Da} = \frac{N_s k_{on}}{4\pi D a}$$

Letters

  • \((\delta C/C)^2_{\text{receptors}}\) — the variance of the receptor reading (eq. 3.3.14) · dimensionless
  • \((\delta C/C)^2_{\text{absorber}}\) — the variance at the counting floor (eq. 3.3.12) · dimensionless
  • \(k_s = 4\pi D a\) — the cell's encounter rate constant (eq. 1.5.1) · µm³/s
  • \(N_s\), \(k_{on}\) — receptor count and per-site association constant · count, µm³/s
  • \(\theta\) — the occupancy · dimensionless
  • \(\mathrm{Da} = N_sk_{on}/(4\pi D\,a)\) — §3.6's referee written for a sphere · dimensionless
  • \(D\), \(a\) — the ligand's diffusion coefficient and the cell's radius · µm²/s, µm

How it is used

§3.7 divides eq. 3.3.14 by eq. 3.3.12. The concentration and the time cancel, leaving the reciprocal of the Damköhler number. A cell reads at the counting limit only if it captures nearly every arrival, Da ≳ 1, and §3.6 showed such a surface depletes its own neighbourhood. "A cell cannot have both an honest reading and a perfect one." The neutrophil (Da ≈ 0.03, \(\theta\) = ½) sits √(2/(0.5 × 0.03)) ≈ 11.5 times above the floor, and one glance still resolves its front from its back. The sim prints the measured gap at 100 s against this formula, and Tab 4.4's "what the model cannot say" quotes the factor of ~11.

Comes back: — in a box. Week 4 Tab 0 lists it among the tools it brings, "the ceiling Tab 4 pays".

Biological exampleE. coli's trade-off, both ways

The referee's E. coli chip: 1,200 receptors, \(a\) = 0.5 µm, \(D\) = 900 µm²/s. Read at \(\theta\) = ½.

  1. Receptors at the diffusion ceiling: Da = 2.4 (eq. 3.3.9).
  2. Gap² = 2/((1 − 0.5) × 2.4) = 1.67, so the gap is 1.3: within a third of the floor.
  3. But fresh, those receptors feel \(C_s = C/(1 + 2.4) = 0.29\,C\) (eq. 3.3.10). Near-perfect counting of a depleted neighbourhood.
  4. \(k_{on}\) dragged two decades lower (the referee sim's suggestion): Da = 0.024.
  5. Gap² = 2/(0.5 × 0.024) = 167, so the gap is 13.
  6. And \(C_s\) = 0.98 \(C\): an honest reading of the bulk.

What it means. The same receptors give either a near-floor reading of a concentration that is not the bulk's, or an honest reading 13 times noisier than the floor. Da sets both, in opposite directions.

Mechanical analogya Geiger counter with dead time

After each click a real Geiger tube is dead for a moment and misses whatever arrives. Now suppose you cannot hear the clicks at all. You can only check, now and then, whether the tube is busy, the way a cell only knows its occupancy. That reading is eq. 3.3.14, and its gap from the ideal counter is eq. 3.3.15.

In the cellIn the machine
a perfect absorber (eq. 3.3.12)an ideal tube: every particle clicks
a bound receptor cannot bindthe tube is dead after a click
\(k_{off}\)one over the dead time
\(\theta\)the fraction of time the tube is dead
reading occupancy, not countingreading how often the tube is found dead
gap, \(\sqrt{2/((1-\theta)\mathrm{Da})}\)the extra error of that reading

Run it. Particles arrive at 1,000 per second and the dead time is 1 ms, so the tube is dead half the time: Langmuir with \(k_{on}C\) = 1,000/s and \(k_{off}\) = 1,000/s gives \(\theta\) = 0.5. Every particle that reaches a live tube registers, so Da = 1. In 10 s the ideal counter gets 10,000 clicks, ±1 %. Reading the dead fraction instead, the gap is \(\sqrt{2/(0.5 \times 1)} = 2\): ±2 %.

Where it breaks. A real tube's dead time is a fixed interval, not a memoryless one, which changes the factor 2 a little. And a real counter does count its clicks; a cell has no click counter, only its occupancy.

Module Tab 4 · Two Readers, One Gradient
3.4.1

The field — a steady source with clearance

Minted in Week 3 §4.1 · The cast · open the module

eq. 3.4.1$$C(r) = \frac{S}{4\pi D\,r}\,e^{-r/\lambda}, \qquad \lambda = \sqrt{D\tau}\ \ (\text{eq. 2.3.7})$$

Letters

  • \(C(r)\) — the concentration at distance \(r\) from the source · µm⁻³
  • \(S\) — molecules released per second · s⁻¹ · the bite's colony ~4 × 10⁵ (assumed)
  • \(D\) — the diffusion coefficient · µm²/s · formyl peptide ≈ 500
  • \(r\) — distance from the source · µm
  • \(\lambda = \sqrt{D\tau}\) — the decay length (eq. 2.3.7) · µm · peptide ≈ 224
  • \(\tau\) — a molecule's mean lifetime before clearance · s · peptide ~100 (assumed)

How it is used

§4.1 writes down the field both readers stand in: Week 2's steady source with clearance, whose length scale was eq. 2.3.7. The module asks for two things before either cell reads it. It falls as \(1/r\) near the source and dies exponentially beyond \(\lambda\), so a usable gradient exists only within a few \(\lambda\) of the colony. And its log slope, \(d\ln C/dr = -(1/r + 1/\lambda)\), is what a spatial reader measures. The cast sets \(S\) so the field crosses \(K_D\) about 100 µm from the colony, and the "neutrophil in the peptide field" sim draws it with sliders for \(S\) and \(\tau\). It feeds eq. 3.4.2 and §4.4's clocks; its one-dimensional cousin \(C_0e^{-x/\lambda}\) was §3.5's morphogen.

Comes back: C1 §2.1 (the steady profile around a source: how far one injured alveolus can call for repair).

Biological examplehow far the itch spreads

Week 2's bite: the mast cell releases about 5 × 10⁷ histamine molecules per second, with \(D\) = 330 µm²/s in tissue and \(\tau\) = 120 s.

  1. Decay length: \(\lambda = \sqrt{330 \times 120} \approx 199\) µm.
  2. Prefactor: \(S/4\pi D = 5\times10^7/(4\pi \times 330) = 12{,}060\) µm⁻².
  3. At the nerve, \(r\) = 120 µm: \(C = (12{,}060/120)\,e^{-120/199} = 100.5 \times 0.547 = 55\) µm⁻³ ≈ 91 nM.
  4. Where it falls to the H1 threshold, about 10 nM = 6.0 µm⁻³: solving gives \(r \approx 350\) µm.
  5. Without clearance (\(\tau \to \infty\)), \(C = 12{,}060/r\) reaches 10 nM only at \(r \approx 2{,}000\) µm.
  6. The log slope at the nerve: \(1/120 + 1/199 = 0.0134\) µm⁻¹, 1.34 % per micron.

What it means. Clearance shrinks the itchy patch from a 2 mm radius to 0.35 mm, the ~350 µm in the module's ledger. Inside the patch the field is steep, 1.34 % per micron at the nerve, plenty for a reader 10 µm across. A few \(\lambda\) out, it is gone.

Mechanical analogya streetlamp in fog

In thick fog, light from a lamp does not travel straight. It bounces from droplet to droplet in a random walk, and a little is absorbed at each bounce. The glow around the lamp is this equation: light spreads like a diffusing molecule, and absorption clears it.

In the cellIn the machine
source \(S\), molecules per secondthe lamp's power
\(D\)how fast light random-walks between droplets
lifetime \(\tau\)how long light survives before a droplet absorbs it
\(\lambda = \sqrt{D\tau}\)the radius of the glow
\(C(r)\)how bright the fog is at distance \(r\)

Run it. If the fog's \(\lambda\) is 5 m (illustrative), the fog 10 m from the lamp is \((2/10)\,e^{-8/5}\) = 4 % as bright as at 2 m. Without absorption, the \(1/r\) alone would leave 20 %.

Where it breaks. Close to the lamp, light is still a beam, not yet a random walk, so the diffusion picture holds only many bounces out; fog droplets also scatter mostly forward. A molecule random-walks from its first nanometre.

3.4.2

The spatial reading — front against back in the bite's field

Minted in Week 3 §4.2 · Reading one: the neutrophil's front and back · open the module

eq. 3.4.2$$\Delta\theta = \theta_{eq}(C_{\text{front}}) - \theta_{eq}(C_{\text{back}}) \;\approx\; \frac{d\theta_{eq}}{dC}\,\Bigl|\frac{dC}{dr}\Bigr|\,2a \;=\; \frac{K_{eq}}{(1+K_{eq}C)^{2}}\cdot C\Bigl(\frac{1}{r}+\frac{1}{\lambda}\Bigr)\cdot 2a$$

Letters

  • \(\Delta\theta\) — the occupancy difference, front minus back · dimensionless
  • \(\theta_{eq}(C)\) — Langmuir's isotherm (eq. 3.2.8) · dimensionless
  • \(C_{\text{front}}\), \(C_{\text{back}}\) — the concentrations at the ends facing toward and away from the source · µm⁻³
  • \(d\theta_{eq}/dC\) — the isotherm's slope · µm³
  • \(|dC/dr|\) — the field's gradient (eq. 3.4.1) · µm⁻⁴
  • \(a\) — the cell's radius; \(2a\) is the baseline · µm · neutrophil 7.5; E. coli 0.5
  • \(K_{eq} = 1/K_D\) — the equilibrium constant · µm³ · neutrophil \(K_D\) = 0.36 µm⁻³ (0.6 nM)
  • \(C\) — the concentration at the cell's centre · µm⁻³
  • \(r\), \(\lambda\) — distance to the source and decay length (eq. 3.4.1) · µm

How it is used

§4.2: Tab 3 issued the licence (Da ≈ 0.03), so each end of the neutrophil reads the field with eq. 3.2.8 and the cell's information is the difference. Because \(K_{eq}C/(1+K_{eq}C)^2 = \theta(1-\theta)\), it is \(\theta(1-\theta) \times \Delta\ln C\): the receptor's ruler slope times the field's fractional change across the body, \((1/r + 1/\lambda)\,2a\). That is eq. 3.3.4 with the field filled in. In the sim, sliding the cell inward raises \(\Delta\theta\) as \(1/r\), and lowering \(K_D\) ten-fold at 400 µm lifts the far-field reading several-fold. The worked example: \(\Delta\theta\) ≈ 0.054 where the field crosses \(K_D\), with the affinity cancelling out. §4.3 runs it for E. coli (\(2a\) = 1 µm): \(\Delta\theta\) = 0.0036, far below the 1,200 receptors' one-glance noise (about 3 % by eq. 3.3.4), so the bacterium reads in time instead.

Comes back: —

Biological examplethe neutrophil far out, and what affinity buys

The cast's field (\(S\) = 4 × 10⁵ /s, \(D\) = 500 µm²/s, \(\lambda\) = 224 µm) and the neutrophil (\(a\) = 7.5 µm, 53,000 receptors), parked 400 µm from the colony.

  1. Field: \(C = \dfrac{4\times10^5}{4\pi(500)(400)}\,e^{-400/224} = 0.159 \times 0.167 = 0.027\) µm⁻³.
  2. Fractional change across the cell: \((1/400 + 1/224) \times 15 = 0.105\).
  3. Native receptor, \(K_D\) = 0.36 µm⁻³: \(K_{eq}C\) = 0.074, \(\theta\) = 0.069, \(\theta(1-\theta)\) = 0.064.
  4. Reading: \(\Delta\theta = 0.064 \times 0.105 = 0.0067\). That is about 180 more bound receptors on the front half (26,500 receptors per half).
  5. A ten-fold tighter receptor, \(K_D\) = 0.036 µm⁻³: \(\theta\) = 0.42, \(\theta(1-\theta)\) = 0.24, \(\Delta\theta = 0.24 \times 0.105 = 0.026\).
  6. One-glance signal/noise (eq. 3.3.4): 3.0 for the native receptor, 6.0 for the tighter one.

What it means. Out at 400 µm the native receptor reads only 0.7 %, though 53,000 receptors still see it at three times the noise. A ten-fold tighter receptor multiplies the signal 3.8 times. Affinity buys where the reading begins, not how large it gets; close in, \(\Delta\theta\) is set by \(2a/r\).

Mechanical analogya two-eyed light-seeking robot in the fog

A small wheeled robot carries two light sensors, one on each side, and steers toward the brighter one (a classic hobby build). In the fog of eq. 3.4.1, the difference between its two sensors is this equation.

In the cellIn the machine
front and back receptorsleft and right light sensors
baseline \(2a\)the spacing of the sensors
\((1/r + 1/\lambda)\,2a\)the fractional brightness difference between them
\(\theta(1-\theta)\), the ruler's slopeeach sensor's sensitivity: flat when dazzled or in the dark
choosing \(K_D\)setting the sensors' gain

Run it. Sensors 10 cm apart, 2 m from the lamp, in fog with \(\lambda\) = 5 m (illustrative): the fractional difference is \(0.10 \times (1/2 + 1/5) = 0.07\). With the sensors mid-range, \(\theta(1-\theta)\) = ¼, the readings differ by 1.75 %. A robot 1 cm wide gets 0.175 %, the bacterium's problem; it would do better to drive a little and compare.

Where it breaks. A photosensor's noise is electronic, not a count, and the robot can stop and stare as long as it likes. A cell's noise is its receptor count, and its independent looks are rationed by \(\tau_c\) (eq. 3.3.13).

Module Tab 5 · Next Week
3.5.1

The membrane's flicker spectrum — previewed here, earned in Week 4

Minted in Week 3 §5.1 · Next week's headline, measured today — the surface that senses is a thermal object · open the module

eq. 3.5.1$$\langle |h_q|^2 \rangle = \frac{k_BT}{A\,(\kappa q^4 + \sigma q^2)}$$

Letters

  • \(h_q\) — the amplitude of the membrane ripple with wavenumber \(q\) · µm
  • \(\langle|h_q|^2\rangle\) — its mean square over time · µm²
  • \(k_BT\) — the thermal energy, 4.28 × 10⁻²¹ J at 310 K. Each ripple mode carries ½\(k_BT\) (Week 1's equipartition)
  • \(A\) — the area of the membrane patch · µm² · the sim's strip: 10 µm × 1 µm
  • \(\kappa\) — the bending stiffness · \(k_BT\) · sim 20 \(k_BT\) = 8.6 × 10⁻²⁰ J. Not §1.2's uptake speed \(\kappa\)
  • \(\sigma\) — the membrane tension · \(k_BT\)/µm² · sim "tense" 2,400 \(k_BT\)/µm² ≈ 0.0103 mN/m
  • \(q\) — the wavenumber, 2π/wavelength · µm⁻¹

How it is used

§5.1 previews Week 4's headline: the surface that carries every receptor is itself a thermal object, shaken by the same bath that kicks ligands off. Tension fights the long ripples (\(q^2\)), bending the short ones (\(q^4\)), and they trade places at \(q^* = \sqrt{\sigma/\kappa}\). In the "ten-micron strip" sim, the floppy membrane (\(\sigma\) = 0) heaves by hundreds of nanometres with an rms that falls as \(1/\sqrt\kappa\); the tense one is pinned to tens of nanometres. Nothing is derived here. Week 4 earns \(\sigma\) and \(\kappa\) from the molecules up, and §5.2's ledger lists "the cell is a rigid sphere" as the assumption it repairs.

Comes back: — (Week 4 earns it).

Biological examplehow much the receptors' floor moves

The Tab 5 strip: \(A\) = 10 µm², \(\kappa\) = 20 \(k_BT\). Its longest ripple puts half a wavelength across 10 µm, so \(q = \pi/10 = 0.314\) µm⁻¹. With \(\kappa\) and \(\sigma\) in units of \(k_BT\), the \(k_BT\) cancels.

  1. Bending term: \(\kappa q^4 = 20 \times 0.314^4 = 0.195\) \(k_BT\)/µm².
  2. Floppy (\(\sigma\) = 0): \(\langle|h_q|^2\rangle = 1/(10 \times 0.195) = 0.51\) µm², an rms of about 0.72 µm.
  3. Tension term for a resting cell, \(\sigma\) = 2,400: \(\sigma q^2 = 2{,}400 \times 0.0987 = 237\) \(k_BT\)/µm².
  4. Tense: \(\langle|h_q|^2\rangle = 1/(10 \times 237) = 4.2\times10^{-4}\) µm², an rms of about 20.5 nm.
  5. Crossover: \(q^* = \sqrt{2{,}400/20} = 11\) µm⁻¹, a wavelength of \(2\pi/q^* \approx 0.57\) µm.

What it means. Tension tames the longest ripple 35-fold, from 0.72 µm to about 20 nm. Bending matters only for ripples shorter than about half a micron. Even so, a receptor rides a surface that heaves by many times its own size, which is what Week 4 must account for.

Mechanical analogya tarp lashed over a trailer in gusty wind

Gusts hit a tarp at random. Loose, it billows in long waves. Cinch the straps and the long billows vanish, leaving short crinkles that only the fabric's own stiffness resists. A canvas tarp crinkles less than thin plastic: that is bending.

In the cellIn the machine
thermal kicks, ½\(k_BT\) per modegusts of wind
tension \(\sigma\)the straps' pull
bending stiffness \(\kappa\)the fabric's stiffness: canvas against thin plastic
long ripples, small \(q\)billows
short ripples, large \(q\)crinkles
\(q^* = \sqrt{\sigma/\kappa}\)the size at which strap and fabric matter equally

Where it breaks. Wind does not give every ripple the same energy, so there is no equipartition. The tarp also has inertia and flaps at its own frequencies, while a membrane's ripples are overdamped in water and simply relax.

Reused this week — earlier equations, as Week 3 uses them

Each keeps the number it was given when first minted. The full entry, with its example and analogy, is one click away.

Featured in HW1 · Problem 4, ChallengeFeatured in HW2 · Problem 1(b), Problem 4(e)
1.5.1

Smoluchowski, as the delivery to a pocket

Re-boxed in Week 3 §1.2 · Which arrivals count: the site, and the stick

eq. 1.5.1 again$$\text{arrivals per second at one pocket} = 4\pi D a_s\,(C - C_s)$$

The encounter constant of Weeks 1–2, \(k_s = 4\pi(D_1 + D_2)(a_1 + a_2)\), for a fixed pocket: \(D\) is now the ligand's diffusion coefficient alone, \(a_s\) the pocket's radius (1 nm), and it is written with the surface concentration it feeds into, \(C\) the bulk and \(C_s\) the liquid touching the pocket. Balanced against the pocket's chemistry, \(k_rC_s\), it yields eq. 3.1.4, \(k_{on} = Pk_s\). With \(C_s = 0\) it is §1.1's 3.8 arrivals per second at 1 nM.

Full entry: eq. 1.5.1, Week 1

1.2.7

Boltzmann, for the energy of a kick

Re-boxed in Week 3 §1.3 · Bombarded: what a bound molecule feels

eq. 1.2.7 again$$P(E_{\text{kick}} > \Delta U) = e^{-\Delta U/k_BT}$$

Week 1's \(C(h) = C_0e^{-U(h)/k_BT}\), the law that tilted the sedimentation column, now applied to the energy a colliding water molecule carries into the bond: the fraction of kicks stronger than the well depth \(\Delta U\), with \(k_BT\) = 4.28 × 10⁻²¹ J at 310 K. The bench's histogram of kick energies shows the exponential tail; multiplied by the kick rate, it gives the kick law, eq. 3.1.6.

Full entry: eq. 1.2.7, Week 1

1.2.7

the odds of sitting ΔU above the bottom

Re-boxed in Week 3 §1.5 · A bond is a well the bath kicks you out of

eq. 1.2.7 again$$\frac{P(\text{rim})}{P(\text{bottom})} = e^{-\Delta U/k_BT}$$

The same law as Week 1's tilted cloud, now for a tracer in a binding well: the chance of finding it up at the rim, a height \(\Delta U\) above the bottom. Multiplied by the rattle rate \(k_0\) at which the tracer tries the rim, it re-derives eq. 3.1.6 with an honest prefactor (\(k_0\) ≈ 10⁷ s⁻¹, not the 10¹³ kicks of §1.3).

Full entry: eq. 1.2.7, Week 1

Featured in HW1 · Problem 1(c)
1.3.5

Fick's first law, across the film

Re-boxed in Week 3 §3.6 · Fine print: is the reading honest, and how fast is it?

eq. 1.3.5 again$$J = -D\,\frac{dC}{dx} \approx D\,\frac{C - C_s}{\delta}$$

Tab 3's fine print uses Week 1's flux law for the delivery side of the relay. Molecules cross an unstirred film of thickness \(\delta\) from the bulk concentration \(C\) down to \(C_s\) at the surface; \(D\) is the ligand's diffusion coefficient and \(J\) the flux per area into the surface. Folding \(D/\delta\) into one speed gives the mass-transfer coefficient \(k_m\) (eq. 3.3.8), and writing the same flux as uptake gives eq. 3.3.7.

Full entry: eq. 1.3.5, Week 1

Week 4 · The Cytoskeleton — From Reading to Moving

Week 3 left the neutrophil able to read a gradient. Week 4 gives it a way to move. Every filament end is Week 3's door again: a subunit arrives at \(k_{on}C\), leaves at \(k_{off}\), and builds the next site. So one growth law (eq. 4.1.1) runs actin's treadmill, a microtubule's dynamic instability and, with a Boltzmann factor added, next week's ratchet (eq. 4.5.1). Motors add force but not speed (eq. 4.2.6–4.2.7), microtubules add stiffness and a slow compass (eq. 4.3.1–4.3.6), and the week ends on one subtraction: the edge moves at polymerization minus retrograde flow (eq. 4.4.3).

3.2.15Michaelis–Menten
Module Tab 1 · The Actin Cytoskeleton
Featured in HW2 · Microscope, Problem 4(d)
4.1.1

Growth speed of a filament end — a door that builds the next door

Minted in Week 4 §1.1 · Actin polymerization: one end, one site, and a clock · open the module

eq. 4.1.1$$v = \delta\,(k_{on}C - k_{off})$$

Letters

  • \(v\) — the net growth speed of one filament end · nm/s
  • \(\delta\) — the length one subunit adds (the rise, not the monomer's size) · nm · 2.7 nm for actin; 8/13 ≈ 0.62 nm for a microtubule
  • \(k_{on}\) — the association rate constant at that end · µM⁻¹s⁻¹ · ATP-actin: barbed end 11.6, pointed end 1.3 (Pollard 1986)
  • \(C\) — the free monomer concentration the end sees · µM
  • \(k_{off}\) — the rate at which the end subunit falls off · s⁻¹ · ATP-actin: barbed end 1.4, pointed end 0.8

How it is used

§1.1 mints it to name what the "barbed end in a monomer bath" sim measured: the slope of the length trace at 0.5 µM, read against the drift line. It is Week 3's revolving door (eq. 3.2.7–3.2.8) with one change. Each subunit that binds makes the next site, so there is no isotherm and no plateau. The worked example feeds one barbed end 10 µM and gets 310 nm/s, as fast as a crawling cell. Its zero crossing is eq. 4.1.3 and two ends make eq. 4.1.4. §3.1 reuses it with tubulin's \(\delta\) and rates (the \(v_g\) of eq. 4.3.2), eq. 4.4.3 feeds it through the Damköhler relay, and eq. 4.5.1 adds a load.

Comes back: C1 §3.3 (the critical stiffness — why repeated injury tips a patch).

Biological examplewhat profilin buys a barbed end

At the leading edge a barbed end draws on two pools (Kiuchi 2011). About 2 µM of G-actin is free, and 9.5 µM is held by profilin, which hands its monomer to a barbed end. The 88 µM bound to thymosin-β4 is a reserve that does not add directly. How fast does one tip grow on the free pool alone, and with profilin's share added? (Profilin-actin is taken to add at the same \(k_{on}\), as §4.3 does.)

  1. ATP-actin barbed end: \(k_{on}\) = 11.6 µM⁻¹s⁻¹, \(k_{off}\) = 1.4 s⁻¹, \(\delta\) = 2.7 nm.
  2. Free pool only, \(C\) = 2.0 µM: \(k_{on}C\) = 23.2 s⁻¹.
  3. \(v = 2.7 \times (23.2 - 1.4) = 2.7 \times 21.8\) ≈ 59 nm/s.
  4. Add profilin-actin, \(C\) = 2.0 + 9.5 = 11.5 µM: \(k_{on}C\) = 133.4 s⁻¹.
  5. \(v = 2.7 \times (133.4 - 1.4) = 2.7 \times 132\) ≈ 356 nm/s ≈ 21 µm/min.

What it means. On free actin alone the tip grows at 59 nm/s, about a third of the slowest neutrophil (170 nm/s). With profilin's share it grows at 356 nm/s, faster than the cell crawls. At both concentrations \(k_{off}\) is a small correction. The supply sets the speed.

Mechanical analogya track-laying train

A track-laying machine extends a railway one fixed panel at a time. Each panel that arrives from the supply wagons is a subunit reaching the tip. The more loaded wagons circulate on the line, the more often a panel arrives, just as arrivals at a tip scale with \(C\). Now and then an inspector rejects the end panel and it is lifted off. The railhead advances one panel length per net panel laid.

In the cellIn the machine
rise per subunit \(\delta\) = 2.7 nmpanel length, 20 m
arrivals \(k_{on}C\), proportional to monomer \(C\)panels arriving, proportional to loaded wagons on the line
losses \(k_{off}\)panels lifted off by the inspector
growth speed \(v\)speed of the railhead

With 30 panels arriving an hour and one lifted, the railhead moves \(v\) = 20 m × (30 − 1) per hour = 580 m/h. Double the wagons and the speed nearly doubles. The lifted panel hardly matters, just as \(k_{off}\) hardly matters at 11.5 µM.

Where it breaks. Every panel that arrives is laid, while a barbed end accepts only about one correctly posed arrival in 150 (§1.1). A monomer also arrives by diffusion, not on a timetable.

4.1.2

Length diffusion coefficient — the noise is the sum of the rates

Minted in Week 4 §1.1 · Actin polymerization: one end, one site, and a clock · open the module

eq. 4.1.2$$D_L = \frac{\delta^2\,(k_{on}C + k_{off})}{2}, \qquad \langle(L - vt)^2\rangle = 2D_Lt$$

Letters

  • \(D_L\) — the diffusion coefficient of the filament's length · nm²/s · 26 nm²/s at 0.5 µM, barbed end
  • \(\delta\) — the rise per subunit · nm · 2.7 nm
  • \(k_{on}C\) — the arrival rate · s⁻¹
  • \(k_{off}\) — the departure rate · s⁻¹
  • \(L\) — the filament's length at time \(t\) · nm
  • \(v\) — the drift speed of eq. 4.1.1 · nm/s
  • \(t\) — elapsed time · s

How it is used

§1.1 mints it from the "forty copies" chip. The mean length climbs at the drift speed of eq. 4.1.1, the variance between copies grows as \(t\), and the panel reads the measured \(D_L\) against \(\delta^2(k_{on}C + k_{off})/2\). The derive box counts arrivals and departures as two independent Poisson numbers. Their means subtract, but their variances add. The worked numbers are 26 nm²/s at 0.5 µM and a 56-nm spread in a minute. It sets up §1.2: at \(C = C_c\) the drift is zero but the noise is not, so a filament at its threshold thrashes in place.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea tip at the edge and a tip at its threshold

Two barbed ends. One sits at the leading edge in a rich pool, 10 µM. The other sits where the free monomer has fallen to its critical concentration, 0.12 µM (illustrative: the module's body pool is far richer). How noisy is each?

  1. \(\delta^2\) = 2.7² = 7.29 nm².
  2. At 10 µM: \(k_{on}C + k_{off}\) = 116 + 1.4 = 117.4 s⁻¹, so \(D_L\) = 7.29 × 117.4 / 2 = 428 nm²/s.
  3. In 1 s it drifts \(vt\) = 310 nm; its spread is \(\sqrt{2D_Lt} = \sqrt{856}\) = 29 nm, about 9 % of the advance.
  4. At \(C_c\) = 0.12 µM: \(k_{on}C = k_{off}\) = 1.4 s⁻¹, sum 2.8 s⁻¹, so \(D_L\) = 7.29 × 2.8 / 2 = 10.2 nm²/s.
  5. In 10 min: drift 0; spread \(\sqrt{2 \times 10.2 \times 600}\) = 111 nm, about 41 subunits.

What it means. In a rich pool the tip is close to a clock: the spread is 9 % of the advance after one second, and that fraction falls as \(1/\sqrt t\). At its threshold the same end goes nowhere on average, yet wanders ±110 nm in ten minutes. Both doors keep running; only their difference has vanished.

Mechanical analogya tank with two dripping taps

A tank has one tap dripping in and one dripping out. Each drop is a subunit added or lost. The level's mean change is set by the difference of the two drip rates. Its spread grows with their sum, because a drop out jostles the level as much as a drop in.

In the cellIn the machine
one subunit, \(\delta\) = 2.7 nmone drop, 0.05 mL
arrivals \(k_{on}C\)drops in, 2 per second
departures \(k_{off}\)drops out, 2 per second
drift \(v\)steady change in volume (zero here)
\(D_L\)spread coefficient, 0.05² × (2 + 2)/2 = 0.005 mL²/s

Run it for an hour. The mean volume does not move, but the spread is \(\sqrt{2 \times 0.005 \times 3600}\) = 6 mL, about 120 drops either way. This is the filament held at \(C_c\).

Where it breaks. A real tap drips almost like a clock, and regular drops would spread far less. The law needs memoryless (Poisson) events, which thermal arrivals at a tip are and a tap mostly is not.

Featured in HW2 · Microscope
4.1.3

Critical concentration — where the door is fair

Minted in Week 4 §1.1 · Actin polymerization: one end, one site, and a clock · open the module

eq. 4.1.3$$C_c = \frac{k_{off}}{k_{on}} = \frac{1}{K_{eq}} \qquad (0.12\ \text{µM for ATP-actin at the barbed end})$$

Letters

  • \(C_c\) — the critical concentration, where growth equals loss · µM · 0.12 µM, ATP-actin barbed end
  • \(k_{off}\) — the departure rate · s⁻¹ · 1.4 s⁻¹
  • \(k_{on}\) — the association rate constant · µM⁻¹s⁻¹ · 11.6 µM⁻¹s⁻¹
  • \(K_{eq}\) — Week 3's equilibrium constant, \(k_{on}/k_{off}\) · µM⁻¹

How it is used

§1.1 mints it as the zero crossing of eq. 4.1.1, which is a straight line in \(C\). It is eq. 3.2.7 in a new hat. For a receptor, \(1/K_{eq}\) was the concentration that half-fills the door; for a filament it is the concentration where the door is fair. The bench is the same "barbed end in a monomer bath" sim: slide \(C\) below 0.12 µM and the trace falls. §1.2 gives each end its own \(C_c\) (eq. 4.1.4). §1.5 and §4.4 use \(C_f/C_c\) ≈ 120 as the "how far from fair" number, and eq. 4.5.1's stall force is a logarithm of \(C/C_c\). The check-yourself drug that doubles \(k_{off}\) doubles \(C_c\).

Comes back: C1 §3.3 (where gain equals loss).

Biological examplewhich of the cell's polymers sits near its threshold?

The same ratio prices three polymer ends in the module's cast (Pollard 1986; Walker 1988). Compare each threshold with the pool a cell offers: about 10 µM of usable actin (free plus profilin) and about 10 µM of free tubulin.

  1. ATP-actin, barbed end: \(C_c\) = 1.4 / 11.6 = 0.12 µM.
  2. ADP-actin, barbed end (the aged form): \(C_c\) = 7.2 / 3.8 = 1.9 µM, sixteen times higher.
  3. Tubulin, microtubule plus end: \(C_c\) = 44 / 8.9 = 4.9 µM.
  4. Pool over threshold: ATP-actin 10 / 0.12 ≈ 83; ADP-actin, if the same 10 µM had no ATP, 10 / 1.9 ≈ 5.3; tubulin 10 / 4.9 ≈ 2.0.

What it means. A fresh actin tip in a cell is far above its threshold, a one-way door. A microtubule end sits at only twice its threshold, so a modest change in tubulin or in a MAP can tip it from growth to loss. That is the regime dynamic instability lives in (eq. 4.3.2).

Mechanical analogya tank filled by a valve and emptied by a pump

A tank is filled through a valve whose flow rises in proportion to the supply's head. A pump drains it at a fixed flow, whatever the level. The level rises when the valve beats the pump and falls when it does not. The supply head that holds the level still is the tank's \(C_c\).

In the cellIn the machine
filament lengthwater level
monomer concentration \(C\)supply head, in metres
\(k_{on}\)valve flow per metre of head, 0.5 L/min per m
\(k_{off}\)the drain pump, 2 L/min
\(C_c = k_{off}/k_{on}\)balance head, 2 / 0.5 = 4 m

Above 4 m of head the tank fills; below it, the tank empties.

Where it breaks. The tank's balance point is a plumbing choice. A filament's \(C_c\) is \(1/K_{eq}\), fixed by the free energy of the bond, and only spending ATP lets the two ends of one filament disagree about it (§1.2).

Featured in HW2 · Problem 4(a)–(b)
4.1.4

A filament with two doors — one grows while the other shrinks

Minted in Week 4 §1.2 · Actin dynamics: two ends, two thresholds, and a conveyor belt · open the module

eq. 4.1.4$$\frac{dL}{dt} = \delta\bigl[(k_{on}^B + k_{on}^P)\,C - (k_{off}^B + k_{off}^P)\bigr], \qquad C_c^B = \frac{k_{off}^B}{k_{on}^B},\quad C_c^P = \frac{k_{off}^P}{k_{on}^P}$$

Letters

  • \(L\), \(t\) — filament length and time · nm, s
  • \(\delta\) — rise per subunit · nm · 2.7 nm
  • \(k_{on}^B\), \(k_{off}^B\) — barbed (+) end rates · µM⁻¹s⁻¹, s⁻¹ · 11.6, 1.4 (ATP-actin)
  • \(k_{on}^P\), \(k_{off}^P\) — pointed (−) end rates · µM⁻¹s⁻¹, s⁻¹ · 1.3, 0.8 (ATP-actin)
  • \(C\) — monomer concentration · µM
  • \(C_c^B\), \(C_c^P\) — the two thresholds · µM · 0.12 and 0.62

How it is used

§1.2 mints it for the "barbed and pointed ends, side by side" sim. Below both thresholds (0.05 µM) both ends shrink; above both (1 µM) both grow, the barbed end about twenty times faster; between them one end grows while the other shrinks. Four sliders set the two doors. Make the ends chemically equal and the window between thresholds closes. At equilibrium both ends would have to share one \(C_c\); they differ fivefold only because ATP is spent (§1.2's deep box). Setting \(dL/dt = 0\) gives eq. 4.1.5. The capping example then shows that capping one end chooses which threshold a filament obeys.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea filament behind the edge, before and after capping

Take a patch where the free monomer has fallen to 0.3 µM (illustrative), between the two thresholds. Follow one uncapped filament, then let capping protein shut its barbed end.

  1. Thresholds: \(C_c^B\) = 0.12 µM, \(C_c^P\) = 0.62 µM; take \(C\) = 0.3 µM.
  2. Barbed end: 2.7 × (11.6 × 0.3 − 1.4) = 2.7 × 2.08 = +5.6 nm/s.
  3. Pointed end: 2.7 × (1.3 × 0.3 − 0.8) = 2.7 × (−0.41) = −1.1 nm/s.
  4. Whole filament (eq. 4.1.4): 2.7 × (12.9 × 0.3 − 2.2) = 2.7 × 1.67 = +4.5 nm/s, the sum of the two.
  5. Capping protein shuts the barbed end. Only −1.1 nm/s is left.
  6. A 1-µm filament then takes 1000 / 1.1 ≈ 900 s ≈ 15 min to dissolve.

What it means. Between the thresholds the filament grows at one end and shrinks at the other. Capping turns a growing filament into a shrinking one, but at 1.1 nm/s it takes a quarter of an hour. A lamellipodium turns over in tens of seconds, which is why §1.4 needs cofilin.

Mechanical analogya train with a yard crew at each end

A freight train sits in a marshalling yard with a crew at each end. Each crew couples cars from a siding at a rate that rises with the number of cars waiting, and uncouples cars at a fixed rate. The front crew is quick to couple; the rear crew couples nine times more slowly but uncouples only about half as fast. Each crew has its own break-even queue.

In the cellIn the machine
barbed end, \(k_{on}^B\) = 11.6, \(k_{off}^B\) = 1.4front crew, quick to couple
pointed end, \(k_{on}^P\) = 1.3, \(k_{off}^P\) = 0.8rear crew, slow to couple
monomer \(C\)cars waiting on the siding
\(C_c^B\), \(C_c^P\)each crew's break-even queue
\(\delta\)one car length
capping proteinlocking the front coupler

With a queue between the two break-evens, the train gains cars at the front and sheds them at the back.

Where it breaks. Nothing stops two yard crews from having different break-evens. A filament's two ends can disagree only because each subunit spends its ATP on the way through; without that, detailed balance forces \(C_c^B = C_c^P\).

Featured in HW2 · Problem 4(a)–(b)
4.1.5

Treadmilling steady state — a filament that holds its length and flows

Minted in Week 4 §1.2 · Actin dynamics: two ends, two thresholds, and a conveyor belt · open the module

eq. 4.1.5$$C_{ss} = \frac{k_{off}^B + k_{off}^P}{k_{on}^B + k_{on}^P}, \qquad J = k_{on}^B C_{ss} - k_{off}^B = k_{off}^P - k_{on}^P C_{ss}$$

Letters

  • \(C_{ss}\) — the monomer concentration at which the length holds · µM · 0.17 µM, ATP-actin
  • \(J\) — the flux of subunits through the filament, barbed end in, pointed end out · s⁻¹ · 0.58 bare; 17.8 with cofilin
  • \(k_{on}^B\), \(k_{off}^B\), \(k_{on}^P\), \(k_{off}^P\) — the four end rates · 11.6, 1.4, 1.3, 0.8 (Pollard 1986)

How it is used

§1.2 sets eq. 4.1.4 to zero. On the "treadmilling" chip at 0.17 µM the length holds and a red-marked subunit rides from the barbed end to the pointed end; the panel reads \(J\) and the transit time. On the "ADP-actin" chip the thresholds nearly coincide and the red subunit never moves. The worked example: bare \(J\) = 0.58 s⁻¹ (1.6 nm/s); cofilin raises the pointed-end off-rate 25-fold and \(J\) to 17.8 s⁻¹ (48 nm/s), the range of retrograde flow. It feeds §1.4's belt, and the check-yourself shows that a monomer with no nucleotide cannot treadmill.

Comes back: —

Biological examplehow long a subunit rides through a filament

A subunit joins the barbed end of a 1-µm filament. How long until it leaves from the pointed end, bare, with cofilin, and with aged ADP-actin that has nothing left to spend?

  1. Bare ATP-actin: \(C_{ss}\) = (1.4 + 0.8) / (11.6 + 1.3) = 2.2 / 12.9 = 0.17 µM.
  2. \(J\) = 11.6 × 0.1705 − 1.4 = 0.58 s⁻¹ (check: 0.8 − 1.3 × 0.1705 = 0.58), so \(J\delta\) = 1.56 nm/s.
  3. Transit through 1 µm: 1000 / 1.56 ≈ 640 s ≈ 11 min.
  4. With cofilin, \(k_{off}^P\) = 20 s⁻¹: \(C_{ss}\) = 21.4 / 12.9 = 1.66 µM; \(J\) = 11.6 × 1.66 − 1.4 = 17.8 s⁻¹, so \(J\delta\) = 48 nm/s and the transit takes 21 s.
  5. ADP-actin (3.8, 7.2, 0.16, 0.27): \(C_{ss}\) = 7.47 / 3.96 = 1.89 µM; \(J\) = 3.8 × 1.886 − 7.2 ≈ −0.03 s⁻¹.

What it means. A bare filament turns a micron over in about eleven minutes. Living lamellipodia do it in tens of seconds, and cofilin gets there (21 s) without touching the barbed end. With no ATP to spend the flux is essentially zero, even slightly backward: no fuel, no belt.

Mechanical analogya bulldozer's track

A crawler track lays a link on the ground at the front and lifts one off at the back. The track's length stays fixed, and every link stays still on the ground while the machine moves over it. Lamellipodial filaments do the same: they stay fixed to the substrate while the cell moves over them (Theriot & Mitchison 1991).

In the cellIn the machine
barbed end adds subunitsfront of the track lays a link
pointed end sheds subunitsrear of the track lifts a link
flux \(J\)links laid per second
\(J\delta\)ground speed
\(C_{ss}\)the one supply at which laying equals lifting
ATP spent per subunitthe engine's fuel

A track with 0.2-m links laying 5 links a second moves at 1 m/s. The bare filament's 0.58 subunits a second against cofilin's 17.8 is the difference between idling and driving.

Where it breaks. A track's links return over the top on a fixed path. A released subunit leaves as free ADP-actin, must recharge with ATP and finds its way back by diffusion (§1.4). The track's speed is also set by a throttle, not by a monomer pool that settles to \(C_{ss}\).

4.1.6

Branching against capping — the sign of one difference decides the network

Minted in Week 4 §1.3 · Actin reinforcement: crosslinking, and why the jiggle matters · open the module

eq. 4.1.6$$\frac{dN_{open}}{dt} = (k_{br} - k_{cap})\,N_{open} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad N_{open} \propto e^{(k_{br}-k_{cap})t}$$

Letters

  • \(N_{open}\) — the number of open (uncapped) barbed ends · count
  • \(t\) — time · s
  • \(k_{br}\) — the rate at which Arp2/3 starts a new branch off each open filament · s⁻¹ · the sim's 0.10 s⁻¹
  • \(k_{cap}\) — the rate at which capping protein shuts each open end for good · s⁻¹ · the capping slider

How it is used

§1.3 mints it for the last two chips of the "patch of cytoplasm" sim. On "Arp2/3 alone" the filament count doubles every few seconds, each branch at 70°, until it hits the display cap. On "Arp2/3 + capping" you walk the capping slider and watch the red theory line tilt. Below \(k_{br}\) the tree still runs away, just more slowly; above it the network shuts down.
