At \(k_{cap} = k_{br}\) the average is flat, but a branching process held at balance is critical and dies with probability one. That is the argument for §1.4: a real lamellipodium is fed at the membrane.

Comes back: C1 §3.3 (growth against loss).

Biological examplean Arp2/3 brush under three capping settings

Take the sim's branching rate and ask what a minute does to a patch of brush at three capping rates.

  1. \(k_{br}\) = 0.10 s⁻¹.
  2. No capping: \(N_{open}\) doubles every ln 2 / 0.10 = 6.9 s. In 60 s it grows by \(e^{6}\) ≈ 400-fold.
  3. \(k_{cap}\) = 0.05 s⁻¹: net 0.05 s⁻¹, doubling every 13.9 s. In 60 s it grows by \(e^{3}\) ≈ 20-fold.
  4. \(k_{cap}\) = 0.20 s⁻¹: net −0.10 s⁻¹. A hundred open ends fall to 100 \(e^{-6}\) ≈ 0.25 in a minute.
  5. \(k_{cap} = k_{br}\): flat on average, but a critical branching process reaches zero with probability one.

What it means. No constant capping rate holds a brush open: too little and it runs away, too much and it closes in a minute, exactly enough and it dies by chance. A steady lamellipodium needs a supply of new ends at the membrane, which is why Rac switches on Arp2/3 there (§4.3). A Listeria bacterium uses the same fix: it activates Arp2/3 only at its own surface, so its comet tail is fed from one place.

Mechanical analogya reactor and its control rods

A fission reactor runs on the same equation. Each free neutron makes new neutrons at one rate and is absorbed by the control rods at another. The population grows or decays exponentially with the difference, and the balance point is called critical.

In the cellIn the machine
open barbed ends \(N_{open}\)free neutrons
Arp2/3 branching, \(k_{br}\)fissions making new neutrons
capping protein, \(k_{cap}\)absorption in the control rods
\(k_{br} = k_{cap}\)a critical reactor
new ends fed at the membranea neutron source plus a controller that moves the rods

Where it breaks. A reactor holds criticality with an enormous neutron population and active feedback, so chance extinction never happens. A lamellipodium has a few hundred open ends per micron, few enough that a critical brush really can die out by chance, which is why the cell feeds it rather than balances it.

4.1.7

Persistence length — bending stiffness written as a length

Minted in Week 4 §1.3 · Actin reinforcement: crosslinking, and why the jiggle matters · open the module

eq. 4.1.7$$L_p = \frac{EI}{k_BT} \qquad (\text{actin: } 7.3\times10^{-26}\ \text{N·m}^2 / 4.28\times10^{-21}\ \text{J} = 17\ \text{µm})$$

Letters

  • \(L_p\) — the persistence length, the distance over which thermal bending randomizes a filament's direction · µm · actin 17.7 µm at 25 °C (Gittes 1993), 17.1 µm at 37 °C
  • \(EI\) — the flexural rigidity, the material's stiffness \(E\) times the second moment \(I\) of the cross-section · N·m² · actin 7.3 × 10⁻²⁶; microtubule 2.2 × 10⁻²³ (Gittes 1993)
  • \(k_BT\) — thermal energy · J · 4.28 × 10⁻²¹ J = 4.28 pN·nm at 37 °C

How it is used

§1.3 mints it: the bath bends a rod with \(k_BT\), the rod resists with \(EI\), and their ratio is a length. The "patch of cytoplasm" sim shows 3-µm filaments sagging and straightening. §3.1 measures it the way Gittes did, by fitting the bending-mode spectrum of three thermal rods in one bath; its worked example gives 5.1 mm for a microtubule at 37 °C (the cast's 5.2 mm is Gittes's own). It feeds eq. 4.1.8's sag, §1.5's stiffness number \(2a/L_p\) ≈ 0.85 (a filament spanning the cell is floppy), and §4.4's dashboard, where a bacterium-sized cell gives 0.06.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea filament across a neutrophil, at two temperatures

Gittes measured actin in a bath at 25 °C; the cell runs at 37 °C. Does the warmer bath change the answer, and how does a filament compare with the cell it must span?

  1. \(EI_{actin}\) = 7.3 × 10⁻²⁶ N·m²; at 37 °C, \(k_BT\) = 4.28 × 10⁻²¹ J.
  2. \(L_p\) = 7.3 × 10⁻²⁶ / 4.28 × 10⁻²¹ = 1.71 × 10⁻⁵ m = 17.1 µm.
  3. At 25 °C, \(k_BT\) = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 298 = 4.11 × 10⁻²¹ J, so \(L_p\) = 17.8 µm, the cast's 17.7. Same rod, a cooler bath bends it less.
  4. Microtubule: 2.2 × 10⁻²³ / 4.28 × 10⁻²¹ = 5.1 mm, 300 times actin's.
  5. Across a neutrophil, \(2a\) = 15 µm: actin 15 / 17.1 = 0.88; microtubule 15 / 5,140 = 0.003.

What it means. One actin filament is about as long as it is persistent, so a filament spanning a neutrophil bends visibly and the cell must build a network to hold a shape. A microtubule is a rod at any cell scale. The rigidity is a property of the rod; the persistence length also depends on the temperature of the bath.

Mechanical analogyspaghetti in a boiling pot

Drop cooked and dry spaghetti into a pot at a rolling boil. The churning water kicks both alike. Cooked strands curl and lose their direction within a few centimetres; dry ones stay straight over their whole 25 cm. The kicks are the same, so the difference is all in the bending stiffness.

In the cellIn the machine
the bath's kicks, \(k_BT\) = 4.28 pN·nmthe boil's churning
actin, \(EI\) = 7.3 × 10⁻²⁶ N·m²cooked spaghetti
microtubule, \(EI\) 300 times largerdry spaghetti
\(L_p\)the length over which a strand forgets its direction
a neutrophil, 15 µm acrossthe pot

Where it breaks. Boiling is not thermal equilibrium: its kicks have a size and direction set by the bubbles. Cooking also changes the strand's own stiffness. A filament's \(EI\) stays put, and only the temperature moves its \(L_p\).

4.1.8

Thermal sag of a pinned segment — halve the span, the sag falls 2.8 times

Minted in Week 4 §1.3 · Actin reinforcement: crosslinking, and why the jiggle matters · open the module

eq. 4.1.8$$\langle y^2\rangle \approx \frac{\ell^3}{48\,L_p}, \qquad y_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{\ell^3}{48L_p}}$$

Letters

  • \(y\) — the midpoint's deviation from the chord, in one transverse direction · nm
  • \(y_{rms}\) — its root-mean-square size · nm · 178 nm for 3 µm of actin, 34 nm for 1 µm, 10 nm for 3 µm of microtubule
  • \(\ell\) — the free length between two pins (crosslinks) · µm
  • \(L_p\) — the persistence length (eq. 4.1.7) · µm · 17.7 µm for actin, as §1.3 uses

How it is used

§1.3 mints it for the "patch of cytoplasm" sim. On "no α-actinin" you read the rms sag against \(\sqrt{\ell^3/48L_p}\). On "α-actinin" the crosslinks shorten \(\ell\) and the sag falls along the \(\ell^{3/2}\) curve. The derive box uses equipartition: a coordinate's thermal variance is \(k_BT\) times its compliance, and a three-point bend has compliance \(\ell^3/48EI\). The verdict is that the jiggle which lets α-actinin's second arm find a partner is switched off by the mesh it builds (about 1 nm at 100-nm spacing). The check-yourself compares 3-µm and 1-µm segments: 5.2 times more sag.

Comes back: —

Biological examplehow close must α-actinin pin a bundle?

α-actinin is a 36-nm dumbbell. In a loose cortex its pins may sit microns apart; in a tight bundle they stack at its own length (Meyer & Aebi 1990). How far does a pinned actin segment jiggle at each spacing?

  1. \(L_p\) = 17.7 µm, so \(48L_p\) = 849.6 µm.
  2. \(\ell\) = 0.5 µm: \(\langle y^2\rangle\) = 0.125 / 849.6 = 1.47 × 10⁻⁴ µm², so \(y_{rms}\) = 12 nm.
  3. \(\ell\) = 0.2 µm: \(\langle y^2\rangle\) = 0.008 / 849.6 = 9.4 × 10⁻⁶ µm², so \(y_{rms}\) = 3.1 nm.
  4. \(\ell\) = 0.036 µm (a tight bundle): \(y_{rms}\) = 0.23 nm, less than a tenth of the 2.7-nm rise.
  5. To reach a neighbour 50 nm away by jiggle alone needs \(\ell^3 = 0.05^2 \times 849.6\) = 2.12 µm³, so \(\ell\) ≈ 1.3 µm of free length.

What it means. A filament pinned every half micron barely jiggles 12 nm and can no longer find a neighbour 50 nm away on its own. A tight bundle at α-actinin's own spacing has stopped being a thermal object. To crosslink further, the cell must first sever the mesh back into long free segments.

Mechanical analogya shelf and its brackets

A long shelf board rests on brackets. The board plays the filament and the brackets play α-actinin. Put a book at midspan and the board sinks by the three-point-bend deflection, which grows as the span cubed. Now bump the board at random with blows of fixed energy instead: its jiggle grows only as the span to the 3/2.

In the cellIn the machine
the filamentthe shelf board
α-actinin pinsbrackets
free length \(\ell\)span between brackets
thermal kicks, \(k_BT\)random bumps of fixed energy
\(y_{rms}\)how far the board's middle jiggles
\(L_p\)the board's stiffness written as a length

Add a bracket at midspan, halving the span. The book now sinks 2³ = 8 times less. The random jiggle falls only 2^{3/2} = 2.8 times, because a fixed energy spreads over a variance that scales with the compliance. The filament obeys the second rule.

Where it breaks. A shelf never moves on its own, and its brackets are screwed in by hand. A filament's sag is the bath's doing, and it is the very motion that brings α-actinin's second arm to a partner.

Featured in HW2 · Problem 5(a)
4.1.9

Péclet number — diffuse there, or be carried?

Minted in Week 4 §1.4 · Actin degradation: taking the network down, and the belt back to the front · open the module

eq. 4.1.9$$\mathrm{Pe} = \frac{vL}{D_G} = \frac{L^2/D_G}{L/v} = \frac{\text{time to diffuse } L}{\text{time to move } L}$$

Letters

  • \(\mathrm{Pe}\) — the Péclet number, time to diffuse over time to be carried · dimensionless
  • \(v\) — the carrying speed: the cell's or the flow's for the monomer belt, a motor's for cargo · µm/s · cell 0.2 µm/s; kinesin ≈ 0.8 µm/s
  • \(L\) — the distance · µm · 5 µm, rear to front of the belt
  • \(D_G\) — the monomer's diffusion coefficient in cytoplasm · µm²/s · 3–6 (McGrath 1998), 14 (Kiuchi 2011); the sim's default 6

How it is used

§1.4 mints it for the "rear to front" sim. On "cofilin + profilin" you read the median monomer trip against \(L^2/2D_G\); doubling \(L\) roughly quadruples the trip but only doubles the carry-back, which is Pe changing. The worked example gives Pe ≈ 0.17 and a 2-s trip, so the belt needs no motor. §1.5 and §4.4 put it on the dashboard as \(v \cdot 2a/D_G\) ≈ 0.2. §3.4 reuses it to decide when a road pays: a vesicle has Pe ≈ 80, and G-actin over a cell length has Pe ≈ 1.3.

Comes back: Week 7 §1.2 (why a neuron cannot wait for diffusion — the Péclet number, for a cargo).

Biological examplea vesicle down an axon

A motor neuron makes membrane and receptors in its cell body and needs them at its far end. Take the module's vesicle (radius 100 nm, \(D\) ≈ 0.1 µm²/s in cytoplasm, an estimate) and kinesin's ≈ 0.8 µm/s.

  1. Over \(L\) = 1 mm = 1000 µm: Pe = 0.8 × 1000 / 0.1 = 8,000.
  2. Diffusion, \(L^2/2D\) = 10⁶ / 0.2 = 5 × 10⁶ s ≈ 58 days. Kinesin, \(L/v\) = 1250 s ≈ 21 min.
  3. Over a typical motor-neuron axon, \(L\) = 1 m (spinal cord to foot): kinesin takes 1.25 × 10⁶ s ≈ 14 days.
  4. Diffusion over 1 m takes 10¹² / 0.2 = 5 × 10¹² s ≈ 160,000 years.
  5. Compare the monomer belt: \(v\) = 0.2 µm/s, \(L\) = 5 µm, \(D_G\) = 6 µm²/s, so Pe = 0.17.

What it means. Pe runs from 0.2 to about 10⁷ across the cell's cargo. For a monomer in a lamellipodium diffusion is free and fast. For a vesicle in an axon, without the road it never arrives in a lifetime. Two weeks on kinesin is slow, but it is finite.

Mechanical analogya parcel in a crowd, or on a conveyor

A parcel must cross a 100-m hall. One way: hand it to a crowd that passes it 1 m once a second in a random direction. The other: put it on a conveyor belt at 0.5 m/s. The crowd is diffusion; the belt is kinesin on a microtubule.

In the cellIn the machine
a vesiclethe parcel
thermal jostling, \(D\)the crowd: 1-m passes once a second, \(D\) = 1²/(2 × 1) = 0.5 m²/s
kinesin on a microtubule, \(v\)the conveyor belt, 0.5 m/s
axon length \(L\)the hall, 100 m
Pe0.5 × 100 / 0.5 = 100

The crowd takes \(L^2/2D\) = 10,000 / 1 = 10,000 s, nearly three hours. The belt takes 200 s.

Where it breaks. A conveyor never drops its parcel. Kinesin lets go after about 100 steps (0.8 µm) and must rebind, so a 1-m haul is over a million short rides joined by short diffusive gaps.

4.1.10

Damköhler number of the leading edge — what the tips actually see

Minted in Week 4 §1.5 · All together: the actin system alone moves a cell · open the module

eq. 4.1.10$$\mathrm{Da}_{edge} = \frac{k_{on}\,\rho_B\,\ell}{D_G}, \qquad G_f = \frac{G_b}{1 + \mathrm{Da}_{edge}}$$

Letters

  • \(\mathrm{Da}_{edge}\) — the Damköhler number of the edge: uptake by the tips over resupply by diffusion · dimensionless · ≈ 6 at full tip density; ≈ 4 in the sim
  • \(k_{on}\) — barbed-end rate constant · µm³/s per molecule · 11.6 µM⁻¹s⁻¹ = 0.0193 µm³/s (1 µM⁻¹s⁻¹ = 1.66 × 10⁻³ µm³/s)
  • \(\rho_B\) — growing tips per area of the front face · µm⁻² · 241 per µm of margin / 176 nm thick ≈ 1,370 (Abraham 1999)
  • \(\ell\) — the supply path, from body to edge · µm · 3 µm
  • \(D_G\) — monomer diffusion in cytoplasm · µm²/s · 14 (Kiuchi 2011)
  • \(G_b\), \(G_f\) — deliverable monomer in the body and at the front · µM · \(G_b\) = 100 µM

How it is used

§1.5 mints it for "the actin cell" sim, which prints the edge speed and Da at the front. At the density the sim reaches, the tips see about a fifth of the body's pool; at full uncapped density, a seventh. Push the tip density up and Da starves the edge. It has the form of Week 3's Damköhler referee (eq. 3.3.9–3.3.10): reaction against transport, now for an edge that eats monomer. The check-yourself halves the tip density: each tip grows 1.7 times faster, but the network's total flux falls. Its \(G_f\) feeds eq. 4.4.3's \(v_{pol}\) and §4.4's dashboard.

Comes back: —

Biological examplehow much of the body's actin reaches a neutrophil's front?

The neutrophil's front is a thin sheet packed with barbed ends. Monomer must diffuse 3 µm from the body to reach them. What concentration do the tips feed on?

  1. Convert \(k_{on}\): 11.6 × 1.66 × 10⁻³ = 0.0193 µm³/s per molecule.
  2. Tip density: \(\rho_B\) = 241 µm⁻¹ / 0.176 µm = 1,370 µm⁻².
  3. \(\mathrm{Da}_{edge}\) = 0.0193 × 1,370 × 3 / 14 = 5.7 ≈ 6.
  4. \(G_f\) = 100 / (1 + 5.7) = 15 µM, about a seventh of the body's pool (the module rounds to 14).
  5. Cap 30 % of the tips (the sim's front, \(\rho_B\) ≈ 960 µm⁻²): Da = 4.0 and \(G_f\) = 20 µM, a fifth.
  6. A shorter supply path, \(\ell\) = 1 µm, at full density: Da = 1.9 and \(G_f\) = 35 µM.

What it means. The edge is limited by supply, not by Pollard's rate constant: diffusion through the crowd of tips is the bottleneck. Capping protein, by shutting tips, raises what each of the rest can eat.

Mechanical analogysprinklers on one long hose

A garden hose runs from the tap to a manifold of sprinklers. Water reaching the manifold must pass the hose's resistance; each open sprinkler draws flow in proportion to the manifold's pressure. Balance the two and the manifold pressure is the tap pressure divided by (1 + total sprinkler conductance / hose conductance), the same form as \(G_f\).

In the cellIn the machine
body pool \(G_b\) = 100 µMtap pressure, 3 bar
resupply \(D_G/\ell\)hose conductance, 10 L/min per bar
one tip's uptake \(k_{on}\)one sprinkler's conductance, 2 L/min per bar
tips per area \(\rho_B\)open sprinklers, 30
\(\mathrm{Da}_{edge}\)30 × 2 / 10 = 6
\(G_f\)manifold pressure, 3 / 7 = 0.43 bar

Each sprinkler flows 0.86 L/min, 25.7 L/min in all. Shut half: Da = 3, the manifold rises to 0.75 bar, and each sprinkler flows 1.5 L/min, 1.75 times more. Total flow falls to 22.5 L/min, just as the check-yourself says.

Where it breaks. Water moves by pressure-driven bulk flow; monomer moves by diffusion (Fick's law), which has the same linear form but no bulk motion. A sprinkler also stays open, while tips are capped and opened at random.

Module Tab 2 · The Motors
4.2.1

Duty ratio — the fraction of its cycle a head holds on

Minted in Week 4 §2.2 · How a myosin walks: one foot planted, the other searching · open the module

eq. 4.2.1$$r = \frac{t_{attached}}{t_{cycle}} \qquad (\approx 0.05 \text{ for myosin II at saturating ATP; near 1 for kinesin})$$

Letters

  • \(r\) — the duty ratio · dimensionless · myosin II 0.050 (Uyeda 1990); myosin V head > 0.7 (De La Cruz 1999); kinesin near 1
  • \(t_{attached}\) — the time per cycle the head is strongly bound · ms
  • \(t_{cycle}\) — the time for one full ATP cycle · ms · myosin II: 1/(20 s⁻¹) = 50 ms (to confirm)

How it is used

§2.2 mints it for the "two feet, one hip" sim of myosin V. The panel reads the duty ratio against De La Cruz's > 0.7 and the step against 36 nm. "No ATP" leaves both feet planted (rigor), and lowering ATP to 50 µM raises the duty ratio further. The one number sorts the motors (Howard 1997): myosin V and kinesin carry cargo alone, while myosin II, off the track 95 % of the time, works only in teams. It is the probability a head is attached in eq. 4.2.6 and eq. 4.2.7.

Comes back: Week 7 §1.3 (the duty ratio, now a cargo's).

Biological examplethree motors, three lifestyles

The cast has three motors built on one kind of engine. How long does each hold on, and could a single molecule stay on its track?

  1. Myosin II: \(t_{cycle}\) = 1 / 20 s⁻¹ = 50 ms.
  2. \(r\) = 0.05, so \(t_{attached}\) = 0.05 × 50 ms = 2.5 ms; the head is off for 47.5 ms of every 50.
  3. One two-headed myosin II, heads independent: both off at once with probability 0.95² ≈ 0.90.
  4. Myosin V: each head bound more than 0.7 of its cycle. If independent, both off 0.3² = 0.09 of the time; the gate between the heads brings that close to zero.
  5. So myosin V stays on for a micron or more, 1000 / 36 ≈ 28 steps. Kinesin (\(r\) near 1) runs about 100 × 8 nm = 0.8 µm.

What it means. The same motor domain, three duty ratios, three jobs. A lone myosin II would drift off its filament nine-tenths of the time, so it must be bundled into minifilaments. Myosin V and kinesin carry a vesicle alone.

Mechanical analogycrossing the monkey bars

A child crossing monkey bars hand over hand is myosin V. One hand grips while the other swings forward to the next bar, and the trailing hand lets go only after the leading hand has closed. Each hand is on a bar for most of the cycle, so the child never falls. Now picture a climber whose two hands each grip only 5 % of the time, independently. Both are off about 90 % of the time. That climber is a lone myosin II, and falls.

In the cellIn the machine
a head (a foot)a hand
binding zones every 36 nmbars along the frame
\(t_{attached}\)time a hand grips
\(t_{cycle}\)time from one grip to the next by the same hand
\(r\) > 0.7 per head, myosin Veach hand on a bar most of the cycle
the gatelet go only after the other hand has closed

Where it breaks. A child swings like a pendulum and carries momentum into the next grab. The free head has no momentum; it searches by thermal wandering within about 10 nm of where its tether left it, and its grip is a chemical state switched by ATP.

4.2.2

Force ceiling from the fuel — work per stroke cannot beat one ATP

Minted in Week 4 §2.3 · Power output of a single motor · open the module

eq. 4.2.2$$F_{step}\,d \le \Delta\mu_{ATP} \quad\Rightarrow\quad F_{step} \lesssim \frac{\Delta\mu_{ATP}}{d} \approx \frac{25\,k_BT}{11\ \text{nm}} \approx 10\ \text{pN}$$

Letters

  • \(F_{step}\) — the steady force one head works against during its stroke · pN · myosin II measured 3–4 pN (Finer 1994)
  • \(d\) — the step or stroke · nm · myosin II 11 nm; kinesin 8 nm; myosin V 36 nm
  • \(\Delta\mu_{ATP}\) — the free energy one ATP releases · pN·nm · ≈ 25 \(k_BT\) ≈ 107 pN·nm (to confirm)
  • \(k_BT\) — thermal energy · pN·nm · 4.28 at 37 °C

How it is used

§2.3 mints it as step 1 of a five-step derivation: one ATP pays for one stroke, and a stroke against force \(F\) does work \(Fd\) at most. This is a stall defined by energy, 10 pN for an 11-nm stroke. The "one head against a load" sim's efficiency readout compares the work the filament receives with \(\Delta\mu_{ATP}\). Step 4 finds the force-balance stall, 3.5 pN; the factor of three between them is where the energy goes (the head's spring stores \(\tfrac12\kappa d^2\) ≈ 19 pN·nm and loses it as heat). §3.4 applies it to kinesin: 6 pN × 8 nm ≈ 11 \(k_BT\), about 45 %.

Comes back: —

Biological examplethe lever is a gear

One ATP buys about 107 pN·nm. How much force can that buy for each motor in the cast, given its step?

  1. \(\Delta\mu_{ATP}\) = 25 × 4.28 = 107 pN·nm.
  2. Myosin II, \(d\) = 11 nm: \(F_{step}\) ≤ 107 / 11 = 9.7 pN. Measured: 3–4 pN.
  3. Kinesin, \(d\) = 8 nm: \(F_{step}\) ≤ 107 / 8 = 13 pN. Measured stall ≈ 6 pN, so 48 / 107 = 45 % of the ATP.
  4. Myosin V, \(d\) = 36 nm: \(F_{step}\) ≤ 107 / 36 = 3.0 pN.
  5. Molloy's 4-nm stroke for myosin II would allow ≤ 27 pN; he measured ≥ 1.7 pN.

What it means. The same fuel buys force or distance, not both. Myosin V's long lever carries cargo 36 nm per ATP, but it can never hold more than about 3 pN. Measured motors sit at a third to a half of their ceiling; the rest of the ATP leaves as heat.

Mechanical analogya pile driver

A pile driver lifts a heavy ram and drops it on a pile. Each blow delivers a fixed energy, the ram's weight times its drop. The pile moves a small "set" against the soil's resistance. Energy per blow caps the resistance it can beat: resistance × set ≤ energy per blow. Pile-driving formulas used on building sites rest on this balance.

In the cellIn the machine
one ATP, \(\Delta\mu_{ATP}\) = 107 pN·nmone blow: 3,000-kg ram dropped 1 m = 29.4 kJ
stroke \(d\) = 11 nmset per blow, 10 mm
\(F_{step}\)soil resistance
ceiling \(\Delta\mu_{ATP}/d\) ≈ 10 pN29.4 kJ / 0.01 m = 2.9 MN
heat, spring storagerebound, heat, compression of the pile

Real piles take less than 2.9 MN for the same set, because part of each blow is lost, as part of each ATP is.

Where it breaks. The ram's energy arrives as one impact with inertia. A head's energy is released as a shape change in a thermal bath, and the inequality is the second law: no cycle can bank more than the fuel's free energy.

Featured in HW2 · Problem 3(b)
4.2.3

Power of one head — force times speed

Minted in Week 4 §2.3 · Power output of a single motor · open the module

eq. 4.2.3$$P = \frac{F\,d}{t_{cycle}} = F\,v$$

Letters

  • \(P\) — mechanical power delivered to the filament · pN·nm/s (1 pN·nm/s = 10⁻²¹ W; 1 aW = 10⁻¹⁸ W)
  • \(F\) — the load the head works against · pN
  • \(d\) — distance the filament moves per stroke · nm · 11 nm unloaded
  • \(t_{cycle}\) — time per ATP cycle · s · ≈ 50 ms at saturating ATP
  • \(v\) — the filament's speed, \(d/t_{cycle}\) · nm/s

How it is used

§2.3 mints it as step 2: power is work per stroke over time per stroke. The second form, \(Fv\), is what the "one head against a load" sim's right-hand chart plots, and it is zero at both ends: at no load nothing resists, at stall nothing moves. The worked example gives 770 pN·nm/s ≈ 0.8 aW at saturating ATP and a third of that at 25 µM (eq. 3.2.15 again). HW2 asks for a motor's power below saturation.

Comes back: —

Biological examplethe power to slide a filament in the gliding assay

In Kron and Spudich's assay, heads on glass slide actin at 4 µm/s. The only load is the water's drag on the filament. How much power does that take, and how does it compare with one head's output?

  1. Drag on a 5-µm filament at 4 µm/s: \(F\) ≈ 0.12 pN (§2.3, step 0).
  2. \(P = Fv\) = 0.12 pN × 4,000 nm/s = 480 pN·nm/s = 0.48 aW.
  3. One head's ceiling, as the module's worked example books it: 3.5 pN over the full 11 nm per 50-ms cycle, \(P = Fd/t_{cycle}\) = 3.5 × 11 / 0.05 = 770 pN·nm/s = 0.77 aW.
  4. The ATP it burns: 107 pN·nm × 20 s⁻¹ = 2,140 pN·nm/s = 2.1 aW.
  5. Efficiency ceiling: 770 / 2,140 = 36 %. A 3.5-pN load in fact stalls the head (eq. 4.2.4); what reaches the filament peaks near 0.19 aW, 9 % of the fuel.

What it means. The water's drag, 0.12 pN, is about a thirtieth of one head's 3.5-pN stall, which is why the gliding assay runs at the unloaded speed. In a cell the load is the network's drag, thousands of times larger. A million engaged heads deliver under a picowatt.

Mechanical analogya cyclist on a hill

A cyclist's legs are the head; the slope is the load. Power at the wheel is the force pushing the bike forward times its speed. On the flat in a low gear the legs spin with little force, so the power is small. Against a wall the force is large and the speed zero, so the power is zero again.

In the cellIn the machine
one headthe cyclist's legs
load \(F\)gravity along the slope
\(d\) per cycledistance per pedal turn
\(t_{cycle}\)time per pedal turn
\(v = d/t_{cycle}\)road speed
\(P = Fv\)power at the wheel

A rider and bike of 80 kg on a 5 % grade push against about 0.05 × 80 × 9.81 = 39 N. At a typical 200 W, the speed is \(v = P/F\) = 200 / 39 = 5.1 m/s, about 18 km/h.

Where it breaks. A bike coasts on its momentum between pedal strokes; a filament has none and stops the moment no head pulls. The cyclist's power also falls at extreme cadences for reasons of physiology, not because \(F\) or \(v\) is zero.

4.2.4

Load line — the speed falls in a straight line to stall

Minted in Week 4 §2.3 · Power output of a single motor · open the module

eq. 4.2.4$$v = v_0\left(1 - \frac{F}{F_{stall}}\right), \qquad F_{stall} = \kappa d \approx 3.5\ \text{pN}, \quad v_0 = d\,k_{cycle}$$

Letters

  • \(v\) — the filament's speed under load · nm/s
  • \(v_0\) — the unloaded speed of one head, \(d\,k_{cycle}\) · nm/s · 11 nm × 20 s⁻¹ = 220 nm/s
  • \(F\) — the steady load pulling the filament back · pN
  • \(F_{stall}\) — the load at which the gain per stroke is zero · pN · ≈ 3.5 pN
  • \(\kappa\) — the stiffness of a strongly bound head · pN/nm · ≈ 0.32, Finer's 3.5 pN / 11 nm (a consistency check, not a measurement)
  • \(d\) — the stroke · nm · 11 nm
  • \(k_{cycle}\) — strokes per second · s⁻¹ · ≈ 20 at saturating ATP

How it is used

§2.3 mints it as step 4, from the force balance on one bound head. The stroke moves the head's spring forward by \(d\); the load takes \(F/\kappa\) of it back; the filament keeps \(d - F/\kappa\), zero at stall. In the "one head against a load" sim, the red zigzag is \(F/\kappa\) and the blue brace is what is kept; the chips are pull (1.5 pN), stall (3.5 pN) and slip (6 pN). Two stalls, one gap: energy allows 10 pN (eq. 4.2.2), this spring holds 3.5. It is a straight-line stand-in; kinesin's measured law (eq. 4.3.5) is not. §4.1's speed ladder uses it to show motors do not set a cell's speed.

Comes back: Week 5 §1.3 (the load line, now dragging a network).

Biological exampleone myosin II head pulling harder and harder

A single head in an optical trap, as in Finer's experiment, at saturating ATP. How fast does the filament move, and how much work reaches it, as the trap's load rises?

  1. \(F_{stall} = \kappa d\) = 0.32 × 11 = 3.5 pN; \(v_0 = d\,k_{cycle}\) = 11 × 20 = 220 nm/s.
  2. At \(F\) = 1.0 pN: each stroke keeps 11 − 1.0/0.32 = 7.9 nm; \(v\) = 220 × (1 − 1.0/3.52) = 158 nm/s.
  3. At half stall, \(F\) = 1.76 pN: \(v\) = 110 nm/s and \(P = Fv\) = 194 pN·nm/s ≈ 0.19 aW, the peak.
  4. Work kept per stroke there: 1.76 × 5.5 = 9.7 pN·nm, 9 % of the 107 pN·nm ATP.
  5. At 3.5 pN: \(v\) = 0 and \(P\) = 0, yet ATP still burns at 20 per second.

What it means. The head is a spring, and the load takes back part of every stroke. It delivers the most power at half its stall force, and even there only 9 % of the fuel reaches the filament. At stall it holds a load and burns fuel for nothing outside, like a muscle holding a weight still.

Mechanical analogya small DC motor's speed–torque line

A permanent-magnet DC motor has the same straight load line. Its speed falls linearly with the load torque, from a no-load speed to a stall torque, and its output power peaks at half the stall torque.

In the cellIn the machine
load \(F\)load torque
\(F_{stall} = \kappa d\)stall torque, 0.05 N·m
\(v_0 = d\,k_{cycle}\)no-load speed, 6,000 rpm = 628 rad/s
\(v = v_0(1 - F/F_{stall})\)the speed–torque line
ATP burnt at stallcurrent at stall, all of it heat

At half stall, 0.025 N·m, the shaft turns at 314 rad/s and delivers 0.025 × 314 = 7.9 W, the most this motor can give.

Where it breaks. The motor's line comes from electromagnetism, not from a compliant head. Real muscle follows Hill's curved relation (the muscle weeks), real kinesin's line is measured and not straight (eq. 4.3.5), and past stall the motor simply turns backward while a head is torn off (eq. 4.2.5).

Featured in HW3 · Problem 2(b)
4.2.5

Bell's law — a bond under force lets go sooner

Minted in Week 4 §2.3 · Power output of a single motor · open the module

eq. 4.2.5$$k_{off}(f) = k_0\,e^{f/f_\beta}$$

Letters

  • \(k_{off}(f)\) — the bond's off-rate under force · s⁻¹ (its lifetime is \(1/k_{off}\))
  • \(k_0\) — the off-rate with no force · s⁻¹
  • \(f\) — the force pulling the bond apart · pN
  • \(f_\beta\) — the force that lowers the barrier by one \(k_BT\), \(k_BT/x_\beta\) · pN · the sim's 2.5 pN
  • \(x_\beta\) — the distance from the bound state to the barrier, in the text not the box · nm · 4.28 / 2.5 = 1.7 nm

How it is used

§2.3 mints it as step 5, past stall. When \(F\) exceeds \(\kappa d\) the load drags the filament back through the bound head, and the bond carries the force. A bond under force does not fail at a threshold. It fails sooner, exponentially, because the load tilts the energy landscape it must climb out of (Week 1's Boltzmann factor, eq. 1.2.7). On the "slip" chip at 6 pN the off-rate is up elevenfold, the head is torn off before its cycle ends, and the filament slips. It is minted here because slip is where it is first seen; the clutch reuses it for other bonds.

Comes back: Week 5 §1.5 (Bell's law, now for the integrin–ligand bond); Week 5 §2.2 (written as the lifetime the panel plots); Week 6 §1.3 (how long a bond lasts under a load \(f\)); C1 §2.4 (Bell, as a lifetime — can a cell pull 40 pN?); R2 §1.5 (Bell's slip bond).

Biological examplea myosin head pulled past stall

A minifilament's head holds a filament while the network behind it is pulled harder and harder, as in the "slip" chip. Using the sim's \(f_\beta\), how much sooner does the head let go at each load?

  1. \(f_\beta\) = 2.5 pN, so \(x_\beta = k_BT/f_\beta\) = 4.28 / 2.5 = 1.7 nm.
  2. At the stall load, 3.5 pN: \(k_{off}/k_0 = e^{3.5/2.5} = e^{1.4}\) = 4.1.
  3. At the "slip" load, 6 pN: \(e^{2.4}\) = 11.
  4. At the fuel's ceiling, 10 pN (eq. 4.2.2): \(e^{4}\) = 55.
  5. In the plotted quantity, the lifetime: a bond lasting 2.5 ms unloaded (one stroke's attached time; illustrative) lasts 2.5 / 11 = 0.23 ms at 6 pN.
  6. Each extra piconewton multiplies the off-rate by \(e^{1/2.5}\) = 1.49.

What it means. There is no breaking force, only a breaking rate. At 6 pN the head lives a tenth of its normal attached time, too short to finish a stroke, so the filament slides back. Next week the same law decides how long an integrin holds a cell to the floor.

Mechanical analogya ratchet winch on a shaking deck

A winch holds a load with a spring-loaded pawl seated in a tooth. On a ship's vibrating deck, each jolt has some chance of lifting the pawl over the tooth's tip. The rope's load pushes the pawl up the tooth face, so the more load, the less any jolt has to do, and the rope pays out a tooth at a time more often.

In the cellIn the machine
head bound to actinpawl seated in a tooth
thermal kicks, \(k_BT\)jolts of the deck
force \(f\) on the bondrope load pushing the pawl up the tooth
\(x_\beta\), the bond's reach to its barrierhow far the pawl must ride to clear the tip
\(k_{off}(f)\)rate of slipping a tooth
slip past stallrope paying out tooth by tooth

Where it breaks. A real pawl holds firmly until a definite load and slips only near it. A protein bond has no threshold: it can let go at any force, just exponentially sooner as the force rises.

4.2.6

Force of a team — force adds with the number of heads

Minted in Week 4 §2.4 · Tug of war: force adds, speed does not · open the module

eq. 4.2.6$$F_{tot} = N\,r\,F_{step} \qquad (60 \times 0.05 \times 3.5\ \text{pN} \approx 10\ \text{pN per minifilament})$$

Letters

  • \(F_{tot}\) — the team's time-averaged force · pN · ≈ 10 pN per minifilament
  • \(N\) — heads on the minifilament · count · ≈ 60 (Billington 2013, count to confirm)
  • \(r\) — duty ratio (eq. 4.2.1) · 0.05
  • \(F_{step}\) — force per attached head · pN · 3.5 pN (Finer 1994)

How it is used

§2.4 mints it for the "heads sharing one filament" sim: read the mean attached count against \(Nr\). Sixty heads pull three times as hard as twenty but slide only about 1.5 times faster (eq. 4.2.7). Load them and the time-averaged force reads about 11 pN, yet the team stops advancing near 5 pN. The gaps when every head is off, \((1-r)^N\), let the load take back what the strokes won. So there are two forces: the holding force \(NrF_{step}\) and a lower sliding stall. It feeds §4.3's rear budget (about 100 minifilaments per micron against the floor) and the \(Nr\) number on §4.4's dashboard.

Comes back: C1 §2.4 (a team's force — can a cell pull 40 pN?); R2 §1.5 (the force of a team).

Biological examplehow many myosin heads equal one kinesin?

Kinesin pulls about 6 pN alone, because it almost never lets go. How many myosin II heads match that, and how many minifilaments does a neutrophil's rear need?

  1. One head's time-averaged pull: \(rF_{step}\) = 0.05 × 3.5 = 0.175 pN.
  2. A minifilament, \(N\) = 60: \(F_{tot}\) = 60 × 0.175 = 10.5 pN.
  3. To match one kinesin, 6 pN: \(N\) = 6 / 0.175 ≈ 34 heads.
  4. The rear against the floor, about 1 nN per µm (§4.3's estimate): 1000 / 10.5 ≈ 95 minifilaments per µm.
  5. The catch: with \(N\) = 60, all heads are off at once 0.95⁶⁰ = 4.6 % of the time, so the sliding stall sits below 10.5 pN.

What it means. A low-duty motor buys force with numbers: thirty-four myosin heads to equal one kinesin. Muscle packs hundreds of heads per thick filament for the same reason, and with that many there are no gaps.

Mechanical analogya tug-of-war team that keeps re-gripping

Picture a tug-of-war team whose members each pull hard but keep letting go to re-grip. The rope's average tension is team size times the fraction of time each one grips times the pull of one grip.

In the cellIn the machine
heads \(N\) = 60team members, 20
duty ratio \(r\) = 0.05fraction of time each grips, 0.5
\(F_{step}\) = 3.5 pNone member's pull, 500 N
\(F_{tot} = NrF_{step}\)average tension, 20 × 0.5 × 500 = 5,000 N
holding vs sliding stallrope tied to a post vs a rope that slips back in the gaps

Where it breaks. A human team takes turns on purpose and the rope's mass carries it through brief gaps. Myosin heads cycle independently and the filament has no momentum, so every moment with no head attached is lost ground.

4.2.7

Speed of a team — speed saturates once one head is always on

Minted in Week 4 §2.4 · Tug of war: force adds, speed does not · open the module

eq. 4.2.7$$v = v_0\left[1 - (1 - r)^N\right], \qquad v_0 = \frac{d}{t_{attached}} = \frac{d}{r\,t_{cycle}}$$

Letters

  • \(v\) — the filament's average sliding speed · µm/s
  • \(v_0\) — the speed while driven, one stroke per attached time · µm/s · 11 nm / 2.5 ms = 4.4 µm/s, which the module rounds to ≈ 4, Kron & Spudich's sliding speed
  • \(r\) — duty ratio · 0.05
  • \(N\) — heads within reach · count
  • \(d\) — stroke · nm · 11 nm
  • \(t_{attached}\), \(t_{cycle}\) — attached time and cycle time · ms · 2.5 ms, 50 ms

How it is used

§2.4 mints it (Uyeda, Kron & Spudich 1990) for the same "heads sharing one filament" sim. One head moves in bursts at about 0.2 µm/s; twenty slide continuously at 2.6 µm/s; sixty reach 3.8 µm/s, close to the ceiling. The derive box multiplies the driven speed \(v_0\) by the fraction of time at least one head is attached, \(1 - (1-r)^N\), assuming the heads are independent. It recovers Kron and Spudich's sliding speed from one head's stroke and a duty ratio. Set beside eq. 4.2.6 it gives the section's title: force adds, speed does not.

Comes back: —

Biological examplesparse heads on glass

Uyeda's experiment spreads myosin thinly on glass and lets actin slide over it. How many heads must be in reach of a filament before it slides near full speed?

  1. \(v_0 = d/(r\,t_{cycle})\) = 11 nm / (0.05 × 50 ms) = 11 nm / 2.5 ms = 4.4 µm/s.
  2. \(N\) = 1: \(v = 4.4 \times 0.05\) = 0.22 µm/s, in bursts with long pauses.
  3. \(N\) = 5: \(1 - 0.95^5\) = 0.23, so \(v\) ≈ 1.0 µm/s.
  4. 90 % of \(v_0\) needs \(0.95^N\) = 0.1: \(N\) = ln 0.1 / ln 0.95 ≈ 45 heads.
  5. 99 % needs \(N\) ≈ 90 heads.
  6. A 60-head minifilament runs at \(1 - 0.95^{60}\) = 95 % of \(v_0\).

What it means. Speed saturates near 45–90 heads while force (eq. 4.2.6) keeps climbing. Beyond a minifilament's sixty heads, more heads buy force, not speed.

Mechanical analogyhauling a barge through mud, hand over hand

A crew hauls a barge along a canal so thick with mud that it stops the instant no one pulls. Each hauler grabs the rope, pulls one arm's length, lets go and reaches forward again. The barge moves at the pulling speed whenever someone holds the rope, and not at all otherwise.

In the cellIn the machine
heads \(N\)haulers
duty ratio \(r\)fraction of time each grips, 0.25
\(v_0 = d/t_{attached}\)pulling speed while gripping, 0.5 m per 1-s grip = 0.5 m/s
\(1 - (1-r)^N\)fraction of time someone holds the rope
\(v\)the barge's average speed

One hauler: 0.5 × 0.25 = 0.125 m/s. Four: 0.5 × (1 − 0.75⁴) = 0.34 m/s. Ten: 0.5 × (1 − 0.75¹⁰) = 0.47 m/s, close to the ceiling.

Where it breaks. Even in mud a barge coasts a little, and haulers coordinate. Myosin heads are independent and the filament has no inertia. Real heads on one filament also share load and interfere, so measured curves saturate a little differently.

Module Tab 3 · Microtubules
4.3.1

Flexural rigidity of a tube — stiffness is cross-section

Minted in Week 4 §3.1 · Why a cell needs microtubules at all — and why they have to be tubes · open the module

eq. 4.3.1$$EI = E\,\frac{\pi\,(r_o^4 - r_i^4)}{4} \qquad (E \approx 1.2\ \text{GPa},\ r_o = 12.5\ \text{nm},\ r_i = 8.5\ \text{nm} \Rightarrow 1.8\times10^{-23}\ \text{N·m}^2)$$

Letters

  • \(EI\) — flexural rigidity of the tube · N·m² · computed 1.8 × 10⁻²³; measured 2.2 × 10⁻²³ (Gittes 1993)
  • \(E\) — the stiffness of the material itself (its Young's modulus, as the module writes it; a later week builds what a modulus is) · Pa · ≈ 1.2 GPa, Gittes's inference for tubulin
  • \(r_o\) — outer radius · nm · 12.5 nm
  • \(r_i\) — inner radius · nm · 8.5 nm

How it is used

§3.1 mints it for the "three thermal rods in one bath" sim: an actin filament, a microtubule, and a solid rod of tubulin's \(E\) at the tube's outer radius. The sim fits \(L_p\) from the bending-mode spectrum, as Gittes did. The solid rod is nearly as stiff for about twice the material. The worked example lands within 20 % of Gittes, and a 3–3.5 nm thread of the same \(E\) brackets actin's measured value: stiffness is cross-section to within a factor of two. Through eq. 4.1.7 it gives \(L_p\) ≈ 5 mm and the same example's verdict that a 10-µm microtubule is a rod (\(L/L_p\) = 0.002) where actin is a rope (0.59).

Comes back: —

Biological examplewhy build the compass out of tubes?

A cell has a fixed budget of tubulin to make a stiff rod. Compare the tube it builds with a solid rod of the same outer radius, and with a solid rod made of the same amount of tubulin.

  1. Tube: \(I = \pi(12.5^4 - 8.5^4)/4 = \pi(24{,}414 - 5{,}220)/4\) = 1.51 × 10⁴ nm⁴ = 1.51 × 10⁻³² m⁴.
  2. \(EI\) = 1.2 × 10⁹ × 1.51 × 10⁻³² = 1.8 × 10⁻²³ N·m² (Gittes measured 2.2 × 10⁻²³).
  3. Solid rod, same outer radius: \(I\) is 24,414 / 19,194 = 1.27 times the tube's, for 156 / 84 = 1.86 times the material.
  4. Solid rod, same material (area π × 84 nm², radius 9.2 nm): the tube is \((r_o^2 + r_i^2)/(r_o^2 - r_i^2)\) = 228.5 / 84 = 2.7 times stiffer.
  5. Persistence length from the computed \(EI\) (eq. 4.1.7): 1.8 × 10⁻²³ / 4.28 × 10⁻²¹ = 4.2 mm; the measured \(EI\) gives 5.1 mm.

What it means. Spreading the same tubulin into a ring 25 nm across nearly triples its stiffness. That is why one microtubule spans a 15-µm cell as a straight rod (\(L/L_p\) ≈ 0.003) and can carry a motor's traffic.

Mechanical analogya scaffold tube against a solid bar

Builders use tubes, not bars, for the same reason. Take a standard steel scaffold tube, 48.3 mm across with a 4.0-mm wall (typical), and a solid steel bar made of the same amount of steel. The material's \(E\) is the same for both, so it cancels from the comparison.

In the cellIn the machine
tubulin, \(E\) ≈ 1.2 GPasteel
outer radius \(r_o\) = 12.5 nm24.15 mm
inner radius \(r_i\) = 8.5 nm20.15 mm
tube over same-material rod, 2.7\((24.15^2 + 20.15^2)/(24.15^2 - 20.15^2)\) = 5.6
actin, a 7-nm threada thin solid bar

The scaffold tube is 5.6 times stiffer than the bar its steel would make. Its wall is thinner relative to its radius than a microtubule's, so it gains more.

Where it breaks. Steel is a continuous material. A microtubule is a lattice of thirteen protofilaments held by bonds, its \(E\) is an inference, and MAPs change its stiffness in a living cell.

4.3.2

Four-parameter model of dynamic instability — grow slowly, collapse fast, switch at random

Minted in Week 4 §3.2 · Dynamic instability · open the module

eq. 4.3.2$$\text{growing at } v_g = \delta_{MT}(k_{on}C - k_{off}),\quad \text{shrinking at } v_s,\quad \text{switching at } f_{cat}\ (\text{grow}\to\text{shrink}),\ f_{res}\ (\text{shrink}\to\text{grow})$$

Letters

  • \(v_g\) — growth speed of a plus end, eq. 4.1.1 with tubulin's numbers · µm/min · ≈ 1.7 µm/min at 10 µM
  • \(\delta_{MT}\) — tube length added per dimer, 8 nm over thirteen protofilaments · nm · 8/13 ≈ 0.62 nm
  • \(k_{on}\), \(k_{off}\) — plus-end rates · µM⁻¹s⁻¹, s⁻¹ · 8.9, 44 (Walker 1988)
  • \(C\) — free tubulin · µM · ≈ 10 µM
  • \(v_s\) — shrinking speed · µm/min · 733 dimers/s × 0.62 nm ≈ 27 µm/min (Walker 1988)
  • \(f_{cat}\) — catastrophe frequency, growth to shrinkage · min⁻¹ · ≈ 0.6 (illustrative)
  • \(f_{res}\) — rescue frequency, shrinkage to growth · min⁻¹ · ≈ 0.3 (illustrative)

How it is used

§3.2 mints it for the "forty microtubules from a nucleating strip" sim. One tracked microtubule saw-tooths while the length histogram settles. The chips are bounded, unbounded (more tubulin, MAPs tipped toward stabilizing) and no rescue, and a negative MAP setting acts like stathmin. Tubulin's GTP here is a switch, not a clock: lose the cap and the end collapses. It feeds eq. 4.3.3's mean length, eq. 4.3.4's search, and the compass clock \(a/v_g + a/v_s\) ≈ 290 s of §3.5 and §4.4.

Comes back: —

Biological exampleone microtubule probing toward the edge

A microtubule grows from the centrosome toward a fibroblast's edge 10 µm away, in 10 µM tubulin. Price each of its four parameters.

  1. \(v_g\) = 0.62 nm × (8.9 × 10 − 44) s⁻¹ = 0.62 × 45 = 27.9 nm/s = 1.7 µm/min.
  2. \(v_s\) = 0.62 × 733 = 454 nm/s = 27 µm/min, sixteen times faster.
  3. A growth phase lasts 1/\(f_{cat}\) = 1/0.6 min = 100 s on average and adds \(v_g/f_{cat}\) = 1.67 / 0.6 ≈ 2.8 µm.
  4. A shrink phase lasts 1/\(f_{res}\) ≈ 200 s and could remove 27 × 3.3 ≈ 90 µm, far more than was built, so most shrinks run back to the centrosome.
  5. Chance one growth phase reaches the edge: \(e^{-f_{cat}R/v_g} = e^{-0.6 \times 10/1.67}\) ≈ 2.8 %.

What it means. A microtubule builds for minutes and tears down in seconds. Each probe is cheap to abandon, but only about one in thirty-six reaches a 10-µm edge. That gap is what §3.3's search pays for.

Mechanical analogya spring-return tape measure

A tape measure is drawn out slowly by hand and, when the lock slips, zips back on its spring. Catching it mid-retraction is a rescue.

In the cellIn the machine
plus end growing, \(v_g\)tape drawn out, 0.1 m/s
shrinking, \(v_s\)spring retraction, 1.6 m/s
catastrophe, \(f_{cat}\)the lock slips
rescue, \(f_{res}\)a thumb catches the tape mid-return
GTP capthe lock
the centrosomethe case

Three metres take 30 s to draw out and 1.9 s to retract, the same sixteen-to-one ratio as tubulin.

Where it breaks. A tape's lock slips when someone presses it. A catastrophe has no operator: it is a random event at a fixed rate, so lengths spread into an exponential distribution.

4.3.3

Mean length when growth is bounded — a cell tunes one denominator

Minted in Week 4 §3.2 · Dynamic instability · open the module

eq. 4.3.3$$\langle L\rangle = \frac{v_g\,v_s}{v_s f_{cat} - v_g f_{res}} \qquad (\text{bounded only while } v_s f_{cat} > v_g f_{res};\ \text{with no rescue, } \langle L\rangle = v_g/f_{cat})$$

Letters

  • \(\langle L\rangle\) — mean microtubule length in steady state · µm · 2.9 µm for the default settings
  • \(v_g\), \(v_s\) — growth and shrinking speeds · µm/min · 1.7, 27
  • \(f_{cat}\), \(f_{res}\) — catastrophe and rescue frequencies · min⁻¹ · 0.6, 0.3 (illustrative)

How it is used

§3.2 mints it (Dogterom & Leibler 1993) for the same sim: read the histogram's mean against the formula. The derive box balances the switching, \(p_g f_{cat} = p_s f_{res}\), and the sign of the mean drift decides bounded or unbounded. With no rescue the mean is simply \(v_g/f_{cat}\), how far an end grows before its first catastrophe. The worked example gives 2.9 µm, and \(f_{res}\) = 10 min⁻¹ tips it unbounded. §3.3 uses the 2.9 µm, a third of the cell's radius, to explain why most searches die before the edge.

Comes back: —

Biological exampleMAPs and destabilizers as dials

A cell changes microtubule length with proteins that move \(f_{cat}\) and \(f_{res}\): stabilizing MAPs lower catastrophe and raise rescue, and a destabilizer such as stathmin does the reverse. Keep \(v_g\) = 1.7 and \(v_s\) = 27 µm/min, so the numerator is 45.9 µm²/min².

  1. Default (0.6, 0.3): \(\langle L\rangle\) = 45.9 / (16.2 − 0.51) = 2.9 µm.
  2. A MAP halves \(f_{cat}\) and doubles \(f_{res}\) (0.3, 0.6): 45.9 / (8.1 − 1.02) = 6.5 µm.
  3. A stronger MAP, \(f_{cat}\) = 0.1 with \(f_{res}\) = 0.6: 45.9 / (2.7 − 1.02) = 27 µm, longer than the cell.
  4. The edge of boundedness: \(f_{cat} = v_g f_{res}/v_s\) = 1.7 × 0.6 / 27 = 0.038 min⁻¹.
  5. A destabilizer doubles \(f_{cat}\) (1.2, 0.3): 45.9 / (32.4 − 0.51) = 1.4 µm.

What it means. Modest changes in two switching frequencies move the mean length from 1.4 to 27 µm without touching the growth chemistry. The denominator, not tubulin itself, sets how far the array reaches.

Mechanical analogya fishing line with a restless angler

A lure drifts away on a current, paying out line slowly. Now and then the angler starts reeling it in fast, and sometimes stops reeling before the lure is home. The average length of line out follows the same formula.

In the cellIn the machine
plus endthe lure
\(v_g\)drift paying out line, 0.5 m/s
\(v_s\)reeling in, 2 m/s
\(f_{cat}\)the angler starts reeling, once a minute
\(f_{res}\)the angler stops mid-retrieve, twice a minute
the cortexthe end of the spool

Mean line out = (0.5 × 2) / (2/60 − 0.5/30) = 1 / 0.0167 = 60 m. If the angler stops mid-retrieve four times a minute, \(v_g f_{res}\) equals \(v_s f_{cat}\), the denominator vanishes, and the line runs out until the spool ends.

Where it breaks. An angler decides; a microtubule's switches are random events at fixed rates. In a cell \(f_{cat}\) also depends on the end's age, the tubulin it sees and whether it presses on the cortex.

4.3.4

Search time — how long until some rod finds the target

Minted in Week 4 §3.3 · Search and capture — where the microtubules point · open the module

eq. 4.3.4$$T \approx \frac{2\pi R}{s}\left(\frac{R}{v_g} + \frac{R}{v_s}\right)\frac{1}{N} \qquad (\text{a target } s \text{ wide on a cell of radius } R,\ N \text{ rods})$$

Letters

  • \(T\) — mean time to the first capture · s
  • \(R\) — cell radius, centrosome to edge · µm · 10 µm in the sim
  • \(s\) — target width on the edge · µm · 1 µm
  • \(v_g\), \(v_s\) — growth and shrinking speeds · nm/s · 28, 450
  • \(N\) — rods searching in parallel · count · 200

How it is used

§3.3 mints it for the "radial array looking for a target" sim, which measures the capture time over repeated trials beside a Monte Carlo of the same rules. A random excursion hits the target with odds \(s/2\pi R\), each costs a round trip, and \(N\) rods search at once. The "growth only" chip leaves about 3 of 200 rods ever hitting; the MAP chip makes capture faster. The estimate assumes every excursion reaches the edge, but only 2.7 % do. So the Monte Carlo sits about eleven times higher (21 min against 2 min): the right scaling, the wrong number.

Comes back: —

Biological examplere-aiming at a neutrophil's new front

A neutrophil turns and its array must find the new front, a broad arc of edge. How long does the scaling estimate say?

  1. \(R\) = 7.5 µm (neutrophil radius); front arc \(s\) = 5 µm (illustrative); \(N\) = 100 rods (§3.5's array).
  2. Excursions needed: \(2\pi R/s\) = 2π × 7.5 / 5 = 9.4.
  3. One round trip: 7,500/28 + 7,500/450 = 268 + 17 = 285 s.
  4. One rod alone: 9.4 × 285 ≈ 2,680 s ≈ 45 min. A hundred rods: \(T\) ≈ 27 s.
  5. But only \(e^{-f_{cat}R/v_g} = e^{-0.01 \times 268}\) ≈ 7 % of growth phases reach 7.5 µm, so 27 s is an underestimate by several-fold (×11 in the module's own case).

What it means. Re-aiming the array at a new front is a minutes-scale job, slower than the map (about 15 s) and the body's crossing (about 75 s). That is why the microtubules are the cell's compass and not its steering wheel.

Mechanical analogycranes searching blind for a pallet

Four telescoping cranes stand at the centre of a round yard 30 m in radius. Each operator, blindfolded, swings to a random bearing, extends the boom slowly to the rim, then retracts it fast. A 3-m pallet sits somewhere on the rim.

In the cellIn the machine
centrosomethe cranes' common base
a rod's growth, \(v_g\)boom extension, 0.5 m/s
shrinkage, \(v_s\)boom retraction, 5 m/s
target \(s\) on a cell of radius \(R\)3-m pallet on a 30-m rim
rods \(N\)cranes, 4

Tries needed: 2π × 30 / 3 = 63. Each costs 60 + 6 = 66 s. With four cranes, \(T\) = 63 × 66 / 4 ≈ 1,040 s ≈ 17 min.

Where it breaks. An operator who remembered the empty bearings would need about half as many tries; a microtubule has no memory. A powered boom also always reaches the rim, while most microtubule excursions end early in a catastrophe.

4.3.5

One kinesin's load line, as measured — load reaches into the chemistry

Minted in Week 4 §3.4 · The motors on the tube — kinesin, dynein, and when a road pays · open the module

eq. 4.3.5$$v(F,[\mathrm{ATP}]) = d\,k_{cycle}, \qquad k_{cycle} = k_{max}(F)\,\frac{[\mathrm{ATP}]}{K_M(F) + [\mathrm{ATP}]}, \qquad v(F_{stall}) = 0$$

Letters

  • \(v\) — kinesin's speed · nm/s · ≈ 0.8 µm/s unloaded (to confirm)
  • \(F\) — the load on the motor · pN
  • \([\mathrm{ATP}]\) — ATP concentration · µM · ≈ 1 mM in a cell
  • \(d\) — step · nm · 8 nm, one ATP per step (Svoboda 1993; Schnitzer & Block 1997)
  • \(k_{cycle}\) — steps per second · s⁻¹
  • \(k_{max}(F)\) — the top stepping rate at load \(F\) · s⁻¹ · ≈ 100 s⁻¹ unloaded (0.8 µm/s ÷ 8 nm)
  • \(K_M(F)\) — the apparent Michaelis constant at load \(F\); rises with load (Visscher 1999) · µM
  • \(F_{stall}\) — the load at which \(v\) = 0; itself depends on ATP · pN · ≈ 6 pN

How it is used

§3.4 mints it for the "vesicle on a microtubule track" sim. On the kinesin chip you read the speed against \(v_0(1 - F/F_{stall})\), the 8-nm staircase and the arrival time, then load it: the speed falls and runs shorten. The box records what Visscher's force clamp found that eq. 4.2.4 cannot say: both \(k_{max}\) and \(K_M\) depend on load, there is no single stall force, and stepping stays tightly coupled throughout. The same section prices kinesin's work at stall with eq. 4.2.2 and decides when a road pays with eq. 4.1.9.

Comes back: —

Biological examplekinesin under load, well fed and starved

Kinesin hauls a vesicle down an axon. How do load and ATP combine? The module quotes no kinesin \(K_M\), so take 50 µM unloaded as an illustrative value and suppose a load doubles it.

  1. Unloaded at 1 mM ATP: \(k_{cycle}\) = 800 / 8 = 100 steps/s, burning 100 ATP/s.
  2. Work per step at the ≈ 6-pN stall: 6 × 8 = 48 pN·nm = 11 \(k_BT\), 45 % of an ATP.
  3. ATP factor at 1 mM: 1000 / 1050 = 0.95 unloaded, 1000 / 1100 = 0.91 if load doubles \(K_M\), a 4.5 % loss.
  4. ATP factor at 100 µM: 100 / 150 = 0.67 unloaded, 100 / 200 = 0.50 loaded, a 25 % loss.
  5. A run lasts about 100 steps = 0.8 µm, so a 10-µm haul is about 12 runs.

What it means. With these numbers, in a well-fed cell load acts mostly through \(k_{max}(F)\). When ATP falls toward \(K_M\), a loaded motor is slowed twice over, once by the load and once by acting starved. A straight load line cannot say this.

Mechanical analogya stepper motor's pull-out curve

A stepper motor turns one fixed step for each current pulse, as kinesin advances 8 nm per ATP. Its makers publish a measured pull-out curve: the fastest pulse rate it can follow at each load torque. Lower the supply voltage and the whole curve drops, as if the motor were starved.

In the cellIn the machine
8-nm step1.8° step, 200 per turn
one ATP per stepone current pulse per step
\(k_{cycle}\)pulse rate
\(k_{max}(F)\)fastest pulse rate at load torque \(F\)
\([\mathrm{ATP}]\) and \(K_M(F)\)supply voltage, and the voltage needed for half the top rate
\(F_{stall}\) depends on ATPholding torque depends on voltage

At 1,000 pulses a second the shaft turns 1,000 × 1.8° = 1,800° a second, 5 turns a second.

Where it breaks. An overloaded stepper skips steps and loses count. Kinesin stays coupled, one ATP per 8-nm step, and instead slows, backsteps or lets go. Its pulses also come from ATP arriving by diffusion, not from a clock.

Featured in HW2 · Problem 5(b), Challenge
4.3.6

Persistent random walk — a whole cell as Week 1's walker

Minted in Week 4 §3.5 · All together — the compass · open the module

eq. 4.3.6$$\langle r^2\rangle = 2v^2\tau_p^2\left(\frac{t}{\tau_p} - 1 + e^{-t/\tau_p}\right) \;\xrightarrow{\,t \gg \tau_p\,}\; 4D_{cell}\,t, \qquad D_{cell} = \frac{v^2\tau_p}{2}$$

Letters

  • \(\langle r^2\rangle\) — mean-squared displacement of the cell's track · µm²
  • \(v\) — speed along the path · µm/s · 0.2 µm/s
  • \(\tau_p\) — persistence time, how long the cell keeps a heading · s · the model: fibroblast ≈ 8 min, neutrophil ≈ 4 min
  • \(t\) — lag time · s
  • \(D_{cell}\) — the cell's diffusion coefficient in 2D · µm²/s · 6 µm²/s for \(\tau_p\) = 5 min

How it is used

§3.5 mints it for the "cell walking in a uniform bath" sim, which fits this curve to the track's mean-squared displacement. Chips switch the array: neutrophil (behind the nucleus), fibroblast (reaching to the front), keratocyte (none). Until the cell has turned several times, the MSD rises as \(t^2\) and only a bound on \(\tau_p\) can be read. It is eq. 1.2.6 with a new meaning: \(\langle r^2\rangle = 2dDt\) with \(d\) = 2, but the walker is a whole cell and each step is a persistent run. The compass sets \(\tau_p\); the skeleton sets \(v\). HW2's last problem uses it.

Comes back: R2 §1.4 (how does a fibroblast reach the middle?).

Biological examplea neutrophil with and without its compass

With no gradient, a neutrophil walks at 0.2 µm/s and keeps its heading for about 4 min in the model. After nocodazole its paths turn circuitous (Xu 2005); take \(\tau_p\) = 1 min as an illustrative value.

  1. \(D_{cell} = v^2\tau_p/2\) = 0.04 × 240 / 2 = 4.8 µm²/s.
  2. At a 30-s lag (\(t \ll \tau_p\)): \(\langle r^2\rangle\) = 2 × 0.04 × 240² × (0.125 − 1 + \(e^{-0.125}\)) = 34.5 µm², so 5.9 µm against the straight-line 6 µm. Ballistic.
  3. In an hour (\(t \gg \tau_p\)): \(r_{rms} = \sqrt{4 \times 4.8 \times 3600}\) ≈ 263 µm, against 720 µm straight.
  4. With \(\tau_p\) = 60 s: \(D_{cell}\) = 1.2 µm²/s and \(r_{rms}\) ≈ 131 µm in an hour.
  5. To spread 300 µm rms without a gradient: \(t = r^2/4D_{cell}\) = 90,000 / 19.2 ≈ 4,700 s ≈ 78 min.

What it means. Persistence is worth distance: cutting \(\tau_p\) fourfold halves the hour's reach. A cell that only wanders needs over an hour to spread as far as the colony 300 µm away, which a straight run covers in 25 min.

Mechanical analogya robot vacuum

A robot vacuum drives straight at a fixed speed and turns to a random new heading every so often. Over short times it travels in straight lines; over long times its track is a random walk with a diffusion coefficient built from its speed and its time between turns.

In the cellIn the machine
the cellthe robot
path speed \(v\)drive speed, 0.3 m/s
persistence time \(\tau_p\)mean time between turns, 5 s
\(D_{cell} = v^2\tau_p/2\)0.09 × 5 / 2 = 0.225 m²/s
the microtubule arraya heading gyro that delays turns

In 10 min on an open floor it spreads \(\sqrt{4 \times 0.225 \times 600}\) ≈ 23 m, against 180 m of driving.

Where it breaks. A robot turns mostly when it hits walls and furniture, and many map the room. A cell's turns come from its own flicker. The formula fits both only because each heading's memory decays as \(e^{-t/\tau_p}\).

Module Tab 4 · The Full System in Action
4.4.1

Local excitation, global inhibition — compare yourself with the cell's average

Minted in Week 4 §4.2 · From a reading to a compass — the second messengers · open the module

eq. 4.4.1$$\tau_e\,\frac{de_i}{dt} = \hat\theta_i - e_i, \qquad \tau_m\,\frac{dm}{dt} = \bar{\hat\theta} - m, \qquad r_i = e_i - m$$

Letters

  • \(\hat\theta_i\) — patch \(i\)'s reading of receptor occupancy · dimensionless · ≈ 0.35 at 300 µm from the colony
  • \(e_i\) — that patch's local excitation, following its own reading · dimensionless
  • \(\tau_e\) — the excitation's fast time constant · s · much shorter than \(\tau_m\)
  • \(m\) — the global inhibitor, following the whole cell's mean reading · dimensionless
  • \(\bar{\hat\theta}\) — the cell's mean reading · dimensionless
  • \(\tau_m\) — the inhibitor's slow memory time · s · 60 s (sim slider)
  • \(r_i\) — the patch's response: frontness if positive, backness if negative (not the duty ratio of eq. 4.2.1) · dimensionless

How it is used

§4.2 mints it for "the signalling layer alone" sim; the cell does not move. On "gradient" the map is far steeper than the reading (outside ≈ 10 %, inside ≈ 70 %). On "uniform bath" a front still forms, its direction chosen by flicker. On "source flips at 60 s" the old front holds for minutes (hysteresis). On "no inhibitor" every patch turns green. Frontness is a saturating function of \(g[r_i]_+\), the wiring of Levchenko and Iglesias. The worked example shows a uniform step flaring and adapting on \(\tau_m\). It feeds eq. 4.4.2 and §4.3's wire.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea puff in a gradient

A neutrophil sits in the colony's gradient. Its front patch reads 2.5 % above the mean occupancy of 0.35 and its back 2.5 % below. Then a puff raises every reading by 30 %. What does each patch report, and for how long?

  1. At rest: front 0.359, back 0.341, \(m\) = 0.35.
  2. Steady responses: \(r_{front}\) = +0.009, \(r_{back}\) = −0.009. These persist.
  3. The puff: \(e_i\) follows within \(\tau_e\), \(m\) lags, so every patch gains \(0.3 \times 0.35 \times e^{-t/60\,s}\) = 0.105 \(e^{-t/60\,s}\).
  4. At \(t\) = 0 the uniform flare, 0.105, is 12 times the gradient's resting signal; at 60 s it is 0.039.
  5. The gradient signal, scaled up 30 % by the puff, is 0.0114. The flare falls below it at \(t\) = 60 ln(0.105 / 0.0114) ≈ 133 s.

What it means. A uniform change flares every patch and adapts away in about two minutes. A gradient's front–back sign never fades. The wiring turns "how much" into "which way".

Mechanical analogyharbour float gauges against a stilling well

A harbour has float gauges along its wall and one tide gauge in a stilling well, a pipe that lets water in through a small hole and so follows only the slow average level. Each float minus the stilling-well level reports the local wave, not the tide.

In the cellIn the machine
patch reading \(\hat\theta_i\)water level at float \(i\)
local excitation \(e_i\), fast \(\tau_e\)the float, quick to follow
global inhibitor \(m\), slow \(\tau_m\)the stilling-well level, slow to follow
response \(r_i = e_i - m\)float height minus well level
a gradientwind piling water against one wall
a uniform stepthe tide coming in

When the tide rises, every float reads high at first, then the well catches up and the readings fade. Water piled against one wall by the wind stays high there.

Where it breaks. A stilling well averages only the water near its hole, while the cell's inhibitor spreads across the whole cell. The cell also adds positive feedback, which lets a front form from noise in a uniform bath; no gauge does that.

4.4.2

Front-end ceiling — no gain beats the count

Minted in Week 4 §4.2 · From a reading to a compass — the second messengers · open the module

eq. 4.4.2$$\mathrm{SNR}_{out} \le \mathrm{SNR}_{in}, \qquad \mathrm{SNR}_{in} = \frac{\Delta\hat\theta}{\sigma_{\hat\theta}}\ \text{from eq. 3.3.14}$$

Letters

  • \(\mathrm{SNR}_{in}\) — the reading's signal-to-noise ratio · dimensionless
  • \(\mathrm{SNR}_{out}\) — the signal-to-noise ratio after any downstream stage · dimensionless
  • \(\Delta\hat\theta\) — the front–back difference in measured occupancy · dimensionless · 5 % of occupancy in the worked example
  • \(\sigma_{\hat\theta}\) — its counting noise, set by Week 3's receptor reading (eq. 3.3.14) · dimensionless

How it is used

§4.2 mints it to pay Week 3 §3.7's promise: no downstream biochemistry can add what the count did not carry. The "signalling layer alone" sim shows the reading's SNR and the amplified map's side by side, and the gain slider moves neither. The worked example solves eq. 3.3.14 for time: about 4 s of counting make a 5 % difference trustworthy at 53,000 receptors, and a gain of 30 multiplies signal and flicker alike. §4.4 shrinks the cell to a bacterium: the counting time rises 53-fold on the dashboard and about 1.2 × 10⁴-fold once its smaller front–back difference is counted.

Comes back: —

Biological exampleZigmond's one-percent gradient

Neutrophils can orient in a difference of about 1 % across the cell (Zigmond 1977). How long must one count to trust that, and can a gain shorten it?

  1. \(N\) = 53,000; \(\theta\) = 0.35, so \(\theta(1-\theta)\) = 0.2275; \(\tau_c = (1-\theta)/k_{off}\) = 0.65 / 0.01 = 65 s.
  2. For a 5 % difference: \(t \approx 2\tau_c/(N\theta(1-\theta)\varepsilon^2)\) = 130 / (53,000 × 0.2275 × 0.0025) = 4.3 s.
  3. For 1 %: 130 / (53,000 × 0.2275 × 10⁻⁴) = 108 s, nearly 2 min.
  4. A map gain of 30 multiplies \(\Delta\hat\theta\) and \(\sigma_{\hat\theta}\) alike, so \(\mathrm{SNR}_{out} = \mathrm{SNR}_{in}\) and the 108 s stand.
  5. Four times the receptors (illustrative) would cut it fourfold, to 27 s.

What it means. At the edge of what it can sense, a neutrophil must count for about two minutes, longer than it takes to cross its own body. No amplifier helps; only more receptors or a steeper gradient do.

Mechanical analogyweighing yourself on a rolling ship

A bathroom scale on a rolling ship jumps ±2 kg from reading to reading. You want to know whether you gained 0.5 kg. One reading has a signal-to-noise ratio of 0.5 / 2 = 0.25. A dial magnified ten times shows 5 units of signal and 20 of jitter: still 0.25. Averaging 16 independent readings gives 0.25 × √16 = 1.

In the cellIn the machine
occupancy readingthe scale's reading
\(\sigma_{\hat\theta}\), counting noisejitter from the ship's roll, ±2 kg
\(\Delta\hat\theta\)the 0.5-kg difference
map gain \(g\)dial magnification
counting time (eq. 3.3.14)number of readings averaged
\(\mathrm{SNR}_{out} \le \mathrm{SNR}_{in}\)no dial beats the readings

Where it breaks. A ship's roll is periodic, so a clever reader can read only at the bottom of each roll and beat plain averaging. Receptor noise is memoryless binding and unbinding, with no phase to exploit.

Featured in HW2 · Problem 4(d)Featured in HW3 · Problem 1(b), Problem 1(c)
4.4.3

Edge speed — polymerization minus flow

Minted in Week 4 §4.3 · The front and the back, wired · open the module

eq. 4.4.3$$v_{edge} = v_{pol} - v_{retro}, \qquad v_{pol} = \delta\,(k_{on}G_f - k_{off})\cos 35^\circ, \quad G_f = \frac{G_b}{1 + \mathrm{Da}}$$

Letters

  • \(v_{edge}\) — the speed of the leading edge · nm/s
  • \(v_{pol}\) — the network's polymerization speed toward the membrane · nm/s · ≈ 250 nm/s from 10 µM
  • \(v_{retro}\) — the retrograde flow pulling the network back · nm/s · 20–100 nm/s (to confirm)
  • \(\delta\), \(k_{on}\), \(k_{off}\) — eq. 4.1.1's rise and barbed-end rates · 2.7 nm, 11.6 µM⁻¹s⁻¹, 1.4 s⁻¹
  • \(G_f\), \(G_b\) — monomer at the front and in the body · µM · \(G_b\) = 100 µM
  • \(\mathrm{Da}\) — the edge's Damköhler number (eq. 4.1.10) · ≈ 6
  • 35° — half of Arp2/3's 70° branch angle (Mullins 1998)

How it is used

§4.3 mints it for "the whole wire" sim. In the wild type you read \(v_{pol}\) and \(v_{retro}\) and subtract them. "No myosin II" removes the flow (the edge is faster) and the rear stops retracting; "no Arp2/3" leaves the map pointing with few tips; "no microtubules" weakens the front. The polymerization term is eq. 4.1.1 through eq. 4.1.10's relay, tilted by the branch angle; the flow term is Tab 2's motors, written as a number. The worked example gives 150–200 nm/s, 9–12 µm/min. §4.1's speed ladder and §4.5's ledger show the flow term carrying much of the answer.

Comes back: Week 5 §1.3 (both terms alive this time).

Biological examplea well-fed edge and a starved one

Run the edge budget with the Damköhler relay, once with the body's full pool and once with the "poor pool" of §1.5. Hold the retrograde flow at 60 nm/s.

  1. Full pool, \(G_b\) = 100 µM, Da ≈ 6: \(G_f\) = 100 / 7 = 14.3 µM.
  2. One tip: 2.7 × (11.6 × 14.3 − 1.4) = 2.7 × 164 = 444 nm/s.
  3. Tilted by the branches: \(v_{pol}\) = 444 × cos 35° = 444 × 0.819 = 364 nm/s.
  4. \(v_{edge}\) = 364 − 60 = 304 nm/s ≈ 18 µm/min, inside the neutrophil's 10–20.
  5. Poor pool, \(G_b\) = 20 µM: \(G_f\) = 2.9 µM; \(v_{pol}\) = 2.7 × (33.1 − 1.4) × 0.819 = 70 nm/s.
  6. \(v_{edge}\) = 70 − 60 = 10 nm/s ≈ 0.6 µm/min.

What it means. The same flow that is a small tax on a well-fed edge eats almost all of a starved one. A fivefold cut in monomer cuts the edge speed thirtyfold: the cell knows where to go and cannot get there.

Mechanical analogywalking against a moving walkway

Walk the wrong way along an airport's moving walkway. Your ground speed is your walking pace minus the belt's speed.

In the cellIn the machine
polymerization at the tips, \(v_{pol}\)walking pace on the belt, 1.4 m/s
retrograde flow, \(v_{retro}\)belt speed backward, 0.6 m/s
edge speed, \(v_{edge}\)ground speed, 0.8 m/s
myosin II pulling the networkthe belt's motor
the clutch (next week)a brake gripping the belt to the floor
\(\cos 35^\circ\)walking at an angle to the belt

A tired walker at 0.7 m/s against the same belt makes 0.1 m/s, the starved edge again.

Where it breaks. A walkway's speed is set by its motor whatever the walker does. In a cell the push and the flow act on the same network, so each changes the other. That is why next week turns \(v_{retro}\) into a force balance.

4.5.1

Brownian ratchet — a tip against a load, previewed

Minted in Week 4 §5.1 · Next week's headline, measured today — a filament tip against a load · open the module

eq. 4.5.1$$v = \delta\left(k_{on}C\,e^{-F\delta/k_BT} - k_{off}\right), \qquad F_{stall} = \frac{k_BT}{\delta}\ln\frac{k_{on}C}{k_{off}} = \frac{k_BT}{\delta}\ln\frac{C}{C_c}$$

Letters

  • \(v\) — the tip's growth speed against the load · nm/s
  • \(\delta\) — the gap a monomer needs, one subunit's rise · nm · 2.7 nm
  • \(k_{on}C\), \(k_{off}\) — arrival and departure rates (eq. 4.1.1) · s⁻¹
  • \(F\) — the load pressing on the tip (membrane, cortex) · pN
  • \(k_BT\) — thermal energy · pN·nm · 4.28
  • \(e^{-F\delta/k_BT}\) — the Boltzmann odds that the bath opens a gap the load wants closed (eq. 1.2.7) · 0.53 at 1 pN
  • \(F_{stall}\) — the load at which growth stops · pN · 7.0 pN at 10 µM; 2.3 pN at the sim's 0.5 µM
  • \(C_c\) — critical concentration (eq. 4.1.3) · µM · 0.12 µM

How it is used

Tab 5 §5.1 previews it with the "tip against a flickering sheet" sim: no load, light (1 pN) and heavy (2 pN). The panel reads the measured chance that a monomer-sized gap is open; the light/no-load ratio is about 0.61 against the free-sheet factor 0.53, because the sim's sheet has stiffness of its own. The stall is logged twice, 2.3 pN at the sim's 0.5 µM and 7.0 pN at the cell's 10 µM. It is eq. 4.1.1 with one Boltzmann factor on the arrivals. §4.5's ledger prices membrane tension with it: 2 pN per tip costs a factor 0.28. Peskin, Odell and Oster's logic is earned next week.

Comes back: Week 5 §1.1 (previewed in Week 4, earned here); Week 5 §1.2 (solved for the stall).

Biological examplea neutrophil's tip under membrane load

A barbed end at the neutrophil's front feeds on \(G_f\) ≈ 14 µM after the Damköhler relay. The membrane presses on it. How much does a 3-pN load cost, and where does the tip stall?

  1. \(C\) = 14 µM, \(C_c\) = 0.12 µM, \(\delta\) = 2.7 nm, \(k_BT\) = 4.28 pN·nm.
  2. No load: \(v\) = 2.7 × (11.6 × 14 − 1.4) = 2.7 × 161 = 435 nm/s.
  3. At \(F\) = 3 pN: \(e^{-3 \times 2.7/4.28} = e^{-1.89}\) = 0.151.
  4. \(v\) = 2.7 × (162.4 × 0.151 − 1.4) = 2.7 × 23.1 = 62 nm/s, a seventh of free growth.
  5. Stall: \(F_{stall}\) = (4.28 / 2.7) × ln(14 / 0.12) = 1.59 × 4.76 = 7.5 pN.
  6. Per micron of edge: 241 tips × 7.5 pN ≈ 1.8 nN.

What it means. A load under half the stall force already slows the tip sevenfold, because the exponential penalizes arrivals long before stall. The stall itself is only a logarithm of the supply. Whether the membrane loads each tip this hard is next week's first question.

Mechanical analogya ratchet jack on a shaking floor

A ratchet jack holds a load. Its pawl can drop into the next tooth only when the load is jostled up by at least one tooth pitch. On a shaking floor such gaps open at random; a heavier load makes them rarer, by the Boltzmann odds \(e^{-F\delta/\text{shake energy}}\).

In the cellIn the machine
gap needed, \(\delta\) = 2.7 nmtooth pitch, 5 mm
thermal flicker, \(k_BT\)the floor's shaking, 0.1 J per jolt
membrane load \(F\)weight on the jack, 20 N
a monomer insertingthe pawl dropping into the next tooth
\(k_{off}\)the pawl slipping back a tooth
ATP keeping \(C\) above \(C_c\)the pawl's spring

Here \(F\delta\) = 20 × 0.005 = 0.1 J, one jolt's energy, so the odds of a gap fall to \(e^{-1}\) = 0.37 of their unloaded value.

Where it breaks. In a truly thermal bath the pawl would jiggle too and slip as often as it catches (Feynman's ratchet), so no net lift. The filament fills gaps one way only because ATP keeps \(C\) above \(C_c\); the energy comes from polymerization, and the flicker is only the opportunity.

Each keeps the number it was given when first minted. The full entry, with its example and analogy, is one click away.

3.2.15

Michaelis–Menten — the motor's cycle rate, with ATP as the substrate

Re-boxed in Week 4 §2.3 · Power output of a single motor

eq. 3.2.15 again$$k_{cycle} = k_{max}\,\frac{[\mathrm{ATP}]}{K_M + [\mathrm{ATP}]}, \qquad K_M \approx 50\ \text{µM}$$

Week 3's door that eats, with the myosin head as the enzyme and ATP as what it eats: \(k_{cycle}\) is the rate per head, \(k_{max}\) its ceiling (≈ 20 s⁻¹, to confirm), and \(K_M\) ≈ 50 µM is Kron and Spudich's half-maximal sliding. At a cell's 1 mM the head runs at 1000/1050 = 95 % of \(k_{max}\); at 25 µM it runs at a third, 6.7 s⁻¹, which drops one head's power from 0.77 to 0.26 aW. Eq. 4.3.5 gives both constants a load dependence for kinesin.

Full entry: eq. 3.2.15, Week 3

Week 5 · Integrins, Focal Adhesions & the Motor–Clutch

Week 5 opens on a neutrophil whose actin stands still on the coverslip while the cell crawls over it. Tab 1 builds the two speeds that fight at the leading edge: a Brownian ratchet pushing the membrane forward, and a myosin load line dragging the network back. The integrin is the force balance between them. Tabs 2 and 3 make the grip local, then let the clutches choose their own number in one feedback loop. Tab 4 spends that loop on the neutrophil, and Tab 5 names Hooke and the modulus for the ground that is about to move.
