Module Tab 1 · The Tug-of-War
5.1.1

The gap probability — the load sets the odds of a step

Minted in Week 5 §1.1 · A filament cannot push. So how does it push? · open the module

eq. 5.1.1$$P(\text{gap} \ge \delta) = e^{-F\delta/k_BT}$$

Letters

  • \(P(\text{gap}\ge\delta)\) — the fraction of the time the membrane sits at least one subunit away from the tip · dimensionless, 0 to 1
  • \(F\) — the load the membrane puts on the filament tip · pN · the panel's default is 2 pN
  • \(\delta\) — the length one subunit adds · nm · 2.7 nm, actin's half-stagger (Week 4)
  • \(k_BT\) — thermal energy · pN·nm · 4.28 pN·nm at 37 °C
  • \(F\delta\) — the work needed to open a gap of one subunit against the load · pN·nm

How it is used

§1.1 mints it to answer a puzzle: what does a growing filament do to a membrane if nothing in it can push? The panel "One filament tip against a load" counts monomers as they reach the tip. At ×0.01 clock you can count how many bounce off for each one that slots in, and that fraction matches the "gap ≥ δ" readout. It is Week 1's Boltzmann law (eq. 1.2.7) with the energy set to \(F\delta\). The temperature slider moves only \(k_BT\), so the panel shows this factor on its own. Put in front of the on-rate, it turns Week 4's growth law into the ratchet, eq. 4.5.1, which is re-boxed right after it and drives every speed in Tabs 1–4.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea neutrophil's tip barely feels its membrane; a keratocyte's does

§1.1 brackets the load on one filament from measured membrane tension: about 0.3 pN in a neutrophil-like cell and about 1.5 pN in a fast keratocyte. What fraction of the monomers that arrive find room to slot in?

  1. Constants: \(k_BT\) = 4.28 pN·nm, \(\delta\) = 2.7 nm.
  2. Neutrophil: \(F\delta\) = 0.3 × 2.7 = 0.81 pN·nm.
  3. \(P = e^{-0.81/4.28} = e^{-0.19}\) = 0.83.
  4. Keratocyte: \(F\delta\) = 1.5 × 2.7 = 4.05 pN·nm.
  5. \(P = e^{-4.05/4.28} = e^{-0.95}\) = 0.39.
  6. The module's default, 2 pN: \(P = e^{-1.26}\) = 0.28.
  7. At 10 µM, monomers arrive at \(k_{on}C\) = 11.6 × 10 = 116 per second. At 2 pN, 116 × 0.28 ≈ 33 per second get in.

What it means. Each extra pN multiplies the odds by \(e^{-2.7/4.28}\) = 0.53, so every piconewton roughly halves the success rate. The neutrophil's tip turns away 17 % of arrivals, the keratocyte's 61 %. The arrival rate never changed. Only the odds did.

Mechanical analogya ratchet and pawl on a shaker table

Take a toothed wheel with a pawl, so it can turn only one way. Hang a weight from its axle and shake the whole frame at random. The wheel advances one tooth only when a kick lifts the weight through one tooth's worth of height. Then the pawl drops in and stops it from slipping back. The shaker plays the thermal bath, one tooth plays one subunit, and the weight plays the membrane.

In the cellIn the machine
one actin subunit addedthe wheel advances one tooth
step \(\delta\) = 2.7 nmthe height the weight rises per tooth
membrane load \(F\)the hanging weight
thermal energy \(k_BT\)the typical size of a kick
\(P(\text{gap}\ge\delta)\)the fraction of kicks big enough to clear a tooth

Suppose the kick energies had an exponential spread with a mean of 0.1 J, and one tooth lifts a 10 N weight by 1 cm (0.1 J of work). Then \(P = e^{-1}\) = 0.37. Double the weight and \(P = e^{-2}\) = 0.14.

Where it breaks. A shaker's kicks are not Boltzmann-distributed, so the exponential would have to be built in. And if the pawl rattles as hard as the wheel, the ratchet gives no net turn. The filament escapes that because each insertion is paid for by binding chemistry (\(k_{on}C\) against \(k_{off}\)), not by the jiggle alone.

5.1.2

The loaded critical concentration — a load raises the bar for growing at all

Minted in Week 5 §1.2 · The ceiling, and who sets it · open the module

eq. 5.1.2$$C^*(F) = C_c\,e^{F\delta/k_BT}$$

Letters

  • \(C^*(F)\) — the free G-actin concentration at which a tip under load \(F\) just holds station · µM
  • \(C_c\) — the unloaded critical concentration, \(k_{off}/k_{on}\) · µM · 1.4/11.6 = 0.12 µM (Pollard 1986, eq. 4.1.3)
  • \(F\) — the load on the tip · pN · the right-hand panel's default is 3 pN
  • \(\delta\) — the subunit step · nm · 2.7 nm
  • \(k_BT\) — thermal energy · pN·nm · 4.28 pN·nm at 37 °C

How it is used

§1.2 mints it by reading the stall (eq. 4.5.1 solved for \(v = 0\)) the other way round. The stall asks what load stops a tip fed at \(C\). This asks what \(C\) a tip needs at a given load. The right-hand chart of "What sets the ceiling" lets you pick a load and read off the concentration needed to hold station. Dropping \(C\) below \(C_c\) removes the idea of a stall force altogether. It is \(C_c\) divided by the gap probability of eq. 5.1.1, and it is why §2.1's cast says growth needs \(C > C_c\), and more than that under load.

Comes back: —

Biological examplewhat Footer's 9 pN would cost

Footer and colleagues (cited in §1.1) worked out that the most one filament could push in a cell is about 9 pN. What monomer pool would that take at the tip?

  1. \(C_c = k_{off}/k_{on}\) = 1.4/11.6 = 0.121 µM.
  2. At 9 pN: \(F\delta/k_BT\) = 9 × 2.7/4.28 = 5.68.
  3. \(C^* = 0.121 \times e^{5.68} = 0.121 \times 292\) = 35 µM.
  4. A keratocyte tip at 1.5 pN: exponent 0.946, so \(C^* = 0.121 \times 2.58\) = 0.31 µM.
  5. At §1.2's 7.0 pN stall: exponent 4.42, so \(C^* = 0.121 \times 83\) = 10.0 µM. That is the stall read backward.

What it means. Every \(k_BT/\delta\) = 1.6 pN of load multiplies the pool the tip needs by e. A keratocyte's 1.5 pN is cheap: 2.6 times \(C_c\). Holding 9 pN needs 35 µM at the tip, three and a half times the 10 µM this module assumes. A cell cannot concentrate its way out of a real load.

Mechanical analogya parts feeder behind a sprung gate

A stacking machine is fed from a vibrating bowl. Parts reach the top of the stack at a rate set by how full the bowl is. A sprung guide lets a part on only when the vibration has lifted it a part's thickness. A wiper knocks parts off the stack at a fixed rate. The stack grows only if accepted arrivals beat removals.

In the cellIn the machine
free G-actin \(C\)how full the feeder bowl is
arrivals \(k_{on}C\)parts reaching the stack per second
load \(F\) and the odds \(e^{-F\delta/k_BT}\)the guide's preload and the fraction of parts it passes
loss rate \(k_{off}\)parts the wiper removes per second
\(C^*(F)\)the least bowl fill that keeps the stack's height

A full bowl delivers 10 parts/s and the wiper removes 2 parts/s. If the guide passes 1 part in 4, the stack needs the bowl at least 2/(10 × 0.25) = 80 % full. Stiffen the guide so it passes 1 in 6 and the stack needs 120 %, which no bowl can supply.

Where it breaks. The guide's pass rate falls with preload in whatever way its designer shaped it. In the cell the exponential is forced by thermal statistics, and nobody designed it.

Featured in HW3 · Problem 1(a)
5.1.3

The oblique step — δ cos θ in both the advance and the work

Minted in Week 5 §1.2 · The ceiling, and who sets it · open the module

eq. 5.1.3$$\delta_{eff} = \delta\cos\theta, \qquad \theta \approx 35^\circ \;\Rightarrow\; v_{pol} = \delta_{eff}\left(k_{on}Ce^{-F\delta_{eff}/k_BT} - k_{off}\right)$$

Letters

  • \(\delta_{eff}\) — how far the membrane advances per subunit · nm · 2.21 nm
  • \(\delta\) — the subunit's length along the filament · nm · 2.7 nm
  • \(\theta\) — the angle between filament and membrane normal · degrees · ≈ 35°, half of Arp2/3's 70° branch
  • \(v_{pol}\) — the edge's growth speed · nm/s · 88 nm/s at 2 pN and 10 µM
  • \(k_{on}\) — the barbed-end on-rate constant · µM⁻¹s⁻¹ · 11.6 (Pollard 1986)
  • \(k_{off}\) — the barbed-end off-rate · s⁻¹ · 1.4
  • \(C\) — free G-actin at the tip · µM · 10 µM
  • \(F\) — the membrane's load on one filament · pN
  • \(k_BT\) — thermal energy · pN·nm · 4.28 pN·nm

How it is used

§1.2 adds it just before §1.3 sets growth against the motors, so that comparison is fair. A monomer still lengthens the filament by \(\delta\), but the membrane moves only \(\delta\cos\theta\), and the work against the load shrinks by the same factor. So \(\delta_{eff}\) replaces \(\delta\) everywhere. Putting \(\cos\theta\) in front of the whole speed, as Week 4's eq. 4.4.3 did, double-counts the penalty: 70 nm/s instead of 88 nm/s at 2 pN. From §1.3 on every \(v_{pol}\) is this one: the speckle panel, break-even (5.1.6), the workbench (5.2.1), §3.1's inset, and §4.3's capstone, which turns 88.2 nm/s into 5.29 µm/min.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea keratocyte's lamellipodium, head-on and at 35°

Take a keratocyte-like load of 1.5 pN per filament and the module's 10 µM pool. How much does the branch angle cost?

  1. \(\delta_{eff}\) = 2.7 × cos 35° = 2.7 × 0.819 = 2.21 nm.
  2. Head-on odds: \(e^{-1.5 \times 2.7/4.28}\) = 0.388.
  3. Head-on speed: 2.7 × (116 × 0.388 − 1.4) = 2.7 × 43.6 = 118 nm/s.
  4. At 35°, odds: \(e^{-1.5 \times 2.21/4.28} = e^{-0.775}\) = 0.461.
  5. \(v_{pol}\) = 2.21 × (116 × 0.461 − 1.4) = 2.21 × 52.0 = 115 nm/s.
  6. The shortcut, \(\cos\theta\) in front only: 118 × 0.819 = 96.5 nm/s.

What it means. The tilt costs this edge 2 % (118 → 115), not the 18 % the shortcut claims. A shorter step is paid back by a cheaper one. At the module's heavier 2 pN load the cheaper step wins outright: 88 nm/s at 35° against 85 nm/s head-on.

Mechanical analogya ratchet jack braced at an angle

A ratcheting jack, set 35° off the normal, pushes a heavy sliding wall. Each click lengthens the jack by one tooth pitch along its own axis. The wall moves only pitch × cos θ, and the work done against the wall per click shrinks by the same factor.

In the cellIn the machine
the filament's axisthe jack's axis
\(\delta\) = 2.7 nm per subunittooth pitch, 10 mm per click
\(\theta\) ≈ 35°the jack's tilt from the wall's normal
\(\delta_{eff} = \delta\cos\theta\)the wall's advance per click, 8.2 mm
work \(F\delta_{eff}\)the work per click against the wall

With a 10 mm pitch at 35°, the wall moves 8.19 mm per click. Against a 500 N wall each click costs 4.1 J instead of the 5.0 J a head-on jack would pay.

Where it breaks. A tilted jack also shoves the wall sideways and needs a braced foot. In a lamellipodium the ±35° filaments come in mirror pairs, so the sideways pushes cancel across the network. And the jack's clicks are driven, not thermal.

5.1.4

The force triangle — the anchor carries the sheet and the motors

Minted in Week 5 §1.3 · Meanwhile, the motors are pulling the other way · open the module

eq. 5.1.4$$f_{anchor} = \underbrace{F_{mem}}_{\text{the sheet pushing back}} \;+\; \underbrace{F_{FA}/N_{fil}}_{\text{this filament's share of the motors}}$$

Letters

  • \(f_{anchor}\) — the forward force the integrin linkage must supply to one filament · pN
  • \(F_{mem}\) — the membrane pushing back on this filament's tip · pN · 2 pN default
  • \(F_{FA}\) — the force the focal adhesion takes off the motors · pN
  • \(N_{fil}\) — the filaments that share that adhesion · count · swept, 60 on the panel

How it is used

§1.3 draws this free body on one filament, after Case A shows that with nothing anchored the motors pull against nothing (\(F = 0\), so \(v_{retro} = v_0\)). Forward is the way the cell goes. The sheet pushes the tip rearward, the motors drag the network rearward, and only the integrin holds forward. The speckle panel's third canvas, "The force triangle on ONE filament", draws it. Switch to "motors + anchors" and the tethers lean as they take the load. The triangle warns that \(F_{FA}\) in eq. 5.1.5 is only the part that comes off the motors. The anchor's burden also includes \(F_{mem}\).

Comes back: —

Biological examplea fibroblast's leading edge at the panel's working point

A fibroblast's leading-edge adhesion takes 120 pN off the motors (§1.4's default grip). The load is shared by 60 filaments, and the membrane presses each tip back with 2 pN. What does each filament's anchor hold?

  1. Motor share per filament: \(F_{FA}/N_{fil}\) = 120/60 = 2.0 pN.
  2. Membrane push on the tip: \(F_{mem}\) = 2.0 pN.
  3. \(f_{anchor}\) = 2.0 + 2.0 = 4.0 pN per filament.
  4. Raise the membrane load to 4 pN: \(f_{anchor}\) = 4.0 + 2.0 = 6.0 pN, up 50 %.
  5. The whole patch holds 60 × 4.0 = 240 pN, twice the 120 pN the motors feel.

What it means. Half of what this anchor holds never shows in the retrograde speed. A taut membrane slows growth (eq. 4.5.1) and loads the anchor at the same time, so the integrin's job is harder than \(F_{FA}\) alone suggests.

Mechanical analogyrams against a wall, on a frame being winched back

Sixty hydraulic rams push a heavy wall forward. A winch drags their common frame backward. Each ram's foot is bolted to the floor, and the bolt is the only thing holding the ram forward.

In the cellIn the machine
one actin filamentone ram
\(F_{mem}\), the sheet pushing backthe wall's push back on each ram
\(F_{FA}/N_{fil}\), the motors' pull shared outthe winch's pull, shared per ram
the integrin linkagethe floor bolt at the ram's foot
\(f_{anchor}\)the shear on each bolt

Each ram meets 2 kN from the wall. The winch drags with 120 kN, shared by 60 rams, so 2 kN each. Each bolt carries 2 + 2 = 4 kN. If the wall's resistance doubles to 4 kN, each bolt carries 6 kN, and the winch never noticed.

Where it breaks. A bolt holds until it shears. An integrin holds for a while and lets go at random, so the triangle closes only on average. And real filaments share the load unevenly (§2.3).

Featured in HW3 · Problem 1(b), Problem 1(c), Challenge
5.1.5

The retrograde speed — the load line with the adhesion as its load

Minted in Week 5 §1.3 · Meanwhile, the motors are pulling the other way · open the module

eq. 5.1.5$$v_{retro} = v_0\left(1 - \frac{F_{FA}}{N_m F_m}\right)$$

Letters

  • \(v_{retro}\) — the speed the actin network slides rearward · nm/s
  • \(v_0\) — the motor team's unloaded sliding speed · nm/s · 120 nm/s (Bangasser 2017's cast)
  • \(F_{FA}\) — the force the focal adhesion takes off the motors · pN
  • \(N_m\) — motor modules in the team · count · 100
  • \(F_m\) — force per module · pN · 2 pN, so \(N_mF_m\) = 200 pN

How it is used

§1.3 derives it in Case B by putting the adhesion's force into Week 4's load line (eq. 4.2.4). Just before, an unnumbered box defines the word: a focal adhesion is \(N_{int}\) integrins side by side, each carrying \(f_{int}\), so \(F_{FA} = N_{int}\bar f_{int}\). §1.4 re-boxes eq. 5.1.5 and measures it on "Where the motor force goes". Press measure, and the bench times a marked subunit and the membrane for 2 s and puts a dot on each of two lines. The equation appears, dashed, only after two dots. The amber dots reach zero at 200 pN (100 pN with half the motors), and changing the membrane load moves only the pink line. §3.2 re-boxes it once more as \(v_a\), the load line driving the network in Tab 3, and eq. 5.3.5 closes the loop with it. The reading the module draws: integrins do not make a cell move; they let a surface push back.

Comes back: Week 6 §1.2 (from the motors to the gel, the whole chain on one spring).

Biological examplea fibroblast's lamellipodium, before and after a myosin inhibitor

Speckle microscopy on a fibroblast's leading edge. Suppose its adhesions take \(F_{FA}\) = 80 pN off a team of 100 motor modules (illustrative). Then a drug halves the working motors while the adhesion still takes 80 pN.

  1. Team stall: \(N_mF_m\) = 100 × 2 = 200 pN.
  2. \(v_{retro}\) = 120 × (1 − 80/200) = 120 × 0.60 = 72 nm/s.
  3. In speckle units: 72 nm/s × 60/1000 = 4.3 µm/min.
  4. Half the motors: \(N_mF_m\) = 50 × 2 = 100 pN.
  5. \(v_{retro}\) = 120 × (1 − 80/100) = 24 nm/s = 1.4 µm/min.
  6. Exchange rate with all 100 motors: each pN of grip removes \(v_0/N_mF_m\) = 0.6 nm/s of flow.

What it means. 4.3 µm/min sits inside the 0.5–7 µm/min that Alexandrova measured in lamellipodia (§2.3). The same grip against half the motors cuts the flow threefold, because it now absorbs a larger share of a weaker team.

Mechanical analogya winch hauling rope through a belay device

An electric winch reels in a climbing rope. Its free line speed is 0.5 m/s and it stalls at 10 kN. Between the winch and the rope's far end, the rope runs through a belay device clipped to a wall anchor, which brakes it.

In the cellIn the machine
the myosin teamthe winch
\(v_0\) = 120 nm/sno-load line speed, 0.5 m/s
\(N_mF_m\) = 200 pNstall pull, 10 kN
\(F_{FA}\)the belay device's braking force
\(v_{retro}\)rope speed through the device
the matrixthe wall anchor the device is clipped to

A 4 kN brake gives a line speed of 0.5 × (1 − 4/10) = 0.30 m/s. Every kN of brake costs 0.05 m/s. At 10 kN the rope stops and the winch stalls.

Where it breaks. A belay device's friction is set by how the rope is threaded. The adhesion's braking force comes from bonds that bind, stretch and let go, so it depends on the very speed it sets. That is Tab 3's loop.

Featured in HW3 · Problem 1(b)
5.1.6

Break-even — the grip a cell needs before it moves at all

Minted in Week 5 §1.4 · The integrin is a force balance · open the module

eq. 5.1.6$$F^*_{FA} = N_m F_m\left(1 - \frac{v_{pol}}{v_0}\right)$$

Letters

  • \(F^*_{FA}\) — the adhesion force at which the edge neither advances nor retreats · pN
  • \(N_mF_m\) — the motor team's stall force · pN · 200 pN
  • \(v_{pol}\) — the growth speed at the edge (eq. 5.1.3) · nm/s · 88 nm/s at 2 pN
  • \(v_0\) — the motors' unloaded sliding speed · nm/s · 120 nm/s

How it is used

§1.4 derives it by setting \(v_{edge} = 0\) in eq. 4.4.3 and substituting eq. 5.1.5. On the bench you bracket the force where the pink dots (edge speed) cross zero, one going backward and one forward, then check the bracket against the formula. The worked example gives 53 pN, 27 % of the team's stall. Past it each pN buys 0.6 nm/s, so 120 pN of grip returns about 40 nm/s. It scales with the motors: halve them and it halves. It feeds §1.5's count of tethers, the \(v_{edge} = 0\) row of §2.1's limits table (\(N^* = F^*_{FA}/\bar f\)), and chapter 6 of §4.1's recap, which asks you to check the traction against it.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea growth cone when its membrane tightens

A neuron's growth cone pushes its lamellipodial veil with Tab 1's cast. If membrane tension doubles the load per filament from 2 to 4 pN, how much more grip does it need just to stop retreating?

  1. At 2 pN: \(v_{pol}\) = 88.2 nm/s (eq. 5.1.3).
  2. \(F^*_{FA}\) = 200 × (1 − 88.2/120) = 200 × 0.265 = 53 pN.
  3. At 4 pN, the odds: \(e^{-4 \times 2.21/4.28} = e^{-2.07}\) = 0.127.
  4. \(v_{pol}\) = 2.21 × (116 × 0.127 − 1.4) = 2.21 × 13.3 = 29.4 nm/s.
  5. \(F^*_{FA}\) = 200 × (1 − 29.4/120) = 200 × 0.755 = 151 pN.
  6. In integrins at about 6 pN each (§1.4's own figure): 53/6 ≈ 9 holding at once, against 151/6 ≈ 25.

What it means. Doubling the load cut growth threefold and nearly tripled the grip needed, from about a quarter of the motors' stall to three quarters. Under high tension a cell must nearly stall its own motors just to stand still.

Mechanical analogya runner on a braked treadmill

A treadmill's belt is driven by a motor whose speed falls in a straight line with load: 4 m/s free, stalled by 1000 N on the belt. A runner jogs forward at 3 m/s relative to the belt. A brake pad can press on the belt.

In the cellIn the machine
growth speed \(v_{pol}\)the runner's pace on the belt
retrograde flowthe belt running backward
\(v_0\) and \(N_mF_m\)the belt motor: 4 m/s free, 1000 N stall
\(F_{FA}\)the brake pad on the belt
\(F^*_{FA}\)the brake needed for the runner to hold station

The runner holds station when \(F^* = 1000 \times (1 - 3/4)\) = 250 N. A tired runner at 1 m/s needs 1000 × 0.75 = 750 N, and the belt motor is nearly stalled.

Where it breaks. The runner's pace does not depend on the brake, and neither does \(v_{pol}\) on \(F_{FA}\), so that part holds. But a belt has inertia and a motor controller, the actin network has neither, and the cell's "brake" is made of bonds that come and go.

5.1.7

Talin's cryptic sites — a switch that opens with load

Minted in Week 5 §1.5 · Reinforcement — and the limit one integrin runs into · open the module

eq. 5.1.7$$P_{open}(f) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-(f-F_T)/\Delta F}}$$

Letters

  • \(P_{open}(f)\) — the chance a talin rod bundle is unfolded, with its vinculin site exposed · dimensionless
  • \(f\) — the load on the talin linkage · pN
  • \(F_T\) — the midpoint load, where half are open · pN · 12 pN: del Rio found 12 pN takes vinculin binding from one site to three
  • \(\Delta F\) — how sharp the switch is · pN · 2.5 pN, labelled illustrative in the module

How it is used

§1.5 mints it to answer a sum. One vinculin–actin tether lasts under a second above about 15 pN (Huang), so the cell needs about 7 tethers at once to reach break-even and about 15 at 120 pN. Talin builds that crowd: load unfolds its bundles, which exposes buried vinculin sites. The reinforcement cascade is an animated illustration, not a simulation. Its eight beats are scripted, and its stats print "Talin open (eq. 5.1.7)". The lumped switch sits beside two measured facts: R3 opens first, near 5 pN (Yao 2016), and bound vinculin blocks refolding, so the linkage latches (Yao 2014). It feeds eq. 5.1.8, and chapter 7 of §4.1's recap marks the clutches whose talin is open.

Comes back: —

Biological exampleone more motor's pull on a fibroblast's talin

How much does one more motor module (\(F_m\) = 2 pN) change the odds a site is exposed? It depends on where the linkage already sits.

  1. At 5 pN, where R3 starts to give: \(P = 1/(1+e^{(12-5)/2.5}) = 1/(1+16.4)\) = 0.057.
  2. At 8 pN: \(P = 1/(1+e^{1.6})\) = 0.17.
  3. At 12 pN: \(P = 1/(1+e^{0})\) = 0.50.
  4. At 14 pN, one module more: \(P = 1/(1+e^{-0.8})\) = 0.69.
  5. At 20 pN: \(P = 1/(1+e^{-3.2})\) = 0.96.
  6. Slope at the midpoint: \(1/(4\Delta F)\) = 0.10 per pN.

What it means. Near 12 pN, one extra 2 pN module lifts the odds from 50 % to 69 %. Below 5 pN almost nothing opens and above 20 pN almost everything has. The switch spans the pull of a few motor modules, so it trips all the time, not only at exotic forces. The engine writes \(\Delta F\) as \(k_BT\) over how far the bundle's end moves as it opens. At 2.5 pN that distance is 4.28/2.5 = 1.7 nm.

Mechanical analogya rip-stitch lanyard

A climber's energy-absorbing lanyard has folds of webbing sewn down with stitching that tears at a rated force. Each torn fold pays out length. In this version, each also exposes a sewn loop that a second line can clip to.

In the cellIn the machine
a folded helical bundlea sewn-down fold
\(F_T\) = 12 pNthe stitching's rated tear force
\(\Delta F\) = 2.5 pNthe scatter in tear force from fold to fold
\(P_{open}(f)\)the fraction of folds torn at load \(f\)
an exposed vinculin sitethe loop a torn fold reveals
contour paid out as talin unfoldswebbing paid out as a fold tears

With folds rated at 2.0 kN and a logistic spread of 0.4 kN, a 2.4 kN load has torn \(1/(1+e^{-1})\) = 73 % of them. Like talin with vinculin bound, a torn fold stays open when the load drops.

Where it breaks. Stitches tear once and are never re-sewn. A bare talin bundle refolds when the load comes off, and it opens by thermal activation, so its spread is set by \(k_BT\), not by manufacturing scatter.

5.1.8

What reinforcement buys — capacity grows with the open fraction

Minted in Week 5 §1.5 · Reinforcement — and the limit one integrin runs into · open the module

eq. 5.1.8$$F_{link}(f) = F_0\left(1 + \gamma\,P_{open}(f)\right)$$

Letters

  • \(F_{link}(f)\) — the force the talin–vinculin–actin linkage can carry · pN
  • \(F_0\) — one actin line's worth of capacity · pN · 11 pN, illustrative
  • \(\gamma\) — extra lines' worth at full opening · dimensionless · 4, so capacity reaches 5 × \(F_0\)
  • \(P_{open}(f)\) — the open fraction from eq. 5.1.7 · dimensionless
  • \(f\) — the load on the linkage · pN

How it is used

§1.5 mints it to say what the exposed sites are worth: each one recruits a vinculin that grows a new actin line in place. The cascade's right-hand chart, "Two running totals", plots it in green. The red line is the load on the single integrin–ligand bond at the bottom of the chain, and a dashed line marks the ≈ 40 pN that one bond can take. \(F_0\) and \(\gamma\) only shape the green curve, and the module says no conclusion depends on them. Between steps 7 and 8 nothing new is built, the motors keep hauling, and the anchor tears off at the one end nobody strengthened. That sets up the next box, Bell's law for the integrin bond.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea nascent adhesion outgrows its own foot

Follow one fibroblast linkage as its load climbs. Compare what it can carry with the ≈ 40 pN the integrin–ligand bond at its foot can take (the dashed line on the cascade's chart).

  1. At 5 pN: \(F_{link}\) = 11 × (1 + 4 × 0.057) = 13.5 pN.
  2. At 12 pN: \(F_{link}\) = 11 × (1 + 4 × 0.50) = 33 pN.
  3. At 15 pN: \(P_{open}\) = 0.77, so \(F_{link}\) = 11 × 4.07 = 44.8 pN.
  4. Fully open: \(F_{link}\) = 11 × 5 = 55 pN.
  5. Capacity passes 40 pN when \(P_{open}\) = (40/11 − 1)/4 = 0.66.
  6. That happens at \(f = 12 + 2.5\ln(0.66/0.34)\) = 13.6 pN.

What it means. Above about 14 pN the linkage can carry more than the one bond beneath it. From then on reinforcement only moves the weak link down to the integrin, and Bell's law says that bond's life gets shorter with every pN it is handed.

Mechanical analogytow straps rigged in parallel, all on one shackle

A recovery crew pulls a stuck truck. As the load rises they rig more straps in parallel, but every strap ends on the same single shackle bolted to the truck.

In the cellIn the machine
one actin line, \(F_0\) = 11 pNone tow strap, rated 11 kN
\(\gamma P_{open}\)the extra straps rigged so far, up to 4 more
\(F_{link}\)the straps' combined capacity, up to 55 kN
the single integrin–ligand bondthe one shackle, rated 40 kN
myosin haulingthe winch truck pulling

With three straps rigged the straps hold 33 kN. With five they hold 55 kN, but the shackle fails at 40 kN, so the fourth strap buys only the last 7 kN and the fifth buys nothing.

Where it breaks. A shackle has a rated strength. The integrin bond has no fixed strength, only a lifetime that falls with load, so given time it can fail well below 40 pN. The cell's way out is many shackles: §2.3's patch.

Module Tab 2 · The Grip, Locally
5.2.1

The whole chain — edge speed, and what the cell gets

Minted in Week 5 §2.1 · Every speed equation, one panel · open the module

eq. 5.2.1$$v_{edge} = \underbrace{\delta_{eff}\!\left(k_{on}Ce^{-F_{mem}\delta_{eff}/k_BT}-k_{off}\right)}_{v_{pol}\;\;(\text{4.5.1 at 5.1.3's angle})} \;-\; \underbrace{v_0\!\left(1-\frac{F_{FA}}{N_mF_m}\right)}_{v_{retro}\;\;(5.1.5)}, \qquad v_{cell}=\min\!\left(v_{edge},\,v_{rear}\right)$$

Letters

  • \(v_{edge}\) — how fast one piece of membrane advances · nm/s
  • \(v_{pol}\) — the growth term: the ratchet at the network's angle · nm/s
  • \(\delta_{eff}\) — the step the membrane sees · nm · 2.21 nm (eq. 5.1.3)
  • \(k_{on}\) — barbed-end on-rate constant · µM⁻¹s⁻¹ · 11.6
  • \(k_{off}\) — barbed-end off-rate · s⁻¹ · 1.4
  • \(k_BT\) — thermal energy · pN·nm · 4.28
  • \(C\) — free monomer at the tip · µM · slider, 10 µM
  • \(F_{mem}\) — the membrane's push on one filament · pN · slider, 2.0 pN
  • \(v_{retro}\) — the flow term: the load line · nm/s
  • \(v_0\) — the motors' unloaded sliding speed · nm/s · 120 nm/s
  • \(N_m\) — motor modules · count · 100
  • \(F_m\) — force per module · pN · 2 pN, so \(N_mF_m\) = 200 pN
  • \(F_{FA}\) — the adhesion's force, \(N\bar f\) · pN · sliders: \(N\) = 20 engaged integrins, \(\bar f\) = 5.5 pN each
  • \(v_{cell}\) — how fast the cell's centre moves · nm/s
  • \(v_{rear}\) — how fast the rear lets go · nm/s · slider, 120 nm/s

How it is used

§2.1 puts every speed equation from Tab 1 on one workbench, wired the way they connect. Its eight case chips (motors off, free network, one anchor, a patch of N, membrane load high, break-even, clutch fully engaged, rear lagging) light the boxes each case needs, and "predict first" makes you choose them before the reveal. An unnumbered box, "eq. 5.2.1's cast", lists where every letter comes from and its value. The same-week re-box, "its limits, one zero at a time", sets each term to zero in turn. \(F_{mem}=0\) gives the ratchet's ceiling. \(v_0=0\) is motors off. \(F_{FA}=0\) is a free network. \(v_{edge}=0\) gives eq. 5.1.6 and \(N^* = F^*_{FA}/\bar f\). \(v_{rear}=0\) pins the cell. The chart "All eight cases at once" shows the growth bar barely moving while the flow bar does everything. Eq. 5.2.5 is its derivative, and eq. 5.2.6 applies its min rule to each side of the cell.

Comes back: —

Biological examplethe workbench default, then a rear that holds on

  1. \(v_{pol}\) = 2.21 × (116 × 0.356 − 1.4) = 88.2 nm/s, at \(C\) = 10 µM and \(F_{mem}\) = 2 pN.
  2. \(F_{FA} = N\bar f\) = 20 × 5.5 = 110 pN.
  3. \(v_{retro}\) = 120 × (1 − 110/200) = 54 nm/s.
  4. \(v_{edge}\) = 88.2 − 54 = 34.2 nm/s.
  5. With \(v_{rear}\) = 120 nm/s: \(v_{cell}\) = min(34.2, 120) = 34.2 nm/s = 2.1 µm/min.
  6. Now let the rear hold on, \(v_{rear}\) = 15 nm/s (illustrative): \(v_{cell}\) = min(34.2, 15) = 15 nm/s.
  7. The front outruns the rear by 34.2 − 15 = 19 nm/s, about 1.2 µm/min of lamellipodium stretch.

What it means. Grip at the front lifts the edge from −32 nm/s (free network) to +34 nm/s without changing growth at all. But a cell whose rear lets go at 15 nm/s moves at 15 nm/s however well its front grips. Its lamellipodium stretches until something gives.

Mechanical analogya walker on a backward travelator, towing a braked trolley

An airport walkway runs backward, driven by a motor that slows when the belt is braked. A traveller walks forward on it at a steady pace. Brake pads clamp the belt. The traveller tows a luggage trolley with partly locked wheels.

In the cellIn the machine
\(v_{pol}\), set by chemistry and loadwalking pace on the belt, 1.5 m/s
\(v_{retro}\), from \(v_0\) and \(N_mF_m\)belt speed: 2.0 m/s free, motor stalls at 1000 N
\(F_{FA} = N\bar f\)\(N\) brake pads at \(\bar f\) each
\(v_{edge}\)the walker's speed over the floor
\(v_{rear}\) and \(v_{cell}\)the trolley's top speed, and the pair's progress

Eleven pads at 50 N give 550 N of brake. The belt slows to 2.0 × (1 − 0.55) = 0.9 m/s, so the walker gains 1.5 − 0.9 = 0.6 m/s over the floor. If the trolley can only roll at 0.3 m/s, the pair progresses at 0.3 m/s.

Where it breaks. A tow rope just goes taut. A lamellipodium stretches and thins for a while before the front has to slow. And a walker chooses a pace, while \(v_{pol}\) is set by chemistry and load.

Featured in HW3 · Problem 2(a)
5.2.2

The loading rate — how fast the flow ramps a bond

Minted in Week 5 §2.2 · One integrin under flow — loaded until it breaks, or holds · open the module

eq. 5.2.2$$r = \frac{df}{dt} = \kappa\,v$$

Letters

  • \(r\) — the loading rate, the module's letter for \(\dot f = df/dt\) · pN/s
  • \(f\) — the force on the bond · pN
  • \(t\) — time since it bound · s
  • \(\kappa\) — the stiffness of the linkage the bond sits in · pN/nm · 0.8 pN/nm in Tab 3's cast
  • \(v\) — the speed the actin flows past the anchor · nm/s

How it is used

§2.2 mints it because a bond in a cell is not held at a constant force. It is ramped: the flow stretches the linkage and the load climbs at \(\kappa v\). This reconciles two numbers that look incompatible. Li's AFM broke α5β1– fibronectin at 69 ± 2 pN at about 2,000 pN/s, while cells apply only about 40 pN (Wang & Ha). A 0.8 pN/nm linkage at 50 nm/s loads at 40 pN/s, fifty times slower. Same bond, different clock. Tab 3 re-boxes it per clutch as \(df/dt = \kappa_c v_a\). There the panel "One clutch, loading and letting go" varies flow and stiffness, and the same \(\kappa v\) gives the same mean force at release. It is the clock of the motor–clutch loop.

Comes back: Week 6 §1.3 (the loading rate, through the chain).

Biological examplean α5β1–fibronectin bond under free flow and under a grip

How long does a freshly bound integrin take to reach 10 pN, where its catch window opens, and 40 pN, the peak cells apply?

  1. \(\kappa\) = 0.8 pN/nm (Tab 3's linkage).
  2. Free flow, \(v = v_0\) = 120 nm/s: \(\dot f\) = 0.8 × 120 = 96 pN/s.
  3. Time to 10 pN: 10/96 = 0.10 s. Time to 40 pN: 40/96 = 0.42 s.
  4. A flow slowed by a good grip, \(v\) = 10 nm/s: \(\dot f\) = 0.8 × 10 = 8 pN/s.
  5. Time to 10 pN: 1.25 s. Time to 40 pN: 5.0 s.
  6. Li's AFM, at about 2,000 pN/s, loaded 21 times faster than free flow and 250 times faster than engaged flow.

What it means. A slow flow gives a bond seconds to reach its catch window. A fast flow drives it through in a tenth of a second. And the flow is set by the grip, which is the loop Tab 3 closes.

Mechanical analogya spring scale caught on a conveyor

A hanging spring scale has one end tied to a fixed post. Its hook has caught on a conveyor belt. The reading climbs steadily until the hook slips free.

In the cellIn the machine
linkage stiffness \(\kappa\)the scale's spring, 200 N/m
retrograde flow \(v\)belt speed, 0.05 m/s
\(\dot f = \kappa v\)the reading climbs at 10 N/s
the bond lets gothe hook slips off the belt
rigid substratethe fixed post

At 200 × 0.05 = 10 N/s, a hook that slips at 40 N lets go after 4 s. Double the belt speed and it lets go after 2 s, at the same 40 N.

Where it breaks. The hook slips at nearly the same force every time. A bond lets go at random, and its typical rupture force rises with loading rate: Li measured 69 pN at 2,000 pN/s and about 120 pN at 18,000 pN/s.

5.2.3

Two ways out — the catch bond and its lifetime peak

Minted in Week 5 §2.2 · One integrin under flow — loaded until it breaks, or holds · open the module

eq. 5.2.3$$k_{off}(f) = \underbrace{k_s\,e^{f/F_s}}_{\text{slip: force opens it}} + \underbrace{k_c\,e^{-f/F_c}}_{\text{catch: force closes it}}, \qquad \tau(f) = \frac{1}{k_{off}(f)}, \qquad f^{*} = \frac{F_sF_c}{F_s+F_c}\,\ln\frac{k_cF_s}{k_sF_c}$$

Letters

  • \(f\) — the force held on the bond · pN · the panel's default is 15 pN
  • \(k_{off}(f)\) — the total rate of leaving the bound state · s⁻¹
  • \(k_s\) — the slip route's unloaded rate; it plays Bell's \(k_0\) · s⁻¹ · 0.1 s⁻¹
  • \(F_s\) — the slip route's force per e-fold; it plays Bell's \(f_\beta\) · pN · 22 pN
  • \(k_c\) — the catch route's unloaded rate · s⁻¹ · 1.1 s⁻¹
  • \(F_c\) — the catch route's force per e-fold · pN · 11 pN
  • \(\tau(f)\) — the mean lifetime, the quantity the panel plots · s
  • \(f^*\) — the force of longest life, where \(dk_{off}/df = 0\) · pN · 23 pN
  • All four rates and scales are a fit to Kong's measured 10–30 pN window, and the module labels them as a fit.

How it is used

§2.2 mints it right after re-boxing Bell as a lifetime. The panel "Slip or catch, one bond at a time" holds a force and lets hundreds of bonds break. The histogram of lifetimes settles under the predicted curve, and a readout gives the share of exits by the catch route. The dashed grey line is eq. 5.2.3 with \(k_c = 0\), which is Bell again. "Both, side by side" shows the slip bond winning at rest and losing badly under load. The slip/catch/reinforce table says what each changes: slip and catch act on one bond's clock \(\tau\), while reinforcement changes how many hold. Tab 3 spends it in the "catch bonds" regime, where traction jumps, and in §3.4, where the regime boundaries slide.

Comes back: C1 §2.4 (slip and catch, as a lifetime); R2 §1.5 (the catch bond, two ways out of one bound state).

Biological examplean integrin in and out of its window, against a Bell bond

  1. Peak: \(f^*\) = (22 × 11/33) × ln(1.1 × 22/(0.1 × 11)) = 7.33 × ln 22 = 7.33 × 3.09 = 22.7 pN.
  2. At rest: \(\tau(0)\) = 1/(0.1 + 1.1) = 0.83 s.
  3. At the peak: \(\tau(f^*) = 1/(0.1e^{1.03} + 1.1e^{-2.06})\) = 1/(0.280 + 0.140) = 2.38 s.
  4. At 10 pN: \(\tau\) = 1/(0.158 + 0.443) = 1.66 s, under the 2 s Kong found for every force below 10 pN.
  5. At 40 pN: \(\tau\) = 1/(0.616 + 0.029) = 1.55 s. The catch route is nearly shut.
  6. A Bell bond with Tab 3's cast at 15 pN: \(\tau\) = 10 \(e^{-7.5}\) = 0.0055 s. The catch bond at 15 pN: 2.09 s, about 380 times longer.
  7. The two lifetime curves cross at 4.3 pN, where both last about 1.2 s.

What it means. Below about 4 pN the slip bond is the better bond. Under load the catch bond outlives it by hundreds of times. An adhesion that has to form before anything pulls on it pays for that at rest.

Mechanical analogya seat belt that locks harder when yanked

A seat belt on an inertia-locking retractor has two ways to let the wearer move. The retractor can spool webbing out, and a sharp pull shuts that exit by tripping the locking pawl. Or the webbing and its anchor can tear, an exit a hard pull opens.

In the cellIn the machine
the bound integrin–fibronectin pairthe belt holding the wearer
catch route, \(k_c e^{-f/F_c}\)the retractor paying out; a yank shuts it
slip route, \(k_s e^{f/F_s}\)webbing and anchor giving way; a harder pull opens it
\(f^*\) ≈ 23 pNthe range of pull where the belt holds best
\(\tau(f)\)how long the belt holds the wearer in place

Where it breaks. A retractor's pawl locks every time past a threshold. The integrin only shifts its odds, so even at its best force it lets go after 2.4 s on average. And no one designed its window; it comes from the molecules' change of shape under load.

5.2.4

Load sharing — the force each bound integrin carries

Minted in Week 5 §2.3 · A patch of integrins slows the flow under it — and when it does not · open the module

eq. 5.2.4$$\bar f(x) = \frac{F_{FA}(x)}{N_{bound}(x)}$$

Letters

  • \(\bar f(x)\) — the mean force on each bound integrin · pN · §2.1's default 5.5 pN
  • \(F_{FA}(x)\) — the adhesion's total force at that piece of edge · pN
  • \(N_{bound}(x)\) — the integrins bound there at this instant · count
  • \(x\) — position along the leading edge (a place, not a stretch) · µm

How it is used

§2.3 mints it for "A strip of leading edge, crawling". Each segment of edge runs its own Monte Carlo of §2.2's bond cycle with Tab 3's cast, so the number gripping is measured, not set. The summed grip is the local \(F_{FA}\). Eq. 5.1.5 turns it into a local flow, and eq. 4.4.3 into how far that piece of membrane gets. The module stresses that \(\bar f\) is an average. Each bond carries what the flow has loaded onto it since it bound, so a patch loses bonds one at a time, not all at once. In Tab 3 it becomes \(\langle f\rangle\) in eq. 5.3.4.

Comes back: C1 §2.4 (load sharing); R2 §1.5 (load sharing).

Biological exampleone stalled module of a fibroblast's adhesion

Changede's modular unit holds about 50 activated integrins. Suppose one such module in a fibroblast is stalled, passing the motors' full \(N_mF_m\) = 200 pN to the ground. How hard is each bound integrin pulled, as the number bound changes?

  1. 25 bound, half the module: \(\bar f\) = 200/25 = 8 pN. That is the vinculin–actin sweet spot of 7–10 pN (§1.5).
  2. 10 bound: \(\bar f\) = 200/10 = 20 pN, inside the integrin's 10–30 pN catch window.
  3. 5 bound: \(\bar f\) = 200/5 = 40 pN, the peak Wang & Ha measured on a single bond.
  4. The share is uneven. Under a 10 nm/s flow a bond is loaded at 0.8 × 10 = 8 pN/s (eq. 5.2.2).
  5. One bound 1 s ago carries 8 pN. One bound 0.25 s ago carries 2 pN.

What it means. The same 200 pN is gentle on 25 bonds and brutal on 5. When a bond drops out, the rest are loaded harder and fail sooner. That is how a slipping patch comes apart one bond at a time.

Mechanical analogya climber's anchor shared over several bolts

A belay anchor is built from several bolts joined by an equalizing sling. The load on the master point is shared by whichever bolts are loaded.

In the cellIn the machine
\(F_{FA}(x)\)the load on the master point
\(N_{bound}(x)\)the bolts actually taking load
\(\bar f\)the load per bolt
the longest-bound bond carries mostthe bolt on the shortest sling leg takes most
one bond lets go, the rest reloadone bolt pops and shock-loads the rest

With 6 kN on three bolts, each takes 2 kN. One pops and the two survivors take 3 kN each. Another pops and the last takes all 6 kN.

Where it breaks. Bolts do not replace themselves. Integrins rebind within about a second, so a patch can recover. And a bolt fails at a rated strength, while a bond has only a force-dependent lifetime.

5.2.5

What one more integrin buys — the derivative and its kink

Minted in Week 5 §2.3 · A patch of integrins slows the flow under it — and when it does not · open the module

eq. 5.2.5$$\frac{dv_{edge}}{dN} = \begin{cases} \dfrac{v_0\,\bar f}{N_mF_m} & F_{FA} < N_mF_m \\[6pt] 0 & F_{FA} \ge N_mF_m \end{cases}$$

Letters

  • \(dv_{edge}/dN\) — the edge speed gained per extra engaged integrin · nm/s per integrin
  • \(N\) — engaged integrins · count
  • \(\bar f\) — the force each carries, held fixed · pN · 5.5 pN default
  • \(v_0\) — the motors' unloaded sliding speed · nm/s · 120 nm/s
  • \(N_mF_m\) — the motors' stall force · pN · 200 pN
  • \(F_{FA} = N\bar f\) — the adhesion force; the case split is whether it has reached the motors' stall · pN

How it is used

§2.3 mints it by differentiating eq. 5.2.1 with respect to \(N\), after Gardel's finding that traction and flow are related biphasically, with a switch at 8–10 nm/s. It gives three regimes. Slipping: few integrins, flow near \(v_0\), a high loading rate, and almost no traction. Engaging: each integrin buys \(v_0\bar f/N_mF_m\), Gardel's inverse branch. Saturated: \(F_{FA}\) has reached the stall, \(v_{edge} = v_{pol}\), and another integrin adds traction and nothing else. The panel "Better or worse — the regimes, computed" plots flow, edge speed and traction against integrins present, and traction against flow on Gardel's axes, from eq. 5.3.6's mean field. On §2.1's workbench the \(N\) bar grows and then vanishes at the stall. §2.4 uses it: a saturated front cannot steer.

Comes back: —

Biological examplewhen do more integrins stop paying at the edge?

Use the workbench's cast: \(\bar f\) = 5.5 pN, 2 pN of membrane load, 10 µM.

  1. Gain per integrin: 120 × 5.5/200 = 3.3 nm/s.
  2. Break-even: \(N^*\) = 53/5.5 = 9.6 integrins (eq. 5.1.6).
  3. Stall: \(F_{FA}\) = 200 pN at \(N\) = 200/5.5 = 36.4 integrins.
  4. From 20 to 21 integrins, \(v_{edge}\) goes from 34.2 to 37.5 nm/s.
  5. Past 36, \(v_{edge} = v_{pol}\) = 88.2 nm/s. The 37th integrin adds 5.5 pN of traction and 0 nm/s.
  6. If each carried 10 pN instead, the gain would be 6 nm/s per integrin, and the stall would come at 20.

What it means. Between about 10 and 36 bound integrins, each one is worth 3.3 nm/s of edge. Past 36 they are worth nothing in speed, only in pull on the ground. Tab 4's neutrophil lives past that kink.

Mechanical analogya tug of war against a winch

A winch reels in a rope, 0.5 m/s free and stalled by 2,000 N. People join the anchor team one at a time, each holding 250 N.

In the cellIn the machine
one bound integrinone person on the anchor team
\(\bar f\)each person's hold, 250 N
\(v_0\) and \(N_mF_m\)the winch: 0.5 m/s free, 2,000 N stall
\(dv_{edge}/dN\)how much each person slows the rope
saturatedrope stopped; more people only strain the ground

Each person slows the rope by 0.5 × 250/2,000 = 0.0625 m/s. Eight people stop it. The ninth adds hold but changes no speed.

Where it breaks. People pull at a steady force. Bound integrins carry what the flow has loaded onto them, so \(\bar f\) itself shifts as the flow slows. That is why the real kink is softer than this one.

5.2.6

Turning — steering from a speed difference

Minted in Week 5 §2.4 · Two sides, and the adhesions that steer them · open the module

eq. 5.2.6$$\omega = \frac{v_L - v_R}{W}, \qquad v_{side} = \min\!\left(v_{edge,side},\; v_{rear,side}\right)$$

Letters

  • \(\omega\) — the rate the cell turns · rad/s
  • \(v_L\) — the speed of the left half · nm/s
  • \(v_R\) — the speed of the right half · nm/s
  • \(W\) — the cell's width · µm
  • \(v_{side}\) — one side's speed: the slower of its front and its rear · nm/s
  • \(v_{edge,side}\) — that side's front protrusion (eq. 5.2.1) · nm/s
  • \(v_{rear,side}\) — how fast that side's rear lets go (eq. 4.2.4) · nm/s

How it is used

§2.4 mints it for the steering panel. The camera is locked to the cell, and four adhesion sliders (front supply and rear grip, left and right) drive themselves so the cell wanders. A ringed adhesion is followed from birth at the front to release behind the rear. The evidence is Allen, Barnhart, Theriot and Mogilner's keratocytes: cells steer from the rear. Eq. 5.2.6 says why. A fast front is saturated, so more front adhesion buys traction but no speed, and only the rear asymmetry changes \(v_L - v_R\). The panel declares itself a kinematic model built from the module's equations, not Allen's feedback model.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea leukocyte whose right rear holds on

A crawling leukocyte about 10 µm wide (typical). Both front halves are saturated and advance at 40 nm/s (illustrative). The left rear lets go at 60 nm/s. The right rear keeps more grip and lets go at 30 nm/s.

  1. Left: \(v_L\) = min(40, 60) = 40 nm/s, limited by its front.
  2. Right: \(v_R\) = min(40, 30) = 30 nm/s, limited by its rear.
  3. \(\omega\) = (40 − 30)/10,000 nm = 1.0 × 10⁻³ rad/s.
  4. In degrees: 0.057°/s, or 3.4° per minute.
  5. A full circle: 2π/\(\omega\) = 6,280 s, about 105 minutes.
  6. Turning radius: the mean speed over \(\omega\) = 35 nm/s ÷ 10⁻³ s⁻¹ = 35 µm.

What it means. The cell turns toward its right, the side whose rear holds on. A bigger left front adhesion would change nothing while both fronts are saturated. That is Allen's rear steering, read off one line.

Mechanical analogya skid-steer loader

A skid-steer loader turns by running its two tracks at different speeds. Each track's speed is whatever its drive and its brake allow.

In the cellIn the machine
the left and right halvesthe left and right tracks
\(W\)the track separation, 1.5 m
\(v_L\), \(v_R\)the two track speeds
\(\min(v_{edge}, v_{rear})\) per sideeach track runs at the slower of drive and brake
\(\omega\)the loader's yaw rate

Tracks at 1.0 and 0.8 m/s, 1.5 m apart, give \(\omega\) = 0.2/1.5 = 0.133 rad/s, or 7.6°/s. The turning radius is 0.9/0.133 = 6.75 m.

Where it breaks. A loader is a rigid body. A cell's width and shape change as it turns, its front can stretch ahead of its rear, and it pivots on its adhesions rather than on a fixed frame.

Module Tab 3 · The Motor–Clutch
5.3.1

The coarse-grained stall — N_m F_m with no duty ratio

Minted in Week 5 §3.2 · The motors, the linkage — and what breaks first · open the module

eq. 5.3.1$$F_{stall} = N_m F_m \quad\text{(no duty ratio: it is already inside } F_m\text{)}$$

Letters

  • \(F_{stall}\) — the most the motor ensemble can hold · pN · 200 pN
  • \(N_m\) — motor modules · count · 100
  • \(F_m\) — force per module, a fitted lump · pN · 2 pN (Bangasser 2017)

How it is used

§3.2 mints a new number for it because these motors are not Week 4's heads. The section's table puts them side by side. A myosin II head pushes \(F_{step}\) ≈ 3–4 pN, slides at about 4 µm/s, and a team's force carries a duty ratio, \(F_{tot} = NrF_{step}\) (eq. 4.2.6). Bangasser's module has \(F_m\) = 2 pN, \(v_0\) = 120 nm/s, and the duty ratio already inside. It sets the ceiling on everything below the motors. The chain bench stops at 200 pN unless something weaker breaks first, the §3.3 bench's "stalled" regime settles there, and §3.4's traction plateau equals \(N_mF_m\) exactly.

Comes back: R2 §1.5 (what the motors can hold).

Biological examplehow many myosin II heads make 200 pN?

  1. Coarse-grained: \(F_{stall}\) = 100 × 2 = 200 pN.
  2. Week 4's head: \(F_{step}\) ≈ 3.5 pN, duty ratio \(r\) = 0.05.
  3. Time-averaged pull per head: 0.05 × 3.5 = 0.175 pN.
  4. Heads needed: 200/0.175 ≈ 1,140.
  5. In Week 4's 60-head minifilaments: 1,140/60 ≈ 19.
  6. The trap: 100 heads × 0.05 × 3.5 pN = 17.5 pN, eleven times short of 200.

What it means. One "motor" here stands for about eleven heads' worth of averaged pull, with the duty ratio already inside \(F_m\). Carry Week 4's formula into this tab and you are out by an order of magnitude, with no visible error.

Mechanical analogya rowing eight rated by its averaged thrust

A rower's blade is in the water for only part of each stroke. A crew can be rated stroke by stroke, or by its averaged thrust, with the in-water fraction already folded in.

In the cellIn the machine
one myosin II headone rower
duty ratio \(r\)the fraction of the stroke the blade is in the water
\(F_{step}\)blade force during the drive
\(F_m\), coarse-grainedeach rower's stroke-averaged thrust
\(N_mF_m\)the crew's averaged thrust

Illustrative numbers: 500 N on the blade for 40 % of the cycle is 200 N averaged per rower, so 1,600 N for the crew. Multiply that crew figure by 0.4 again and you get 640 N, the in-water fraction counted twice.

Where it breaks. Rowers pull in time with each other. Myosin heads act independently, which is why their duty ratio averages out so cleanly. And \(F_m\) is fitted to cell-scale traction, not measured on any one motor.

5.3.2

A bound clutch's force — the stretch is the force

Minted in Week 5 §3.2 · The motors, the linkage — and what breaks first · open the module

eq. 5.3.2$$f_i = \kappa_c\,x_i, \qquad x_{sub} \equiv 0 \;\text{(rigid ground)}$$

Letters

  • \(f_i\) — the force on bound clutch \(i\) · pN
  • \(\kappa_c\) — the linkage's stiffness · pN/nm · 0.8 pN/nm
  • \(x_i\) — how far that linkage has been stretched since it bound · nm
  • \(x_{sub}\) — how far the ground has moved · nm · zero by assumption: rigid ground

How it is used

§3.2 mints it to say where the stretch lives. The ground never moves, so as the actin drags a bound clutch's inner end rearward, all of that motion stretches the linkage. Talin is the spring. The panel "One clutch, loading and letting go" (flow 60 nm/s, \(\kappa\) = 0.8 pN/nm) plots force against time bound. You raise the flow, then the stiffness at the same \(\kappa v\). A same-week re-box, "Hooke, now for the filament", writes \(f = \kappa_a x\) with Kojima's 43.7 pN/nm for a micron of actin. That feeds the strength sum of eq. 5.3.3. Eq. 5.3.2 also feeds the per-clutch loading rate and the traction sum, eq. 5.3.4. The course mints Hooke's law by name later, as eq. 5.5.1.

Comes back: —

Biological exampletalin in a clutch, against the actin it holds

At the panel's default flow of 60 nm/s a clutch binds. How long until it carries 12 pN, talin's vinculin threshold, and how far does the actin stretch under that force?

  1. The stretch grows at \(\dot x_i = v_a\) = 60 nm/s.
  2. After 0.25 s bound: \(x_i\) = 60 × 0.25 = 15 nm.
  3. \(f_i = \kappa_c x_i\) = 0.8 × 15 = 12 pN.
  4. The same 12 pN on a micron of actin: \(x\) = 12/43.7 = 0.27 nm.
  5. On a 2 µm filament, half as stiff (21.9 pN/nm): 0.55 nm.

What it means. The linkage stretches 55 times more than a micron of actin under the same force, and the filament barely notices. That is why the module puts all the give in the clutch.

Mechanical analogya dog on a bungee leash tied to a lamp post

A dog strains away from a lamp post on a bungee leash. The post does not move, so every bit of the dog's progress past slack goes into stretching the leash.

In the cellIn the machine
rigid substrate, \(x_{sub} \equiv 0\)the lamp post
the talin linkage, \(\kappa_c\)the bungee leash, 50 N/m
the actin end dragged at \(v_a\)the dog walking away
\(x_i\)the leash's stretch
\(f_i = \kappa_c x_i\)the pull on the dog's collar

Forty centimetres past slack, the leash pulls with 50 × 0.4 = 20 N. A steel chain leash at 50,000 N/m would stretch only 0.4 mm under the same 20 N. That chain is the actin.

Where it breaks. A bungee stays elastic out to a long stretch. A talin linkage changes stiffness as its bundles unfold (eq. 5.1.7), and a clutch lets go at random, not when the dog stops pulling.

5.3.3

Stretch to failure — strength over stiffness

Minted in Week 5 §3.2 · The motors, the linkage — and what breaks first · open the module

eq. 5.3.3$$x_{fail} = \frac{F_{break}}{\kappa}, \qquad\text{and in a chain the force is shared, so the first to go is the smallest } F_{break}\text{ — not the largest stretch}$$

Letters

  • \(x_{fail}\) — how far an element stretches before it fails · nm
  • \(F_{break}\) — the force at which it fails · pN · actin ≈ 600 pN (Tsuda); one integrin–ligand bond ≈ 40 pN (the module's per-bond limit)
  • \(\kappa\) — its stiffness · pN/nm · actin 43.7 pN/nm per micron (Kojima); linkage 0.8 pN/nm

How it is used

§3.2 mints it to meet next week's idea of a strength: a force at which a piece fails outright. The bench "Pull the chain until something gives" pulls motors, filament and adhesion in series against rigid ground. Force builds along the load line until the first element reaches its \(F_{break}\). A micron of actin fails at 600/43.7 ≈ 14 nm, 1.4 % of its length. The linkage fails at 40/0.8 = 50 nm. At 40 pN the linkage has taken 98 % of the stretch. \(N\) bonds in parallel are \(N\) times stronger and \(N\) times stiffer, so they still fail at 50 nm. That cancelling of size is the move Week 6 makes when it divides by area and length.

Comes back: —

Biological example400 motor modules against a 20-bond adhesion

This is the chain bench's third task: give the motors 400 modules and the adhesion 20 bonds.

  1. Motor ceiling: 400 × 2 = 800 pN.
  2. Adhesion: 20 × 40 = 800 pN strength, and 20 × 0.8 = 16 pN/nm stiffness.
  3. Adhesion's \(x_{fail}\) = 800/16 = 50 nm, the same as one bond.
  4. Filament: \(F_{break}\) = 600 pN and \(\kappa\) = 43.7 pN/nm, so \(x_{fail}\) = 13.7 nm.
  5. The smallest \(F_{break}\) is 600 pN, so the filament fails first.
  6. At that moment the filament has stretched 600/43.7 = 13.7 nm and the adhesion 600/16 = 37.5 nm.

What it means. The adhesion stretched almost three times as far and survived. The filament, which barely moved, snapped. In series the weakest piece goes, not the most stretched one.

Mechanical analogya nylon recovery strap in series with a short chain

A stretchy nylon recovery strap and a short steel chain are shackled end to end between a truck and a stuck car.

In the cellIn the machine
the actin filamentthe chain: stiff, but the weaker piece
the adhesion of \(N\) bondsthe nylon strap: stretchy, and stronger
\(F_{break}\)each piece's breaking load
\(\kappa\)each piece's stiffness
\(x_{fail} = F_{break}/\kappa\)how far each stretches before it breaks

Illustrative numbers: the strap breaks at 80 kN after 1.2 m of stretch, so \(\kappa\) = 67 kN/m. The chain breaks at 60 kN with \(\kappa\) = 6 MN/m, so \(x_{fail}\) = 10 mm. Pull, and the chain breaks at 60 kN, when the strap has stretched 0.9 m.

Where it breaks. A chain has a fairly sharp breaking load. A bond's "strength" depends on how fast it is loaded (Li's spectrum, §2.2), so the adhesion's 40 pN is a declared choice, not a constant.

5.3.4

The traction — the bound clutches' forces, summed

Minted in Week 5 §3.3 · The loop — and this really is the whole model · open the module

eq. 5.3.4$$F_{FA} = \sum_{i\,\in\,\text{bound}} \kappa_c x_i = N_b\,\langle f\rangle = N_c\,n\,\langle f\rangle$$

Letters

  • \(F_{FA}\) — the traction the adhesion puts into the ground · pN
  • \(\kappa_c\) — the linkage's stiffness · pN/nm · 0.8 pN/nm
  • \(x_i\) — the stretch of bound clutch \(i\), so \(\kappa_c x_i\) is its force (eq. 5.3.2) · nm
  • \(N_b\) — clutches bound right now · count
  • \(\langle f\rangle\) — the mean force per bound clutch · pN · a few pN; §2.1's \(\bar f\)
  • \(N_c\) — clutches under this patch of edge · count · 75 in the cast
  • \(n = N_b/N_c\) — the bound fraction · 0 to 1

How it is used

§3.3 mints it as the second of the loop's three equations. First a cast table separates the several things called \(N\): \(N_c\), \(N_b\), \(N_m\), and talin's eleven vinculin sites, which this model lumps inside one clutch. §2.1's \(F_{FA} = N\bar f\) comes back with \(N = N_b\) and \(\bar f = \langle f\rangle\). The motor–clutch bench draws every clutch as its own spring, and its ledger prints the traction row as \(N_b\) times the mean force. That is what eq. 5.3.5's load line turns into a flow.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea snapshot of clutches, then the cast's average

Snapshot (illustrative): a small adhesion has \(N_c\) = 20 clutches. Five are bound, stretched 2, 5, 8, 12 and 20 nm.

  1. Forces: 0.8 × (2, 5, 8, 12, 20) = 1.6, 4.0, 6.4, 9.6, 16.0 pN.
  2. Sum: \(F_{FA}\) = 37.6 pN.
  3. \(N_b\) = 5, so \(\langle f\rangle\) = 37.6/5 = 7.5 pN, and \(n\) = 5/20 = 0.25.
  4. Check: \(N_c n\langle f\rangle\) = 20 × 0.25 × 7.52 = 37.6 pN.
  5. Tab 3's cast (\(N_c\) = 75) settles with \(n\) ≈ 0.13, \(N_b\) ≈ 9.9, \(\langle f\rangle\) ≈ 5.6 pN (the steady state §3.4 solves).
  6. \(F_{FA}\) ≈ 9.9 × 5.6 = 55 pN, about a quarter of \(N_mF_m\).

What it means. At the default cast only about one clutch in eight holds at any instant, each gently: 55 of the motors' 200 pN. In the snapshot, the newest-bound clutch carries a tenth of what the oldest does.

Mechanical analogya ship held against a current by mooring lines

A ship lies alongside a quay in a current. Crew make lines fast and cast them off. Each line's tension is set by how far it has been stretched.

In the cellIn the machine
\(N_c\), clutches availablebollards on the quay
\(N_b\), clutches boundlines made fast right now
\(x_i\) and \(\kappa_c x_i\)each line's stretch and tension
\(F_{FA}\), summedthe total hold against the current
\(\langle f\rangle\)the average line tension

Four lines at 2, 3, 5 and 6 kN hold the ship with 16 kN, an average of 4 kN per line.

Where it breaks. Deckhands make lines fast and cast them off on purpose. Clutches bind by chance at \(k_{on}\) and let go on their own at a force-dependent rate.

5.3.5

The loop closed — the flow depends on itself

Minted in Week 5 §3.3 · The loop — and this really is the whole model · open the module

eq. 5.3.5$$v_a = v_0\left(1 - \frac{F_{FA}(v_a)}{N_m F_m}\right)$$

Letters

  • \(v_a\) — the actin flow, \(v_{retro}\) in the clutch literature's name · nm/s
  • \(v_0\) — the motors' unloaded sliding speed · nm/s · 120 nm/s
  • \(N_mF_m\) — the motors' stall force · pN · 200 pN
  • \(F_{FA}(v_a)\) — the traction (eq. 5.3.4), which itself depends on the flow · pN

How it is used

§3.3 mints it as the third loop equation. It is implicit, with \(v_a\) on both sides, and that is the content. An unnumbered box, "the loop, wired", names every hand-off. The flow stretches each bound clutch at \(\dot x_i = v_a\). The stretch sets its force (5.3.2), and the force sets its off-rate (4.2.5 or 5.2.3). The off-rate enters Langmuir's \(dn/dt\) (3.2.4), and \(n\) gives \(N_b = N_cn\) and the traction (5.3.4). The load line returns \(v_a\). Only eq. 3.2.4 has a \(d/dt\), so the loop's clock is about \(1/k_{on}\) ≈ 1 s. The bench runs it clutch by clutch, with pills for free slip, partial grip, stalled and catch bonds. Its ledger prints both fluxes, and an autocorrelation panel finds no cycle. §3.4 solves its steady state (eq. 5.3.6).

Comes back: —

Biological examplesolving the loop for Tab 3's cast, then for the neutrophil

For 75 slip-bond clutches, get \(F_{FA}(v_a)\) at a given flow from §3.3's steady Langmuir balance, \(\bar n = k_{on}/(k_{on} + \langle k_{off}\rangle)\), times the mean force per bound clutch (the recipe §3.4 writes out as eq. 5.3.6). Then go round the loop.

  1. Guess free flow, \(v_a\) = 120 nm/s: \(F_{FA}\) = 46.2 pN.
  2. Load line: \(v_a\) = 120 × (1 − 46.2/200) = 92.3 nm/s.
  3. At 92.3 nm/s: \(F_{FA}\) = 53.5 pN, so \(v_a\) = 87.9 nm/s.
  4. At 87.9 nm/s: \(F_{FA}\) = 55.0 pN, so \(v_a\) = 87.0 nm/s.
  5. Settles at \(v_a\) ≈ 86.8 nm/s, \(F_{FA}\) ≈ 55.3 pN.
  6. Edge: 88.2 − 86.8 = 1.4 nm/s. Barely past break-even.
  7. With 300 clutches (§4.2's ledger): \(v_a\) ≈ 0.19 nm/s, \(F_{FA}\) ≈ 199.7 pN. Stalled.
  8. Edge: 88.2 − 0.19 = 88.0 nm/s = 5.28 µm/min.

What it means. With 75 clutches the flow eats almost all the growth and the edge creeps. With 300 the flow stops and the edge runs at the full tip speed, inside Tsai's measured 5–10 µm/min. Nothing was set by hand; the loop picked both.

Mechanical analogya car's clutch whose plates grip harder as they stop slipping

The module's own picture. The engine is the motors, the clutch is the adhesion, the road is the matrix. Dry friction grips harder near zero slip than at speed (static beats kinetic). So as the plates slip less, they grip more, and they slip less still, until they lock.

In the cellIn the machine
the motors, \(v_0\) and \(N_mF_m\)the engine: free revs and stall torque
\(v_a\), the retrograde flowslip speed across the clutch plates
\(F_{FA}(v_a)\)torque the slipping clutch passes on, set by slip
more bound at slower flowmore friction at lower slip
stalledclutch locked: no slip, engine at its stall load

Where it breaks. A dry clutch's friction is set by pedal pressure and lining, not by a count of bonds, so it does not flicker clutch by clutch. An engine also has inertia, which the actin network does not. And §3.4 finds no load-and-fail cycle on rigid ground for a reason the car cannot show: each clutch loads its own private spring, so nothing synchronises their failures until Tab 5 gives them one shared ground.

5.3.6

The mean field — the loop solved rather than sampled

Minted in Week 5 §3.4 · Three states — and something that should be here and is not · open the module

eq. 5.3.6$$F = N_c\,\bar n\,\langle f\rangle, \qquad \bar n = \frac{\langle t_{on}\rangle}{\langle t_{on}\rangle + 1/k_{on}}, \qquad \langle t_{on}\rangle = \int_0^\infty\! S\,dt, \quad \langle f\rangle = \frac{\int_0^\infty\! f(t)S(t)\,dt}{\int_0^\infty\! S(t)\,dt}$$

Letters

  • \(F\) — the steady traction · pN
  • \(N_c\) — clutches under the patch · count · 75
  • \(\bar n\) — the time-averaged bound fraction · 0 to 1
  • \(\langle t_{on}\rangle\) — the mean time a clutch stays bound · s
  • \(1/k_{on}\) — the mean wait to rebind · s · 1 s at \(k_{on}\) = 1 s⁻¹
  • \(S(t)\) — the chance a clutch that bound at \(t = 0\) is still bound at \(t\) · 0 to 1
  • \(f(t)\) — its force at time \(t\), \(\kappa_c v_a t\) · pN
  • \(\langle f\rangle\) — the force averaged over the time bound · pN

How it is used

§3.4 mints it as the grey dashed line on the "Sweeping the clutch count" charts: the same steady state, solved instead of sampled. Every clutch is replaced by an average one that binds at \(k_{on}\), lives \(\langle t_{on}\rangle\) and carries \(\langle f\rangle\). The sweep moves through three states: free slip, partial grip, and stalled, where the traction sits at \(N_mF_m\). §2.3's regime charts are this same mean field. The module points at a trap it fell into: \(\langle f\rangle\) is averaged over the time bound, not over the force at rupture. An earlier version averaged rupture forces and got a traction three times too high. And on rigid ground there is no load-and-fail cycle; that waits for Tab 5's moving ground.

Comes back: —

Biological exampleone average clutch at Tab 3's working flow

Take the loop's fixed point, \(v_a\) = 86.8 nm/s (eq. 5.3.5), with Tab 3's Bell clutches: \(k_0\) = 0.1 s⁻¹, \(f_\beta\) = 2 pN, \(\kappa_c\) = 0.8 pN/nm.

  1. Loading rate: \(\kappa_c v_a\) = 0.8 × 86.8 = 69.4 pN/s, so \(f(t) = 69.4\,t\) (pN, with \(t\) in s).
  2. \(S(t)\) falls as Bell's off-rate, \(k_0 e^{f(t)/f_\beta}\), builds up over the time bound.
  3. \(\langle t_{on}\rangle = \int S\,dt\) = 0.152 s, against 10 s unloaded.
  4. \(\langle f\rangle\) = 5.58 pN.
  5. \(\bar n\) = 0.152/(0.152 + 1) = 0.132.
  6. \(F\) = 75 × 0.132 × 5.58 = 55.3 pN.
  7. Check: 120 × (1 − 55.3/200) = 86.8 nm/s. Self-consistent.
  8. The trap: the mean force at the moment of rupture is 10.6 pN, 1.9 times \(\langle f\rangle\).

What it means. At this flow a clutch lives about a sixty-sixth of its unloaded life and spends most of it lightly loaded. Averaging rupture forces would nearly double \(\langle f\rangle\) at this flow, and feeding that back through the loop is how the earlier page tripled the traction.

Mechanical analogya rope tow up a steepening slope

On a ski rope tow, skiers grab the rope, ride, and let go. On a slope that steepens with distance, each skier's pull grows the longer they hold on, and most let go where it is hardest.

In the cellIn the machine
a clutcha skier
\(1/k_{on}\)the wait to grab again, 20 s
\(\langle t_{on}\rangle\)the average ride, 40 s
\(\bar n\)the fraction of skiers on the rope at once
\(\langle f\rangle\) against the rupture forcepull averaged over the ride, against the pull at let-go
\(F\)the load on the tow motor

\(\bar n\) = 40/(40 + 20) = 0.67, so 20 of 30 skiers are on the rope. At 150 N each, averaged over the ride, the motor carries 3.0 kN. Use the 300 N pull at let-go and you would say 6.0 kN.

Where it breaks. The tow rope runs at a fixed speed whatever the load. The actin's speed is part of the solution, which is why the mean field has to be solved round the loop. And skiers let go by choice, not at a rate that rises with force.

Featured in HW3 · Problem 3(b), Challenge
5.5.1

Hooke — force against displacement

Minted in Week 5 §5.1 · Force against displacement · open the module

eq. 5.5.1$$F = k\,x$$

Letters

  • \(F\) — the force on the spring · pN
  • \(k\) — its stiffness, the slope of the force–displacement line · pN/nm · panel default 0.8 pN/nm, a talin linkage
  • \(x\) — the displacement · nm · panel default 30 nm

How it is used

§5.1 names it for the first time, before the module takes away "the ground does not move". "You have been using this all week without naming it." The clutch was a spring of \(\kappa_c\) = 0.8 pN/nm, and §3.2's whole argument was that its stretch is the force. The panel "A spring, and its slope" asks you to set 0.8 pN/nm and find the displacement for 12 pN, talin's unfolding threshold, then halve the stiffness. It is the language Tab 5 needs for ground that gives. §5.3 puts one spring, \(\kappa_s\), under the whole adhesion, and traction then peaks at an intermediate stiffness, where the load-and-fail cycle appears. Eq. 5.5.2 divides its geometry out.

Comes back: Week 6 §1.5 (the gel under the adhesion is a spring); Week 6 §2.2 (force control and displacement control); R2 §1.8.

Biological exampletalin to its threshold, then the ground under an adhesion

  1. A talin linkage, \(k\) = 0.8 pN/nm, pulled to 12 pN: \(x = F/k\) = 12/0.8 = 15 nm.
  2. Halve the stiffness to 0.4 pN/nm: \(x\) = 12/0.4 = 30 nm for the same 12 pN.
  3. The panel's default: 0.8 pN/nm × 30 nm = 24 pN.
  4. Ground as a spring at §5.3's default, \(\kappa_s\) = 1 pN/nm, loaded by the motors' full 200 pN: \(x\) = 200 nm.
  5. Ten times stiffer ground, 10 pN/nm: \(x\) = 20 nm.

What it means. A soft ground under a stalled adhesion moves 200 nm, more than ten talin stretches' worth. That is the displacement Tabs 1–4 forbade and Tab 5 finally allows. Week 6 measures it by watching beads in the gel.

Mechanical analogya luggage spring scale

A hand-held luggage scale is a spring with a pointer. The bag's weight stretches the spring until the spring pulls back as hard as the bag pulls down.

In the cellIn the machine
force \(F\)the bag's weight
stiffness \(k\)the scale's spring
displacement \(x\)how far the hook drops
talin, 0.8 pN/nma stiff scale, 2,000 N/m
soft grounda soft scale: more travel per newton

A 20 kg bag weighs 196 N. On a 2,000 N/m spring the hook drops 9.8 cm. On a 1,000 N/m spring it drops 19.6 cm.

Where it breaks. A steel spring stays straight-line and elastic over its working range. Talin's stiffness changes as its bundles unfold, and real matrix creeps and relaxes (§5.4), so its "stiffness" depends on how fast you pull.

5.5.2

Stress, strain and the modulus — dividing the geometry out

Minted in Week 5 §5.2 · Stress against strain — dividing the geometry out · open the module

eq. 5.5.2$$\sigma = \frac{F}{A}, \qquad \varepsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L}, \qquad \sigma = E\,\varepsilon \quad\Longrightarrow\quad k = \frac{EA}{L}$$

Letters

  • \(\sigma\) — stress, force per area carrying it · Pa (1 pN/µm² = 1 Pa)
  • \(F\) — the force · pN
  • \(A\) — the cross-section carrying it · µm² · panel default 1 µm²
  • \(\varepsilon\) — strain, stretch per length · dimensionless
  • \(\Delta L\) — the stretch · nm
  • \(L\) — the length being stretched · µm · panel default 2 µm
  • \(E\) — Young's modulus, a property of the material · Pa · panel default 10 kPa
  • \(k = EA/L\) — the object's spring constant (eq. 5.5.1) · pN/nm

How it is used

§5.2 mints it because \(k\) belongs to an object, not a material. A short fat piece of collagen and a long thin piece of the same collagen have different spring constants. The panel "Same material, different shape" lets you change \(L\) and \(A\): \(k\) moves on the left while the stress–strain line refuses to move on the right. The section sets brain against the dish: Elkin's 0.14–0.31 kPa at cell scale, Stewart's 1.56 ± 0.75 kPa at millimetre scale, and polystyrene at 3 GPa = 3 × 10⁶ kPa. It warns that measured stiffness depends on the scale you probe. §3.2's eq. 5.3.3 had already shown size cancelling out. This is where the course divides it out for good.

Comes back: Week 6 §3.1 (from a spring to a modulus); C1 §3.1 (why fibroblasts are quiet in a healthy lung); R2 §1.5.

Biological examplethe same pull on gel, brain and dish

A fibroblast's adhesion pulls with the motors' full 200 pN on a plug of matrix 1 µm² across and 2 µm long, the panel's default shape.

  1. Stress: \(\sigma = F/A\) = 200 × 10⁻¹² N / 10⁻¹² m² = 200 Pa.
  2. On a 10 kPa gel: \(\varepsilon = \sigma/E\) = 200/10,000 = 0.02, so \(\Delta L\) = 0.02 × 2 µm = 40 nm.
  3. Spring constant: \(k = EA/L\) = (10⁴ Pa)(10⁻¹² m²)/(2 × 10⁻⁶ m) = 5 × 10⁻³ N/m = 5 pN/nm. Check: 200/5 = 40 nm.
  4. On brain-like 1 kPa: \(\varepsilon\) = 0.2, \(\Delta L\) = 400 nm, and \(k\) = 0.5 pN/nm.
  5. On polystyrene, 3 × 10⁹ Pa: \(k\) = 1.5 × 10⁶ pN/nm, and \(\Delta L\) ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ nm.
  6. Double \(L\) to 4 µm on the gel: \(k\) halves to 2.5 pN/nm, while \(E\) and the stress–strain line stay put.

What it means. The same 200 pN strains brain-like matrix by 20 % and the dish by essentially nothing. A dish is rigid ground, which is why Tabs 1–4's assumption worked on a coverslip, and why it fails in tissue. A 20 % strain is also near the edge of where a straight-line law can be trusted.

Mechanical analogytwo steel wires of different length

Two wires are cut from the same steel. Steel's modulus is 200 GPa (typical). Hang the same load on each.

In the cellIn the machine
force \(F\)the hanging load, 200 N
cross-section \(A\)the wire's cross-section, 1 mm²
length \(L\)the wire's free length, 1 m or 2 m
\(E\)steel's modulus, 200 GPa
\(k = EA/L\)the wire's spring constant

The 1 m wire has \(k\) = 200 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁶/1 = 2 × 10⁵ N/m, and 200 N stretches it 1.0 mm. That is a stress of 200 MPa and a strain of 0.001. The 2 m wire has \(k\) = 10⁵ N/m and stretches 2.0 mm, with the same stress and strain.

Where it breaks. Steel is uniform, elastic and the same at every scale you test it. Tissue is porous and viscoelastic (§5.4), and its measured modulus changes fivefold between a cell-sized probe and a millimetre one.

Each keeps the number it was given when first minted. The full entry, with its example and analogy, is one click away.

4.5.1

The Brownian ratchet — previewed in Week 4, earned here

Re-boxed in Week 5 §1.1 · A filament cannot push. So how does it push?

eq. 4.5.1 again$$v = \delta\!\left(k_{on}\,C\,e^{-F\delta/k_BT} - k_{off}\right)$$

§1.1 earns the ratchet by deriving why the load touches only the on-rate. Adding a subunit needs a gap, so the on-rate is gated by eq. 5.1.1, and losing one does not. Here \(v\) is a head-on tip's growth speed, with \(\delta\) = 2.7 nm, \(k_{on}\) = 11.6 µM⁻¹s⁻¹ and \(k_{off}\) = 1.4 s⁻¹ (Pollard), \(C\) the free G-actin (10 µM), and \(F\) the membrane's load. At 2 pN it gives 85 nm/s, and the §1.1 panel counts insertions so the dot on the curve is measured.

Full entry: eq. 4.5.1, Week 4

Featured in HW3 · Problem 1(a)
4.5.1

Solved for the stall

Re-boxed in Week 5 §1.2 · The ceiling, and who sets it

eq. 4.5.1 again$$F^* = \frac{k_BT}{\delta}\,\ln\!\frac{C}{C_c}, \qquad C_c = \frac{k_{off}}{k_{on}}$$

Setting \(v = 0\) gives the load \(F^*\) a tip can just hold, with \(C_c\) = 0.12 µM. At 10 µM, \(F^* = (4.28/2.7)\ln(10/0.121)\) = 7.0 pN, with no motor and no ATP term in sight. Doubling \(C\) buys only \((k_BT/\delta)\ln 2\) = 1.1 pN. The §1.2 panel plots \(F^*\) against \(C\). Read the other way round, it becomes eq. 5.1.2.

Full entry: eq. 4.5.1, Week 4

Featured in HW2 · Problem 4(d)Featured in HW3 · Problem 1(b), Problem 1(c)
4.4.3

The edge speed — both terms alive this time

Re-boxed in Week 5 §1.3 · Meanwhile, the motors are pulling the other way

eq. 4.4.3 again$$v_{edge} = v_{pol} - v_{retro}$$

Week 4 minted it with \(v_{retro}\) set to zero. Here both terms are alive. \(v_{pol}\) is the ratchet at 35° (eq. 5.1.3; 88 nm/s at 2 pN), and \(v_{retro}\) is the network's rearward flow. With motors on and nothing anchored, \(v_{retro} = v_0\) = 120 nm/s and the edge goes backward at 32 nm/s. The speckle panel reads all three speeds off a lab-frame ruler.

Full entry: eq. 4.4.3, Week 4

4.2.4

The load line, now dragging a network

Re-boxed in Week 5 §1.3 · Meanwhile, the motors are pulling the other way

eq. 4.2.4 again$$v = v_0\left(1 - \frac{F}{F_{stall}}\right), \qquad F_{stall} = N_m F_m \;\;\text{(eq. 4.2.6)}$$

Same law, new cast. \(v\) is the network's retrograde speed, \(v_0\) = 120 nm/s the motor team's unloaded speed, and \(F_{stall} = N_mF_m\) = 100 × 2 pN = 200 pN. §3.2 later gives this duty-ratio-free stall its own number, 5.3.1. With nothing anchored \(F = 0\) and \(v = v_0\) (Case A). With an adhesion, \(F = F_{FA}\), and out falls eq. 5.1.5 (Case B).

Featured in HW3 · Problem 2(b)
4.2.5

Bell's law, now for the integrin–ligand bond

Re-boxed in Week 5 §1.5 · Reinforcement — and the limit one integrin runs into

eq. 4.2.5 again$$k_{off}(f) = k_0\,e^{f/f_\beta}$$

Week 4 minted it for a myosin head letting go of actin. Here \(f\) is the load on the single integrin–ligand bond at the foot of the talin–vinculin linkage, \(k_0\) its off-rate with nothing pulling, and \(f_\beta\) the force per e-fold. That bond is in series with everything reinforcement builds above it (eqs. 5.1.7–5.1.8), so its off-rate climbs as the linkage strengthens. The anchor tears off at the one end nobody reinforced.

Full entry: eq. 4.2.5, Week 4

Featured in HW3 · Problem 2(b)
4.2.5

Bell's law, written as the lifetime the panel plots

Re-boxed in Week 5 §2.2 · One integrin under flow — loaded until it breaks, or holds

eq. 4.2.5 again$$\tau(f) = \tau_0\,e^{-f/f_\beta} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad k_{off}(f) = \frac{1}{\tau(f)} = k_0\,e^{f/f_\beta}, \qquad \tau_0 = \frac{1}{k_0}, \qquad f_\beta = \frac{k_BT}{x_\beta}$$

Here Bell is written as the lifetime \(\tau\) on §2.2's vertical axis. With Tab 3's cast, \(k_0\) = 0.1 s⁻¹ gives \(\tau_0\) = 10 s, and \(f_\beta = k_BT/x_\beta\) = 2 pN. Then 4 pN shortens the life \(e^2\) ≈ 7-fold, and 10 pN \(e^5\) ≈ 150-fold, to 0.07 s. It is the red slip curve beside the catch bond, and the first term of eq. 5.2.3 (\(k_s \equiv k_0\), \(F_s \equiv f_\beta\)).

Full entry: eq. 4.2.5, Week 4

3.2.4

Langmuir, now counting clutches

Re-boxed in Week 5 §3.3 · The loop — and this really is the whole model

eq. 3.2.4 again$$\frac{dn}{dt} = k_{on}(1-n) - k_{off}(f)\,n, \qquad n = \frac{N_b}{N_c} \in [0,1]$$

Week 3's occupancy \(\theta\) becomes \(n\), the fraction of clutches bound. The actin streaming past is always there, so \(k_{on}\) is a plain rate (1 s⁻¹ in the cast). The force-dependent \(k_{off}(f)\) (eq. 4.2.5 or 5.2.3) couples it to the flow. Setting \(dn/dt = 0\) gives \(\bar n = k_{on}/(k_{on} + \langle k_{off}\rangle)\). At the default cast that is about 0.13, roughly 10 of 75 clutches holding, and the bench's ledger prints both fluxes so you can watch them balance.

Full entry: eq. 3.2.4, Week 3

Week 6 · The Ground Gives — Stiffness, Viscoelasticity & Traction

Week 5's clutch pulled on a floor that could not move; this week the floor gives. Tab 1 hangs the clutches on a gel spring \(\kappa_s\) and follows that spring through the load's build-up (6.1.2), the bond's race to talin (6.1.3) and the adhesion's shared give (6.1.4), then reads the pull back from beads (6.1.5–6.1.6). Tab 2 rebuilds the ground from springs and dampers joined by two rules, Tab 3 trades a spring for a modulus, a strain and a traction so that a number belongs to the gel rather than to one grip, and Tab 5 sends the nucleus through a pore as the same standard linear solid.
