6.1.1

The chain — clutches and gel in series, softer than either

Minted in Week 6 §1.2 · From the motors to the gel — the whole chain on one spring · open the module

eq. 6.1.1$$\frac{1}{\kappa_{eff}} = \frac{1}{n\,\kappa_c} + \frac{1}{\kappa_s} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \kappa_{eff} = \frac{n\,\kappa_c\,\kappa_s}{n\,\kappa_c + \kappa_s}$$

Letters

  • \(\kappa_{eff}\) — the effective stiffness of the whole chain, from the actin to far ground · pN/nm
  • \(n\) — the number of bound clutches, side by side · no unit · 10 in §1.2's table and bench
  • \(\kappa_c\) — one clutch's stiffness: integrin, talin and the ligand stretched as one small spring · pN/nm · 0.8 pN/nm, the same on glass or on brain
  • \(\kappa_s\) — the ground's spring: the force to drag the patch of gel under the adhesion one nanometre · pN/nm · about 0.1 on a very soft gel to thousands on glass

How it is used

§1.2 mints it to say what the motors actually pull against: the actin's slide \(\Delta\) is shared between stretching the clutches and moving the gel, so \(F_{FA} = \kappa_{eff}\Delta\). The §1.1 scene shows the gel's springs lean while each clutch's own stretch falls, and §1.2's table reads the shares: ten clutches on a dish leave 99 % of the stretch in the clutches, while on a 1 pN/nm gel 89 % goes into the gel. \(\kappa_{eff}\) sets the load time \(\tau_L\) of eq. 6.1.2 and, with one clutch, the loading rate of eq. 5.2.2. The week re-boxes it twice: §1.3 with \(n = 1\) (0.44 pN/nm on a 1 pN/nm ground) and §2.1 as two springs in series, \(k = k_Ak_B/(k_A + k_B)\); §2.7 then tries putting an element's \(k_{eff}(t)\) where \(\kappa_s\) stood.

Comes back: R2 §1.6 (the chain, as the cell waits for the wound to stiffen).

Biological examplea neutrophil's young adhesion, on soft dermis and on glass

A neutrophil crawling through the dermis grips with a young adhesion of four bound clutches. Under it is soft matrix; in a dish it would be glass. How does a 40 pN pull split between the clutches and the ground, and how far must the actin slide to build it?

  1. Four clutches side by side: \(n\kappa_c = 4 \times 0.8 = 3.2\) pN/nm.
  2. Soft ground (illustrative): \(\kappa_s\) = 0.5 pN/nm.
  3. The chain: \(\kappa_{eff} = (3.2 \times 0.5)/(3.2 + 0.5) = 1.6/3.7 = 0.432\) pN/nm.
  4. Shares of the stretch: clutches \(0.432/3.2\) = 13.5 %; gel \(0.432/0.5\) = 86.5 %.
  5. Hold \(F_{FA}\) = 40 pN: \(\Delta = 40/0.432\) = 92.5 nm, of which 12.5 nm is clutch and 80 nm is gel.
  6. On glass, \(\kappa_s \approx 1000\) pN/nm: \(\kappa_{eff} = 3200/1003.2 = 3.19\) pN/nm, and \(\Delta\) = 12.54 nm (gel 0.04 nm).
  7. At the free flow \(v_0\) = 120 nm/s the actin needs at least 92.5/120 = 0.77 s on the soft ground, and 0.10 s on glass.

What it means. Each integrin carries the same 10 pN and its clutch stretches the same 12.5 nm on both grounds. The series rule changes only how far the actin must slide to get there, here 7.4 times further. That extra slide is time, and time is what a loaded bond does not have (eq. 6.1.3).

Mechanical analogya pocket-sprung mattress on a sprung base

Lie on a pocket-sprung mattress. The coils under your hip stand side by side, so they share your weight and their stiffnesses add: they are the \(n\) clutches. The mattress sits on a base. On a concrete floor the base cannot give, which is Week 5's rigid ground. On a sprung slatted base, the base is a second spring end to end with the coils: the gel. How far you sink is set by the chain.

In the cellIn the machine
\(n\) bound clutches side by side, \(n\kappa_c\)20 coils under the hip, 1 kN/m each: 20 kN/m
the gel under the adhesion, \(\kappa_s\)the sprung base, 5 kN/m (or a concrete floor)
the adhesion's force \(F_{FA}\)the hip's load, 400 N
the actin's slide \(\Delta = F_{FA}/\kappa_{eff}\)how far the hip sinks
each clutch's stretch \(F_{FA}/n\kappa_c\)how far the coils compress

With these illustrative numbers \(\kappa_{eff}\) = (20 × 5)/(20 + 5) = 4 kN/m, so the hip sinks 400/4000 m = 10 cm: 2 cm in the coils and 8 cm in the base. On the concrete floor it sinks only the coils' 2 cm. The coils feel the same squeeze either way; the base decides how far you travel to load them.

Where it breaks. Your weight is a force applied at once, while the motors build \(F_{FA}\) by sliding the actin; and a mattress coil never lets go and rebinds the way a clutch does.

Featured in HW3 · Challenge
6.1.2

The build-up — the load climbs to the motors' stall on one clock

Minted in Week 6 §1.2 · From the motors to the gel — the whole chain on one spring · open the module

eq. 6.1.2$$F_{FA}(t) = N_m F_m\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau_L}\right),\qquad v_{retro}(t) = v_0\,e^{-t/\tau_L},\qquad \tau_L = \frac{N_m F_m}{\kappa_{eff}\,v_0}$$

Letters

  • \(F_{FA}(t)\) — the force the adhesion holds, a time \(t\) after the clutches bind · pN
  • \(N_m\) — the number of myosin motors · 100
  • \(F_m\) — the force one motor holds at stall · pN · 2 pN, so the stall \(N_mF_m\) = 200 pN
  • \(v_{retro}(t)\) — the actin's retrograde speed · nm/s
  • \(v_0\) — the free speed, with nothing holding the actin · 120 nm/s
  • \(\tau_L\) — the load time: how long the build would take at its starting rate · s
  • \(\kappa_{eff}\) — the chain's stiffness, eq. 6.1.1 · pN/nm
  • \(t\) — time since the clutches bound · s

How it is used

§1.2 mints it by putting the motors' law (eq. 5.1.5 again) into the chain: the force climbs at \(\kappa_{eff}v_{retro}\), that rate falls in step with the force still left, and so the stretch left decays on \(\tau_L\). The bench plays the run from binding with eq. 6.1.2 dashed under the solver: the dashed starting line meets the end value at \(\tau_L\), the force is 63 % of the way at one \(\tau_L\), and with ten clutches \(\tau_L\) is 0.21 s on rigid ground, 1.9 s on 1 pN/nm and 17 s on 0.1 pN/nm. The end is the same on every ground (200 pN, \(N_mF_m/n\) per integrin, the gel moved \(N_mF_m/\kappa_s\)); only the time changes. Its starting rate \(\kappa_{eff}v_0\) is §1.3's loading rate, its stall and its ramp are two of the four loadings Tab 2 puts on every element, and §2.7 shows why a time-varying \(k_{eff}(t)\) cannot simply be dropped into \(\tau_L\).

Comes back: —

Biological examplea fibroblast's leading edge on a soft and a stiffer gel

A fibroblast's leading edge, with Week 5's cast, has five clutches bound, first on a soft gel and then on one ten times stiffer. How long does each integrin take to reach talin's 12 pN, and how far does the gel end up moving? (In §1.2 the clutches hold on, so this is the build alone.)

  1. The stall: \(N_mF_m = 100 \times 2 = 200\) pN; five clutches: \(n\kappa_c\) = 4 pN/nm.
  2. Soft gel, \(\kappa_s\) = 0.2 pN/nm: \(\kappa_{eff} = (4 \times 0.2)/4.2 = 0.190\) pN/nm.
  3. Its load time: \(\tau_L = 200/(0.190 \times 120)\) = 8.75 s.
  4. Stiffer gel, \(\kappa_s\) = 2 pN/nm: \(\kappa_{eff} = 8/6 = 1.33\) pN/nm, so \(\tau_L = 200/(1.33 \times 120)\) = 1.25 s.
  5. Each integrin ends at 200/5 = 40 pN on both gels; the gel ends 200/0.2 = 1000 nm or 200/2 = 100 nm from where it started.
  6. Each integrin reaches 12 pN at \(t = -\tau_L\ln(1 - 5 \times 12/200) = 0.357\,\tau_L\): 3.1 s on the soft gel, 0.45 s on the stiffer one.
  7. At \(t = \tau_L\) on either gel: \(F_{FA} = 200(1 - e^{-1})\) = 126 pN and \(v_{retro} = 120\,e^{-1}\) = 44 nm/s.

What it means. The soft gel gives the same final force, ten times the displacement and a build seven times slower. Three seconds to reach 12 pN is long for a bond whose lifetime falls from 10 s unloaded to 0.025 s at 12 pN (eq. 4.2.5). On the soft gel almost no bond would get there, and §1.3 turns that race into odds.

Mechanical analogya winch hauling through a stretchy recovery rope

A winch is a motor team with a load line: unloaded it reels in at full line speed, and at its stall pull it stops. Hook it to a stuck truck, a far ground that does not move, through a rope. The rope plays the chain, and the line the winch reels in is the actin's slide. A stretchy nylon recovery rope is the soft gel; a steel cable is the dish.

In the cellIn the machine
myosin team, stall \(N_mF_m\) = 200 pNwinch, stall pull 40 kN
free actin speed \(v_0\) = 120 nm/sno-load line speed 0.1 m/s
the chain, \(\kappa_{eff}\)the rope: nylon 20 kN/m, steel 2000 kN/m
\(F_{FA}(t)\) climbing on \(\tau_L\)the line pull climbing as the winch slows
the gel's final give \(N_mF_m/\kappa_s\)the rope's final stretch

With these illustrative numbers \(\tau_L\) = 40 000/(20 000 × 0.1) = 20 s through nylon and 0.2 s through steel. Both end at 40 kN, and at one \(\tau_L\) the pull is 25 kN (63 %). The nylon ends 2 m longer, the steel 2 cm. A soft line gives the same final pull, slowly, with a lot of travel.

Where it breaks. The winch drum and the truck have mass, so a real haul can jerk and overshoot; and a rope does not let go at random under load the way §1.3's bonds do.

6.1.3

The race to talin — the ground costs a factor of its own

Minted in Week 6 §1.3 · How the ground's give changes the force on the integrin · open the module

eq. 6.1.3$$P(\text{reach }F_T) = \underbrace{e^{-K/\kappa_c}}_{\text{the clutch: rigid ground}}\;\times\;\underbrace{e^{-K/\kappa_s}}_{\text{what the ground costs}},\qquad K = \frac{k_0 f_\beta}{v_0}\left(e^{F_T/f_\beta}-1\right)$$

Letters

  • \(P(\text{reach }F_T)\) — the probability that a bond ramped from zero lives to reach talin's threshold · no unit
  • \(F_T\) — talin's unfolding threshold · 12 pN (del Rio 2009)
  • \(K\) — the threshold stiffness: everything fixed by the bond, talin and the flow · pN/nm · 0.67 pN/nm for the cast
  • \(\kappa_c\) — the clutch's stiffness · 0.8 pN/nm
  • \(\kappa_s\) — the ground's spring · pN/nm
  • \(k_0\) — the bond's unloaded off-rate, \(k_{off,0}\) · s⁻¹ · 0.1 s⁻¹
  • \(f_\beta\) — Bell's force scale · 2 pN
  • \(v_0\) — the free actin flow · 120 nm/s

How it is used

§1.3 mints it to say how the ground's give changes the force on one integrin. A Derive box solves Bell's rate as a differential equation under the ramp \(f = \dot f t\); because \(1/\dot f\) splits into a clutch part and a ground part (eq. 6.1.1 with \(n = 1\)), the odds split into a product. The bench races five bonds slowed ten times and tallies thousands more in the background, so the fraction reaching 12 pN is measured and laid beside eq. 6.1.3: 43 % on rigid ground, 22 % on 1 pN/nm, 0.05 % on 0.1 pN/nm. A ground as stiff as \(K\) cuts the odds to 1/e of the rigid value. The mechanism, bonds on soft ground letting go before talin can unfold, is the rigidity threshold Elosegui-Artola and colleagues measured; it sets up §1.4's best ground, and §2.7 uses it to show that a \(k_{eff}\) falling to zero gives a bond no chance.

Comes back: Week 7 §2.4 (a stellate cell's clutch on a normal lobule and on a scar); C1 §2.4 (its integral form, with eq. 5.2.3's rate); R2 §1.6 (why the cell waits for the wound to stiffen).

Biological examplea liver stellate cell's bond, before and after the matrix scars

A stellate cell's integrin binds on soft ground; months of injury stiffen the matrix around it tenfold. Take one bond on each ground and ask how often it lives long enough to unfold talin and reinforce.

  1. The threshold stiffness: \(K = (0.1 \times 2/120)(e^{6} - 1) = 0.00167 \times 402\) = 0.671 pN/nm.
  2. The clutch's own factor, as on rigid ground: \(e^{-0.671/0.8}\) = 0.432.
  3. Soft ground (illustrative), \(\kappa_s\) = 0.3 pN/nm: the ground's factor is \(e^{-0.671/0.3} = e^{-2.24}\) = 0.107.
  4. Odds on soft ground: \(P = 0.432 \times 0.107\) = 0.046, about one bond in 22.
  5. Scarred ground, \(\kappa_s\) = 3 pN/nm: the factor is \(e^{-0.224}\) = 0.800, so \(P\) = 0.346, about one in three.
  6. Why, as rates (eqs. 6.1.1 and 5.2.2, \(n = 1\)): soft, \(\kappa_{eff}\) = 0.218 pN/nm, \(\dot f\) = 26 pN/s, 0.46 s to 12 pN.
  7. Scarred: \(\kappa_{eff}\) = 0.632 pN/nm, \(\dot f\) = 76 pN/s, 0.16 s to 12 pN.

What it means. The bond itself did not change. A tenfold stiffer ground loads it three times faster, so it reaches talin's threshold before its lifetime runs out 7.5 times as often. On the soft ground 95 % of bonds let go before their 0.46 s ramp is done; on the scar a third of them reinforce.

Mechanical analogya suction-cup hook, a winch and a trip latch

Picture a suction-cup hook on a tile wall. Unloaded it holds for a long time; under load it leaks and pops sooner. Suppose its hold time falls e-fold for every extra 20 N, a Bell-like rule (illustrative). A winch takes up a line from the hook at 0.05 m/s, and in the line is a spring latch that trips at 100 N, which is the job you want done. Whether the latch trips before the cup pops depends on how fast the line loads, and that is set by the line's stiffness.

In the cellIn the machine
integrin–ligand bond, \(k_0\) = 0.1 s⁻¹suction cup, unloaded hold about 100 s (\(k_0\) = 0.01 s⁻¹)
Bell's scale \(f_\beta\) = 2 pN20 N per e-fold
talin's threshold \(F_T\) = 12 pNthe latch trips at 100 N
actin flow \(v_0\)winch line speed 0.05 m/s
ground spring \(\kappa_s\)a bungee (200 N/m) or a stiff strap (20 kN/m)

Run eq. 6.1.3's threshold stiffness at machine scale: \(K = (0.01 \times 20/0.05)(e^{5} - 1)\) ≈ 590 N/m. Through the bungee, \(e^{-590/200}\) = 0.05: the cup almost always pops first. Through the strap, \(e^{-590/20000}\) = 0.97: the latch nearly always trips. Same cup and same latch; only the loading rate changed, 10 N/s against 1000 N/s.

Where it breaks. A suction cup leaks by air seeping under its rim, not by thermal kicks, so its hold time is not exactly Bell's exponential; and a cup that has popped does not re-stick by itself.

6.1.4

The shared ground — every bound clutch shares one give

Minted in Week 6 §1.4 · An adhesion on a spring — and the best ground · open the module

eq. 6.1.4$$F_{FA} = \kappa_s\,x_s = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\kappa_c\,(\Delta_i - x_s) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_s = \frac{\kappa_c\sum_{i}\Delta_i}{\kappa_s + n\,\kappa_c}$$

Letters

  • \(F_{FA}\) — the adhesion's force, which the gel carries (Week 5's "traction") · pN
  • \(\kappa_s\) — the ground's spring · pN/nm
  • \(x_s\) — the gel's give under the adhesion, shared by every bound clutch · nm
  • \(\kappa_c\) — one clutch's stiffness · 0.8 pN/nm
  • \(\Delta_i\) — how far the actin has slid since clutch \(i\) bound · nm
  • \(\Delta_i - x_s\) — clutch \(i\)'s own stretch, so its force is \(\kappa_c(\Delta_i - x_s)\) · nm
  • \(n\) — the number of clutches bound at that moment · up to 75

How it is used

§1.4 mints it as the force balance under an adhesion whose clutches bound at different moments; it ran Week 5 §5.3's bench without a number and gets one here, because §1.1 showed every green spring leaning by the same \(x_s\). With every \(\Delta_i\) equal it gives back eq. 6.1.1, and with \(\kappa_s \to \infty\) Week 5's rigid model, which the harness checks. The bench is Week 5 §5.3's with \(\kappa_s\) on the slider and a sweep of sixteen springs: the rigid floor returns about 57 pN, and the traction peaks near 1 pN/nm at about double that. On a ground that gives, a clutch letting go lets the gel spring back and re-loads the survivors, so the adhesion loads and fails together. That peak makes durotaxis a prediction (Lo 2000); §2.6 puts a standard linear solid in place of the spring in the same balance, and the capstone (Tab 4) runs it under each front corner of the neutrophil.

Comes back: —

Biological examplethree clutches in a neutrophil's adhesion, and one lets go

Three clutches bound at different moments, so the actin has dragged them 12, 15 and 18 nm. They share one patch of ground of 1 pN/nm. What does each carry, and what happens to the other two when the most-stretched one lets go?

  1. \(\kappa_c\sum\Delta_i = 0.8 \times (12 + 15 + 18)\) = 36 pN.
  2. \(\kappa_s + n\kappa_c = 1 + 3 \times 0.8\) = 3.4 pN/nm.
  3. The shared give: \(x_s = 36/3.4\) = 10.6 nm.
  4. Clutch forces \(0.8(\Delta_i - 10.6)\): 1.13, 3.53 and 5.93 pN; together 10.6 pN, which is \(\kappa_sx_s = F_{FA}\).
  5. The 18 nm clutch lets go: \(x_s = 0.8 \times 27/(1 + 1.6) = 21.6/2.6\) = 8.31 nm, so the gel springs back 2.3 nm.
  6. Survivors: \(0.8(12 - 8.31)\) = 2.95 pN and \(0.8(15 - 8.31)\) = 5.35 pN, each up by 1.82 pN.
  7. On a rigid floor (\(x_s\) = 0) the same clutches carry 9.6, 12 and 14.4 pN, and a failure hands the survivors nothing.

What it means. On a ground that gives, a failure is passed on: 62 % of the lost clutch's load reappears on the survivors. With \(f_\beta\) = 2 pN, an extra 1.82 pN cuts each survivor's Bell lifetime by \(e^{1.82/2}\), about 2.5 times. That is how an adhesion on soft ground loads and fails together.

Mechanical analogymooring lines to one sprung pontoon

A ship is drifting off a quay. Three mooring lines were made fast at different moments, so each has paid out a different amount by now, and all three are tied to the same floating pontoon, held to the sea bed by a spring anchor. The ship's drift is the actin, each line is a clutch, and the pontoon's spring is the gel. Because all three pull one pontoon, they share its give.

In the cellIn the machine
actin's travel since each bond, \(\Delta_i\)each line's pay-out since it was made fast: 12, 15, 18 cm
clutch stiffness \(\kappa_c\)each line, 80 N/cm
ground spring \(\kappa_s\)the pontoon's anchor spring, 100 N/cm
shared give \(x_s\)how far the pontoon is dragged
a clutch lets goa line parts

With these illustrative numbers the pontoon is dragged 10.6 cm and the lines carry 113, 353 and 593 N. When the 593 N line parts, the pontoon springs back 2.3 cm and the two survivors jump to 295 and 535 N. Each survivor is now more heavily loaded, which is how one parted line can start a chain of them.

Where it breaks. A parted line does not re-make itself the way a clutch rebinds, and a ship and a pontoon have mass, so a parting line whips and the loads overshoot.

Featured in HW3 · Problem 3(b)
6.1.5

The reach of a pull — one over distance, twice as far in line

Minted in Week 6 §1.5 · Measuring it — traction force microscopy · open the module

eq. 6.1.5$$u(r) = u_0\,\frac{a}{r}\times\begin{cases}\tfrac23 & \text{in line with the pull}\\[3pt] \tfrac13 & \text{beside the pull}\end{cases}\qquad\qquad u_0 = \frac{F}{\kappa_s}$$

Letters

  • \(u(r)\) — how far a bead at distance \(r\) moves, along the pull · nm
  • \(u_0\) — how far the gel under the adhesion moves · nm
  • \(a\) — the adhesion's radius · µm · 1 µm in Tabs 1 and 2
  • \(r\) — the bead's distance from the adhesion's centre · µm
  • \(\tfrac23\), \(\tfrac13\) — the direction factors for a bead in line with the pull and one beside it
  • \(F\) — the adhesion's pull · pN
  • \(\kappa_s\) — the ground's spring under that adhesion · pN/nm

How it is used

§1.5 mints it as the forward half of traction force microscopy: what one adhesion does to the beads around it. The bench pulls a 1 µm adhesion along +x through a bead-seeded gel and reads the row in line with the pull and the column beside it: at 100 pN on 1 pN/nm, \(u_0\) = 100 nm, and a bead 2 µm out reads 33 nm in line and 17 nm beside (the exact beads read 33 and 18). It is good to about 0.1 % in line from two radii out and 9 % low beside at two radii; a Derive box gets it from Cerruti's half-space solution, in which the gel's own stiffness cancels. It is the kernel eq. 6.1.6 sums over many adhesions, and §3.2 reads strain from its \(1/r\) fall.

Comes back: C1 §3.1 (how far the ground gives, in a healthy and a stiff lung); R2 §1.6 (how far the pull reaches in a healing wound).

Biological examplehow far a fibroblast's pull reaches through soft gel

A fibroblast pulls 50 pN through a 1 µm adhesion on a soft gel whose spring under that adhesion is 0.25 pN/nm. How far do the beads around it move, and how far out can a microscope still see the pull?

  1. Under the adhesion: \(u_0 = F/\kappa_s = 50/0.25\) = 200 nm.
  2. A bead 5 µm ahead, in line: \(u = 200 \times (1/5) \times \tfrac23\) = 26.7 nm.
  3. A bead 5 µm to the side: \(200 \times (1/5) \times \tfrac13\) = 13.3 nm.
  4. A bead 20 µm ahead, about a cell length: \(200 \times (1/20) \times \tfrac23\) = 6.7 nm.
  5. The same pull on a 1 pN/nm gel: every number falls four-fold, and the 20 µm bead moves 1.7 nm.

What it means. The pull is felt a cell length away, but 6.7 nm is below the 10–40 nm position error of a real bead image (§1.5). The far field carries almost no usable signal; the beads within a few microns carry the measurement. A softer gel scales every displacement up by the same factor, so for the same noise it gives a cleaner reading.

Mechanical analogydragging a coin glued to a deep tray of jelly

Glue a coin to the top of a deep tray of firm jelly and drag it sideways. The coin is the adhesion, the jelly is the gel, and dots drawn on the surface are the beads. The surface under the coin moves with it, and every dot moves too, less and less with distance.

In the cellIn the machine
adhesion of radius \(a\) = 1 µmcoin of radius 1 cm
gel under it moves \(u_0\)coin dragged 3 mm
bead 5 µm ahead, in linedot 5 cm ahead: 3 mm × (1/5) × ⅔ = 0.4 mm
bead 5 µm besidedot 5 cm to the side: 0.2 mm
a half-space of geljelly much deeper than the coin is wide

The rule needs only \(u_0\) and the ratio \(a/r\), so it scales: with these illustrative numbers a dot 20 cm ahead moves 0.1 mm. Keep the tray deep. In a shallow tray the glued floor holds the jelly back, and dots far out barely move.

Where it breaks. Do not swap the jelly for a trampoline: a pre-stretched sheet passes a pull on through its tension, and its dip fades only logarithmically with distance, not as \(1/r\). And jelly, like collagen, stops being linear when dragged far.

6.1.6

The bead sum — every bead reports every adhesion

Minted in Week 6 §1.5 · Measuring it — traction force microscopy · open the module

eq. 6.1.6$$\mathbf u(\mathbf x) = \sum_k \mathbf K(\mathbf x - \mathbf x_k;\,a_k)\,\mathbf F_k$$

Letters

  • \(\mathbf u(\mathbf x)\) — the displacement of a bead at position \(\mathbf x\) · nm (a vector)
  • \(\mathbf x_k\) — where adhesion \(k\) sits · µm
  • \(a_k\) — adhesion \(k\)'s radius · µm
  • \(\mathbf K\) — the displacement one adhesion causes per piconewton of its pull · nm/pN (a 2 × 2 matrix: a pull along x can move a bead along x and y)
  • \(\mathbf F_k\) — adhesion \(k\)'s pull · pN (a vector)
  • \(k\) — counts the adhesions; the sum runs over all of them

How it is used

§1.5 mints it because the gel is linear: a bead's displacement is the sum of eq. 6.1.5's reach, once per adhesion (the page uses the exact adhesion, not the far-field rule). Read forwards, it is what the second bench does to its beads. Read backwards, it is the measurement: with the adhesions' sites known it is a small least-squares problem that returns the forces exactly from clean beads and within a few percent with realistic noise; with a force on every patch it is ill-posed, and 10–40 nm of bead error makes the bare answer nonsense until a penalty \(\lambda\) smooths it. §3.5 contrasts it with a thin film that reads locally, and the capstone's chapter 4 inverts the neutrophil's own beads this way (10 nm of noise, \(\lambda = 3 \times 10^{-4}\)) and checks the map with eq. 6.3.6.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea fibroblast's two adhesions, read from three beads

A fibroblast has two 1 µm adhesions 10 µm apart, A at x = 0 and B at x = 10 µm, each pulling 80 pN toward the other on a 1 pN/nm ground. Use eq. 6.1.5's in-line rule as the kernel, \(K(r) = \tfrac23(a/r)/\kappa_s\).

  1. The kernels: \(K(5)\) = 0.133, \(K(3)\) = 0.222 and \(K(13)\) = 0.0513 nm/pN.
  2. The bead midway, 5 µm from each: \(u = 0.133 \times 80 - 0.133 \times 80\) = 0 nm.
  3. A bead 3 µm behind A, outside the cell: \(u = 0.222 \times 80 - 0.0513 \times 80 = 17.8 - 4.1\) = 13.7 nm, toward the cell.
  4. A bead 3 µm beyond B: −13.7 nm, by symmetry.
  5. Backwards, with both sites known: \(0.222F_A - 0.0513F_B = 13.7\) and \(0.0513F_A - 0.222F_B = -13.7\).
  6. Solve: \(F_A = F_B = 13.7/(0.222 - 0.0513)\) = 80 pN, both pulls recovered.
  7. Noise: a 10 nm position error is 73 % of a 13.7 nm reading.

What it means. The bead between two hard-pulling adhesions does not move at all. A still bead does not mean no force, because each bead reports a sum. The forces come back only by modelling every pull at once, and with real noise two beads cannot do it; hundreds can, if you know where the adhesions are.

Mechanical analogystrain gauges weighing trucks on a bridge

Bridge weigh-in-motion systems weigh trucks with strain gauges under the deck. Each gauge's reading is the sum of every axle's effect on it, and each axle's effect is its load times an influence line: how much one unit of load at that spot moves this gauge. The influence line is \(\mathbf K\); the axle loads are the \(\mathbf F_k\).

In the cellIn the machine
bead displacement \(\mathbf u(\mathbf x)\)one gauge's reading
adhesion \(k\) and its pull \(\mathbf F_k\)axle \(k\) and its load
the kernel \(\mathbf K(\mathbf x - \mathbf x_k)\)the influence line from axle to gauge
sites known from a fluorescent adhesion proteinaxle positions from axle detectors
penalty \(\lambda\) for a force on every patchsmoothing when the axles must be found too

With the axles located, a few gauges and a least-squares fit give each axle's load, which is the bench's left-hand pill. Ask the gauges to find the axles as well, and two neighbouring axles become almost interchangeable, just as neighbouring patches did under the \(1/r\) reach.

Where it breaks. A bridge girder spreads load along a beam, so its influence lines are not \(1/r\), and moving trucks shake the deck, adding inertia the gel never has.

Module Tab 2 · Springs and Dampers
6.2.1

The two rules — series shares the force, parallel shares the displacement

Minted in Week 6 §2.1 · Series and parallel — two ways to join any two elements · open the module

eq. 6.2.1$$\text{series:}\quad F = F_A = F_B,\;\; x = x_A + x_B \qquad\qquad \text{parallel:}\quad x = x_A = x_B,\;\; F = F_A + F_B$$

Letters

  • \(F\), \(x\) — the force on the pair and the pair's displacement · pN, nm
  • \(F_A\), \(F_B\) — the force on element A and on element B · pN
  • \(x_A\), \(x_B\) — each element's own displacement, its change in length · nm

How it is used

§2.1 mints the rules from a massless joint (series: the two pulls on it balance) and two rigid bars (parallel: both elements stretch by the bar's shift); neither argument cares what A and B are. The bench joins two springs, a clutch (0.8 pN/nm) and its ground (1 pN/nm), either way and under either control: series points fall on a line of slope \(k_Ak_B/(k_A + k_B)\), which the section re-boxes as eq. 6.1.1, and parallel points on \(k_A + k_B\). The key it hands Tab 2: controlling the quantity the joint shares is direct, while controlling the one that adds needs a split first, and later a differential equation. Every element after it (eqs. 6.2.3–6.2.5 and the tree solver), §3.1's bar of cubes, §3.3's cut and §3.5's free cell is this rule at a joint.

Comes back: C1 §3.2 (every breath, what a stretch does to a stiff patch); R2 §1.7 (why the wound does not stop).

Biological examplea fibroblast pulling on a collagen fibre in soft gel

A fibroblast's adhesion grips a patch of soft gel with a stiff collagen fibre in it. Take the fibre as a spring of 2 pN/nm and the gel as 0.5 pN/nm (illustrative). If the fibre runs along the pull, anchored beside the gel, the two are in parallel. If the pull must cross soft gel to reach the fibre, they are in series.

  1. Parallel, force control (split first): the motors' stall of 200 pN gives one shared \(x = 200/(2 + 0.5)\) = 80 nm.
  2. So the fibre carries \(F_A = 2 \times 80\) = 160 pN and the gel \(F_B = 0.5 \times 80\) = 40 pN.
  3. Series, force control (direct): \(x_A = 200/2\) = 100 nm, \(x_B = 200/0.5\) = 400 nm, so \(x\) = 500 nm.
  4. Parallel, displacement control (direct): the actin drags the patch 50 nm, so \(F = 2 \times 50 + 0.5 \times 50\) = 125 pN.
  5. Series, displacement control (split first): \(k = (2 \times 0.5)/2.5\) = 0.4 pN/nm, so \(F = 0.4 \times 50\) = 20 pN.
  6. Then \(x_A = 20/2\) = 10 nm and \(x_B = 20/0.5\) = 40 nm.

What it means. The same two materials make a ground of 2.5 pN/nm or of 0.4 pN/nm, six times apart, by how they are joined. A fibre the cell grips directly makes stiff ground; the same fibre behind soft gel hardly counts, because in series the soft part takes the stretch.

Mechanical analogytwo bungee cords on a roof rack

Strap a kayak to a roof rack with two bungee cords. Hook them side by side to the same buckle and they are in parallel: the buckle moves once, both stretch by that much, and their pulls add. Hook one to the end of the other to reach further and they are in series: one pull runs through both, and their stretches add.

In the cellIn the machine
collagen fibre, \(k_A\) = 2 pN/nmstiff cord, 200 N/m
soft gel, \(k_B\) = 0.5 pN/nmsoft cord, 50 N/m
motors at stall, force controlpulling the buckle with 100 N
actin drags 50 nm, displacement controlmoving the buckle 0.2 m
the massless jointthe hook between the cords

With these illustrative numbers, 100 N in parallel moves the buckle 0.4 m with the cords carrying 80 and 20 N; in series they stretch 0.5 m and 2.0 m, 2.5 m in all. Move the buckle 0.2 m: in parallel it takes 50 N at once; in series the pair is one 40 N/m spring, so 8 N, split as 4 cm and 16 cm. The stiffer cord carries more force in parallel; the softer cord takes more stretch in series.

Where it breaks. Bungee cords stiffen as they stretch, and a metal hook has mass, so under a sudden jerk two cords in series do not carry the same force at the same instant; the massless joint fits molecules far better than hardware.

Featured in HW3 · Challenge
6.2.2

The damper — force follows speed, not distance

Minted in Week 6 §2.3 · The Newtonian damper — force control and displacement control · open the module

eq. 6.2.2$$F = \eta\,\dot x$$

Letters

  • \(F\) — the force on the damper · pN
  • \(\eta\) — its viscosity: the force to move the piston at 1 nm/s · pN·s/nm · a slider; 2 pN·s/nm by default
  • \(\dot x\) — the rate of stretching, \(dx/dt\) · nm/s

How it is used

§2.3 mints the second part: a piston in a cylinder of oil, which answers how fast, not how far. Under force control you integrate (a held force drifts for ever at \(F_0/\eta\); a ramp gives a parabola); under displacement control you differentiate (a drag at \(v\) costs \(\eta v\) at once, and a true step would cost an infinite force, so the bench's "step" is a fast ramp over \(t_r\)). The bench, which like every Tab 2 bench starts at rest, loads at \(t = 0\) and lets go at \(t_{off}\), shows that a damper held still carries nothing however far it has moved, and that let go it stops dead and keeps everything. In the cell it stands for matrix with no crosslinks (collagen before it gels, mucus): a bead moving steadily reads \(\eta v\), and a stopped bead reads zero. It is the second part of Maxwell (eq. 6.2.3), Kelvin–Voigt (eq. 6.2.4) and the standard linear solid (eq. 6.2.5).

Comes back: —

Biological examplea neutrophil's adhesion on collagen that has not gelled

Put the adhesion on collagen that has not yet gelled, a damper of 2 pN·s/nm (illustrative). Can a bond on it ever reach talin's 12 pN?

  1. \(\eta\) = 2 pN·s/nm.
  2. The engaged actin drags the patch at \(v\) = 5 nm/s ("about 5 nm/s under load", §2.1's table of loadings): \(F = \eta v = 2 \times 5\) = 10 pN, from the first instant, for as long as the drag lasts.
  3. Talin's threshold is 12 pN, and 10 pN never gets there, however long the bond holds.
  4. The drag speed that would reach it: \(v = 12/2\) = 6 nm/s.
  5. Now force control, the motors at stall: \(\dot x = 200/2\) = 100 nm/s, so the gel under the adhesion moves 1000 nm in 10 s and never stops.
  6. The cell lets go: \(F = 0\), so \(\dot x = 0\), and the 1 µm dent stays.

What it means. On a damper the force is set by speed alone, so a slow, engaged clutch meets a ceiling of \(\eta v\), and waiting does not help. Under a held force the adhesion sinks at 100 nm/s for as long as the force is held. On such matrix the cell cannot hold a load, only keep pulling, and every pull leaves a dent.

Mechanical analogya car's shock absorber, off the car

Take the shock absorber off a car and work it by hand. Push slowly and it barely resists; push fast and it fights; stop pushing and it stops where it is, carrying nothing. The shock is the damper, the rod's speed is \(\dot x\), and its damping coefficient is \(\eta\).

In the cellIn the machine
unlinked collagen, \(\eta\) = 2 pN·s/nmshock absorber, 2000 N·s/m
actin's drag at \(v\) = 5 nm/spushing the rod at 0.05 m/s: 100 N
a fast draga pothole at 1 m/s: 2000 N
motors at stall, force control100 N hung on the rod: it sinks at 5 cm/s, never stopping
the bench's "step" over \(t_r\)a 3 cm jolt in 0.01 s: 6000 N, then nothing

With these illustrative numbers the shock answers every push with \(\eta\dot x\) and nothing else. Hold the rod still at any length and it carries zero force, which is why a car needs springs as well.

Where it breaks. A real shock absorber works through valves, so its force is not proportional to speed and differs between compression and rebound, and its oil heats and thins as it works.

Featured in HW3 · Challenge
6.2.3

Maxwell — a spring and a damper in series, a fluid

Minted in Week 6 §2.4 · Maxwell — a spring and a damper in series · open the module

eq. 6.2.3$$\dot F + \frac{F}{\tau} = k\,\dot x, \qquad \tau = \frac{\eta}{k}$$

Letters

  • \(F\), \(\dot F\) — the force through both parts, and its rate of change · pN, pN/s
  • \(\dot x\) — the rate of the total displacement (spring stretch plus piston slide) · nm/s
  • \(k\) — the spring's stiffness · pN/nm · 1 pN/nm on the bench
  • \(\eta\) — the damper's viscosity · pN·s/nm · 2 pN·s/nm on the bench
  • \(\tau = \eta/k\) — the relaxation time · s · 2 s on the bench

How it is used

§2.4 mints it from the series rule written for rates: force control is direct (add the spring's jump to the damper's drift), but displacement control needs this equation. The bench and its Derive box solve it: a held stretch relaxes, \(F = kx_0e^{-t/\tau}\), all the way to zero; a steady drag levels off, \(F = \eta v(1 - e^{-t/\tau})\); let go, it jumps back by \(F/k\) and keeps the damper's slide as a permanent set. The worked example drags a ground with \(\tau\) = 2 s at 5 nm/s: 0.95 pN after 0.2 s, like a spring, and 9.93 pN after 10 s, like a damper. In the cell it is a matrix whose crosslinks let go; §2.7 tabulates its four \(k_{eff}(t)\), and §2.8 shows that a bead on it reports speed, not distance.

Comes back: —

Biological examplean adhesion holds a dent in weakly crosslinked collagen

A mature adhesion forms over a patch of weakly crosslinked collagen, drags it 200 nm in a fraction of a second, and holds it there; the cell lets go 30 s later. Take the patch as a Maxwell ground of \(k\) = 0.5 pN/nm and \(\eta\) = 5 pN·s/nm (illustrative).

  1. \(\tau = \eta/k = 5/0.5\) = 10 s.
  2. Just after the fast drag the spring has taken it all: \(F(0^+) = kx_0 = 0.5 \times 200\) = 100 pN.
  3. Held: \(F(10\ \text{s}) = 100\,e^{-1}\) = 36.8 pN; \(F(30\ \text{s}) = 100\,e^{-3}\) = 5.0 pN.
  4. Let go at 30 s: the spring jumps back by \(F/k = 5.0/0.5\) = 10 nm.
  5. Kept for ever: \(x_0(1 - e^{-3}) = 200 \times 0.950\) = 190 nm.
  6. Compare a steady drag at 5 nm/s instead of a hold: the force levels at \(\eta v\) = 25 pN.

What it means. Holding the gel still does not hold the force: after three \(\tau\) the gel pulls back with 5 pN, below talin's 12. To keep a load on such matrix the cell must keep dragging it, and then the ceiling is \(\eta v\), set by speed. And the gel remembers: 190 nm of the 200 nm dent is still there after the cell has gone.

Mechanical analogySilly Putty, stretched and clamped

Roll Silly Putty into a bar, stretch it quickly and clamp both ends. It pulls back hard at first and then lets its pull fade, because its long molecules slide past each other while the stretch is held. Unclamp it and it shrinks back a little, then stays long. Drop a ball of it and it bounces; leave it on a table and it puddles.

In the cellIn the machine
crosslinks stretching, the spring \(k\)the putty's elastic stretch, 50 N/m
crosslinks letting go, the damper \(\eta\)molecules sliding, 500 N·s/m
\(\tau = \eta/k\) = 10 s\(\tau\) = 10 s
adhesion drags 200 nm and holdsa 2 cm stretch, clamped
the cell lets go at 30 sunclamping at 30 s

With these illustrative numbers the clamped bar pulls with 1.0 N at first, 0.37 N after 10 s and 0.05 N after 30 s. Unclamped then, it snaps back 1 mm and keeps 1.9 cm: the same equation in the same proportions as the collagen patch. A bounce lasts milliseconds, far shorter than \(\tau\), so the putty answers as its spring; an hour on the table is far longer, so it answers as its damper.

Where it breaks. Real putty has a spread of relaxation times, not one, and stiffens or tears when pulled far; one spring and one damper catch only its middle.

6.2.4

Kelvin–Voigt — a spring and a damper side by side, a solid with a delay

Minted in Week 6 §2.5 · Kelvin–Voigt — a spring and a damper in parallel · open the module

eq. 6.2.4$$F = k\,x + \eta\,\dot x$$

Letters

  • \(F\) — the total force, the spring's plus the damper's · pN
  • \(k\), \(x\) — the spring's stiffness and the shared displacement · pN/nm, nm
  • \(\eta\), \(\dot x\) — the damper's viscosity and the shared rate · pN·s/nm, nm/s
  • \(\tau = \eta/k\) — the creep time, which appears when the law is solved under force control · s

How it is used

§2.5 mints it from the parallel rule. Under displacement control it is direct (add the spring's \(kx\) to the damper's \(\eta\dot x\)), and a fast "step" costs a spike \(kx_0 + \eta x_0/t_r\) that grows without limit as \(t_r\) shrinks. Under force control it needs \(\dot x + x/\tau = F/\eta\): a held force creeps to \(F_0/k\) on \(\tau\) and stops, a solid with a delay, and let go it creeps back to zero on the same \(\tau\), never jumping. The bench runs it alone or beside Maxwell with the same \(k\) and \(\eta\), which sorts a crosslinked gel from a solution of unlinked chains. In the cell it is a crosslinked gel with its water counted in, whose beads lag the force; §2.7 and §2.8 read its surrogates and its bead tracks.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea water-filled gel under the motors' stall

The motors stall and hold the adhesion's 200 pN on a crosslinked, water-filled gel, here \(k\) = 0.5 pN/nm and \(\eta\) = 2.5 pN·s/nm (illustrative). The cell lets go at 15 s. What do the beads under the adhesion do, and what would a spring-law reading say?

  1. \(\tau = \eta/k = 2.5/0.5\) = 5 s.
  2. The creep: \(x(t) = (200/0.5)(1 - e^{-t/5})\), heading for \(F_0/k\) = 400 nm.
  3. \(x(5\ \text{s}) = 400(1 - e^{-1})\) = 253 nm; \(x(15\ \text{s}) = 400(1 - e^{-3})\) = 380 nm.
  4. A spring-law reading of the bead at 5 s: \(kx = 0.5 \times 253\) = 126 pN, against the 200 pN actually held: 37 % low.
  5. Let go at 15 s: no jump, and \(x = 380\,e^{-(t-15)/5}\).
  6. Five seconds later the bead is still 140 nm out; fifteen seconds later, 19 nm.

What it means. The beads keep moving for about three \(\tau\) after the force has stopped changing, so a spring reading taken at one \(\tau\) understates the pull by 37 %, and an earlier one by more. After the release the beads creep home on \(\tau\), so §1.5's reference picture must wait several \(\tau\), or it carries leftover displacement into every bead.

Mechanical analogya car's spring and shock absorber

Each wheel of a car hangs on a coil spring with a shock absorber beside it: Kelvin–Voigt at machine scale. Load the boot and the car settles, not at once but over a moment; unload it and the car rises back the same way, without a jump. Hit a pothole and the shock, asked to move fast, pushes back hard.

In the cellIn the machine
the gel's elastic network, \(k\)coil spring, 30 kN/m
water moving through the mesh, \(\eta\)shock absorber, 3 kN·s/m
\(\tau = \eta/k\) = 5 s\(\tau\) = 0.1 s
the motors' stall, force control600 N of luggage: settles 2 cm, 63 % of it in 0.1 s
a displacement "step" over \(t_r\)a 3 cm pothole climbed in 0.01 s

With these illustrative numbers the pothole costs a spike of \(kx_0 + \eta x_0/t_r\) = 900 + 9000 = 9900 N, then 900 N once the wheel stops rising. The spring sets where the car ends up; the shock sets how long it takes to get there, and how much a fast jolt costs.

Where it breaks. A car body has mass, so a real car overshoots and bounces, which a massless Kelvin–Voigt element cannot do; and the tyre is a spring in series that takes the edge off the infinite spike.

6.2.5

The standard linear solid — two stiffnesses and two clocks

Minted in Week 6 §2.6 · Anything more complex is just another element added · open the module

eq. 6.2.5$$F + \tau\,\dot F = k_\infty\,x + \tau\,k_0\,\dot x, \qquad k_0 = k_1 + k_\infty,\quad \tau = \frac{\eta}{k_1},\quad \tau_\varepsilon = \tau\,\frac{k_0}{k_\infty}$$

Letters

  • \(F\), \(\dot F\) — the force and its rate · pN, pN/s
  • \(x\), \(\dot x\) — the displacement and its rate · nm, nm/s
  • \(k_\infty\) — the lone spring: the equilibrium stiffness, all a slow pull meets · pN/nm
  • \(k_1\), \(\eta\) — the Maxwell arm's spring and damper · pN/nm, pN·s/nm
  • \(k_0 = k_1 + k_\infty\) — the instantaneous stiffness, both springs at once · pN/nm
  • \(\tau = \eta/k_1\) — the relaxation time, seen under a held displacement · s
  • \(\tau_\varepsilon = \tau k_0/k_\infty\) — the creep time, seen under a held force · s

How it is used

§2.6 mints it by adding one lone spring beside §2.4's Maxwell arm. Under displacement control the answer is direct (a held stretch relaxes from \(k_0x_0\) to \(k_\infty x_0\) on \(\tau\)); under force control it needs this equation (a held force creeps from \(F_0/k_0\) to \(F_0/k_\infty\) on \(\tau_\varepsilon\)); let go, it jumps back by \(F/k_0\) and creeps home on \(\tau_\varepsilon\). The builder bench measures both clocks and their ratio \(k(0^+)/k(\infty)\), and the worked example (\(k_1\) = 3, \(\eta\) = 6, \(k_\infty\) = 1) relaxes on 2 s and creeps on 8 s. The drop-in bench then puts it under Tab 1's adhesion through eq. 6.1.4: at \(k_0\) = 2.82 and \(k_\infty\) = 0.141 pN/nm the traction sits near 100 pN for \(\tau\) of 0.01–0.1 s, above either spring alone (93 and 81 pN), as Gong and colleagues found. It is the ground of the capstone's chapter 3 and the nucleus of eq. 6.5.1.

Comes back: —

Biological examplethe drop-in's ground, under a neutrophil's adhesion

Take the ground the drop-in bench uses by default, stiff for a moment and soft at rest: \(k_0\) = 2.82 pN/nm, \(k_\infty\) = 0.141 pN/nm, \(\tau\) = 0.1 s. What does each clock mean for one adhesion?

  1. The arm: \(k_1 = 2.82 - 0.141\) = 2.68 pN/nm, and \(\eta = \tau k_1\) = 0.268 pN·s/nm.
  2. The creep clock: \(\tau_\varepsilon = 0.1 \times 2.82/0.141\) = 2.0 s.
  3. The gel dragged 20 nm and held (displacement control): \(F\) starts at \(2.82 \times 20\) = 56 pN and relaxes to \(0.141 \times 20\) = 2.8 pN within a few tenths of a second.
  4. The motors' stall held (force control, 200 pN): the gel jumps to \(200/2.82\) = 71 nm and creeps toward \(200/0.141\) = 1420 nm on 2 s.
  5. A bond reaches talin's 12 pN in about 0.1–0.3 s at Tab 1's rates (§2.7), close to \(\tau\): it loads on a ground still near \(k_0\).
  6. It then holds for a second or so, between \(\tau\) and \(\tau_\varepsilon\), as the ground softens toward \(k_\infty\).

What it means. This ground is twenty times stiffer to its first tenth of a second than at rest. A bond loads while the ground is stiff and holds while it softens, which is why the drop-in finds more traction, about 100 pN, than either spring gives alone.

Mechanical analogymemory foam under a hand

Press a hand into memory foam. It dents a little at once, then keeps sinking slowly; lift the hand and the foam springs back part way at once, then fills in over several seconds. That is the standard linear solid: a lone spring (the foam's frame) beside a spring-and-damper arm (air squeezing through its cells).

In the cellIn the machine
instantaneous stiffness \(k_0\)5 kN/m to a quick press
equilibrium stiffness \(k_\infty\)1 kN/m once settled
relaxation time \(\tau\)2 s
creep time \(\tau_\varepsilon = \tau k_0/k_\infty\)10 s
the motors' stall, force controla hand pressing with 50 N

With these illustrative numbers the hand sinks 1 cm at once and creeps toward 5 cm on 10 s. Lift it after 10 s, at 3.5 cm: the foam jumps back 1 cm, to 2.5 cm, and fills in on 10 s, with 0.9 cm left after another 10 s. Hold a 2 cm dent instead and the push it takes falls from 100 N to 20 N on 2 s: the same foam, the shorter clock.

Where it breaks. Memory foam's clocks depend strongly on temperature, it stiffens sharply once its cells collapse, and it has a spread of relaxation times rather than one.

6.2.6

The single-spring surrogate — a stiffness that belongs to the experiment

Minted in Week 6 §2.6 · Anything more complex is just another element added · open the module

eq. 6.2.6$$k_{eff}(t) = \frac{F(t)}{x(t)}$$

Letters

  • \(k_{eff}(t)\) — the stiffness a spring would need to give this force at this displacement, at this moment · pN/nm
  • \(F(t)\) — the element's force at time \(t\) · pN
  • \(x(t)\) — its displacement at time \(t\) · nm
  • \(t\) — time since the loading began · s

How it is used

§2.6 mints it as the one number that puts any element back under a clutch, which only knows springs; its two ends are \(k(0^+)\), every damper rigid, and \(k(\infty)\), every damper slack. For the Maxwell ground dragged at a steady speed it reads 0.95 pN/nm after 0.2 s and 0.2 pN/nm after 10 s, Week 5's "stiffness is a rate" in a number. §2.7 writes it out for five elements under four loadings, names the relaxation stiffness \(k_x(t)\) and the creep stiffness \(k_F(t)\), shows \(k_x \le k_F\), and on the "four gels" bench feeds each reading into Tab 1's chain as \(\dot f\); after the release it reads zero on every gel still displaced, as if a gel springing back had no stiffness. Its problems (there is no single \(k_{eff}\), it multiplies where the physics sums a history, and its clock is the loading's) lead to eq. 6.2.7.

Comes back: Week 7 §2.3 (which stiffness did it read: a probe's twenty milliseconds against the cell's ten seconds).

Biological examplea probe's quick poke against a fibroblast's long pull

A probe indents a fast-relaxing gel and reads it 20 ms later; a fibroblast on the same gel holds a steady pull for 10 s. Take the gel as a standard linear solid with \(k_\infty\) = 0.5 pN/nm, \(k_1\) = 1.5 pN/nm and \(\tau\) = 1 s (illustrative). What stiffness does each report, and what loading rate would each give a bond?

  1. \(k_0 = 1.5 + 0.5\) = 2.0 pN/nm, and \(\tau_\varepsilon = 1 \times 2.0/0.5\) = 4 s.
  2. The probe, a held displacement, at 20 ms: \(k_x = 0.5 + 1.5\,e^{-0.02}\) = 1.97 pN/nm.
  3. The cell, a held force, at 10 s: \(k_F = 1/\big(1/0.5 - (1/0.5 - 1/2.0)\,e^{-10/4}\big) = 1/(2 - 0.123)\) = 0.533 pN/nm.
  4. Same gel, two readings 3.7 times apart.
  5. Into Tab 1's chain for one bond (eq. 6.1.1, \(n = 1\)) with \(\dot f = \kappa_{eff}v_0\): 1.97 gives \(\kappa_{eff}\) = 0.569 pN/nm and \(\dot f\) = 68 pN/s.
  6. And 0.533 gives \(\kappa_{eff}\) = 0.320 pN/nm and \(\dot f\) = 38 pN/s.

What it means. Both numbers are honest, and neither is the gel's stiffness: each belongs to the experiment that produced it. A bond fed the probe's number is loaded 1.8 times faster than one fed the cell's, so which \(k_{eff}\) you quote decides what Tab 1 predicts.

Mechanical analogya shoe midsole in a drop test and under a standing nurse

A shoe lab measures a foam midsole by dropping a weight on it, an impact of about 20 ms. A nurse stands on the same midsole for minutes. Each reports a force over a squash, \(F/x\), and each is right; they disagree because the foam is a standard linear solid.

In the cellIn the machine
the gelthe foam midsole
the probe's poke, a held displacementthe drop rig, a 20 ms impact
the cell's steady pull, a held forcestanding still for 10 s
relaxation stiffness \(k_x\)the drop rig's reading
creep stiffness \(k_F\)the standing reading

Run the same equations with illustrative foam values, \(k_\infty\) = 50 kN/m, \(k_1\) = 150 kN/m and \(\tau\) = 1 s: the drop test reads 197 kN/m, and ten seconds of standing read 53 kN/m. A footfall and a long stand meet very different stiffnesses in the same shoe.

Where it breaks. Foam is nonlinear: it stiffens as its cells collapse, so its \(F/x\) depends on how far it is squashed as well as on when, which no linear element captures.

6.2.7

Boltzmann's superposition — the force now is a weighted history

Minted in Week 6 §2.7 · One number for the ground? — a \(k_{eff}(t)\) for each element, to put into Tab 1 · open the module

eq. 6.2.7$$F(t) = \int_0^t k_x(t - t')\,\dot x(t')\,dt'$$

Letters

  • \(F(t)\) — the element's force now · pN
  • \(t\) — now · s
  • \(t'\) — an earlier time, between 0 and now · s
  • \(\dot x(t')\,dt'\) — the small step of displacement made at \(t'\) · nm
  • \(k_x(t - t')\) — the relaxation stiffness: how much force a unit step made \(t - t'\) ago still carries · pN/nm

How it is used

§2.7 mints it after listing the problems with plugging \(k_{eff}(t)\) into Tab 1. A relaxation stiffness is not a spring constant that drifts; it is a weight over the past, and the force now is every earlier step times what is left of it (a starting jump adds \(k_x(t)\,x(0^+)\)). A Derive box gets it from nothing but linearity and checks it twice: it turns Maxwell's step answer into its drag answer, and it returns a held force exactly. The "four gels" bench's bottom chart plots the standard linear solid's true force, the product \(k_x(t)\,x(t)\) and this sum: holding 10 pN for 8 s, the product says 7.6 pN and the sum 10.0 pN, and after the cell lets go only the sum returns to zero, because it counts the release as one more step. It is the honest way to use a relaxation stiffness, measured under a held displacement, on any other loading.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea bead under a clutch, dragged and then held

On a Maxwell gel with \(k\) = 0.5 pN/nm and \(\eta\) = 1.5 pN·s/nm (illustrative), a clutch drags a bead at 20 nm/s for 2 s, to 40 nm. Then the clutch stops and holds it, and at 5 s the cell lets go. Did the gel's force ever pass talin's 12 pN?

  1. \(\tau = 1.5/0.5\) = 3 s, so the relaxation stiffness is \(k_x(s) = 0.5\,e^{-s/3}\).
  2. At 2 s, the sum: \(F = kv\tau(1 - e^{-2/3}) = 0.5 \times 20 \times 3 \times 0.487\) = 14.6 pN.
  3. The product at 2 s: \(k_x(2)\,x(2) = 0.5\,e^{-2/3} \times 40\) = 10.3 pN, 30 % low.
  4. At 5 s, three seconds into the hold, the sum: \(kv\tau(e^{-3/3} - e^{-5/3}) = 30 \times (0.368 - 0.189)\) = 5.37 pN; the product says 3.78 pN.
  5. Let go at 5 s: the gel jumps back \(5.37/0.5\) = 10.7 nm and keeps 29.3 nm.
  6. The true force is now zero, but the product still claims \(0.5\,e^{-5/3} \times 29.3\) = 2.8 pN.

What it means. The true force crossed talin's 12 pN before the drag ended; the product says it never did. Read through a relaxation stiffness, a bead's displacement means nothing without its history, and here the history decides whether the adhesion could reinforce.

Mechanical analogypumping up a slowly leaking tyre

Pump a tyre that has a leak. Every stroke adds a little pressure, and from that moment the leak starts bleeding that stroke's share away. The pressure now is the sum of every stroke, each weighted by how much of it is left. That is eq. 6.2.7 with a pump in place of a clutch.

In the cellIn the machine
a small step \(\dot x(t')\,dt'\)one pump stroke, +0.1 bar
relaxation stiffness \(k_x(t - t')\)how much of a stroke is left after the leak
the force now, \(F(t)\)the gauge pressure now
the product \(k_x(t)\,x(t)\)all the pumping, leaked as if done at the first stroke
the cell lets goopening the valve

With an illustrative leak time of 60 s and ten strokes 2 s apart, the gauge just after the last stroke reads \(0.1\sum_{j=0}^{9}e^{-2j/60}\) = 0.86 bar. Treating all 1.0 bar as pumped at the first stroke, as the product does, gives \(e^{-18/60}\) = 0.74 bar, 14 % low. The early strokes have leaked longer than the late ones, and only the sum knows it.

Where it breaks. A real puncture's leak is not exactly proportional to the gauge pressure, so the tyre is only nearly linear; eq. 6.2.7 rests on the linearity that the gel's springs and dampers really have.
