6.3.1

The ground's spring from a modulus — grip size times gel stiffness

Minted in Week 6 §3.1 · From a spring to a modulus — force becomes stress, displacement becomes strain · open the module

eq. 6.3.1$$\kappa_s = \frac{4}{9}\,\pi E\,a \;\approx\; 1.4\,E\,a \qquad (E \text{ in kPa},\ a \text{ in µm},\ \kappa_s \text{ in pN/nm})$$

Letters

  • \(\kappa_s\) — the ground's spring under one adhesion · pN/nm
  • \(E\) — the gel's Young's modulus, a property of the material · kPa · brain 0.14–0.31 kPa by AFM, muscle ≈ 12 kPa, culture gels 1–100 kPa, a dish ≈ 3 × 10⁶ kPa
  • \(a\) — the adhesion's radius · µm · 1 µm by default; a nascent adhesion's 0.19 µm² is 0.25 µm
  • \(\tfrac49\pi\) — the shape number for a uniform sideways pull on an incompressible half-space (\(\nu = \tfrac12\)) · ≈ 1.40

How it is used

§3.1 mints it right after building \(\sigma = E\varepsilon\) from cubes (eq. 5.5.2 again): \(\kappa_s\) is a modulus times a shape, as \(k = EA/L\) was for a bar, and here the shape is the grip's radius. It was derived in §1.5's Derive box by adding the half-space answer over a disc, and it is eq. 2 of Saez 2005 at \(\nu = \tfrac12\). The bench reads \(F/u_0\) against \(a\), one straight line per gel, and redraws §1.4's sweep against \(E\) with brain and muscle marked. Tab 1's best ground of 1 pN/nm is 0.72 kPa under a 1 µm adhesion, 1.4 kPa under 0.5 µm and 0.36 kPa under 2 µm, so the optimum is set by \(E\cdot a\). The capstone uses it under each front corner of the neutrophil to turn the gradient's modulus into a spring.

Comes back: Week 7 §2.4 (a stellate cell's grip spring from the liver's modulus); C1 §3.1 (a fibroblast's ground in a healthy and a stiff lung); R2 §1.6 (the wound's spring from its modulus).

Biological exampleone bond's ground on brain and on muscle, through two grips

A cell grips brain-soft matrix (0.3 kPa, the top of the AFM range) or muscle (12 kPa), through a nascent adhesion or a 1 µm one. What spring does each grip make, and what does it cost a bond racing to talin (eq. 6.1.3, \(K\) = 0.67 pN/nm)?

  1. The shape number: \(\tfrac49\pi\) = 1.40.
  2. Brain, 1 µm grip: \(\kappa_s = 1.40 \times 0.3 \times 1\) = 0.42 pN/nm.
  3. Muscle, 1 µm grip: \(1.40 \times 12 \times 1\) = 16.8 pN/nm.
  4. A nascent adhesion: \(a = \sqrt{0.19/\pi}\) = 0.25 µm, so 0.105 pN/nm on brain and 4.2 pN/nm on muscle.
  5. The ground's factor \(e^{-K/\kappa_s}\): nascent on brain, \(e^{-0.67/0.105}\) = 0.0017; 1 µm on muscle, \(e^{-0.67/16.8}\) = 0.96.
  6. The gel that makes Tab 1's best 1 pN/nm under the nascent grip: \(E = 9 \times 1000/(4\pi \times 0.25)\) pN/µm² = 2.9 kPa.

What it means. From a small grip on brain to a large one on muscle the ground's spring rises 160-fold, and its factor in a bond's odds goes from almost nothing to almost one. Growing an adhesion from 0.25 to 1 µm stiffens its ground four times on any tissue, so a cell can change the ground it feels without changing the ground.

Mechanical analogya puck glued to a thick rubber block

Glue a flat puck to the top of a thick block of soft rubber and push it sideways with a force gauge. Force over sideways travel is a spring, and it depends on two things: how stiff the rubber is and how big the puck is. Double the puck's radius and the spring doubles; use a rubber twice as stiff and it doubles again.

In the cellIn the machine
the gel's modulus \(E\)the rubber's modulus, 1 MPa
the adhesion's radius \(a\)the puck's radius, 1 cm
the ground's spring \(\kappa_s\)the sideways spring you feel
gel thick beside the adhesiona block many puck-widths deep
1 kPa × 1 µm = 1 pN/nm1 MPa × 1 cm = 10 kN/m

Run eq. 6.3.1 with these illustrative values: \(\kappa_s\) = 1.40 × 10⁶ Pa × 0.01 m = 14 kN/m, or 14 N per millimetre. A 2 cm puck gives 28 kN/m, and a 10 kPa jelly under the 1 cm puck only 140 N/m. Rubber, like gel, keeps its volume, so the same \(\tfrac49\pi\) applies.

Where it breaks. A rigid puck carries more of its load at its rim than a uniform pull does and is about 4/π ≈ 1.27 times stiffer (Mindlin's problem, which §1.5 notes); and a block not much deeper than the puck is wide is stiffer still, because the floor is close.

6.3.2

Strain from beads — a stretch is a difference of displacements

Minted in Week 6 §3.2 · Strain, read between two beads — a stretch is a difference of two displacements · open the module

eq. 6.3.2$$\varepsilon = \frac{(\mathbf u_2 - \mathbf u_1)\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}}{L} \;\;\xrightarrow{\;L\to0\;}\;\; \varepsilon_{xx} = \frac{\partial u_x}{\partial x},\quad \varepsilon_{yy} = \frac{\partial u_y}{\partial y},\quad \gamma_{xy} = \frac{\partial u_x}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_y}{\partial x}$$

Letters

  • \(\varepsilon\) — the strain between two beads: stretch over separation · no unit (per cent)
  • \(\mathbf u_1\), \(\mathbf u_2\) — the two beads' displacements · nm
  • \(\hat{\mathbf e}\) — the unit vector along the line from bead 1 to bead 2
  • \(L\) — the beads' separation · µm · 1 µm is the closest pair on the bench
  • \(u_x\), \(u_y\) — the displacement's components at a point · nm
  • \(x\), \(y\) — position · µm
  • \(\varepsilon_{xx}\), \(\varepsilon_{yy}\) — the stretch along x and along y at a point · no unit
  • \(\gamma_{xy}\) — the shear strain: the change in a small square's corner angle · no unit (radians)

How it is used

§3.2 mints it from Tab 1's clutch, whose stretch was already a difference (\(\Delta_i - x_s\)): a piece of gel between two beads is stretched by the part of \(\mathbf u_2 - \mathbf u_1\) along the line joining them, over their separation, and as \(L \to 0\) that becomes a derivative. The bench reads a chosen pair on §1.5's cell and maps all three components plus the area strain \(\varepsilon_{xx} + \varepsilon_{yy}\): the gel is squeezed under the middle of the cell, and at the edge of the field beads still move (eq. 6.1.5's \(1/r\)) while the strain nearly vanishes. §3.4 uses the two diagonals of a shear to tie \(G\) to \(E\), and §3.5 uses the shear \(\gamma = u/h\) on a thin film.

Comes back: —

Biological examplebeads ahead of and behind a fibroblast's adhesion

A fibroblast pulls 100 pN along +x through a 1 µm adhesion on a 1 pN/nm ground (about a 0.72 kPa gel, eq. 6.3.1), so \(u_0\) = 100 nm. Beads in line with the pull move by eq. 6.1.5, \(u = u_0(a/r)\tfrac23\), all along +x. Where is the gel stretched, where squeezed, and how fast does strain fade?

  1. Beads 2 and 3 µm ahead move 33.3 nm and 22.2 nm.
  2. Their strain: \(\varepsilon = (22.2 - 33.3)\ \text{nm}/1000\ \text{nm}\) = −1.1 %, squeezed ahead of the pull.
  3. Beads 3 and 2 µm behind also move 22.2 and 33.3 nm along +x; from the far one to the near one, \(\varepsilon = +11.1/1000\) = +1.1 %, stretched behind.
  4. The point value 2.5 µm ahead: \(\varepsilon_{xx} = \partial u_x/\partial x = -\tfrac23 u_0a/r^2 = -\tfrac23 \times 100/6.25\) = −10.7 nm/µm = −1.07 %.
  5. Far out, beads 10 and 11 µm ahead move 6.67 and 6.06 nm, so \(\varepsilon\) = −0.061 %.

What it means. Displacements fall as \(1/r\) but strain falls as \(1/r^2\): from the 2–3 µm pair to the 10–11 µm pair the displacement drops five-fold and the strain eighteen-fold. A bead that moved 7 nm far from the cell sits in gel that is barely deformed; strain says where the cell is actually working the gel.

Mechanical analogya clip-on extensometer on a tensile test

In a tensile test the machine's crosshead reports one displacement: how far the grip moved. That number includes the grips slipping and the frame flexing, so it says little about the bar itself. An extensometer clips two knife edges to the bar a set gauge length apart and reads the difference of their displacements, which is the strain.

In the cellIn the machine
bead displacements \(\mathbf u_1\), \(\mathbf u_2\)the two knife edges' movements
separation \(L\)gauge length, 50 mm
one bead's displacement alonethe crosshead's travel
\(\varepsilon = (\mathbf u_2 - \mathbf u_1)\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}/L\)(0.30 − 0.20) mm / 50 mm = 0.2 %
a dense field of beads, \(L \to 0\)a speckle pattern and a camera (image correlation)

With these illustrative readings the crosshead might have moved 1.5 mm while the bar itself strained 0.2 %. Only the difference over a known length says what the material did.

Where it breaks. The extensometer averages over its 50 mm, so near a hole or a weld, where strain changes over millimetres, it misses the peak; the \(L \to 0\) limit needs a fine grid, which the beads give.

Featured in HW3 · Problem 3(c)
6.3.3

The traction on a cut — stress turns a direction into a force per area

Minted in Week 6 §3.3 · Force per area, with a direction — the traction on a cut · open the module

eq. 6.3.3$$\mathbf t = \boldsymbol\sigma\,\mathbf n:\qquad t_x = \sigma_{xx}n_x + \sigma_{xy}n_y,\quad t_y = \sigma_{xy}n_x + \sigma_{yy}n_y,\qquad t_n = \mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n,\quad t_s = \mathbf t\cdot\mathbf s$$

Letters

  • \(\mathbf t\) — the traction: force per area across a cut, with a direction · Pa (pN/µm²); the 2D lattice uses pN/µm
  • \(\boldsymbol\sigma\) — the stress: \(\sigma_{xx}\) and \(\sigma_{yy}\) across the x- and y-cuts, and \(\sigma_{xy} = \sigma_{yx}\) along them · Pa
  • \(\mathbf n = (n_x, n_y) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\) — the unit normal, straight across the cut
  • \(t_x\), \(t_y\) — the traction's components · Pa
  • \(t_n = \mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n\) — its normal part, pulling the two sides apart (+) or together (−) · Pa
  • \(t_s = \mathbf t\cdot\mathbf s\) — its shear part along the cut, with \(\mathbf s = (-n_y, n_x)\) · Pa

How it is used

§3.3 mints it from force balance on a small triangle of gel, the massless-joint argument of Tab 2's series rule, and shows why \(\sigma_{xy} = \sigma_{yx}\) (or a small square would spin). The bench loads a spring lattice by stretch and shear, cuts it at any angle, sums the forces of the springs that cross, and lays the measured \(t_n\) and \(t_s\) over eq. 6.3.3 computed from the three stresses: pure shear pulls the 45° cut straight apart and pushes the 135° cut together, and the normal tractions on any two perpendicular cuts add to \(\sigma_{xx} + \sigma_{yy}\). The gel's own surface is the cut that matters to the cell, and the traction there is almost all shear. §3.4 uses the 45° cut to tie \(G\) to \(E\), and §3.5 reads the traction on a thin film's top face.

Comes back: —

Biological exampleinside the gel under a mature adhesion

Take x along the cell's pull and y up out of the gel. Under a mature adhesion the surface carries a shear traction of about 5.5 kPa (Balaban's 5.5 nN per µm² of adhesion), the cell does not lift the gel, and suppose the gel just behind it carries a tension of 2 kPa along x (illustrative). So \(\sigma_{xy}\) = 5.5 kPa, \(\sigma_{yy}\) = 0 and \(\sigma_{xx}\) = 2 kPa. What acts on a plane inside the gel tilted at 30°?

  1. The surface, \(\mathbf n = (0, 1)\): \(t_x = \sigma_{xy}\) = 5.5 kPa and \(t_y = \sigma_{yy}\) = 0, pure shear, the traction TFM reports.
  2. The 30° cut: \(\mathbf n\) = (0.866, 0.5).
  3. \(t_x = 2 \times 0.866 + 5.5 \times 0.5\) = 4.48 kPa; \(t_y = 5.5 \times 0.866 + 0\) = 4.76 kPa.
  4. Normal part: \(t_n = 4.48 \times 0.866 + 4.76 \times 0.5\) = 6.26 kPa, pulling the plane open.
  5. Shear part, with \(\mathbf s\) = (−0.5, 0.866): \(t_s = -2.24 + 4.12\) = 1.88 kPa.
  6. Check on the perpendicular 120° cut: \(t_n\) = −4.26 kPa, and 6.26 − 4.26 = 2.0 = \(\sigma_{xx} + \sigma_{yy}\).

What it means. The cell only slides the surface, yet a plane inside the gel is pulled open at 6.3 kPa, more than the shear the cell applied. Stresses of this size are comparable to the modulus of many culture gels (1–100 kPa), which is where gel stops behaving like a small-strain spring.

Mechanical analogya scarf joint in timber

Two boards are joined by gluing their ends along a long slanted cut, a scarf joint, and the board is pulled along its length. The glue line is a cut through the board, and what it carries depends on its angle. Square across, the glue is pulled straight apart; slanted, it is mostly sheared, which glue resists far better.

In the cellIn the machine
the gel's stress \(\boldsymbol\sigma\)the board's tension, \(\sigma_{xx}\) = 10 MPa
a cut through the gel, normal \(\mathbf n\)the glue line, its normal at \(\theta\) to the board's axis
\(t_n\), pulling the cut apartpeel on the glue
\(t_s\), sliding along the cutshear on the glue
the gel's surface under the cellthe face of the glue line

With an illustrative 10 MPa, a butt joint (\(\theta\) = 0°) puts the full 10 MPa across the glue as peel. A scarf whose normal sits at 80° to the axis gives \(t_n = 10\cos^2 80^\circ\) = 0.30 MPa and a shear of \(10\sin 80^\circ\cos 80^\circ\) = 1.71 MPa: the same tension, turned mostly into shear by choosing the cut.

Where it breaks. Eq. 6.3.3 holds at a point for any material, but a real scarf's stress is not uniform: it peaks at the joint's thin tips, where glue lines usually fail first, so one board-wide \(\sigma\) understates the worst spot.

6.3.4

Three material constants — E, ν and G, tied by one rule

Minted in Week 6 §3.4 · Two more numbers a material needs — the narrowing ν, the shear modulus G, and how the three are tied · open the module

eq. 6.3.4$$\sigma_{xx} = E\,\varepsilon_{xx},\qquad \varepsilon_{yy} = -\nu\,\varepsilon_{xx},\qquad \sigma_{xy} = G\,\gamma_{xy},\qquad G = \frac{E}{2(1+\nu)} \qquad\Big(\text{triangular lattice: } E = \tfrac{2k}{\sqrt3},\ \nu = \tfrac13,\ G = \tfrac{\sqrt3 k}{4}\Big)$$

Letters

  • \(\sigma_{xx}\), \(\varepsilon_{xx}\) — stress and strain along a pull · Pa, no unit
  • \(E\) — Young's modulus, the slope of a stretch · Pa (kPa for gels)
  • \(\varepsilon_{yy}\) — the narrowing across the pull · no unit
  • \(\nu\) — Poisson's ratio · ½ for biology (incompressible); polyacrylamide 0.480 ± 0.012 (Boudou 2006); the lattice ⅓
  • \(\sigma_{xy}\), \(\gamma_{xy}\) — shear stress and shear strain · Pa, no unit
  • \(G\) — the shear modulus, the slope of a lean · Pa · \(E/3\) at \(\nu = \tfrac12\): 333 Pa for a 1 kPa gel
  • \(k\) — the spring constant of the bench's triangular lattice, which sets its \(E\) and \(G\) (per unit length, in 2D)

How it is used

§3.4 mints the two numbers a material needs beyond \(E\). The narrowing \(\nu\) is fixed at ½ because water-filled gels keep their volume: a block stretched by \(\varepsilon\) and narrowed by \(\nu\varepsilon\) on two sides keeps its volume only if \(\nu = \tfrac12\). A Derive box ties the shear modulus to the other two by reading a shear as a stretch along one diagonal and a squeeze along the other, \(G = E/2(1+\nu)\). The bench stretches and shears a triangular spring lattice, measures \(E\), \(\nu\) and \(G\), and checks the tie with the measured numbers, not the predicted ones. At \(\nu = \tfrac12\) it gives \(G = E/3\) for §3.5's thin film, and it turns the general grip spring \(\pi Ea/\big((1+\nu)(2-\nu)\big)\) into eq. 6.3.1's \(\tfrac49\pi Ea\).

Comes back: C1 §3.3 (the shear modulus, in the critical stiffness that tips a lung patch).

Biological examplea strip of muscle-stiff matrix, stretched and then sheared

Normal muscle has \(E\) ≈ 12 kPa (Engler 2004) and, like every water-filled tissue, \(\nu = \tfrac12\). Stretch a strip of it by 4 %, then shear it by the same 4 %.

  1. \(G = E/2(1+\nu) = 12/(2 \times 1.5)\) = 4 kPa.
  2. Stretch by 4 %: \(\sigma_{xx} = 12 \times 0.04\) = 0.48 kPa.
  3. The narrowing: \(\varepsilon_{yy} = -\tfrac12 \times 4\ \%\) = −2 % in each direction across.
  4. The volume: 1.04 × 0.98 × 0.98 = 0.999, kept to small-strain accuracy.
  5. Shear by 4 %: \(\sigma_{xy} = 4 \times 0.04\) = 0.16 kPa, a third of the stretch's stress.
  6. With polyacrylamide's measured 0.48 instead: \(G = E/2.96\) = 0.338\(E\), 1.4 % above \(E/3\).

What it means. Matrix that keeps its volume is three times softer to a lean than to a stretch, and a cell sliding a surface leans it. Rounding \(\nu\) from 0.48 to ½ moves \(G\) by 1.4 %, far less than the five-fold gap between brain's two measured moduli, so ½ costs nothing.

Mechanical analogya rubber stopper and a cork in a bottle neck

Push a rubber stopper into a bottle neck a little narrower than it. Rubber, like gel, keeps its volume: squeezed across, it must lengthen, so it bulges and jams. A cork has a Poisson's ratio near zero (a standard textbook value; its cells collapse instead of pushing sideways), so it shrinks its girth without growing longer, which is why corks go in.

In the cellIn the machine
water-filled gel, \(\nu = \tfrac12\)rubber stopper, \(\nu\) ≈ ½
a material free to change volumecork, \(\nu\) ≈ 0
\(\varepsilon_{yy} = -\nu\varepsilon_{xx}\)squeezed 5 % across, rubber grows about 10 % longer; cork hardly at all
\(G = E/3\)rubber of \(E\) = 3 MPa has \(G\) = 1 MPa
a cell sliding the gel's surfacetwisting the stopper in the neck

With these illustrative numbers the stopper resists a twist with a third of the modulus it shows to a straight pull, exactly as the gel does. Cork, with \(\nu \approx 0\), has \(G \approx E/2\).

Where it breaks. A stopper is squeezed far beyond small strain, where rubber is not linear, and cork's cells are prisms, so it is not the same in every direction; one \(\nu\) simplifies both.

6.3.5

Thin-film traction — each bead reads the traction above it

Minted in Week 6 §3.5 · Everything back to tractions — and why bother · open the module

eq. 6.3.5$$\gamma = \frac{u}{h},\qquad \sigma_{xy} = G\gamma,\qquad t = \frac{G\,u}{h}$$

Letters

  • \(\gamma\) — the film's lean, its shear strain · no unit
  • \(u\) — how far a bead at the film's top surface moved sideways · nm
  • \(h\) — the film's thickness, glued to a rigid floor · µm · 0.5 µm on the bench
  • \(\sigma_{xy}\) — the shear stress in the film · Pa
  • \(G\) — the shear modulus, \(E/3\) · Pa · 333 Pa for a 1 kPa gel
  • \(t\) — the traction the cell puts on the surface above the bead · Pa (pN/µm²)

How it is used

§3.5 mints it by treating a thin film as §3.1's bar loaded sideways: the lean \(\gamma = u/h\) (eq. 6.3.2), the shear stress \(G\gamma\) (eq. 6.3.4), and the traction on the top face (eq. 6.3.3). Each bead then reports the traction directly above it with no inversion, and a bead error \(\delta u\) becomes an error \(G\,\delta u/h\) and nothing worse; a thick gel instead spreads every pull by eq. 6.1.5 and must be inverted through eq. 6.1.6. The bench runs the same cell on both gels with noise and \(\lambda\), and the worked example turns 180 nm on a 0.5 µm film of 1 kPa gel into 120 Pa, and over a 0.7 µm adhesion into the planted 185 pN.

Comes back: —

Biological exampleWeek 5's adhesion on a thin film

Week 5's lamellipodial module pulls about 100 pN through a 1 µm-radius adhesion. Pour a 1 kPa gel as a 0.5 µm film, the bench's thickness, and read the bead above the adhesion.

  1. The traction: \(t = 100\ \text{pN}/(\pi \times 1^2\ \text{µm}^2)\) = 31.8 Pa.
  2. The film: \(G = 1\ \text{kPa}/3\) = 333 Pa.
  3. The lean: \(\gamma = t/G = 31.8/333\) = 0.0955.
  4. The bead: \(u = \gamma h = 0.0955 \times 0.5\ \text{µm}\) = 48 nm.
  5. Read backwards with 10 nm of bead noise: \(\delta t = G\,\delta u/h = 333 \times 0.010/0.5\) = 6.7 Pa, 21 % of the signal.
  6. On a 0.25 µm film the same pull moves the bead only 24 nm, and the noise becomes \(333 \times 0.010/0.25\) = 13.3 Pa, 42 %.
  7. Why not pour 2 µm for more signal? The formula would claim 191 nm, more than the 72 nm this adhesion moves even an infinitely deep gel (\(F/\kappa_s\), with \(\kappa_s\) = 1.40 pN/nm from eq. 6.3.1). A film twice as thick as the grip's radius is not thin, and its beads no longer read locally.

What it means. A thin film converts nanometres to pascals by one factor, \(G/h\), so every bead is its own gauge. The thinner the film, the fewer nanometres each pascal makes, so the same position noise costs more: half the thickness gives twice the relative error. Thickening the film buys signal only while it stays thin next to the grip (\(h \ll a\), the bench's condition).

Mechanical analogya rubber bearing pad under a bridge

Bridge decks sit on flat rubber pads. As the deck grows and shrinks with temperature, the top of each pad slides with it while the bottom stays on the pier. Each pad is a thin film loaded sideways: it leans by its top's travel over its thickness and pushes back with \(G\) times that lean.

In the cellIn the machine
thin gel film on a rigid floorrubber pad on a concrete pier
\(h\) = 0.5 µm\(h\) = 50 mm
\(G\) = 333 Pa\(G\) ≈ 1 MPa (typical bearing rubber)
bead moves \(u\) = 48 nmdeck moves 10 mm
traction \(t = Gu/h\)\(t\) = 1 MPa × 10/50 = 0.2 MPa

Over an illustrative 300 × 300 mm pad that traction is 0.2 MPa × 0.09 m² = 18 kN. Each pad's force is read from its own lean, with no need to model its neighbours, which is the thin film's whole advantage.

Where it breaks. Real bearing pads are layered with steel plates so they do not bulge under the deck's weight, and their rubber is linear only for modest leans.

6.3.6

The free-cell balance — a cell's tractions sum to zero

Minted in Week 6 §3.5 · Everything back to tractions — and why bother · open the module

eq. 6.3.6$$\sum_k \mathbf t_k\,\Delta A_k = \mathbf 0,\qquad \sum_k \mathbf x_k\times\mathbf t_k\,\Delta A_k = 0$$

Letters

  • \(\mathbf t_k\) — the traction recovered on patch \(k\) · Pa (pN/µm²)
  • \(\Delta A_k\) — patch \(k\)'s area · µm², so \(\mathbf t_k\Delta A_k\) is a force in pN
  • \(\mathbf x_k\) — patch \(k\)'s position · µm
  • \(\mathbf x_k \times \mathbf t_k\Delta A_k\) — that force's moment, its turning effect about the origin · pN·µm
  • \(k\) — counts the patches of the map

How it is used

§3.5 mints it as the one check that is free on any traction map: a cell adhering to nothing but the gel exerts no net force and no net moment on it, which is Tab 2's massless-joint argument with the cell as the joint. A nonzero sum flags a bad reference image, a drifted stage or an over-smoothed inverse. The bench reads the net force on both the thin-film map and the inverted thick-gel map, and asks whether pushing \(\lambda\) up changes it. The capstone's chapter 4 checks the neutrophil's own inverted map against it.

Comes back: —

Biological examplea fibroblast's map, and a stage that drifted 20 nm

A fibroblast's map, on the thin film of eq. 6.3.5 (\(G\) = 333 Pa, \(h\) = 0.5 µm), shows three adhesions, each as its force \(\mathbf t\Delta A\): front-left (−40, −10) pN at (20, 5) µm, front-right (−40, +10) pN at (20, −5) µm, and rear (+80, 0) pN at (−20, 0) µm.

  1. Net force along x: −40 − 40 + 80 = 0 pN; along y: −10 + 10 + 0 = 0 pN.
  2. Net moment, \(\sum(xF_y - yF_x)\): [20(−10) − 5(−40)] + [20(10) − (−5)(−40)] + 0 = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0.
  3. Now suppose the stage drifted 20 nm along x between the two pictures, so every bead reads 20 nm extra.
  4. On the thin film that is a uniform false traction, \(G\,\delta u/h = 333 \times 0.020/0.5\) = 13.3 Pa.
  5. Over the cell's footprint, say 470 µm² (illustrative): 13.3 × 470 ≈ 6300 pN of net force.
  6. Against the three real pulls, 41 + 41 + 80 = 162 pN in all: a residual almost forty times larger.

What it means. A drift the size of one bead's position error (10–40 nm in a real image) is invisible bead by bead but glaring in the sum, because it adds the same small error over the whole footprint. A cell cannot push the world, so any net force in its map is a measurement error.

Mechanical analogythe spokes of a bicycle wheel on a free hub

A spoked wheel off the bike is a free body. Thirty-two spokes pull on the hub from every side, and because nothing else touches the hub, the pulls must add to zero, as forces and as turning effects. A wheel builder who measures every spoke with a tension gauge can check the gauges this way.

In the cellIn the machine
the cell, touching only the gelthe hub, touching only the spokes
each adhesion's force \(\mathbf t_k\Delta A_k\)each spoke's tension
the traction mapthe gauge readings
a drifted stage or a bad referencea gauge that reads one spoke 10 % high
eq. 6.3.6the hub's forces and moments adding to zero

With illustrative tensions of 1000 N, a gauge that reads one spoke 10 % high claims a 100 N net pull on a hub that is not moving. The balance catches the bad reading without knowing which spoke it was.

Where it breaks. A wheel on the road is not free, because the ground pushes up through the rim; the balance holds only for a wheel touching nothing else, as eq. 6.3.6 holds only for a cell touching nothing but the gel.

Module Tab 5 · Next Week
6.5.1

The nucleus through a pore — a creep that must reach the gap

Minted in Week 6 §5.1 · Next week's headline, measured today — the cell itself gives · open the module

eq. 6.5.1$$x(t) = F_0\left[\frac{1}{k_\infty} - \left(\frac{1}{k_\infty} - \frac{1}{k_0}\right)e^{-t/\tau_\varepsilon}\right] = \Delta \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t_{pass} = -\tau_\varepsilon\,\ln\frac{F_0/k_\infty - \Delta}{F_0/k_\infty - F_0/k_0}$$

Letters

  • \(x(t)\) — how far the nucleus has been squeezed by time \(t\) · nm
  • \(F_0\) — the steady push on the nucleus · pN · 2 nN on the bench
  • \(k_0\), \(k_\infty\) — the nucleus's instantaneous and equilibrium stiffness · pN/nm · 3 and 0.6 pN/nm, illustrative
  • \(\tau_\varepsilon\) — the creep time, \(\tau k_0/k_\infty\) · s · 25 s, from \(\tau\) = 5 s
  • \(\Delta = D_{nucleus} - D_{pore}\) — how much wider the nucleus is than the pore · µm · the bench's nucleus is 8 µm wide
  • \(t_{pass}\) — the time for the squeeze to reach \(\Delta\) · s

How it is used

§5.1 previews next week by posing the pore as eq. 6.2.5's creep under a held push: the nucleus passes when its squeeze reaches \(\Delta\). A Derive box solves the creep for that time, which gives three regimes: at once if the instantaneous squeeze \(F_0/k_0\) already covers \(\Delta\), never if even the equilibrium squeeze \(F_0/k_\infty\) does not, and in between a wait set by \(\tau_\varepsilon\) that grows without bound as \(\Delta\) nears \(F_0/k_\infty\). The bench pushes a nucleus into a channel with a set force, times it, and plots the transit time against pore width beside eq. 6.5.1. Its numbers for the nucleus are illustrative, and next week replaces them with measured ones.

Comes back: Week 7 §3.3 (into three dimensions, where the nucleus is the limit).

Biological examplea migrating cancer cell's nucleus at three gaps in collagen

A cancer cell crawling through collagen meets gaps narrower than its 8 µm nucleus and pushes with 2 nN. Use the module's illustrative nucleus: \(k_0\) = 3 pN/nm, \(k_\infty\) = 0.6 pN/nm, \(\tau\) = 5 s.

  1. The creep clock: \(\tau_\varepsilon = 5 \times 3/0.6\) = 25 s.
  2. The two limits at 2000 pN: at once, \(F_0/k_0\) = 667 nm; at most, \(F_0/k_\infty\) = 3333 nm.
  3. A 5.5 µm gap, \(\Delta\) = 2.5 µm: \(t_{pass} = -25\ln\big((3333 - 2500)/(3333 - 667)\big) = -25\ln 0.3125\) = 29 s.
  4. A 5 µm gap, \(\Delta\) = 3 µm: \(t_{pass} = -25\ln 0.125\) = 52 s.
  5. A 4.5 µm gap, \(\Delta\) = 3.5 µm: more than 3.33 µm, so never at 2 nN.
  6. Push 3 nN at that gap: the limits become 1000 and 5000 nm, so \(t_{pass} = -25\ln(1500/4000)\) = 24.5 s.

What it means. One micron of gap separates a half-minute squeeze, a one-minute squeeze and no passage at all at 2 nN. The clock is the creep time, 25 s, five times the relaxation time, because the cell sets its push, not the nucleus's shape; pushing harder moves the "never" limit out.

Mechanical analogya foam ball pushed into a narrow pipe by a weight

Hang a weight on a plunger that pushes a memory-foam ball into a pipe narrower than the ball. The foam squashes a little at once, then creeps. If the creep reaches the gap, the ball slips through; if even its full creep falls short, it sticks for ever.

In the cellIn the machine
the nucleus, a standard linear solidthe memory-foam ball (the foam of 6.2.5)
\(k_0\), \(k_\infty\)5 kN/m and 1 kN/m
\(\tau_\varepsilon\) = 25 s\(\tau_\varepsilon\) = 10 s
the push \(F_0\) = 2 nNa 50 N weight
\(\Delta = D_{nucleus} - D_{pore}\)how much wider the ball is than the pipe

With these illustrative numbers the ball squashes 1 cm at once and 5 cm at most. A ball 3 cm too wide passes after \(-10\ln\big((5 - 3)/(5 - 1)\big)\) = 6.9 s; one 0.8 cm too wide drops straight through; one 6 cm too wide never goes.

Where it breaks. The pipe's wall rubs the foam, which the model ignores, and a squashed ball must also lengthen along the pipe; a nucleus squeezing through a pore faces both.

Reused this week — earlier equations, as Week 6 uses them

Each keeps the number it was given when first minted. The full entry, with its example and analogy, is one click away.

Featured in HW3 · Problem 1(b), Problem 1(c), Challenge
5.1.5

The motors' load line — the retrograde speed, with the adhesion carrying the load

Re-boxed in Week 6 §1.2 · From the motors to the gel — the whole chain on one spring

eq. 5.1.5 again$$v_{retro} = v_0\left(1 - \frac{F_{FA}}{N_m F_m}\right)$$

Week 5's motors' law, unchanged: \(N_m\) = 100 motors of \(F_m\) = 2 pN slide the actin at \(v_0\) = 120 nm/s when nothing holds it and stop at the 200 pN stall. What is new is where \(F_{FA}\) comes from: it is the force in the chain of clutches and gel (eq. 6.1.1), so putting this law into \(dF_{FA}/dt = \kappa_{eff}v_{retro}\) gives the build-up of eq. 6.1.2.

Full entry: eq. 5.1.5, Week 5

Featured in HW3 · Problem 2(a)
5.2.2

The loading rate — now through the chain

Re-boxed in Week 6 §1.3 · How the ground's give changes the force on the integrin

eq. 5.2.2 again$$\dot f = \frac{df}{dt} = \kappa_{eff}\,v_{retro} \;\approx\; \kappa_{eff}\,v_0$$

Week 5's loading rate (written \(r\) there; the dot replaces it here) now carries the whole chain's stiffness, eq. 6.1.1 with one clutch, instead of the clutch's alone. One bond's 12 pN slows the motors by only 6 %, so \(v_{retro} \approx v_0\) and \(\dot f\) is 96 pN/s on rigid ground, 53 pN/s on 1 pN/nm and about 11 pN/s on 0.1 pN/nm. It is the only door through which the ground reaches the bond's odds in eq. 6.1.3.

Full entry: eq. 5.2.2, Week 5

Featured in HW3 · Problem 2(b)
4.2.5

Bell's lifetime — how long a bond lasts under a load f

Re-boxed in Week 6 §1.3 · How the ground's give changes the force on the integrin

eq. 4.2.5 again$$\tau(f) = \tau_0\,e^{-f/f_\beta}, \qquad \tau_0 = 1/k_0$$

Bell's law for the integrin–ligand bond, with \(k_0 = k_{off,0}\) = 0.1 s⁻¹ (so \(\tau_0\) = 10 s) and \(f_\beta\) = 2 pN: 10 s unloaded and 0.025 s at talin's 12 pN. Here \(\tau(f)\) is the bond's lifetime, not §1.2's load time \(\tau_L\). Written as a rate, \(k_{off} = k_0e^{f/f_\beta}\), and fed the ramp \(f = \dot f t\), it is the race that eq. 6.1.3 scores.

Full entry: eq. 4.2.5, Week 4

Featured in HW3 · Problem 3(b), Challenge
5.5.1

Hooke — the gel under the adhesion is a spring

Re-boxed in Week 6 §1.5 · Measuring it — traction force microscopy

eq. 5.5.1 again$$F = \kappa_s\,u_0$$

Hooke's law for the gel under one adhesion: \(F\) is the adhesion's pull, \(\kappa_s\) is Week 5 §5.3's ground spring, and \(u_0\) is how far the gel under the adhesion moves. A 100 pN pull on a 1 pN/nm ground moves it 100 nm; run backwards, it turns §1.5's worked bead (\(u_0\) = 90 nm) into a 90 pN pull, and eq. 6.1.5 carries \(u_0\) out to every other bead.

Full entry: eq. 5.5.1, Week 5

Featured in HW3 · Problem 3(b), Challenge
5.5.1

Hooke — the spring, under force control and displacement control

Re-boxed in Week 6 §2.2 · Hooke's spring — force control and displacement control

eq. 5.5.1 again$$F = k\,x$$

The spring as Tab 2's first element, with \(k\) its stiffness in pN/nm and \(x\) its stretch in nm. Under force control you divide (\(x = F/k\)), under displacement control you multiply (\(F = kx\)); there is no clock, and let go it is back at once. Read as Tab 1's ground \(\kappa_s\), it holds 200 nm under the motors' stall on 1 pN/nm, and it is the one element whose \(k_{eff}(t)\) (eq. 6.2.6) is the same under every loading.

Full entry: eq. 5.5.1, Week 5

5.5.2

Stress, strain and the modulus — built from cubes and the two rules

Re-boxed in Week 6 §3.1 · From a spring to a modulus — force becomes stress, displacement becomes strain

eq. 5.5.2 again$$\sigma = \frac{F}{A}, \qquad \varepsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L}, \qquad \sigma = E\,\varepsilon \quad\Longrightarrow\quad k = \frac{EA}{L}$$

Week 5 previewed this box; Tab 3 builds it from a bar of 1 µm cubes and eq. 6.2.1: cubes side by side add, cubes end to end divide, so \(k = k_1n_A/n_L = EA/L\). \(\sigma\) is force per area (1 pN/µm² = 1 Pa), \(\varepsilon\) is stretch per length (no unit), and \(E\) is the gel's modulus, with 1 kPa × 1 µm = 1 pN/nm. Eq. 6.3.1 is the same exchange rate for a grip instead of a bar.

Full entry: eq. 5.5.2, Week 5

  1. Pick your level (466 or 566) in the bar below. The parts marked 566 are folded away at 466 and the written parts carry one extra question at 566, exactly as the two exams differ.
  2. Work each scenario in order. It is built like a midterm scenario: a situation, then parts that chain, then a written part. No part names its relation; working out which relation a situation needs is the skill the exam tests. Each numeric part checks itself, has a free three-rung hint ladder, and offers show this part after three misses. The written part has no self-check: write first, then compare with the model answer.
  3. When a scenario is finished, its summary chains your own numbers, and two reveals open: the certified answers, and the list of relations the scenario used, by number, each linked into the equation compendium, the week tabs above.
  4. Nothing here is recorded. Your answers stay in this browser only; there is no sign-in and no export. Calculators allowed; on the exam there is no formula sheet, so try each part without the compendium open first.

How this practice is built, and how the exam differs

The midterm has three scenarios, each with three multiple-choice numeric parts and one written part, for 45 minutes. This practice has five scenarios, one per week-block, so that every relation on the instructor’s list appears at least once, and nothing off the list appears at all. The numeric parts are answered with a number here (the exam gives four choices); the written parts are the exam’s shape. Expect it to take longer than the exam: it is practice, not a timed rehearsal.

ScenarioWeeksWhat the parts ask you to combine
1 · The clot1–2thermal speed · Stokes–Einstein · the walk in 2-D and 3-D · the absorber’s halo and catch · 566 arrivals from a burst · Péclet in the written part
2 · The wound’s edge3two mobile partners meeting · arrive-then-stick · a still layer against a surface · one-way doors · two-way doors · the kick law · 566 the counting floor
3 · The keratocyte4a tip as a door · the critical concentration · Péclet for the belt · the load line read backwards · the gap and the ratchet · edge speed · 566 the cell as a walker

5 · The stem cell6a modulus becomes a spring · the chain · the race to talin on two gels · the gel that ends the race · 566 the build-up · 566 a ground that flows
Stuck on which relation? That struggle is the point. Ask three questions — what is pushing or pulling, what is resisting, and what is the geometry or the clock? — then open the compendium’s entry list for that week and read the “How it is used” lines against your answers. The hint ladder trains the same move; there are no hints on the exam.
